title: One person is dead, several others injured in incident involving Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia
text:
Police say one person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia. Cobb County police said the incident took place Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles northwest of Atlanta.
Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate. This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park
One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller coaster Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.
Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta. Detectives will investigate the circumstances, according to the Cobb County Police Department.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller coaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster. The roller coaster, which was opened in 2006, goes as fast as 70 mph (about 113 kph) and reaches heights of 200 feet (61 meters), the park’s website reports. During about 3 1/2 minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” according to the website.
This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, whose practice areas include amusement park accidents.
Last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental.

title: Varsity Maine football honor roll for Week 6
text:
Lars Bruhn, Fryeburg Academy: Bruhn reeled in three touchdown passes (52, 15 and 90 yards) and ran for a score in a 35-34 loss to Kennebunk.
Isaac Bulger, Winslow: Bulger rushed for 190 yards and a score on 13 carries, and had a 17-yard TD catch as the Black Raiders downed MCI, 38-6. Bulger also had a sack on defense.
Ethan Closson, Old Town: Closson threw four touchdown passes (24, 55, 23 and 28 yards), ran 69 yards for a score and returned a kickoff 91 yards for a TD in the Coyotes’ 60-20 win over Lake Region. Closson finished 15 of 26 passing for 289 yards and ran for 151 yards on seven carries.
Adam Cote Jr., Sanford: Cote scored four touchdowns, including a 2-yard run with 17.8 seconds remaining that gave the Spartans their first win of the season, 44-36 over Scarborough. Cote also ran for 23-, 17- and 65-yard scores.
Bradley Farrell, Kennebunk: The running back’s second touchdown pass, a 5-yarder to quarterback Giovanni D’Elia with 7.5 seconds to play, lifted the Rams to a 35-34 win over Fryeburg. Farrell also threw a 41-yard TD pass to Charlie Pentland late in the first half.
Darren Flagg, Leavitt: Flagg scored five touchdowns and intercepted two passes in the Hornets’ 48-7 triumph over Gardiner. Flagg scored on runs of 4 and 47 yards, caught 12- and 27-yard touchdown passes from Landon Marquis, and returned his second interception 35 yards for a score.
Dylan Jewett, Spruce Mountain: Jewett rushed for three touchdowns — all longer than 50 yards (56, 72 and 87) — and gained 260 yards on 12 carries to propel the Phoenix to a key 40-24 win over Cape Elizabeth. Jewett also threw a 14-yard TD pass to Levi Richards, made 14 tackles (13 solo) and had a pass deflection.
Lucas Klehn, Bonny Eagle: The Scots quarterback set the tone with his weaving, tackle-breaking 61-yard touchdown run for the first score in a 45-6 win against Oxford Hills. Klehn rushed for 170 yards and four touchdowns on 10 carries, and completed 4 of 5 passes for 91 yards, highlighted by a 67-yard TD pass to Drew Gervais.
Fin Minkel, Messalonskee: Minkel helmed a potent offense in the Eagles’ 41-26 victory over Mt. Blue. He completed 12 of 22 passes for 234 yards and two scores, ran for two touchdowns and gained 39 yards on eight carries.
Owen Ross, Falmouth: Ross scored four touchdowns — on runs of 10, 4, 70 and 14 yards — for the Navigators in their 35-12 win over Gorham.
Brennan Tabor, Thornton Academy: Tabor’s strong performance on both sides of the ball helped the Golden Trojans overcome a 14-point deficit to defeat Noble, 53-20. Tabor carried 13 times for 161 yards and four touchdowns, was in on 14 tackles (seven solo, two for loss) and forced a fumble.

title: Wet and ugly tomorrow into Wednesday, clear but chilly Thursday, more rain possible Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will continue moving through the state tonight before a low pressure system moves through the state tomorrow bringing mainly a cold rain. There is a chance for a wintry mix far to the north as well. The rain will stick around until Wednesday midday before clearing to the east. This system will probably bring a beneficial inch or so of rain before clearing off. Thursday will be a clearer day but it will be noticeably chillier. Another system moves in Friday bringing more rain and some gusty winds before a calmer weekend.
Tonight: Getting chillier before showers arrive
A mostly dry cold front will move from north to south across the state tonight as temps cool off quickly. A few sprinkles are possible through the evening hours especially north of the Millinocket area. Temps will drop noticeably behind the front as lows will fall into the 30s for most. Showers will likely arrive by the early morning hours as well with the approaching low. NW winds will gust to near 25 mph as well.
Tuesday: Wet, ugly and cold
Rain will arrive by the early morning hours from west to east across the state covering the entire region by a little after noon. It will be a cold rain with most places not escaping the 40s tomorrow and some barely getting out of the 30s. It is possible that in some of our colder spots there will be some wintry mix that may fall early on in the storm. The rain will stick around most of the day into the overnight hours.
Tuesday night: Still rainy and chilly
The rain will likely continue into the overnight hours Tuesday. Some downpours are possible as well. Temps won’t move much only dropping to the low 40s with the cold spots into the 30s. It will stay breezy with NE winds at about 10-20 mph.
Wednesday: Getting better as the day goes on
Wednesday will likely be a half and half day especially for western areas. Some showers will be around in the morning especially the further east you go and the clearing will come from west to east. Sun may arrive by late in the day Wednesday for most. Rain totals when it’s all said and done likely are going to be between .75 and 1.50 inches of rain depending on where heavier rain sets up. Lows will be in the 30s and 40s. Winds will swing back around to the NW at about 10-15 mph.
Wednesday night and beyond: Clear night and pretty nice day Thursday, more rain late week
Wednesday night will be generally clear and Thursday will probably be the nicest day of the week. Temps will be chilly only in about the 50s for highs but the sun will return.
Another system moves in Friday bringing the likelihood of more rain and wind but we will work out all those details as we get closer.
Tonight: Getting chilly with lows in the 30s for most. Winds NW at 10-15 mph
Tuesday: Chilly and rainy. Highs only in the low 40s. Winds NE at 10-15 mph.
Tuesday night: Rain continues. Lows in the 40s. Winds E at 5-10 mph
Wednesday: Showers early and clearing late. Highs in the 50s for most. Winds N at 5-10 mph

title: 911 call transcript from botched Christa Pike execution released
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - What happened the night Christa Pike’s attempted execution failed? Authorities released the transcript of the 911 call made from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution that night, providing new details about what occurred.
Metro Nashville Emergency Communications Center released the transcript Monday, a little over one week after the botched execution.
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications, or DEC, first received notification of the incident at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution through a 911 call at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30.
DEC said following a review by Metro Legal, it was determined that the original 911 audio call is exempt from public disclosure under Tennessee Code.
“While recognizing this exemption, DEC has made a good-faith effort to provide additional information by preparing a written account of the initial call based on a review of the audio recording,” a spokesperson for DEC said.
What happened the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution?
The failed attempt happened after a day of back-and-forth among courts about whether the procedure would proceed.
Pike was scheduled to be executed at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the morning of Sept. 30, but shortly before, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered that her execution be paused.
The pause was issued because the court believed that she should be allowed to challenge the legality of her sentence. Pike’s attorneys then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to maintain the pause while a federal appeals court reviewed a new legal challenge.
That evening, the Supreme Court said in a 6-3 decision that the execution would be allowed to proceed. She would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She is the only woman on death row in the state.
But things went wrong when they attempted to administer the two doses of pentobarbital.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” witnesses heard Pike say as she was undergoing lethal injection.
The state administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be lethal, but witnesses and her attorneys said that they did not have the intended effect. Instead, one witness said, “Heavy snoring is the best description we can get you for the noises she was making.”
Shortly after, WSMV observed ambulances arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution and leaving soon after, followed by police.
Pike was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Attorneys later confirmed that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. It was revealed that on Oct. 5, her attorneys and medical team believed she was brain dead and would be taken off life support within days, but she regained consciousness the following morning.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey, said.
Pike’s attorneys announced on Saturday that she had been released from the hospital and was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years.
Why is Christa Pike on death row?
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
The case revealed that Pike, who was 18 at the time, worked with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson to plan and carry out the killing, which became known as the “Job Corps murder.” Pike and Slemmer had both been Job Corps members at the time of the murder, which took place on the University of Tennessee campus.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville chief of police during the 1995 murder, described it as “an incredibly grotesque crime scene, one of the most brutal” he ever saw.
According to Keith, Pike had tortured Slemmer for nearly an hour with a box cutter, “carving a pentagram on her chest before she crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.”
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her upbringing was not given enough consideration in her case. According to her defense, Pike was a victim of child abuse and multiple rapes, details they say were kept from the jury during her trial.
Tennessee previously claimed Pike was lying about her childhood, but has since acknowledged the abuse in open court.
For Keith, her upbringing is not an excuse.
“If everyone that had an abusive lifestyle killed someone, there’d be a lot more murders in this country,” he said. “This is not about how she’s become reformed, or that those days are past. Her values or morals have been set for a long time, and somewhere along the way, they got twisted.”
While Keith said that Pike never showed any remorse for the crime, Pike’s friend, Misty Armstrong, said otherwise.
According to Armstrong, Pike spent much of her time in prison trying to help other inmates.
“It took years of therapy for her to get there, but she did,” she said. “She changed and became a completely different person.”

title: Nearly a third of Americans admit to shoplifting, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As prices climb, more Americans say they are willing to risk a criminal record to cover basic necessities.
A new LendingTree survey of 2,000 Americans found 30% admit to shoplifting, up from 23% just a couple of years ago. Most respondents who shoplifted blame inflation and financial strain.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said the actual number is likely even higher than reported.
“The truth is that the numbers are actually probably higher than what we state, because there’s certainly some people who have done it who aren’t going to admit that even anonymously in a survey,” Schulz said.
Schulz said the findings are troubling for retailers and help explain why more stores are scaling back self-checkout options. He said the willingness to risk the consequences of shoplifting reflects how financially strained many households currently are.
“What our numbers showed is that most people are doing this out of necessity, and they’re not stealing things like diamond necklaces from jewelry stores,” Schulz said. “It’s more likely to be a loaf of bread and a pound of ground beef from your local grocery store.”
Schulz said the survey also revealed a generational gap, with younger Americans far more likely to report having shoplifted.
Schulz said there are better options available than stealing, including local groups, food banks and community organizations that can offer assistance to those facing financial hardship.

title: Actor Selma Blair taken into custody by police responding to physically abusive passenger on plane
text:
Actor Selma Blair was taken into custody after a flight from Los Angeles to New York for being physically abusive and injuring two flight attendants, authorities said Monday.
Police took Blair, 54, into custody late Sunday night when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. There was no immediate response to a request for comment from the airline.
Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said.
The FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, declined to release details.
“Yesterday, we were informed by our partners at Port Authority Police Department of a potential assault aboard a flight that arrived into JFK. As per long-standing DOJ policy, we do not comment on ongoing investigations,” said Sydney Kleinmann, a spokesman for the FBI NY.
Messages seeking comment were not immediately returned by the state and federal prosecutors’ offices in New York.
A message left with Blair’s publicist seeking comment was not immediately answered.
In a statement to several media outlets, a Blair representative said she had a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct.
Blair had major roles in films including 1999’s “Cruel Intentions,” 2001’s “Legally Blonde” and 2004’s “Hellboy.”
In recent years she has been an advocate for disability rights. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018. In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.
___
Associated Press journalist Michael R. Sisak contributed reporting.

title: Are you a real Maine deer hunter if you wait out bad weather in the recliner?
text:
I like hunting under blue skies and in temperatures somewhere around freezing as much as anyone. But when it comes to hunting Maine’s whitetails, it makes little difference what Mother Nature throws my way.
I have a few exceptions when I’ll stick close to the home fires, including monsoon-like rain and a nor’easter-like blizzard. But despite a slight breeze, gently falling snow or sleet and drizzling rain, I’m usually out there.
Maine’s 2026 deer season runs for three months, Sundays excluded, for a total of 80 days. I’m hoggish and selfish enough to say that’s not long enough. So until Dec. 12, when muzzleloader and expanded archery seasons end, or I tag out, whichever comes first, most weather conditions be damned, I’m taking advantage of the time we have and hunting every single day.
Over the years, I’ve learned a few important things that have stuck with me and guided me every time I step into the deer woods. One is that deer live 24/7, every day of their existence exposed to the elements. Whether the day brings a gentle drizzle or a torrential downpour, softly falling snowflakes or a full-blown blizzard, deer have to deal with it. It is what it is.
No matter how miserable the weather gets, deer can’t stay home or leave the woods to go somewhere else. The woods are home. It’s an obvious fact hunters often forget. So why should hunters stay home or quit the woods early simply because adverse weather makes it tempting to do so? I’ll argue that in most cases, we shouldn’t.
I’ve read books and magazine articles and heard plenty of discussions around hunting camps about how weather affects deer activity, particularly during severe conditions. Is it worth hunting on rain-soaked days or when snow is falling, or is the time better spent at home until the weather clears? Hunters also debate whether the hours before an approaching front and after it passes are among the best times to be in the deer woods.
I’ve hunted Maine whitetails for a long time and, based on personal experience, believe some of what I’ve read and heard over the years. Some of it, I don’t. But one thing I know for sure: It’s next to impossible to fill a deer tag from a La-Z-Boy.
Whether hunting during inclement weather is worthwhile is a complex subject involving humidity, barometric pressure and other factors. But I’ve hunted long enough and had enough blown opportunities I’d rather forget to know that a deer’s keen senses of smell, hearing and sight are never completely diminished.
Those survival tools may become less effective depending on the severity of the weather, but they’re part of a deer’s DNA and are always at work. During extreme weather, such as a heavy downpour, deer may bed down and hold tight until conditions improve. Still, I’ve shot plenty of deer on rain-soaked and snowy days to know they will continue moving around and feeding. Bucks are also increasingly focused on finding does at this time of year.
For the most part, a deer’s daily routine continues despite what the weather throws at it. With that in mind, I see few reasons to stay home simply because the forecast looks unpleasant.
I gave up being a fair-weather deer hunter long ago. Drizzly days at this time of year, especially when a light to moderate snow is falling, often bring a drop in temperature. That combination can get deer moving or keep them on their feet, making those conditions some of my favorite times to be in the woods.
Granted, the weather can be miserable. But if you dress properly, the potential reward can be memorable. I’ve killed several deer, including some of my best bucks, in weather conditions that might have encouraged me to stay indoors. My experience continues to suggest deer are no less active on drizzly or snowy days, particularly before a major front moves in and after it passes.
There are other advantages, too. Once the foliage drops, deer become easier to spot, especially after snow falls. In my experience, bad weather can also make it harder for deer to detect a hunter, giving me an advantage in the woods. But the biggest reason I hunt in bad weather is simple: I love being out there.
Aside from torrential rain, the condition most likely to keep me indoors is wind, particularly strong, swirling winds that seem to change direction constantly.
I dislike those conditions because I’m primarily a stationary hunter. During archery season, I hunt exclusively from a tree stand. During rifle season, if I’m not in a stand, I usually sit tight for the duration and rarely move.
There’s considerable hunting pressure and plenty of echoing rifle shots in my neck of the woods during rifle season, which tends to keep deer moving. I’ve learned it’s better to have deer moving toward me than away from me.
During archery season, and generally speaking, deer also tend to hold tight during high winds, especially when the wind swirls. In my experience, deer seem to move less when strong, shifting winds make it harder for them to detect danger.
We’re still early in Maine’s deer season, with plenty of hunting days left before it ends. Given Maine’s weather at this time of year, there’s little doubt Mother Nature will throw just about everything at us before the season is over.
Each hunter has to decide where his or her “stay home” factor is.
Where’s yours?

title: Business summit to address Maine’s new paid leave program
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) -The Central Aroostook Chamber of Commerce is hosting a business summit this week to help local businesses navigate new and old challenges.
The summit will cover a range of topics, from leadership and marketing strategies to working with ChatGPT. Chamber of Commerce Executive Director LaNiece Sirios said one of those topics will be the paperwork and rules that come with Maine’s new Paid Family and Medical Leave program.
“Now that it’s in full swing, how do we make sure that the paperwork is getting done properly and we’re understanding all of those rules that go with it?” Sirios said. “And Reggie Parson from the MaineDOL is going to be here to help explain to us and make sure that we’re all doing everything according to the plan.”
Business owners and affiliates can register online at centralaroostookchamber.com. The summit costs 75 dollars to attend and takes place Thursday, October 15th at the Best Western Caribou Inn.

title: Name-calling politics birthed ‘Oxford County bear’ symbol
text:
In Oxford County in the 1800s, what was at first a political insult became a point of pride as the image of a bear emerged as a symbol for a hearty and resilient people.
Larry Glatz, a historian who has written extensively about the early history of western Maine, researched the use of the “Oxford bear” in the 19th century — a political symbol first, but later a geographical one.
The term took some time to evolve, and the groundwork for it was laid beginning in 1805, when Oxford County was established — at a time when county politics were more powerful than they are today.
“Today’s politics are nothing compared to then,” said Glatz, who recently presented a program on the Oxford bear at the Paris Cape Historical Society.
In the early 1800s Maine was still part of Massachusetts, and representatives to that legislature were chosen at the county level.
Much of Oxford County at that time was made up of Democrats, who adhered to the Jeffersonian philosophy of limited government, agrarianism and individual liberty. They opposed the Federalists (later to become the Whigs), derived from John Adams, who were the driving force all over New England, except in interior Maine, according to Glatz.
Newspapers were a key player in local politics, Glatz said, and the Oxford Advertiser of Norway was among them. “Newspapers were very political,” he said, with the editors and writers striving and writing to get their candidates elected.
The differences had to do with culture and lifestyle. On Paris Hill, he said, “Everyone was a Democrat and a Baptist. There was a real tension here. On the surface it looks like politics. But from the perspective of Boston and Portland, Oxford County was backwoods, uncultured, and uncivilized.”
Oxford County became “a proving ground for Democratic politicians who were influential,” said Glatz.
In 1834, after Maine had become a state, the Boston Courier newspaper wrote about inhabitants of interior Maine, describing them as “furrow-turners.”
“A farmer never looks so well as when he has a hand upon the plough; with his huge paw upon the statues what can he do? It is as proper for a blacksmith to attempt to repair watches, as a farmer, in general, to legislate,” the paper wrote.
“The ‘huge paws’ struck a chord,” said Glatz. “The Oxford Democrats liked it.
“They used it against their opponents, and it appeared in every local editorial,” he said. “It was a good political hammer to use on the other side.”
The Democrats did very well in subsequent elections, according to Glatz.
A few years later, a Whig writer changed the “huge-pawed” farmer reference to “backwoods bears.” Soon after, a debate took place in the legislature regarding keeping bounties on various animals. A Washington County representative singled out Oxford County representative and Oxford Advertiser Editor John J. Perry, who was on the side of maintaining bounties, and said, “If this Legislature doesn’t repeal this law someone will soon be bringing here the scalp of this old Oxford Bear himself for a bounty.”
“Perry loved it,” said Glatz. “Folks here loved it.” They signed letters they wrote to the newspaper with bear-related names and adjectives.
The political bear symbolism continued into the mid-1800s, Glatz said, with the formation of the Oxford Bears Association, which met annually at different Maine locations.
But after the Civil War, the political focus of the local newspapers eased as people became more focused on joining social and other organizations, and that became the subject of more news writing.
The political sense of the Oxford bear symbol faded, “and became geographic instead,” said Glatz, referring instead to someone who was simply a resident of Oxford County.
The gatherings of the Bears Association also took on more of that focus, he said, with large numbers of former Oxford County residents often arriving in train excursions for the social event. A stuffed bear joined the tradition when the 1887 meeting took place in Norway.
By the late 1800s, however, the interest in the meetings waned, as the primary organizers aged and passed away, said Glatz. The last use of the Oxford bear symbol in the Oxford Advertiser newspaper was in 1926. Then it disappeared.
By the time the Oxford County Commissioners decided the county should have an official seal, in 1982, no one had heard of the bear and the seal was created without it.
Had they known, said Glatz, it would have been an easy decision to incorporate it.
The Oxford bear was resurrected in 2005 for the county bicentennial. Glatz was the chairman of that organizing committee, and wrote an article about the bear for “Maine History,” a publication of the Maine Historical Society.
Glatz wrote in the conclusion of that article, “the Bear provides an interesting study of the interaction between politics and place in the New England experience.”
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: What November’s vote means for the future of the Penobscot County Jail
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Penobscot County voters will decide this November if the county jail can move out of Bangor.
If passed, the ballot question would allow the Penobscot County Jail and its accompanying services to move out of Bangor. It does not specify where the jail would be moved, but county officials have paid to hold a location in a Hampden industrial park.
“[This vote] gives us the breathing room to look around and say, ‘OK, what’s the next best step?’” Penobscot County Commissioner Chair David Marshall said.
The ballot question is the first step in which voters have a voice in a complicated process to build a new jail. Here’s what we know — and don’t know — about what voting “yes” or “no” on the ballot question means for the jail and Penobscot County residents.
What are Penobscot County residents voting on?
Penobscot County residents will see this question on their ballot: “Do you favor authorizing the Penobscot County Commissioners, as required under Title 30‑A, §122, to relocate the county correctional facility and any related buildings to a site outside of the county seat?”
The ballot measure will decide if the Penobscot County Commissioners are authorized to relocate the Penobscot County Jail, and related buildings, outside of Bangor. The vote and its approval is required by state law before a new jail can be built outside the county seat, where the jail has been operating for more than 150 years.
A “Yes” vote would allow the commissioners to relocate the facility to any town in Penobscot County. A “No” vote would not.
County officials have said the related buildings are for jail operations and do not include the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
The question does not say where the jail will be built or how much it will cost. Commissioners are paying to hold a lot in a Hampden industrial park, but the question does not limit them to just that space.
“What we’ve looked at the last three years has been disappointing for a host of reasons. And then we looked across [to Hampden], we saw this, and my goodness, this is just perfect,” Marshall said.
Penobscot County residents will not be voting on any funding for a new jail in this year’s election.
Why does this vote matter?
Voter approval to relocate the jail would allow county commissioners to move forward with building a new facility outside of Bangor. Commissioners are working toward plans to build a new facility in Hampden but need voter approval before issuing requests for proposals for engineering and construction.
If it were voted down, commissioners would have to create and propose a new plan or present the same ballot question at a later election.
The last time a jail proposal was met with voter disapproval was in 2019. The criticism forced commissioners to create new plans.
Why does the county want to build a new jail?
The Penobscot County Jail has been operating in its current location for more than 150 years.
Penobscot County Sheriff Troy Morton has often described the facility’s cracking foundation, leaking plumbing and aging boilers as costly defects that drive up maintenance expenses. Upgrades and renovations were made since the facility opened in 1869, with the most recent being in 1988, but the jail still has aging infrastructure.
Others, including Marshall and Hampden Town Council Chair Matt LaChance, have said the aging facility makes correctional officers less safe at work and doesn’t allow inmates to receive needed medical services.
“The building has deteriorated. It was built 23 years before electricity came to Bangor, and the infrastructure is just falling apart, and it costs more to try and repair it every year. We’re looking at a building that is unsuitable,” Marshall said.
These costs, coupled with the expense of boarding out inmates when the jail is at capacity, have cost taxpayers millions of dollars. The county spent more than $2 million to board out more than 60 inmates in 2024. The current facility holds 157 inmates.
County commissioners and officials have said Penobscot County Jail’s expenses, which have been underfunded by the state, caused the county’s multimillion-dollar financial crisis. A new facility has been presented as a way to save, and potentially earn, county funds.
County and local officials have said building a new facility would eliminate boarding and maintenance costs because it would have more beds and updated technology, saving county taxpayers money.
“It’s like there’s a hole in the bathtub. County tax dollars are washing right out the bottom of it, We’ve got to put a plug in it,” LaChance, who supports a new jail, said.
The No Penobscot County Jail Expansion group has said a jail with more beds is not needed, and county officials should fund diversion programs instead of a new facility. Building a new jail would not incentivize police or county officials to divert inmates, the group’s members have said.
What does this vote mean for Bangor?
If approved, the Penobscot County Jail could be relocated outside of Bangor, but it would not happen immediately. County officials have said it would take approximately three years to build a new facility and begin operating. The existing jail would still be used during that time.
Once a new jail is built and operational, county commissioners would be able to decide how to use the current jail facility. Commissioners and county officials have discussed how the building could be used, but nothing has been decided, Marshall said.
“Once we get a new facility, those are decisions that are down the road. I have my idea of what I’d like to do, but this is a little bit too early to speak about that,” Marshall said.
What does this vote mean for Hampden?
While Hampden is not specified as the new location on the ballot, it’s the only town that county commissioners have publicly shown interest in for building a new jail. A site has not been purchased and a jail design has not been decided.
Hampden residents would see changes if a facility was built in their community, LaChance said. Building the jail in the town would create more calls for police, fire and emergency services to the facility, meaning Hampden would have to add employees to provide the same level of services to its residents, LaChance said.
“The fear is overextending the capabilities or the capacity of our current staffing levels, which might require adding more personnel to the police and fire department through either paramedics or police officers, so then all of that could compound into a bigger cost to the Hamden taxpayers, specifically without any type of gain because the jail wouldn’t be contributing to the tax pool,” LaChance said.
LaChance, who is part of a group of local leaders who have helped the county’s jail efforts, said the proposed Hampden location is a good choice “geographically speaking” but does raise questions for residents, and not all of them have been answered.
To offset the potential tax hike, Hampden Councilors asked county officials for a tax break to offset costs for additional staff. Hampden councilors have not heard a response from the county, LaChance said.
Other concerns some residents have had, including a reduction in property values or an uptick in crime, are not supported by analytics from other communities, LaChance said.
There may be other options to lessen the burden on Hampden taxpayers, including changing town lines to place the proposed plot in Bangor or creating a mutual-aid agreement, but nothing has been decided yet, LaChance said.
What would happen next?
If the relocation passes this year, another vote would be held to approve funding for the new facility in 2027. The vote would likely happen in the November election, Marshall said.
Before residents vote on the proposed funding, the county will share information about the proposed costs, building design and location, Marshall said.
“By that time, trust me, everybody’s going to know exactly what we’re offering, why we’re offering it, what impact it’s going to have, what it’s going to cost, what savings they can expect to see. We’re going to be very, very transparent about that,” Marshall said.
Because a design and bid have not been selected, details for funding haven’t been finalized. Marshall said discussions have focused on a 35-year bond for a modular design. Recent cost estimates for a 258-bed facility were between $72.7 million and $84.5 million, but it’s unclear what the yearly cost would be for bond payments.
It’s unclear what next steps county officials would take if voters deny the relocation.
When asked what would happen if it’s denied, Marshall said; “I have no answer to that. It’s just like if you asked me ‘After you die, what do you think you’re going to do?’ I have no clue.”
Marshall said he expects the vote to pass.
The last time residents disapproved of a proposed Penobscot County Jail in 2019, commissioners were forced to find a new design and location. This November’s vote is the first proposal since 2019.

title: Many GOP states have imposed new voting rules this year, some mirroring Trump's midterm proposals
text:
President Donald Trump has pushed Congress to pass a proof-of-citizenship law, signed an executive order seeking a national voter ID requirement and tried to limit mail voting through U.S. Postal Service changes.
None of those moves succeeded in time to affect this year’s midterm elections. It’s a different matter in the states.
More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of Trump’s stalled proposals. They include changes to what IDs are acceptable to register for the first time and requirements to show proof of citizenship, an issue the Republican president has tried but failed to get through Congress.
“Trump’s attacks on our elections are deeply damaging, but they are not happening in isolation,” said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Project. ”Across the country, states are also advancing restrictions that make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.”
Some new laws seek to make voting easier. Others continue a trend in Republican-controlled states of imposing restrictive rules that began in 2021 after Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. Trump’s continued false claims have resonated with Republican voters, a majority of whom believe Biden was not legitimately elected despite all evidence to the contrary. Trump lost dozens of court challenges, his own attorney general found no evidence of widespread fraud, and reviews, audits and recounts in the battleground states where he contested his loss all affirmed Biden’s victory.
Among the changes confronting voters as early voting gets underway: Students in New Hampshire can no longer use student IDs; Utah voters returning mail ballots must include more information on the envelope; and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports to verify their identities.
Changes to voter ID requirements are challenged
Republican lawmakers who support the tighter voting laws, especially around voter ID, describe them as common sense changes.
New Hampshire state Rep. Donald McFarlane said he sponsored the bill to eliminate student IDs as acceptable for voting because colleges don’t have the same controls when issuing those cards as government agencies.
“The change removes a special exception and applies the same government-issued ID standard to all voters,” he said, adding that his bill had bipartisan support.
Students, he said, can still get state IDs free of charge.
The new requirements have not gone unchallenged.
In South Dakota, the ACLU has filed a lawsuit seeking to halt a new law that includes requiring voters registering for the first time to present the most common forms of ID — driver’s licenses, Tribal IDs and non-driver state IDs. They must be presented in person at places that accept registration.
“Proof of citizenship in itself is not terrible,” said Kathryn Johnson, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota.
Her concern is the requirement to present the IDs in person.
“We’re kind of a remote state, so sometimes it takes a drive, and you have to coordinate, you have to take off work, and all of these kinds of things,” she said.
Ohio seeks to scrub voter rolls
Ohio has a proof of citizenship requirement in effect for the first time this year for those registering to vote or updating their voter registration information at a Bureau of Motor Vehicles location. The state also eliminated its four-day grace period for mail ballots, which now must be received at local election offices by Election Day.
Yet the biggest concern for voting rights groups is an ongoing purge of the state’s voter rolls. The databases used to check citizenship against voter registration lists can be outdated, said Freda Levenson, legal director of the ACLU of Ohio, which has sued to overturn the law.
“Vast numbers of perfectly eligible voters are vulnerable to being disenfranchised,” she said.
Republican state Sen. Theresa Gavarone, one of the primary sponsors of the bill, challenged the ACLU’s legal action and said the problem it addresses is a real one.
“In the past two years, hundreds of noncitizens have been removed from Ohio’s voter rolls,” she said in an email. “Every single vote cast by a noncitizen disenfranchises a lawful Ohio voter.”
Voters have mixed views on the changes
Outside an early voting center in Wayne County, Ohio, retired steel worker Dan Walter, an independent voter, said he opposes requiring documentary proof of citizenship to vote.
“It’s to keep people from voting, it sounds to me like,” he said.
His wife, Jody, a retired aerospace executive and a Democrat, said she felt the same way about Ohio’s new requirement for registering to vote.
“A driver’s license doesn’t prove citizenship, and that’s all they ask for now,” she said. “It’s going to be an obstacle for so many people.”
Genia Fortune had a different view. A nurse, the Millersburg resident described herself as an independent and said she voted for President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and later for Trump. She believes Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen and sees requiring documentary proof of citizenship as a necessary precaution.
“I just feel like you need to be a citizen and show proof of ID,” she said.
Voting and election laws have become a regular target for legislatures
The Trump administration has pushed multiple strategies to influence this year’s midterm elections, most of them stymied by Congress or the courts.
Chris Diaz, the director of legislative tracking at the Voting Rights Lab, which tracks state legislation, said the group has seen several versions of the Republican president’s proposals passed by his allies in the states.
A recently released report by the group highlighted some of the key areas drawing Republican lawmakers’ attention, including mail balloting, voter ID and the hunt for noncitizens on voter rolls.
Noncitizen voting has been a focus of the Trump administration despite it being a rare problem. The U.S. Department of Justice recently announced it had brought charges in roughly 90 cases for various types of election misconduct, including 50 against people who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. The U.S. had 227 million registered voters for the 2024 presidential election.
The Brennan Center for Justice has identified nearly 40 laws in 21 states taking effect this election season that will make it harder for eligible voters to register, stay on the rolls or cast ballots.
The report from the center, part of the New York University School of Law, found that many of the new laws target subsets of voters.
“What I want voters to take away from this is that elections are still run by the states and there are still people in many states who are trying to make it harder for you to vote,” said Sean Morales-Doyle, senior director of the center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program. “But that’s all the more reason to go make a plan to vote and participate.”
___
Fields reported from Washington, and Smyth reported from Wooster and Millersburg, Ohio.

title: Quentin Tarantino’s Play Reveals Premiere Date and Plot Details
text:
Quentin Tarantino’s First Play Reveals Premiere Date and Plot Details
Quentin Tarantino’s writing and directing his first play, The Popinjay Cavalier, and now the show’s opening night and its premise are both confirmed.
Tickets for the show are now on sale for performances to The Popinjay Cavalier at the Phoenix Theatre in London starting on February 23.
As for the premise...
Set in 1830s Europe, this rambunctious tale of deception and disguise is Tarantino’s first-ever play, inspired by the grand adventure epics and sparkling romances of stage and screen, including the works of Hollywood’s golden greats – George Bruce, Ernest Vajda and Jesse Lasky Jr. Follow Rupert Sebastian Thomas Jr., the world’s greatest actor, as he heads to Paris to perform for the illustrious Comédie-Française. But after a few ill-advised words about the French land him in hot water, Rupert the Magnificent’s triumphant trip across the Channel takes a decidedly more dangerous turn…
Borat himself, Sacha Baron Cohen, plays Rupert Sebastian Thomas Jr (the world’s greatest actor). As part of hyping tickets for the show going on sale today, the play also posted several videos on Instagram, including this one of Tarantino signing in to work at the Phoenix Theatre.
READ MORE: Every Tarantino Movie Ranked, From Worst to Best
The Popinjay Cavalier’s official website says you can “expect Tarantino’s signature style and rapier wit in a sweeping celebration of theatre, complete with acrobatics, swordplay, daring deeds, dastardly acts and an incredible cast whose virtues put the very saints to shame.”
It’ll be a busy few months for Tarantino. While prepping his first play he’s also got the sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood coming this fall. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth was written by Tarantino, stars Brad Pitt as Cliff, and was directed by David Fincher. It premieres on Netflix on December 23.
I’m sure I speak for Tarantino fans everywhere (but London) when I say: Why isn’t this coming to Broadway rather than the West End?? Oh well; maybe a transfer to New York will happen in the future. If you’re based in the U.K. and want to get tickets for The Popinjay Cavalier they are on sale now.

title: Super PAC buys Troy Jackson attack ad in Portland, Oregon
text:
A Republican-supporting Super PAC purchased about $25,000 in attack ads against Maine’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson in the Portland, Oregon, region.
The ads, paid for by the Defending Maine Street Super PAC, ran in more than 260 zip codes in Oregon between Oct. 8 and 11, according to the Google Ads Transparency Center. It was updated on Monday to cover Maine.
“The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend,” a spokesperson for Defending Main Street said in an email Monday. “No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error.”
They were shown more than 1.2 million times, according to the center. Approximately $25,000 was spent on the ads.
The PAC’s spokesperson also included a statement from its vendor, the 1903 Group, which said: “This was 100% a Cross Screen Media error.” Cross Screen Media is a political and public affairs advertising company that is owned by the 1903 Group, a holding company.
“Susan Collins’ allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map,” Dan Gottlieb, a spokesperson for Jackson’s campaign, said in a written statement. “Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in.”
A spokesperson for Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.

title: Audit found $2.6M deficit in Rockland school board budget
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — Regional School Unit 13 board members voiced concerns at their Wednesday night meeting over audit findings that found numerous deficiencies in financial operations in the district.
The business manager said the finance department has responded to those findings and are working to ensure they do not occur again.
The 2024-25 audit also reported a deficit of about $2.6 million in the overall budget of more than $41 million. The deficit was due largely to the district not receiving the MaineCare reimbursement it had expected to cover some of the special education costs.
Business Manager Katherine Hunt said the district had budgeted $2.2 million in revenues from MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for 2024-2025 but received none.
She said RSU 13 and other Maine districts had gone to a training session by the Maine Department of Health and Human Services in February 2024. The reimbursement would have been for speech therapy, occupational therapy and physical therapy for students. DHHS and the Maine Education Department said the process would be straightforward and a way to take the burden off property taxes.
She said when the federal administration changed at the end of 2024, the process for reimbursement changed from when she had done similar reimbursement work in a prior job.
The district did not budget for any MaineCare revenue in the next year’s budget but the business manager said she expects the district will now receive revenues from MaineCare and reduce the deficit. The district has been putting in for reimbursement since February 2026.
The audit being discussed was for the 2024-2025 school year. That audit was completed in May and the board’s budget and finance committee reviewed it in July. The management letter from the auditing firm pointed out some deficiencies.
“I’m quite concerned by the number of deficiencies,” board member Brad Choyt said.
Board member Katrina Saucier said she was frustrated that the management letter from the auditor wasn’t sent to the board in a more timely manner. Hunt noted paper copies of all the materials were at the central office.
Superintendent John McDonald said all audit materials in the future will be emailed to all board members, not just members of the budget and finance committee.
The management letter from RHR Smith & Co. of Buxton, dated June 1, 2026, stated “During our audit we became aware of several matters referred to as ‘management letter comments’ that offer opportunities for strengthening internal controls and improving operating efficiencies of Regional School Unit 13.”
The deficiencies found in the audit were:
— “The general ledger accounts were not consistently reconciled throughout the year. In several instances, account balances were not supported by underlying documentation or did not agree to subsidiary ledgers or supporting schedules. Routine reconciliation procedures are a key component of an effective internal structure and are necessary to ensure the accuracy and completeness of financial information.”
— “Certain cash accounts were not reconciled in a timely or accurate manner.”
— “Investment activity was not recorded in the general ledger throughout the year.”
— “Certain budget cost center totals exceeded the School Board’s statutory transfer authority under Maine law. Pursuant to Maine statute, the regional school unit board may transfer an amount not exceeding 5% of the total appropriation for any cost center to another cost center or among other cost centers without voter approval.”
— “Failure to properly close out completed grant, special revenue, and capital project funds.”
“Student activity transactions were not consistently recorded in the accounting records during the year.”
— “Purchase orders were not consistently prepared and approved prior to the commitment of funds. In several instances, purchase orders were generated after goods or services had already been received.”
— “The general ledger inventory balance was not adjusted to agree with the detailed inventory records maintained by the Food Service Department at year end.”
The auditor also pointed out that the number of audit adjustments indicate that controls over financial reporting are not operating effectively.”
Hunt in her response told the auditor that the district takes the matters seriously and has implemented corrective actions on each of the concerns raised.
The business manager said the Maine Department of Education will be conducting a review of the district’s food service department since last year’s review did not go well. Hunt said the district had not had a state review of its food service program in nearly 10 years and the district has gone through a couple of food service managers.
Meal count procedures, components of a reimbursable meal, better inventory process and more training for staff have been undertaken. The district hired a new food service director in July who has served as a director for another district. The district and state are working closely, she said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: ‘Breaking Bad’ actor, disability rights activist RJ Mitte dies at 34
text:
(Gray News) - Actor and disability rights activist RJ Mitte, known for his role in “Breaking Bad,” has died. He was 34 years old.
Representatives for Mitte confirmed his death on Monday, saying he died in Texas.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” they told Deadline.
TMZ was the first to confirm Mitte’s death.
In acting, he was best known for his role as Walter White Jr. in the hit television show “Breaking Bad,” though he had several other roles, appearing in “Switched at Birth,” “The Guardians of Justice,” “Triumph,” and more.
Like his character, Mitte had cerebral palsy and worked to bring about disability awareness and inclusion.
He was an ambassador for the organizations United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children.
He was also the founder of the nonprofit The Mitte Foundation, which offered grants and scholarships to “enrich people’s lives, as well as bringing hope to those in need,” according to the foundation website.
His cause of death was not immediately known.

title: Campaign finance reform needs to be our top priority
text:
Beth Franklin of Cumberland worked on Capitol Hill for a Mississippi congressman and has lived in Maine for the last 32 years.
Given the eye-popping revelations about Sen. Susan Collins’ involvement with a pay-to-play arrangement with a campaign donor, it may be time to reexamine how Collins and her opponent, Troy Jackson, are funding their campaigns.
A quick check of Federal Election Commission contribution reports reveals who is giving
money to Collins in her bid to retain the Senate seat she has held since 1997.
The biggest donors in the last several months include the following people: Matthew Steinmetz of Illinois, attorney, whose practice focuses on leveraged buyouts ($100,000); Konstantine Sokolov of Illinois, private equity investor ($100,000); Edward C. Levy Jr. of Michigan, owner of a construction materials company and former president of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee ($250,000); Adam Freede of California, investor ($100,000); Michelle and David Kroin of New York, lawyer and investor ($400,000); Gary Rosenthal of Texas, private equity investor ($50,000); Michael Kassen of Connecticut, investor and former president of the American Israel Political Action Committee ($100,000); J. Blair Frank of Utah, equity portfolio manager and philanthropist ($200,000); Barry MacLean, president of a manufacturing company in Illinois ($50,000).
The most recent entries on the FEC campaign report show that only 24 of the last 100 donors who gave directly to Susan Collins gave under $10,000. All the rest gave what some might refer to as “real money.”
This doesn’t include the donations to the Pine Tree Results Political Action Committee
supporting Sen. Collins. 
Of the most recent donors this year, the top giver to Pine Tree Results was Kenneth Griffin, CEO of Citadel, LLC, a multinational hedge fund based in Florida ($2.5 million). Second runner-up was Stephen Schwarzman, CEO of the Blackstone Group in New York, the world’s largest alternative asset manager ($1 million). Next were Jude and Christopher Reyes, co-chairs of Reyes Holdings in Florida ($1 million, or $500,000 each). More than 20 of the most recent 100 donors to Pine Tree Results gave $100,000 or more.
So, what about Troy Jackson? Given his recent entry into the race, his first FEC report won’t be coming out until October. A quick search of various news outlets painted a different picture of the kinds of donations received by the Jackson campaign.
One report stated that Troy Jackson had 58,000 unique donors in the first few days following his nomination. Another report stated that while Jackson had received a “massive” small donor influx, it was dwarfed by the large sums that continued to pour into the Collins camp.
You don’t have to believe these reports; just watch the evening news. The ads are beginning to all look alike and surely voters are tuning them out. The negative ads about Jackson are double the number that you see about Collins. And if you listen to the fast talk at the end, all those negative ads about Troy Jackson are funded by Pine Tree Results.
What does this say about our candidates? There is no question that Susan Collins’ campaign is being financed by large corporations and investment interests. Does that make her beholden to them? Recent reports about Collins’ alleged “pay-to-play” arrangement with Navatek suggest it may.
But this also points to the broader problem of how campaigns are financed. “Elon Musk-like” money does not always win, but negative ads can sway enough voters to help wealthy interests get the candidates and outcomes they paid for. It’s only when the public makes campaign finance reform their highest priority that this will change.

title: Passengers injured in deadly Grace Bailey mast failure sue schooner’s owners
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Three people injured in a deadly schooner accident off the coast of Rockland are now suing the boat’s owners.
Just over three years ago, the mast of the schooner Grace Bailey broke during a four-day cruise, killing Dr. Emily Mecklenburg and injuring five others. A sixth passenger was injured when they fell down the galley ladder to avoid the falling mast.
A Coast Guard investigation found that severe internal rot had weakened the mast and that it had not received proper preservation treatments. Court documents say 33 people were on board: 26 passengers and seven crew members.
Three injured passengers are suing Grace Bailey Navigation Company and the schooner, seeking compensation for physical and emotional damages. One of the three is also suing crew members, inspectors, repair workers and the ship’s former owners.
One plaintiff, who lived in Montville at the time of the cruise, was working aboard the vessel as a musician. She says she suffered “serious and numerous physical and emotional injuries” as a result of the incident.
A man from Lubec, who says he was struck by falling debris, also filed a lawsuit. He says he was injured a second time while helping other passengers. His wife, who was also a passenger, joined the suit in an amended filing. She said she heard a “loud crack from above, looked up, [and] saw the mast split and begin to fall.” The complaint says that although she was not physically injured, she was at risk “of traumatic physical harm.”
A Massachusetts woman is the plaintiff in the third lawsuit. According to court documents, she was the passenger injured when she fell down the galley ladder while trying to avoid the mast.

title: Woman with custody of teenager charged after authorities say he shot friend to death
text:
WALHALLA, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A woman who has custody of a teenager accused of accidentally shooting his friend in the head has been arrested.
Davina Jill Browne, 33, was arrested and charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk of harm, according to the Oconee County Sheriff’s Office.
According to the arrest warrant, Browne allowed the 15-year-old to have a Taurus 900 handgun. She allegedly knew the teen had a gun and did not take proper preventative measures.
The 15-year-old boy was charged with involuntary manslaughter after the gun went off while he was handling it, killing 15-year-old Thaddaeus Justice Terezakis, according to the sheriff’s office.

title: How to save money on heating costs this winter
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story was originally published in October 2022.
Winter and freezing temperatures are going to cover the state soon, so now is the time to make sure your home is as ready for winter as possible. There are several things you can do to winterize your residence that not only save you money on heating bills, but that you can do yourself at a minimal cost, according to energy and heating experts.
Some won’t cost you a dime.
“People might not have the resources for large-scale winterization projects,” said Judy Long, communications manager at Versant Power. “But there are things they can do to maximize the efficiency of their homes and save money on energy.”
Keep the cold air outside
Cold outside air can creep into your home any number of ways, meaning your furnace will have to work hard to keep your surroundings warm. Depending on the fuel used, that can waste oil, propane, natural gas or wood.
In fact, the warmth of your home will work to pull cold from outside to inside as the warm air rises, “sucking” in the colder air.
To counteract what is known as the “stack effect,” try to eliminate those entry points. Use a door snake — this can be as simple as a long, thin bag filled with dried peas, rice or beans — to block the bottom of doorways leading outside.
Another sneaky way cold air finds its way inside is around electrical outlets. Outlet insulators are available from home improvement or hardware stores. These are simple foam sheets you place behind the outlet’s face plate to block the cold air.
Also make sure your windows close tightly and caulk the areas around the frame that let the cold air in.
Use windows to their heating advantage
Once your windows are sealed, you can create a pocket of air between the glass and your living space using plastic film that is available in easy-to-install kits. The clear film uses that air to create a very effective insulation.
On sunny days, make sure your drapes and curtains are fully open to let in passive solar heat. Then, at night, close them to prevent that heat from escaping when the sun sets.
Reverse the ceiling fan rotation
If you have a room or rooms with ceiling fans, reverse the direction of the fan so instead of creating a cooling downdraft, it is pulling warm air up. The reverse rotation will then force that warmer air back down.
Rugs and blankets
While you are at it, if you have bare floors, consider placing wool or other forms of insulated rugs down. These block heat from escaping downward. You can also place warm blankets on chairs and couches so they are ready to grab in case you get a chill.
Check filters and chimneys
Whatever the source of heat, make sure it is functioning as efficiently as possible. Now is the time to remove and inspect filters on heat pumps and furnaces. Depending on their condition, they can be cleaned and put back in or replaced with new filters.
Chimneys should be cleaned out before you light the first fire of the season to remove creosote or other detritus that built up at the end of last winter.
Inspect generators
Warmer weather is also a good time to check your generator, if you have one, and make sure that you have the fuel to run it should you need it. Make sure it is placed in a location where any fumes that are created when it’s running can’t seep into your house. Also confirm it is installed in such a way that it won’t create a hazard to linemen working during a power outage. When in doubt, according to Long, have a licensed electrician inspect your generator set up.
Space heater safety
Safety, Long said, is every bit as important as saving money on heating.
“A lot of people like to use space heaters to supplement their main heat source or add comfort in a smaller room,” Long said. “Those can be a real concern if they are used in a space not designed for them.”
When used improperly, space heaters can become fire or electrical hazards.
“Be sure to follow all the safety guidelines when you are placing a space heater and plugging it in,” Long said. “And never leave them on when you are sleeping or leaving the house.”
While a space heater can provide some quick warmth, Long cautioned they can also be costly to operate.
Get more information
The federal government is predicting energy and heating costs will remain high throughout the winter. The Maine Governor’s Energy Office has updated its winter resource heating guide in light of those forecasts with information on how to keep your home warm and on available heating assistance.

title: LaGrange Shooting Leads To Arrests Of Two Convicted Felons In Penobscot County
text:
Deputies Arrest LaGrange Men On Firearms Charges After Weapons Were Discharged Earlier This Week
Deputies in Penobscot County arrested two men from LaGrange Thursday afternoon, following reports that a weapon had been discharged in the area.
Read More: Maine Man Charged After Allegedly Breaking Into Ex's Home In Passadumkeag
According to the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office, 37-year-old Guy Shurman and 44-year-old Daniel Turner were arrested, with help from the Maine State Police, and without incident, and taken to the Penobscot County Jail, following reports from folks in town that a shooting had taken place near or around a residence in the area.
"During the investigation, deputies determined that gunfire had crossed the roadway and struck a residence located across the street, creating a potentially dangerous situation for nearby residents. As the investigation progressed, deputies obtained a search warrant for the suspects’ residence. Investigators confirmed that both individuals were convicted felons and prohibited from possessing firearms."
Authorities say this is a great example of "see something, say something" (or, in this case, "hear something") in action.
Read More: Maine Man Shot And Killed In Indian Township, Suspect Arrested
Authorities arrested both men and charged them with Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person.
In the state of Maine, prohibited people include felons, those involved with domestic violence cases, mental illness cases, and juvenile offenders.
Convicted felons like Turner and Shurman, who are found guilty of possession of a firearm, could face up to 10 years in prison and up to $20,000 in fines.
Others might only face up to 5 years in prison and a fine of up to $5,000. In either case, the minimum jail sentence is at least 2 years for felons, and 1 year for others found guilty of firearm possession by a prohibited person.

title: 911 call transcript from botched Christa Pike execution released
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - What happened the night Christa Pike’s attempted execution failed? Authorities released the transcript of the 911 call made from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution that night, providing new details about what occurred.
Metro Nashville Emergency Communications Center released the transcript Monday, a little over one week after the botched execution.
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications, or DEC, first received notification of the incident at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution through a 911 call at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30.
DEC said following a review by Metro Legal, it was determined that the original 911 audio call is exempt from public disclosure under Tennessee Code.
“While recognizing this exemption, DEC has made a good-faith effort to provide additional information by preparing a written account of the initial call based on a review of the audio recording,” a spokesperson for DEC said.
What happened the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution?
The failed attempt happened after a day of back-and-forth among courts about whether the procedure would proceed.
Pike was scheduled to be executed at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the morning of Sept. 30, but shortly before, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered that her execution be paused.
The pause was issued because the court believed that she should be allowed to challenge the legality of her sentence. Pike’s attorneys then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to maintain the pause while a federal appeals court reviewed a new legal challenge.
That evening, the Supreme Court said in a 6-3 decision that the execution would be allowed to proceed. She would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She is the only woman on death row in the state.
But things went wrong when they attempted to administer the two doses of pentobarbital.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” witnesses heard Pike say as she was undergoing lethal injection.
The state administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be lethal, but witnesses and her attorneys said that they did not have the intended effect. Instead, one witness said, “Heavy snoring is the best description we can get you for the noises she was making.”
Shortly after, WSMV observed ambulances arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution and leaving soon after, followed by police.
Pike was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Attorneys later confirmed that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. It was revealed that on Oct. 5, her attorneys and medical team believed she was brain dead and would be taken off life support within days, but she regained consciousness the following morning.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey, said.
Pike’s attorneys announced on Saturday that she had been released from the hospital and was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years.
Why is Christa Pike on death row?
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
The case revealed that Pike, who was 18 at the time, worked with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson to plan and carry out the killing, which became known as the “Job Corps murder.” Pike and Slemmer had both been Job Corps members at the time of the murder, which took place on the University of Tennessee campus.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville chief of police during the 1995 murder, described it as “an incredibly grotesque crime scene, one of the most brutal” he ever saw.
According to Keith, Pike had tortured Slemmer for nearly an hour with a box cutter, “carving a pentagram on her chest before she crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.”
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her upbringing was not given enough consideration in her case. According to her defense, Pike was a victim of child abuse and multiple rapes, details they say were kept from the jury during her trial.
Tennessee previously claimed Pike was lying about her childhood, but has since acknowledged the abuse in open court.
For Keith, her upbringing is not an excuse.
“If everyone that had an abusive lifestyle killed someone, there’d be a lot more murders in this country,” he said. “This is not about how she’s become reformed, or that those days are past. Her values or morals have been set for a long time, and somewhere along the way, they got twisted.”
While Keith said that Pike never showed any remorse for the crime, Pike’s friend, Misty Armstrong, said otherwise.
According to Armstrong, Pike spent much of her time in prison trying to help other inmates.
“It took years of therapy for her to get there, but she did,” she said. “She changed and became a completely different person.”
