title: Why CMP is suing the state of Maine over a new revenue blocking law
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Power sued Maine regulators Friday to stop the implementation of a new state law that would block the utility from collecting a $4.6 million boost in investment return.
The law, LD 2038, requires transmission line owners in Maine — CMP, Versant and the utility-owned Maine Electric Power Co. — to join a regional group that operates the lines and manages the flow of electricity.
CMP, MEPCO and Versant are already voluntary members of that group, called ISO New England — which means they are eligible for a federal profit incentive that goes to companies that choose to participate in such collectives. By requiring the utilities to participate, lawmakers hoped to eliminate that federal incentive.
Maine regulators and consumer advocates asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to block utilities from collecting that incentive on Sept. 1. CMP, meanwhile, wants to get the state law thrown out.
The lawsuit comes amid an ongoing fight between CMP and regulators over the utility’s proposed rate hike — and again puts the CMP’s allowed investment profit center stage.
MEPCO joined CMP’s lawsuit against the Maine Public Utilities Commission, public advocate and Department of Energy Resources; Versant did not.
Here’s what to know about the incentive, the state law and the arguments on either side.
THE ‘ADDER’
A 2005 federal law spells it out: For voluntarily joining ISO New England and allowing it to operate CMP’s transmission lines, federal regulators allow CMP to earn an extra 0.5% return on equity — the profit it can make on its built infrastructure.
That 0.5% is an “adder,” as FERC puts it. Utilities all around the country benefit from it.
For CMP, that adder is worth about $4.6 million this year, the Office of the Public Advocate said in March testimony on the bill. Combined, Versant and MEPCO earned $1.35 million.
In 2024, Maine ratepayers paid about $700,000 extra on their bills for this 0.5% “adder,” according to a Sept. 1 complaint from the OPA and Maine regulators. Ratepayer costs are split between New England states.
Congress intended for the incentive to compensate utilities for “surrendering operational control of their facilities” and for maintaining the lines, CMP and MEPCO said in the lawsuit. Without the adder, the company may not be able to afford to keep up its infrastructure and attract outside investment, the lawsuit says.
The adder also helps “handle growing demand for electricity from changing weather patterns due to climate change, the construction of data centers, and the rapid electrification of cars, heating and cooling, home appliances, and other consumer products,” the companies wrote.
CMP, by its own account, is hurting financially. After Maine regulators denied a $7 per month rate increase this month, the company said that it would need to defer upgrades to grid infrastructure, pause hiring and “consider workforce reductions.” CMP’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in its rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
A spokesperson for CMP declined to comment.
THE STATE LAW
Maine’s LD 2038, passed mostly along party lines this spring, followed the lead of Maryland and Connecticut, which approved similar legislation this year and brought their case to federal regulators shortly thereafter.
California and Ohio have similar laws or rules, too — FERC recently denied the adder for utilities in those states. Federal appeals courts backed up FERC’s decisions last year.
The law was always meant to be the first of two steps, Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in January testimony in favor of the bill.
Like the other states, officials in Maine planned to petition federal regulators to remove the adder for Maine utilities as soon as the law was implemented. Maine did so Sept. 1, and three other New England states joined the complaint three weeks later.
“It is long past time to eliminate this ROE adder, which adds millions of dollars to customer bills,” former Public Utilities Commission Chair Philip Bartlett said in a September news release. “Maine has joined other states in the region in requiring transmission owner participation in ISO-New England, providing a clear pathway to reducing this inflated return on equity.”
Maine’s law, like the others, was born out of a concern for affordability and high electricity rates. By most measures, Maine’s rates rank in the top five most expensive in the country, and the effort, when combined with Connecticut’s new law, was estimated to save Maine customers $2 million per year — $5 million if all New England states enacted the same law.
“Given the urgency of electricity affordability issues, this is a simple and easy solution that will have immediate impact,” Sanborn told legislators.
Sanborn declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation. A spokesperson for the PUC did not respond to a request for comment.
CMP argued in its lawsuit that Maine attempted to supersede federal law, in violation of the Constitution, by interrupting transmission rates that had already been approved by FERC.
CMP also said the new law violated its contractual right to withdraw from ISO New England — a scenario the public advocate called “highly unlikely” in its bill testimony. It also argued that the law essentially made it so it no longer owned its transmission property.
The utility also blasted the new Maine law in a response to the Sept. 1 complaint. CMP said the Maine lawmakers enacted an “unlawful state statute in a naked attempt to interfere with FERC’s authority” over transmission rates.
WHAT NOW?
A federal judge will review the case in the coming weeks, and FERC will continue to consider the complaint from the public advocate and PUC.
CMP’s state-level rate case will continue in the meantime, too. Maine regulators recently rejected a $7 per month increase — but the larger rate hike, worth about $18 per month to the average household, will remain under consideration until the spring.

title: ProPublica report, outrageous? Yes it is, senator.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Confronted with credible accusations that Sen. Susan Collins received large contributions from someone seeking a lucrative contract with the federal government, the senator and her campaign responded by calling it “outrageous.”
I agree. It certainly is outrageous that such payments appear to have been accepted under those circumstances. It’s also outrageous that we have an electoral system that allows such payments under any circumstances, and an economy so dominated by a wealthy few who are able to virtually control our governing institutions.
Troy Jackson doesn’t seek or accept contributions like that. In truth, I doubt they would be offered anyway, because when Troy gets to Washington he will work with fellow progressives to fix our corrupt political system and promote a more equal and fair economy.
I can’t wait.
Mike Roland
Bowdoinham

title: 24-year-old hiker missing in Great Smoky Mountains found dead after dayslong search
text:
BLOUNT COUNTY, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A 24-year-old man was hiking in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park when his phone became untraceable, setting off a dayslong search that ended in tragedy.
Sahil Jilani, 24, went missing while hiking in the Great Smoky Mountains. Park officials say he was last seen around 8 p.m. last Monday at the Riverstone Campground in Townsend. His car was found at the Abrams Falls trailhead Wednesday.
The next day, divers found Jilani’s body in the water at Abrams Falls, according to his family. His phone, keys and clothes were also found near the falls.
While waiting for official reports, Jilani’s family believes he drowned after getting caught in powerful currents near the waterfall.
“With heavy hearts, we share the loss of our beloved brother, Sahil Jilani... Sahil was a pure, kind, generous soul who always cared for others. He dreamed of helping Mom retire, taking on her bills and helping Dad with dental procedures. A new uncle, he couldn’t wait to spoil his niece and teach her martial arts and self-defense. His absence leaves an irreplaceable void,” said Jilani’s sister, Asma Jilani Bustamante.
Bustamante says the family asked for help the day Jilani went missing due to the fact that their mother felt something was “terribly wrong.”
“He never went hours without checking in, but his location sharing stopped in a dead zone. We requested a welfare check from rangers the next day, but were told hikers often lose service. We kept requesting help as our fear grew,” Bustamante said.
Jilani’s family is now asking for help through donations, prayers and sharing their story, as they work to get his body back to Houston, Texas, and cover other bills related to the incident. Among these is getting care for Jilani’s mother, who was hospitalized “after losing her precious son,” according to Bustamante.
The family also hopes to raise awareness about water safety in honor of Jilani.
“I am determined to honor Sahil by helping save lives. If his story saves even one life, his memory will continue to protect others,” Bustamante said.
She is urging others to be aware of their surroundings, even when engaging in something beautiful like a waterfall.
“Beauty can turn deadly in an instant. Please heed warning signs, especially where lives have been lost. Share travel plans, prepare for cellular dead zones and consider carrying a satellite communication device in remote areas,” Bustamante said. “An upset or disappointed loved one who turns back from dangerous water is infinitely better than a deceased one.”
Official reports about the incident are pending.

title: Credit union employee accused of stealing more than $28,000 from dead people
text:
BETTENDORF, Iowa (KWQC/Gray News) - An employee at an Iowa credit union is facing charges after police say she stole more than $28,000 from seven people, six of whom were dead.
Amanda N. Tincher, a 38-year-old employee at IH Mississippi Valley Credit Union, was booked on several felony charges Friday after Bettendorf Police say she stole money from the accounts of six dead people and one living person.
A credit union official contacted police July 2 about an employee who had made multiple suspicious transactions on the account of someone who had died, according to court documents.
Police say Tincher made multiple withdrawals from the person’s account and created cashier’s checks in her name, transferred money to a CashApp in her name and made multiple cash withdrawals. She stole $21,279.51 from the account, officials say.
Police met with Tincher at the credit union July 3 and asked her about the suspicious transactions.
“It’s pretty clear what was done,” Tincher reportedly said.
Officials say Tincher denied taking money from other accounts, but the credit union later found she had made similar transactions on six more accounts. Court documents show six of the seven accounts belonged to someone who was dead. She took a total of $28,326.28 from the accounts.
Police say Tincher transferred money from the one living person’s account to the account of a dead person to cover money she took when the beneficiaries noticed the money was missing.
Tincher is facing the following charges:
- First-degree theft, a felony
- Ongoing criminal conduct, unlawful activity, a felony
- First-degree fraudulent practice, a felony
- Second-degree theft, a felony
- Second-degree fraudulent practice, a felony
- Four counts of third-degree theft, an aggravated misdemeanor
- Four counts of third-degree fraudulent practice, an aggravated misdemeanor
- Fifth-degree theft, a simple misdemeanor
- Fifth-degree fraudulent practice, a simple misdemeanor
Tincher was released on bond last Friday afternoon. She has a preliminary hearing scheduled this coming Friday.

title: A Spanish-language radio show overflows with voters' frustration in Pennsylvania battleground
text:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. (AP) — Una sola cosa. Just one thing. That’s all Victor Martinez wanted from listeners of his Spanish-language radio station — tell him one positive thing about President Donald Trump.
The calls started rolling in. Someone mentioned the $5,000 payout that Trump promised if Republicans keep control of Congress, which Martinez thought was so hilarious that he played a laugh track.
Then a trucker shared a silver lining from high diesel prices — he was expecting to take an unplanned vacation because he could no longer afford to fill up his rig.
Martinez has been hosting his show for nearly a decade in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, where Latinos have gone from a fifth to nearly a quarter of the population over the same time period. He added an hour of politics to his morning talk show at the end of Trump’s first term, and listeners flooded his phone with their worries about the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, their unhappiness with inflation and their concern over Joe Biden’s age.
Now, at the halfway mark of Trump’s second term, Martinez said people are just as frustrated as they were then. They’re angry about higher prices for fuel and groceries, and Republicans could face the consequences in the midterm elections.
“It’s the economy, stupid. That’s what it is. I mean, things have gotten so bad,” Martinez said. “People didn’t think Biden did a good job. Everything was expensive and now it’s worse.”
Latinos make up a key part of a winning coalition
Martinez broadcasts from a fourth floor studio with hardwood floors and a view of an old church in downtown Allentown. He operates the show’s control board like an orchestra conductor and sits in front of a poster with campaign signs for Democrats and Republicans.
The studio is located in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, where freshman incumbent Ryan Mackenzie faces Democratic challenger Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter and union official, in one of the most closely watched races in the country.
Latinos are about a quarter of the district’s population, and they were a key part of Trump’s winning coalition two years ago.
Both candidates have organized Latino outreach efforts.
Brooks calls his “Bombero Bob” — Spanish for firefighter — and recently stopped by a Mexican restaurant and a barber shop with a Dominican flag hanging inside. Mackenzie’s campaign has promoted support from Latino voters and officials, and the congressman opened a district office in downtown Allentown with Spanish-speaking staff.
Martinez is a longtime critic of the president, and this year is backing Brooks. But he said his political roots are in the Republican Party. He supported candidates like Marco Rubio and Jeb Bush, and he opposed Biden’s decision to seek reelection because he was too old.
Martinez said he uses his show to keep people engaged with politics when some have despaired about the prospect of things getting better .
“I got a call yesterday from a guy that said that he was just not going to vote,” Martinez said. “I understand that feeling of frustration, but not doing nothing is not the answer.”
Economic stress looms over the campaign
Republicans know Martinez’s show is an avenue to reach voters, and they’re buying advertising time on it.
Jackie Rivera, vice chair of Lehigh County Republicans, said the party wants to hold on to the support from Latino voters that Trump won over two years ago, and that means connecting with them on issues like “faith and family.”
Although Trump often brags about the economy under his leadership, she said her party wasn’t making the same mistake as Democrats did before.
“We’re not pretending everything is great right now,” she said. “You have to be honest with them so that they can believe in you and actually trust in what you’re stating to them.”
Matt Tuerk, Allentown’s Democratic mayor, said this year’s election has the “same vibes” as two years ago, when Biden was trying to convince people that the economy was strong.
“People on the street were like, ‘Yeah, but my monthly childcare bill is higher and then my monthly mortgage, the price of groceries is ridiculously high,’” he said. “That’s the same story that you hear right now. There’s been no improvement.”
Gas and grocery prices contribute to living ‘day by day’
Claudia Parrales-DeLeon, a Democratic listener from Allentown, said Martinez’s show helps people feel connected as they pay more for gas and groceries and face Trump’s immigration crackdown.
“I don’t know if it makes people less afraid, as much as it makes people more informed,” she said.
She recalled listening one day when a particular caller’s story brought tears to her eyes.
“This one gentleman who shared how he just lost his job, he can’t find work, doesn’t even know where he’s going to get his next meal for him and his children,” she said.
Alberto Pena isn’t a regular listener to Martinez, but his concerns are similar. For nearly two decades, Pena and his wife have run a Dominican restaurant in Allentown, where the aroma of crispy pastelillos and savory rice fill the dining room.
He voted for Trump hoping he’d turn things around after high inflation under Biden. But they’re still “living day by day,” and he’s leaning toward Brooks this year.
“This is not what we expected,” he said. “The economy is completely on the ground.”

Maine should expect an early flu season, experts say
text:
Maine could experience an early peak of influenza cases this flu season, public health experts said, urging residents to not delay getting immunized.
“We are seeing the beginnings of influenza circulating earlier than we have had in recent seasons, said Anna Krueger, an epidemiologist with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
While flu season runs from October to May, typically cases crest in late December, January or February. Cases peaked around the winter holidays during last flu season, with a high of 1,347 reported for the week ending Jan. 3, according to Maine CDC data.
So far this flu season, Maine has recorded 104 cases through Oct. 3, compared to 36 for the same time period in 2025.
During the 2023-24 and 2024-25 flu seasons, cases in Maine peaked in February, while in 2022-23, influenza crested in mid-December. Sometimes, Maine is hit with a second wave of flu cases in March or April. But Krueger said if cases peak early, that does not mean Maine is more likely to get a second wave.
Krueger said with the early uptick in cases, this season’s flu could peak here in November, which is why they are urging people to not wait to get their flu shot. Krueger said they worry that influenza could surge before many people have received their annual shot.
What Maine is seeing coincides with the U.S., which is also expecting an early flu season, experts say. Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, told National Public Radio last week that the nation should anticipate flu to arrive sooner this season.
The flu shot — recommended for everyone 6 months and older — is currently widely available at pharmacies, primary care providers, clinics and many healthcare settings. It is typically free, even for those without insurance.
Krueger said the flu shot appears to be a good match for circulating strains of the virus, which currently is influenza A. That means this year’s shot should be especially effective against the most common strain. Scientists update the flu shot every year, and try to match what they anticipate will be the season’s circulating strains.
Dr. Dora Anne Mills, chief health improvement officer for MaineHealth, advised Maine residents to get their flu shots now because signs are pointing to an early onset of cases.
“I usually wait until mid- to late-October, but I didn’t wait this year. I got my flu shot already,” Mills said.
Mills said a higher-dose flu shot is recommended for those 65 and older.
Mills said it’s also a good idea to get COVID-19 and influenza vaccines during the same appointment. The COVID-19 vaccine is updated every year to match mutations in the virus.
She said some may be afraid of worse side effects if getting both at the same time, but there’s “no evidence” that receiving both vaccines at the same appointment results in more side effects.
COVID-19 levels are currently considered “very low” in Maine, according to state data.

title: Cheverus, Lincoln Academy, Maranacook claim state golf championships
text:
Cheverus High School in Portland, Newcastle’s Lincoln Academy and Maranacook High School of Readfield captured Maine state golf championships at the Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro over the weekend.
In the Class A championships held on Friday, Cheverus made it two in a row by registering a score of 304, 10 strokes better than Falmouth. Rounding out the top 10 were Messalonskee of Oakland (324), Thornton Academy of Saco (328) a tie involving South Portland and Gorham (340s), Bangor (346), Brewer (350), Deering High of Portland (353) and Camden Hills of Rockport (372).
Sophomore Sam Sirois from Cheverus was the medalist with an even-par 72. Eight players tied for second with 76s: Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, Falmouth’s Dante Iannetta, Cheverus’ Keane McGrath and Joe Stratman, Gorham’s Charlie Sands, Greyson Dooley from Messalonskee, Caleb Greenleaf from Mt. Ararat in Topsham and Sawyer Poland from Oxford Hills High School in South Paris.
There are no girls teams, so the girls play on the boys teams and have a separate individual competition.
Cheverus’ Jacquelin Sirois and Camden Hills’ Lila Dailey shared the A title with 97s. Mia Binnette from Kennebunk, Stella Veilleux from Windham and Bailey Begin from Greely High in Cumberland Center all shot 99s. Emma Mathieu from Windham had a 100, Paige Jordan from Hampden Academy shot a 103, Oxford Hills’ Riley Pulkkinen had a 106, Brewer’s Finnley Collins had a 117 and Hampden Academy’s Lydia Adamo posted a 119.

Yarmouth was next at 334, followed by Cape Elizabeth and Fryeburg Academy at 341, Lake Region of Naples (344), Leavitt of Turner (348), Gray-New Gloucester (351), Belfast (353), and John Bapst of Bangor and Nokomis of Newport (356).

Kathryn Peterson of Lake Region and Carla Ferraris from Fryeburg Academy shared the girls B individual title with 90s. Emma Kane from Cape Elizabeth shot a 97 and rounding out the top 10 were Kamilia Martinez from Fryeburg (99), Vivi Nemeth from John Bapst (100), Alice Korzekwa from Presque Isle and Kate Geary from Yarmouth (101s), Svea Kark from Lincoln Academy (102), Addy Dowsland from Bar Harbor’s Mount Desert Island High School (103) and Mya Betters from Old Town (106).
In the Class C competition, Maranacook shot a 317 and won by the slimmest of margins, one stroke, over Winthrop. Calais was third (328) and completing the top 10 were Dexter (332), Houlton (336), Mattanawcook Academy of Lincoln (350), Narraguagus of Harrington and North Yarmouth Academy (352s), Orono (356) and Dirigo of Dixfield (362).
Jack Fontaine of Maranacook shot a 73 to finish one shot better than runnerup Ryan Farnsworth of Dexter. Drew Mertzel of Winthrop, Beckett Peabody of Houlton and Chris Johnson of Kents Hill shot 76s, Jacob Footer of Calais posted a 78 and recording 79s were Wyatt Corson of Dexter, Sam Corgan of Winthrop, Grady Hreben of Maranacook, Burren Absalom from Narraguagus and Isiah Barrett from Jonesport-Beals.
Kayden Allaire of Winthrop shot an 83 to win the girls championship by seven shots over Skylar Bard of Mattanawcook Academy. Presley Goodwin from Houlton was third with a 92 followed by Penobscot Valley of Howland and Kents Hill’s Caitlin Powers (98s), Averie Smith of Ashland (101), Chloe White of Fort Fairfield (109) and Rebecca O’Leary of Mars Hill’s Central Aroostook High School (111).

title: Here’s how Susan Collins secured my vote
text:
My wife is French, holds an EU passport and has multiple advanced degrees in engineering. She applied for a green card to live and work permanently in Maine. Immigration officials instructed us to wait until we received further notice. We heard nothing.
My wife was forced to repeatedly renew her driver’s license and carry a substantial file of immigration documents with her when traveling. We contacted Sen. Susan Collins’ office. Her staff investigated the situation to discover that the paperwork was sent to Portland, Oregon, not Portland, Maine. Their intervention finally moved the process forward.
Today, my wife owns her own engineering LLC and works as an independent contractor on advanced engineering projects in Maine and across the country. She’s contributing her education and professional experience to the U.S. economy — all made possible because of the assistance we received from Sen. Collins and her staff.
That is what effective representation looks like. And that is why Susan Collins has my vote this November.
Mark Zimmer
South Berwick

title: Volunteers give seniors the feeling of wind in their hair through bike rides
text:
SEVERNA PARK, Md. (Aging Untold) — A global nonprofit called Cycling Without Age is giving older adults a chance to ride through their communities on trishaws, bicycles equipped with a passenger seat, as volunteers pedal.
Dolores Ring, 95, took a ride in a trishaw along a Maryland trail.
“Well, I just enjoyed the whole thing because like I say, I have never been in anything like this,” Ring said.
“And the greens, you know, it’s so green,” Ring said. “And of course, this summer it’s been so beautiful because of all the rain we’ve had.”
Volunteers pedal passengers through the trail
Volunteers pedaled Ring and 79-year-old Diane Bockman along the trail, where they took in the sight of beautiful flowers.
Cycling Without Age’s mission is to give everyone the feeling of wind in their hair, no matter their mobility.
The trishaws picked up passengers at Sunrise of Severna Park, which offers seniors independent living, assisted living and memory care.
A chance to reminisce
Tim Stevens is a volunteer for the county’s chapter of Cycling Without Age, which is one of 3,500 chapters across the world.
“You know, I love asking questions, finding out about, you know, people’s background,” Stevens said. “And that’s the type of thing that they love too. They want somebody that’s going to listen to them.”
Julez Marsh, a Sunrise employee, said the rides bring passengers near tears.
“When they come back, they’ve got a smile on their face,” Marsh said. “And it just uplifts their soul.”
How the program started locally
Sandy Bishop was researching options for her daughter, who has a disability, to get to work when she came across Cycling Without Age’s website.
“The volunteers, the pilots, on the back of the bike, enjoy the experience,” Bishop said. “From exercise to being outdoors to interacting with the passengers. To be involved in something that just feels good.”
Bishop said the trishaws are meant to go slow enough for riders to interact with their environment, including people around them, make eye contact, say hello and stop to chat.
For many riders, the rides spark memories and fuel conversation.

title: The first indigenous peoples’ day film festival held in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The first Indigenous Peoples’ Day Film Festival took place in Bangor Sunday.
It was held at the Unitarian-Universalist Church in Bangor, and showed seven films, all following the theme of Environmental Justice.
Sunlight Media Collective, a group of filmmakers from Wabanakik, produced six of the films, along with one film produced by Bullfrog Films.
The event aimed to show films that asked the question, “What is environmental justice, and why is it so important right now?”
The films covered topics including the Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion, and the proposed AI data center in Passamaquoddy bay.
“These films all fundamentally tell a story that we as Wabanaki people are still here, fighting for and caring for our land and cultures in ways that we’ve been doing for thousands of years,” said Darren Ranco, Professor of Anthropology & Chair of the Native American Program at UMaine.
“Native, non-native people working together in a native framework, is actually one of the key elements of political change and social cultural change that we’re advocating for,” said Ranco.
The film screenings were followed by a “Harvest Potluck Supper” and traditional frybread was served.
For more information about the event, you can email the Peace and Justice Center at peacectr@gmail.com.

title: UMaine Extension offers virtual backyard bird learning series for kids
text:

Participants will learn to identify common backyard birds while exploring bird beaks, diets and habitats and developing observation and documentation skills through regular feeder observations. No previous bird identification experience is required. The series will be led by Carolyn Reece, leader of the Pollinator Protectors 4-H club, and Erin McDonald, a 4-H Youth Development Professional in York County. The sessions are modeled after the national Project Feeder Watch program. Families have the option to participate in that program for an additional fee, however it’s not required.

title: Volunteers give seniors the feeling of wind in their hair through bike rides
text:
SEVERNA PARK, Md. (Aging Untold) — A global nonprofit called Cycling Without Age is giving older adults a chance to ride through their communities on trishaws, bicycles equipped with a passenger seat, as volunteers pedal.
Dolores Ring, 95, took a ride in a trishaw along a Maryland trail.
“Well, I just enjoyed the whole thing because like I say, I have never been in anything like this,” Ring said.
“And the greens, you know, it’s so green,” Ring said. “And of course, this summer it’s been so beautiful because of all the rain we’ve had.”
Volunteers pedal passengers through the trail
Volunteers pedaled Ring and 79-year-old Diane Bockman along the trail, where they took in the sight of beautiful flowers.
Cycling Without Age’s mission is to give everyone the feeling of wind in their hair, no matter their mobility.
The trishaws picked up passengers at Sunrise of Severna Park, which offers seniors independent living, assisted living and memory care.
A chance to reminisce
Tim Stevens is a volunteer for the county’s chapter of Cycling Without Age, which is one of 3,500 chapters across the world.
“You know, I love asking questions, finding out about, you know, people’s background,” Stevens said. “And that’s the type of thing that they love too. They want somebody that’s going to listen to them.”
Julez Marsh, a Sunrise employee, said the rides bring passengers near tears.
“When they come back, they’ve got a smile on their face,” Marsh said. “And it just uplifts their soul.”
How the program started locally
Sandy Bishop was researching options for her daughter, who has a disability, to get to work when she came across Cycling Without Age’s website.
“The volunteers, the pilots, on the back of the bike, enjoy the experience,” Bishop said. “From exercise to being outdoors to interacting with the passengers. To be involved in something that just feels good.”
Bishop said the trishaws are meant to go slow enough for riders to interact with their environment, including people around them, make eye contact, say hello and stop to chat.
For many riders, the rides spark memories and fuel conversation.

title: Political groups invest in Bangor City Council race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Political groups are spending money on Bangor City Council races, with speakers at a Monday event citing public safety, police staffing, needle exchanges and homelessness among their concerns.
Jonathan Bush, a former gubernatorial candidate and founder of Maine for Keeps, said he hopes the group’s investment in local races across Maine — including Waterville, Lewiston and Bangor — will reach six figures.
“I gave, as you know, 50,000 bucks, which is all I had left in Maine for Keeps,” Bush said. “And I’m hoping to get another 50 from the other folks that are concerned.”
Bush said Maine for Keeps focuses on voter education and policy advocacy rather than endorsing candidates. He said city councils are a place where he believes his group can have the most influence.
Bangor group backs three candidates
Concerned Citizens of Bangor is supporting three of the 12 declared candidates running for City Council, said Philip Henry, a member of the group.
“We have a PAC set up. We have funding coming in from the local Bangor community. And so, we are supporting three candidates,” Henry said. “We don’t want the vote to get diluted.”
Henry said the group wants transparency and metrics on efforts to fully staff the Police Department. He said there is bipartisan support for the group’s calls for change.
Maine Republican Party Chairman Jim Deyermond urged voters to support Republicans, saying the goal was to “put sane Republicans and conservatives on this city council.” Bush said his group was fully committed to the three races in Bangor, Waterville, and Lewiston.
Organizer criticizes election spending
Bangor resident and progressive organizer Mitchell Cooper criticized the spending, calling it an attempt by wealthy people to influence an election. He said the money should instead go toward solutions, including needle return boxes, a needle bounty program and funding to fully staff the Police Department.

title: Central Maine Medical Center nurses vote to unionize as UMaine students prepare to enter workforce
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As University of Maine nursing students prepare to enter Maine’s health care workforce, nurses at Central Maine Medical Center (CMMC) voted 204-21 on Sept. 24 to join the Maine State Nurses Association/National Nurses Organizing Committee (MSNA/NNOC), following concerns over working conditions and allegations of retaliation.
The vote comes as UMaine nursing students prepare to enter a workforce where labor conditions are increasingly under scrutiny. Four out of five alumni in the nursing program report working within an hour of their hometown, and 93% begin their careers in Maine, according to internal student demographic and project evaluation data shared with the Maine Campus.
In a Sept. 25 press release announcing the vote, National Nurses United (NNU) shared that “since Prime began operating CMMC, nurses have cited increased patient loads, a lack of necessary patient care supplies… and unilateral cuts to nurses’ pay and benefits.”
Efforts began in response to Prime Healthcare, a for-profit health care company, purchasing the hospital. According to a July 12 Bangor Daily News article, Central Maine Healthcare lost 572 employees within the first five months of Prime Healthcare’s ownership.
“We are beyond thrilled to win our union election. Prime Healthcare thought they could silence us,” registered nurse Aaron McDaniel said in a separate Sept. 24 NNU press release. “We’re so proud to join NNOC because we know we will win a contract that will make a drastic difference for our patients and for us as nurses to build a healthier community.”
According to statements from NNU, before the union vote, registered nurses at CMMC held an informational picket in support of striking NNU nurses at Olympia Fields Hospital in Illinois and the six nurses there who had been fired. Subsequently, 20 CMMC nurses faced disciplinary action, with 15 being fired. One nurse, Katie Grinnell, said that CMMC suspended her without pay within the same night that she attended the picket. The union has criticized this move as illegal.
Prime Healthcare has denied that the disciplinary actions were related to union activity, maintaining that the employees violated hospital policies and standards, according to reporting by Maine Public.
“Their cruelty toward us just made us stronger,” Grinnell stated in the Sept. 25 NNU press release. “We are more determined than ever to win improvements to the lives of nurses and patients at our hospital. Prime should not profit off the backs of us nurses, at the expense of our patients.”
This follows eight months of bargaining by unionized nurses at Eastern Maine Medical Center (EMMC), resulting in a final tentative agreement, as well as a vote by unionized nurses at Maine Medical Center to ratify a new contract. With this union vote, the three biggest hospitals in the state each now have chapters representing MSNA/NNOC.
The Maine Campus reached out to fourth-year nursing student Nadia Tarbell for comment via email.
“As a nurse, it is our duty to advocate for and provide the best patient care we can, and this situation has reinforced the importance of having a workplace where nurses feel supported and comfortable speaking up about concerns,” Tarbell wrote in the email. “Although this situation makes me concerned about entering the profession, it also reminds me how important it is for nurses to stand together and advocate for the changes needed to protect both themselves and their patients.”
Tarbell expressed trepidation about the prospect of a private healthcare company owning a hospital she worked at, positing that it could result in nurses having greater access to resources and funding, but may also result in a prioritization of profit over patient outcomes.
“If the nurses at CMMC are successful in creating meaningful changes through unionization, it could inspire nurses at other hospitals to consider the possibility as well, leading to greater conversation about staffing, compensation, workplace safety and patient care,” Tarbell wrote. “Ultimately, supporting nurses and advocating for better working conditions is essential because nurses spend more time directly with patients than other healthcare professionals and their working conditions have a direct impact on patient safety, quality of care and the overall patient experience.”
Following the vote, nurses at CMMC will begin selecting representatives for their bargaining team and preparing to negotiate their first collective bargaining agreement with Prime Healthcare, according to MSNA.

title: Deadheads, meet drag: Bertha brings Grateful Dead tribute to Portland
text:
If you’re a Deadhead, or just someone who wants to have a really good time dancing and grooving on Saturday night, you need to know about the show at the State Theatre, when an all-drag Grateful Dead tribute act called Bertha: Grateful Drag will be taking the stage by storm.
I’ve never been a Grateful Dead fan. Heck, I didn’t know until about five minutes ago that they have a song named “Bertha,” which is where this band got its name.
But I’ve always respected the musicianship of the band and how dedicated Dead fans are – and continue to be – more than 30 years after the death of Jerry Garcia. Co-founder Bob Weir died earlier this year, and Phil Lesh two years ago.
Mad props to every musician involved with the Grateful Dead and its many spinoffs. I love it when people are passionate about music, and Deadheads excel at this.
Bertha: Grateful Drag is a Nashville, Tennessee-based roots collective that formed in 2023 for what was supposed to be a one-time benefit performance when their home state tried to ban drag performances. None of the seven musicians in the band had ever performed in drag, but thought they’d merge the world of Dead music with drag ensembles.
The show went over so well, they’re still at it and have since released a live album and live recordings of “Touch of Grey” and “Jack Straw.”
I got to to see them at the Newport Folk Festival in 2024. I had never heard of Bertha, but was intrigued by the thought of a drag Dead tribute act and I knew festival organizers don’t book mediocre acts, so surely there had to be something special about them.
Their performance was one of the most talked about sets of the weekend.
The set kicked off with “Truckin'” and I was immediately blown away by the musicianship, paired with the spectacle of over-the-top flashy outfits, that made for an unbelievable performance.
The crowd lost their minds.
Bertha: Grateful Drag is Melody Walker (Daddy Bertha) on vocals and percussion, Caitlyn Doyle (Mommy Bertha) on vocals and percussion, Jacob Groopman (Big Sissy Bertha) on vocals and bass, Mike Wheeler (Baby Bobby Barbie Bertha) on vocals and guitar, Justin Volp (Cousin Bertha) on drums and Alex Joran (Cousin Bertha) on keys.
Walker, Doyle and Wheeler trade off lead vocals, shifting keys when needed, as the band taps into the Dead sound of the late ’70s and early ’80s.
Still skeptical? Know this: Grateful Dead publicist Dennis McNally caught Bertha’s two-night run in San Francisco and said “Jerry would have loved this.”
8 p.m. Saturday. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $26 in advance, $31 day of show. statetheatreportland.com.

title: 5 fun things to do in Freeport
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tawni Whitney was drawn to the charm of Freeport’s downtown when she moved to town 14 years ago.
Her connection to the community deepened when she served a stint on the Town Council. Now, through her current role as the executive director of the Greater Freeport Chamber of Commerce, she works with business leaders to envision the future of downtown.
“I just loved the vibe of the residents and the businesses, and, on top of that, we’re right on the ocean,” she said.
Whitney recently took a few minutes to answer some questions about Freeport. While the big-brand shops are a great draw, Whitney said, there’s plenty of local businesses and off-the-beaten-path attractions in Freeport, too.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Where do you like to eat?
I like to eat at Tuscan Bistro and the Lobster Cooker, the Bakeshop and Lily’s Food Cart, which is right behind Starbucks. (Lily’s is a) charming little hidden gem in Freeport. Right in front of you, she makes fried rice and these incredible dumplings.
Where do you like to go for a drink?
M.A.D.E. has a coffee shop in it that’s just darling. On warmer days, you can sit outside on their gorgeous, sunny porch, but it’s also in this historic old building that just feels so nice to be inside. I feel like I’m on the set of “Gilmore Girls.” It’s so precious, and centrally located to where I work downtown. We often host meetings over there, or I can meet my kids there after school.
As far as going out for a drink, we are a little bit limited, and I’d like more, but Tuscan Bistro would be that spot. It’s a beautiful restaurant.
Where do you connect with nature?
Wolfe’s Neck State Park. The first time I went there, I couldn’t even believe that we had this asset in Freeport. It is stunning to walk these trails and see an osprey next to you while you’re looking at this gorgeous water with these beautiful colors, and I was just blown away.
The other one is Wolfe’s Neck Farm itself. I remember taking my kids there one time, and they were like, ‘Mom, you gotta come over here, this cow is giving birth.’ Lo and behold, the cow gave birth in front of me and my kids. Of course, there was a farmer there to assist. Not only did this cow give birth in front of us, but all the other cows were out to pasture, and they were just peacefully doing what cows do, eating grass, and then as soon as she gave birth, they all came to her.
Our world is so hectic and noisy, and to watch something like that, and have that whole experience evolve before your eyes is something I’ll never forget.
Where do you shop local?
I still love national (stores). I think the psychology of someone in Freeport is that we have great deals here, and I think that that’s so true. Like, if you ever need to get something simple, we have places you can get a pair of sweatpants, or socks, or what have you — Under Armour, Old Navy, Gap, American Eagle — and they’re going to have the trendy things that you’re seeing.
But we also have some things that make Freeport special, like (local clothing and home stores) Loom and Gingham, and even the Freeport Community Thrift Shop are really great places to get unique items that you can’t find on Amazon.
What’s one more thing you can’t miss in Freeport?
Experiencing the Desert of Maine is something that is a must-do. It has changed so much over the years. I can remember going there as a child, and being in awe of it.
Now they have new ownership, and they have really cranked up the natural beauty (that) enhances how you can experience this natural wonder. They have really helped us understand the history, but made it really fun. It’s something kids can take in, or adults. They have a really fun mini golf and snack shack; it is a treasure.
Five Things is a feature in which locals give our readers suggestions for exploring the state of Maine, town by town. Have a city or town you think we should explore in the future? Tell News & Culture Editor Katherine Lee at [email protected].

title: She was a janitor at this hospital. Now she’s returning as a physician
text:
NEW HAVEN, Conn. (InvestigateTV) — In 2011, Shay Taylor-Allen was working as a janitor at Yale New Haven Hospital when she was 18. She is now returning years later to the hospital as a resident physician.
Taylor-Allen said she took the janitor job after finishing high school because her mother told her she needed to either work or go to school.
“And that’s when I got a call back that I got a job as a janitor,” Taylor-Allen said.
Taylor-Allen said her mother, Shema, became sick, and doctors did not have answers. She said a doctor asked her a question that changed her outlook.
“The doctor pulled me to the side and was like, ‘Does your mother have a history of mental illness?’ And I’m like, ‘Why’d you ask me that?’” Taylor-Allen said.
Taylor-Allen said she began researching health care disparities. She then emailed the hospital’s CEO.
“I am the janitor that cleans your office. And this is what my mom is going through and I don’t think is right. Is there any way that you can help us?” Taylor-Allen said. “Within that day, she emailed me back. They ended up switching her team and they found out that she had vocal cord dysfunction, and I just got to see advocacy happen so fast. And I was very motivated by that.”
Taylor-Allen said that experience led her to want to work as a doctor. She knew that she wanted to help people and “be that doctor that my mom didn’t have at the time.”
“It was very personal to me,” Taylor-Allen said.
At 28, Taylor-Allen enrolled at Howard University College of Medicine in Washington, D.C. She said she had no mentorship and did not know anyone in her family who was a doctor.
During that time, she met Kenton Allen, who became her husband.
“She doesn’t take no for an answer. She wakes up every single day and she’s like, ‘I need to get this done,’ and she always accomplishes it,” Kenton Allen said.
Taylor-Allen, now 32, graduated from Howard University College of Medicine in May 2026. She is returning to Yale New Haven Hospital as a resident physician specializing in anesthesiology.
Black women make up 2.8% of physicians in the United States, according to a study published in The Lancet.
“I had people who say, you pushed me to go get my masters at 50 years old,” Taylor-Allen said. “I think the biggest lesson is that the sky’s the limit. I think a lot of people love this story because it’s the American dream that we always want, right? You work hard, you can eventually get what you want.”
Her husband, Kenton Allen, is heading to Georgetown University to earn his master’s degree in AI management.

I am writing to express my strong support for Dakota Dupuis for Hancock County Sheriff. My background and experience have given me a clear understanding of the leadership this position demands.
I have served in law enforcement for more than 35 years, including 33 years with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office, where I held leadership positions as Patrol Staff Sergeant and Chief Deputy. Shortly after retiring, I was appointed Chief Deputy at the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office.
I am also a parent who has experienced the devastating loss of a child to an overdose. This personal tragedy has given me firsthand knowledge of the challenges substance abuse creates for families and communities. Addressing these issues requires compassion, accountability, effective resources and strong leadership.
Over the past couple of years, I have worked closely with Dakota and witnessed his commitment to moving the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office forward. He prioritizes providing deputies with current training and appropriate equipment whenever fiscally feasible. He supports his employees while maintaining high standards of professionalism and accountability.
Dakota understands that effective leadership means listening to employees, building trust, encouraging professional growth, and ensuring deputies have the tools necessary to perform their duties safely and effectively. He has also been actively involved in the budget process, working toward responsible solutions that benefit the agency and Hancock County residents.
Dakota recognizes the challenges involving mental health and substance abuse. He understands that incarceration is not always the appropriate answer and values working with community resources to address underlying problems while maintaining public safety.
After more than three decades in law enforcement and years of leadership experience, I do not take my decision lightly. A sheriff must demonstrate integrity, sound judgment, accountability and a genuine commitment to the people they serve.
Based on my experience working alongside Dakota, I believe he possesses these qualities. I am confident in his ability to lead the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office, support its employees, and serve our communities effectively.

title: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
text:
(AP) — President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP.
“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.
___

title: Why CMP is suing the state of Maine over a new revenue blocking law
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Power sued Maine regulators Friday to stop the implementation of a new state law that would block the utility from collecting a $4.6 million boost in investment return.
The law, LD 2038, requires transmission line owners in Maine — CMP, Versant and the utility-owned Maine Electric Power Co. — to join a regional group that operates the lines and manages the flow of electricity.
CMP, MEPCO and Versant are already voluntary members of that group, called ISO New England — which means they are eligible for a federal profit incentive that goes to companies that choose to participate in such collectives. By requiring the utilities to participate, lawmakers hoped to eliminate that federal incentive.
Maine regulators and consumer advocates asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to block utilities from collecting that incentive on Sept. 1. CMP, meanwhile, wants to get the state law thrown out.
The lawsuit comes amid an ongoing fight between CMP and regulators over the utility’s proposed rate hike — and again puts the CMP’s allowed investment profit center stage.
MEPCO joined CMP’s lawsuit against the Maine Public Utilities Commission, public advocate and Department of Energy Resources; Versant did not.
Here’s what to know about the incentive, the state law and the arguments on either side.
THE ‘ADDER’
A 2005 federal law spells it out: For voluntarily joining ISO New England and allowing it to operate CMP’s transmission lines, federal regulators allow CMP to earn an extra 0.5% return on equity — the profit it can make on its built infrastructure.
That 0.5% is an “adder,” as FERC puts it. Utilities all around the country benefit from it.
For CMP, that adder is worth about $4.6 million this year, the Office of the Public Advocate said in March testimony on the bill. Combined, Versant and MEPCO earned $1.35 million.
In 2024, Maine ratepayers paid about $700,000 extra on their bills for this 0.5% “adder,” according to a Sept. 1 complaint from the OPA and Maine regulators. Ratepayer costs are split between New England states.
Congress intended for the incentive to compensate utilities for “surrendering operational control of their facilities” and for maintaining the lines, CMP and MEPCO said in the lawsuit. Without the adder, the company may not be able to afford to keep up its infrastructure and attract outside investment, the lawsuit says.
The adder also helps “handle growing demand for electricity from changing weather patterns due to climate change, the construction of data centers, and the rapid electrification of cars, heating and cooling, home appliances, and other consumer products,” the companies wrote.
CMP, by its own account, is hurting financially. After Maine regulators denied a $7 per month rate increase this month, the company said that it would need to defer upgrades to grid infrastructure, pause hiring and “consider workforce reductions.” CMP’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in its rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
A spokesperson for CMP declined to comment.
THE STATE LAW
Maine’s LD 2038, passed mostly along party lines this spring, followed the lead of Maryland and Connecticut, which approved similar legislation this year and brought their case to federal regulators shortly thereafter.
California and Ohio have similar laws or rules, too — FERC recently denied the adder for utilities in those states. Federal appeals courts backed up FERC’s decisions last year.
The law was always meant to be the first of two steps, Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in January testimony in favor of the bill.
Like the other states, officials in Maine planned to petition federal regulators to remove the adder for Maine utilities as soon as the law was implemented. Maine did so Sept. 1, and three other New England states joined the complaint three weeks later.
“It is long past time to eliminate this ROE adder, which adds millions of dollars to customer bills,” former Public Utilities Commission Chair Philip Bartlett said in a September news release. “Maine has joined other states in the region in requiring transmission owner participation in ISO-New England, providing a clear pathway to reducing this inflated return on equity.”
Maine’s law, like the others, was born out of a concern for affordability and high electricity rates. By most measures, Maine’s rates rank in the top five most expensive in the country, and the effort, when combined with Connecticut’s new law, was estimated to save Maine customers $2 million per year — $5 million if all New England states enacted the same law.
“Given the urgency of electricity affordability issues, this is a simple and easy solution that will have immediate impact,” Sanborn told legislators.
Sanborn declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation. A spokesperson for the PUC did not respond to a request for comment.
CMP argued in its lawsuit that Maine attempted to supersede federal law, in violation of the Constitution, by interrupting transmission rates that had already been approved by FERC.
CMP also said the new law violated its contractual right to withdraw from ISO New England — a scenario the public advocate called “highly unlikely” in its bill testimony. It also argued that the law essentially made it so it no longer owned its transmission property.
The utility also blasted the new Maine law in a response to the Sept. 1 complaint. CMP said the Maine lawmakers enacted an “unlawful state statute in a naked attempt to interfere with FERC’s authority” over transmission rates.
WHAT NOW?
A federal judge will review the case in the coming weeks, and FERC will continue to consider the complaint from the public advocate and PUC.
CMP’s state-level rate case will continue in the meantime, too. Maine regulators recently rejected a $7 per month increase — but the larger rate hike, worth about $18 per month to the average household, will remain under consideration until the spring.

title: When hunting moose, help is always available
text:
A flatbed truck hauling a bull moose slowed as it approached our group of four pickups, nine guys and one gal holding an infant parked in a turnoff on a remote gravel road. The driver offered a friendly wave and a brief, “how you doing?” before starting to turn.
“You want some chicken wings?” shouted one of our hunting party who was dutifully tending the grill on his tailgate.
“Sure,” replied the driver who, along with his father, joined our party for an hour of eating and swapping stories.
That’s not an unusual occurrence in the North Woods during moose season. More than any other pursuit, moose hunting in Maine is a very social experience. Sure, deer camp is social, but most of the socializing occurs at camp, after each day’s hunt. Turkey hunting tends to be more enjoyable when done with a partner, but two’s company and three’s a crowd.
A moose hunting crew might consist of two or three folks per truck, and possibly several trucks. Many eyes are handy, but many bodies are handier still when you’ve got 800-1,000 pounds of moose on the ground. The help often extends beyond individual hunting parties.
We were parked at the bottom of a dead-end road one morning, awaiting shooting light, when we noticed lights on the road below us and went down to investigate. A gentleman hunting with his 10-year-old son had a flat tire. Our crew of five, several of whom just happen to be mechanics, eagerly jumped in, and we had the father and son on their way in time for both groups to make our destination before sun-up.
Two years prior, we were just finishing up field dressing a moose when two truckloads of hunters stopped to investigate. When they saw we had a bull down, they all eagerly volunteered to help us load it into the truck.
And the willingness to help doesn’t end there.
Most hunters get only six days to fill their tag. Some need all six, while others tag out early. The latter are in the North Woods with time to kill, and many will eagerly jump in with another crew to help them find their bull.
As a side note, Maine guides typically book one hunter for a week-long hunt. If their hunter tags out early, that means they are free and available. For someone who decided to go the DIY route but is struggling, it might be worth making a few phone calls or checking social media toward the end of the week.
Even, and perhaps especially, if you start with a guide, you’ll find the same ethic. Everyone in camp wants to be part of the hunt. Guides and their tagged-out hunters are often eager to join others in camp to help out in any way they can.
I’ve been fortunate to fall in with a group of guys who love to hunt moose and are good at it. Our forces were spread a little thin this year because three among us drew tags. That won’t be the case next year, but some among us will have a friend or relative who pulls a permit, and we’ll rally our resources to see they have all the help they need. For all of us, even those who live near and work in the North Woods, it’s a chance to get away into the woods for a week and be hunters.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Church deacon, teacher arrested for reportedly kicking children off bus, leaving them on side of road
text:
ALBANY, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — A deacon for a church in Georgia, who is also a teacher, is facing charges after allegedly kicking a group of young kids off his bus and leaving them on the side of the road.
According to the incident report from the Albany Police Department, officers were called on Sunday, Oct. 11, to Oakridge Baptist Church. When officers got there, they talked to a woman who said her three children (ages 12, 11, and 9) and their 10-year-old friend who they had invited to church, had been kicked off the church bus.
She reported that her mother called her and told her the church deacon, Erin Menefee, had called and said he had put the kids off the bus because they were cursing.
The mom said she was told Menefee left the kids at an intersection about three miles away. She said it was too far for the kids to walk home. The mom says she got in her car and went looking for her kids, but couldn’t find them. She did, however, spot the church bus on the road and tried to flag it down.
According to police, the mom spoke with Menefee, who said he’d left the kids down the road. At that point, the mom went to the church to speak with the pastor and got a call from someone telling her the kids had been brought home by a stranger.
In the report, the grandmother claimed she was told the children were put off the bus because they were cursing and hitting each other and the bus driver, “Don’t play that.”
Officers spoke with Menefee about these accusations. Menefee reportedly told officers he had about 20 kids on the bus and this particular group of kids was being disruptive, and he needed to put them off the bus for his safety. Police asked Menefee how he thought the kids were going to get home, and he claimed he called their grandmother.
Police say Menefee acknowledged he should’ve waited for someone to come pick them up.
At this point, officers arrested Menefee. He was charged with multiple counts of reckless conduct. According to the incident report, Menefee is also a teacher at Mitchell County High School.

title: Maine hunter shoots 1st 200-pound buck with a bow
text:
Devon Polley’s first archery buck was also his first deer to weigh 200 pounds. But with almost no blood to follow after the shot, recovering it required help from a tracking dog.
Polley shot the buck at about 10:30 a.m. last Wednesday during Maine’s regular archery season in Vassalboro. He had been hunting the deer since last year, when he spotted it but couldn’t get close enough for a shot. After running trail cameras in the area for two years, he changed his approach.
“I focused on not intruding into the woods and playing the wind effectively,” he said.
The day before the hunt, Polley spotted the buck feeding on acorns with several does and another large, six-point buck. He returned the next morning and settled into a tree stand near where he had seen it.
The buck appeared around 9 a.m. but stayed out of range. About an hour later, it returned along a rock wall. After watching it for nearly half an hour, Polley got his opportunity as it passed through a gap in the trees.
He released an arrow from about 30 yards away. A camera mount he made for his phone recorded the shot, allowing him to review the footage and assess the hit.
The buck had been walking parallel to Polley before turning slightly toward him as he released the arrow. The arrow passed through one lung, the liver and intestines before exiting in front of the back leg.
Polley believed the wound was lethal but knew the deer might not drop immediately. He determined the hit was a bit low and contacted Susanne Hamilton, a large-game tracker who had helped his family recover deer before.
They waited about 10 to 12 hours before Hamilton arrived with her dog, Fritzi.
The open hardwood forest was covered in leaves, with no visible sign of the wounded deer, Hamilton said. Fritzi quickly picked up the scent and followed the trail. About 50 yards in, they found half of Polley’s arrow and a single drop of blood. The dog followed the trail another 165 yards to the buck.
“Because of the terrain, this would’ve been an incredibly hard track for a dog if it had been mucked around,” Hamilton said. “I was so impressed with how he handled his situation.”
The buck weighed exactly 200 pounds on an official scale at Toby’s Grocery near South China and Windsor. Polley plans to register it with Maine’s Big Buck Club.

title: Here’s how Susan Collins secured my vote
text:
My wife is French, holds an EU passport and has multiple advanced degrees in engineering. She applied for a green card to live and work permanently in Maine. Immigration officials instructed us to wait until we received further notice. We heard nothing.
My wife was forced to repeatedly renew her driver’s license and carry a substantial file of immigration documents with her when traveling. We contacted Sen. Susan Collins’ office. Her staff investigated the situation to discover that the paperwork was sent to Portland, Oregon, not Portland, Maine. Their intervention finally moved the process forward.
Today, my wife owns her own engineering LLC and works as an independent contractor on advanced engineering projects in Maine and across the country. She’s contributing her education and professional experience to the U.S. economy — all made possible because of the assistance we received from Sen. Collins and her staff.
That is what effective representation looks like. And that is why Susan Collins has my vote this November.
Mark Zimmer
South Berwick

title: After Lewiston shooting, Troy Jackson found the courage to change his mind
text:
In less than half an hour on Maine’s darkest day, a man gunned down 18 people in Lewiston and left at least 13 more injured, some of them grievously.
For me, a former Connecticut journalist, the Oct. 25, 2023 mass shooting brought back memories of the Sandy Hook school shooting in 2012. This is the kind of horror that ought to lead to sweeping policy changes.
Here in America, though, too many people just shrug their shoulders every time bullets fly and innocent people die as a result. They insist there’s nothing we can do about it.
Today, Troy Jackson knows better.
During a rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders in Lewiston on Sunday, Jackson told the crowd supporting his Senate bid that when he “watched this community bury 18 people,” he realized he’d taken the wrong position on some gun-related proposals.
“Eighteen funerals changed me,” Jackson said. “Because sometimes leadership means having the guts to admit that what you believed before isn’t good enough anymore. I couldn’t look at those families and tell them nothing had to change. So I changed.”
Sadly, most politicians looking at the same situation refused to reconsider their positions. But some did.
Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who opted not to run for reelection to Congress this year, backed a ban on assault rifles after the Lewiston mass shooting. He called his earlier position a failure and asked for forgiveness from victims’ families and the community at large.
A more careful Sen. Susan Collins called only for limits on “very high capacity” magazines and suggested she might agree to raise the age limit for buying them from 18 to 21.
“We cannot keep treating these mass shootings like they’re a natural disaster, like some terrible thing that just happens in America and there’s nothing that we can do about it. Because there is,” Jackson said on Sunday. “I learned right here in Lewiston that those 18 people deserve more than our grief. We owe them the courage to change.”
Before the shooting, Jackson earned top marks from pro-gun groups and voted against a number of measures aimed at stemming gun violence, including a proposed 72-hour waiting period for gun purchases, background checks and a ban on devices that allow modification of rifles to allow them to be fired more rapidly.
“I grew up around guns,” Jackson said. “I’m a sportsman — and for a long time I opposed some of the gun laws that people in my own party wanted me to support.”
After the Lewiston shootings, Jackson fought for stronger background checks, a waiting period for gun purchases and a red flag law to allow law enforcement to temporarily confiscate firearms from people considered a threat.
“When a family knows somebody they love is in danger to themselves or others, they ought to be able to do something before it’s too late,” he told the crowd.
To my mind, the 2012 Sandy Hook nightmare that left 20 children blown to bits in their classroom by a high-powered semi-automatic rifle should have been enough to cause every political leader to embrace gun control. But better late than never.
After Lewiston, Jackson and Golden fessed up to their mistaken policy choices. It’s refreshing to see politicians admit they had it wrong.

title: Windham-area schools are adopting a new learning model. What is it?
text:
Middle and high schools in Windham and Raymond are among 94 schools in Maine using the Building Assets, Reducing Risks model of education.
Kayla Vangelist, BARR coordinator for Windham Middle School, as well as Jordan Small Middle School in Raymond, said BARR is a data-driven framework used by schools across Maine centered around relationships between students and their teachers and peers.
Lindsay Hanson, who serves as coordinator for Windham High School, said the BARR model was implemented at the high school level by forming teams of around 75 students, classroom teachers from each of the core subjects, counselors and administrators, with social work and special ed included in the larger framework. Each team’s teachers meet frequently to discuss students and put plans in place to help them succeed.
Vangelist said each BARR team looks at three metrics: academic success, student behavior and attendance rates. Each team updates these measures regularly and puts supports in place based on the data.
According to the Maine Department of Education, 71 schools statewide began adopting BARR in the 2023-24 school year, funded by $10 million in federal emergency relief funds. In Windham, the model was first implemented as a pilot program at Windham High School, expanding district-wide by the following school year.
At the time, the Department of Education said the model was meant to support students and educators in recovering from the impact the pandemic had on educational well-being.
RSU 14 Superintendent Christopher Howell said BARR has allowed for a framework in which, when a student is struggling, a team of educators is ready to come together to support them and make sure they don’t slip through the cracks.
As part of BARR, students and teachers participate in 30-minute weekly activities focused on topics such as community building and goal setting.
Hanson said the BARR framework has “moved the needle” in terms of attendance and failure rates at the high school level and improved the school’s culture. She said these results make the teachers involved in the program feel more seen and supported, while students feel like teachers genuinely care about them. Howell pointed to a reduction of freshmen failing classes, as well as student attendance rates ticking up.
Regarding the next steps for BARR, Vangelist said the seventh- and eighth-grade teams at Jordan Small Middle School are set to be “fully implemented” by the end of the school year, while Windham Middle School is only in its first year of implementation.
Howell said, as the schools prepare to merge into a new building next year, having Vangelist help lead the work of bringing the schools’ teams together is setting them up to be prepared once the new middle school opens. The teams will be a mix of teachers who are experienced with BARR and those who have only used the framework for one year.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 13 to correct Lindsay Hanson’s name.

title: Woman dies in head-on collision in Poland

title: Skowhegan-area schools take precautions after receiving threat
text:
SKOWHEGAN — A threat of violence has prompted additional security measures Tuesday at Maine School Administrative District 54 schools.
As of Monday, which was a holiday, district officials were expecting to have schools open Tuesday under “lockout” protocol. That means classes inside school buildings proceed as normal, while outdoor activities are limited and access to school buildings is more restricted than usual.
The district is also planning for an increased police presence at its schools in coordination with the Skowhegan Police Department and the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office.
A field hockey game and other extracurricular activities on school grounds were proceeding as scheduled Monday, with police planning to be on site, Superintendent of Schools Jon Moody said in a telephone call Monday morning.
The precautions were put in place after the district received an anonymous email threatening violence on Tuesday toward “schools in the district,” Moody wrote in a letter sent to families Sunday.
District officials immediately contacted Skowhegan police and the sheriff’s office, Moody wrote.
“Both agencies have worked closely with the district and coordinated with state authorities to assess the situation,” he wrote. “Based on the information available at this time, law enforcement does not believe the threat to be credible.”
The threat was “nonspecific,” which led district leaders and police to determine canceling school was not necessary, Moody said Monday.
“This is similar to other threats that have gone on over the last year” in Maine, Moody said.
The writer, identified as “scabzone” in the email text and “aa awea” in the sender’s name, purported to be part of a terrorist group called No Lives Matter and said group members were planning a shooting, according to a copy of the threat email that Moody shared with the Morning Sentinel. It did not say specifically where it would occur or contain any information specific to MSAD 54.
Moody received the message Friday afternoon. He said the letter to families about the threat did not go out until Sunday, after law enforcement had assessed the situation and discussed a plan with school district leaders.
Moody said he was planning to check in with police later Monday to confirm the plan for Tuesday.
Local police were working with the state law enforcement officials, including the Maine Information and Analysis Center, Moody said. The center is Maine’s clearinghouse for intelligence on criminal activity and terrorism.
MSAD 54 serves Canaan, Cornville, Mercer, Norridgewock, Smithfield and Skowhegan. Its largest elementary school, middle school and high school are in Skowhegan, which has its own police department. Two smaller elementary schools are in Canaan and Norridgewock, where the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office is the primary law enforcement agency.
“The safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our highest priority,” Moody wrote to families. “We are grateful for the ongoing partnership and support of our local and state law enforcement agencies. We will continue to work closely with them, monitor any new information, and communicate promptly with families should circumstances or guidance change.”

title: Tiger that killed man who entered enclosure won’t be euthanized, reports say
text:
