title: ‘Thousands’ of dead fish discovered along Androscoggin River
text:
Local environmental advocates say scores of river herring were killed in the turbines of the Brunswick-Topsham dam while attempting to move down the Androscoggin River recently.
Free the Andro, a local group that has been advocating for better fish passage at the dam during its federal relicensing period, has reported thousands of dead herring “lining the shores” along the river. Many of these dead fish are visible along Water Street in Brunswick.
The group said the young fish were killed while attempting to move downriver through dam turbines.
“This fish kill is, unfortunately, not a surprise,” said Free the Andro founder Chip Spies. “These occurrences are the reason we founded Free the Andro and are working to create safe and effective upstream and downstream fish passage requirements for the Brunswick dam by (the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission). This is one more, very obvious example of what is wrong with the existing facility and how it impacts migratory species that rely on the Androscoggin to complete their life cycles.”
A spokesperson for the dam owner, Brookfield Renewable, said Monday evening that the company is aware of the weekend’s fish mortality event. The hydroelectric dam has been offline since Saturday to prevent further deaths, said spokesperson David Heidrich.
“(Brookfield White Pine Hydro) had been notified of an anticipated outmigration associated with water level changes upstream and, as is the protocol for such circumstances, implemented overnight operational shutdowns at the Brunswick Project to facilitate the safe passage of out-migrating fish,” Heidrich said in an email. “After project personnel observed fish mortality downstream of the dam on Saturday morning, we expanded those measures and shut down generation completely while we assessed conditions and coordinated with resource agencies.”
Another local environmental nonprofit, Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, issued a complaint to FERC, which is currently considering relicensing the dam, on Monday. In its complaint, FOMB wrote that the only way for migratory fish to pass downstream is through a pipe immediately next to turbines.
The fish observed in Brunswick were killed by decapitation, direct concussive strikes and the sudden difference in pressure, FOMB said.
Heidrich said fish protection is an “important operational priority” for Brookfield.
“We are continuing to review the circumstances and will work closely with state and federal resource agencies to better understand what occurred,” he said.
Spies, of Free the Andro, began hearing about the fish kill Sunday morning, he said.
The dam owner’s license expires in 2029. In the coming years, FERC will determine whether to renew the license for another 50 years and what conditions should be imposed. This could include a new fish passage system or even dam removal.
Most fish are not making it through the current fish ladder at the Brunswick dam, en route to their historic breeding grounds, according to counts conducted by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
“This recurring kill emphasizes that all potentially safe passage possibilities must be thoroughly vetted, including and especially dam removal; since any time safe passage is dependent on human intervention, a certain amount of failure is inevitable,” Friends of Merrymeeting Bay wrote in its complaint to FERC.

Bradley Farrell, Kennebunk: The running back’s second touchdown pass, a 5-yarder to quarterback Giovanni D’Elia with 7.5 seconds to play, lifted the Rams to a 35-34 win over Fryeburg. Farrell also threw a 41-yard TD pass to Charlie Pentland late in the first half.
Darren Flagg, Leavitt: Flagg scored five touchdowns and intercepted two passes in the Hornets’ 48-7 triumph over Gardiner. Flagg scored on runs of 4 and 47 yards, caught 12- and 27-yard touchdown passes from Landon Marquis, and returned his second interception 35 yards for a score.
Dylan Jewett, Spruce Mountain: Jewett rushed for three touchdowns — all longer than 50 yards (56, 72 and 87) — and gained 260 yards on 12 carries to propel the Phoenix to a key 40-24 win over Cape Elizabeth. Jewett also threw a 14-yard TD pass to Levi Richards, made 14 tackles (13 solo) and had a pass deflection.
Lucas Klehn, Bonny Eagle: The Scots quarterback set the tone with his weaving, tackle-breaking 61-yard touchdown run for the first score in a 45-6 win against Oxford Hills. Klehn rushed for 170 yards and four touchdowns on 10 carries, and completed 4 of 5 passes for 91 yards, highlighted by a 67-yard TD pass to Drew Gervais.
Fin Minkel, Messalonskee: Minkel helmed a potent offense in the Eagles’ 41-26 victory over Mt. Blue. He completed 12 of 22 passes for 234 yards and two scores, ran for two touchdowns and gained 39 yards on eight carries.
Owen Ross, Falmouth: Ross scored four touchdowns — on runs of 10, 4, 70 and 14 yards — for the Navigators in their 35-12 win over Gorham.
Brennan Tabor, Thornton Academy: Tabor’s strong performance on both sides of the ball helped the Golden Trojans overcome a 14-point deficit to defeat Noble, 53-20. Tabor carried 13 times for 161 yards and four touchdowns, was in on 14 tackles (seven solo, two for loss) and forced a fumble.

title: 6 events and 1 exhibit to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 25 Lewiston mass shootings
text:
Oct. 25 will mark the three-year anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which killed 18 and wounded 13 at two locations in 2023.
As the anniversary draws closer, the following public tributes have been planned in Lewiston.
Tuesday, Oct. 13
The Maine Resiliency Center is hosting a Community Night at Just-In-Time Recreation, 24 Mollison Way, from 6-8 p.m. The event is free to everyone and will feature food and fun, but organizers say it will also celebrate connection and community. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 17
The Maine Resiliency Center is having a community pumpkin carving from noon-2 p.m. outside Just-In-Time Recreation. There will also be painting and crafts. In the days following the mass shootings, pumpkins were carved with words and symbols of remembrance, love, and hope and left outside the bowling center. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 24
TB Events is hosting the third annual Lewiston Stronger Community Cornhole tournament. There will be two tournaments that day: noon to 4 p.m. and 5-11 p.m. Playing costs $20, with all proceeds going to the Maine Resiliency Center. The organization will raffle off its “Lewiston Stronger” cornhole boards after the tournaments. (facebook.com/TB.Mobile.Events)
Central Maine Healthcare and the American Red Cross are holding a commemorative blood drive from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. to honor the lives of those affected by the mass shootings. It will take place in Conference Room ABC in CMMC in the lower half of 12 High St. (redcrossblood.org)
Sunday, Oct. 25
I Love You Gardens is partnering with the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor to host a community planting and care day from 9 a.m. to noon. It commemorates those whose lives were lost, with attendees planting bulbs and seeds at one of four locations across the Twin Cities: outside the Maine MILL in Lewiston, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Beech streets, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Cross streets, and Auburn’s Bonney Park. Attendees will meet outside the Maine MILL that morning and be sent to one of the four locations. The event is free, and there will be an American Sign Language interpreter. (iloveyougardens.com)
The Maine Resiliency Center is holding a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Memorial Park,46 Beech St., from 6-8 p.m. It will begin at the entrance of the park, with attendees walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.
Ongoing exhibit at Maine MILL
Although the Maine MILL doesn’t have any events in October specific to the third anniversary, the museum has an exhibit dedicated to the Lewiston shootings. The exhibit, “Preserved,” features items in the days following the tragedy, including the doors from Just-In-Time Recreation, which are the exhibit’s entry point, and a light fixture from Schemengees Bar and Grille, with visible bullet holes. The space also features 3D-replicated pumpkins that were carved and left outside by community members at Just-In-Time Recreation.
This display will stay up until October 2027, with a new exhibit in its place to honor the four-year anniversary. For more information, go to mainemill.org.

title: Penobscot Valley Country Club’s bunker renovation is underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot Valley Country Club is in Phase 1 of its bunker renovation on the course.
“The difficulty is trying to do it while there’s play on the golf course. There’s not a good time to do golf course maintenance in the state of Maine where you only have a six-month season,” said Michael Webb, general manager of golf operations, PVCC and Lucerne Golf Club.
Course staff is about halfway through removing the sand traps that are not part of the original 1924 Donald Ross design by the middle of next month.
“This golf course means a lot to the greater Bangor community and the town of Orono. To bring it back to the original design is one of the big projects the owner wants to have done,” said Webb.
“In the day, the ball didn’t go that far. You know, the ball only went 200 yards. If you were a big hitter back in the ’20s, if you could hit it 200 yards, but now with the equipment and everything, those bunkers, they’re basically obsolete unless you’re a beginning golfer,” said Mark Hall, PGA golf professional.
Phase 2 will start next spring and will focus on greenside bunker condition updates throughout the 2027 season.
“We want to get the course in shape so we can host a Maine Amateur again or at least a qualifier,” said Hall.
The bunker work comes after last year’s green restorations.

title: Enjoy A Mild Monday Before Rain Arrives Tuesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front will travel southward across the state today giving us a chance for some scattered showers through the afternoon. The best chance of showers will be north of Dover-Foxcroft and Lincoln. Otherwise... expect a partly to mostly cloudy sky for our Monday. It’ll be a warmer day too... and likely the warmest day we see for quite some time. Temperatures will top off in the 60s to near 70° this afternoon.
As the front moves through... the wind will turn out of the northwest and increase this afternoon... with gusts to around 25 MPH possible. This northwest wind will usher colder air into the state behind the departing cold front... making for a colder night tonight. We’ll see mostly cloudy skies tonight with lows dropping to the 30s to near 40°.
Low pressure approaching from the Great Lakes Region Tuesday will bring some much needed rain to the area... developing from west to east across the state by mid-late morning through the afternoon. There’s a chance that it may be cold enough at the onset for some snow or rain/snow mix... mainly over northern and western locales... especially in the higher terrain... otherwise it looks like a mainly rain event. The combination of clouds... rain... a cooler air mass... and an easterly breeze will make for a cool day with highs in the 40s.
Rain will continue through Tuesday night then taper off from west to east Wednesday morning followed by brightening skies and drier weather Wednesday afternoon. Rainfall totals by Tuesday morning through noontime Wednesday will range from .5” to 1.5”.
Temperatures will be better on Wednesday with highs climbing to the 50s. As the system exits Wednesday will be strengthening as it moves up into the Maritimes Thursday. This will cause the pressure gradient to tighten up... leading to a breezy day Thursday with a gusty northwest wind up to 30-40 MPH at times. Thursday overall looks like the nicest day of the week with a good deal of sunshine and highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s. Clouds will move back in Thursday night with another storm system bringing more beneficial rain for Friday and Friday night with another .5” to 1” or so of rain possible. There are some indications too that we could see some wintry precipitation... possibly some accumulating snow... mainly over Northern Aroostook County so stay tuned for updates as we get closer. It looks like we’ll see drier, breezy and chilly weather for the upcoming weekend.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly cloudy. Scattered showers possible. Highs between 59°-69°. Winds will become northwest 5-15 MPH with gusts to around 25 MPH possible.
Tonight: Mostly cloudy. Colder with lows in the 30s to around 40°. East/northeast wind 5-15 MPH.
Tuesday: Mostly cloudy. Rain developing west to east by late morning through the afternoon. Cooler with highs mainly in the 40s. East wind 5-15 MPH with gusts to around 25 MPH possible.
Wednesday: Morning showers possible then brightening skies during the afternoon. Highs in the 50s.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny. Breezy. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Friday: Rain likely. Some rain/snow mix possible across the north. Highs in the 40s to near 50°.

title: Irate about government-funded Trump ads
text:
I was watching “CBS Sunday Morning” last weekend and was shocked to see President Donald Trump in an ad for himself. What was more shocking was seeing the notation at the end that it was paid for by the U.S. government. I understand it was also on during some NFL games.
Sen. Susan Collins, to my knowledge, has not said one word about this. I have called and written to her office and received no response. Other Republican senators have spoken out against it. How is government funding being used for this; who appropriated it?
Needless to say, I am outraged.
Susan Rephan
Portland

title: When hunting moose, help is always available
text:
A flatbed truck hauling a bull moose slowed as it approached our group of four pickups, nine guys and one gal holding an infant parked in a turnoff on a remote gravel road. The driver offered a friendly wave and a brief, “how you doing?” before starting to turn.
“You want some chicken wings?” shouted one of our hunting party who was dutifully tending the grill on his tailgate.
“Sure,” replied the driver who, along with his father, joined our party for an hour of eating and swapping stories.
That’s not an unusual occurrence in the North Woods during moose season. More than any other pursuit, moose hunting in Maine is a very social experience. Sure, deer camp is social, but most of the socializing occurs at camp, after each day’s hunt. Turkey hunting tends to be more enjoyable when done with a partner, but two’s company and three’s a crowd.
A moose hunting crew might consist of two or three folks per truck, and possibly several trucks. Many eyes are handy, but many bodies are handier still when you’ve got 800-1,000 pounds of moose on the ground. The help often extends beyond individual hunting parties.
We were parked at the bottom of a dead-end road one morning, awaiting shooting light, when we noticed lights on the road below us and went down to investigate. A gentleman hunting with his 10-year-old son had a flat tire. Our crew of five, several of whom just happen to be mechanics, eagerly jumped in, and we had the father and son on their way in time for both groups to make our destination before sun-up.
Two years prior, we were just finishing up field dressing a moose when two truckloads of hunters stopped to investigate. When they saw we had a bull down, they all eagerly volunteered to help us load it into the truck.
And the willingness to help doesn’t end there.
Most hunters get only six days to fill their tag. Some need all six, while others tag out early. The latter are in the North Woods with time to kill, and many will eagerly jump in with another crew to help them find their bull.
As a side note, Maine guides typically book one hunter for a week-long hunt. If their hunter tags out early, that means they are free and available. For someone who decided to go the DIY route but is struggling, it might be worth making a few phone calls or checking social media toward the end of the week.
Even, and perhaps especially, if you start with a guide, you’ll find the same ethic. Everyone in camp wants to be part of the hunt. Guides and their tagged-out hunters are often eager to join others in camp to help out in any way they can.
I’ve been fortunate to fall in with a group of guys who love to hunt moose and are good at it. Our forces were spread a little thin this year because three among us drew tags. That won’t be the case next year, but some among us will have a friend or relative who pulls a permit, and we’ll rally our resources to see they have all the help they need. For all of us, even those who live near and work in the North Woods, it’s a chance to get away into the woods for a week and be hunters.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Wabanaki Alliance celebrates Indigenous Peoples Day in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Native peoples and their allies gathered Monday in Augusta for a celebration of Indigenous Peoples Day.
The event, hosted by the Wabanaki Alliance, included music, dancing, films and demonstrations of Wabanaki culture.
“We have all the tribes represented here. We have drumming and dancing. We have an ash basket demonstration,” said Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance. “I’m just always so excited when everyday Mainers get to come together with Wabanaki people because we are all neighbors and friends.”
Holiday replaced Columbus Day in 2019
The holiday replaced Columbus Day in Maine in 2019, a change organizers say reflects an ongoing effort to recognize Indigenous history and sovereignty, rather than Christopher Columbus’ history of exploiting Indigenous peoples.
“It got to a point where I didn’t even want to talk about Columbus anymore. Why go there?” said Barry Dana, former chief of the Penobscot Nation. “It’s Indigenous Peoples Day. We’re going to focus on Indigenous people, our survival traits and who we are.”
Organizers focus on education
For organizers, the gathering was also a chance to bring people together around Indigenous education outside of the legislature.
“It feels good to connect around a celebration and it feels good to just focus on education,” Bryant said. “Why not do some education and some cultural things as well?”
The Wabanaki Alliance says it hopes to make the gathering an annual event.

title: 31 comics coming to Maine to make you laugh into next year
text:
Human beings need to laugh, and that includes Mainers. It’s good for the soul and enables us to take a break and better confront our problems.
A bunch of comedians, from familiar faces to fresh ones — including some with specials you can check out on streaming services — are coming to Maine stages to help provide that humor to soothe our souls. Here is a list of comedy shows at venues across the state over the coming months.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Comic Jason Salmon’s style is described as getting “the best advice you’ve ever gotten … from the dumbest guy you know.” His TV credits include “Orange Is the New Black,” “30 Rock” and “At Home with Amy Sedaris,” along with appearances on HBO and Comedy Central. For a preshow serving of Salmon, view his standup special, “Biscuits and Gravity,” on YouTube.
7 p.m. Sunday. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $20-$45. statetheatreportland.com.
New York City’s Lucas Zelnick has been featured on Comedy Central and has headlined the Netflix is a Joke Festival. Film credits include “Regular” and “Fade to Black.” Be ready to be cracked up by a guy who earned an MBA from Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business.
7:30 p.m. Sunday and Dec. 5. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $42.50-$83.50. jonathansogunquit.com.
Mainer Bob Marley has been cracking people up with his wicked funny humor for decades. Along with the shows in Ogunquit, Marley will be doing his thing Saturday at the Waterville Opera House. Tickets are $46.50 at watervillecreates.org. Marley also has five shows on the calendar at Stone Mountain Arts Center in Brownfield, starting on Dec. 5. Tickets are $36.50 at stonemountainartscenter.com.
7 p.m. Oct. 22. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $24.26, $29.53 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Emma Dalenberg and Sunny Laprade are best friends who are hitting the road together for a co-headlining tour. Expect a wild night from the queer comics, who will be spilling the tea on many topics.
8 p.m. Nov. 5. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $42-$72. statetheatreportland.com.
Writer, actor, radio presenter, podcaster and comic Marc Maron brings his candid brand of humor to the State Theatre with a stop on his Yammering Into The Void tour. As host of the long-running “WFT with Marc Maron” podcast, his galaxy of celebrity guests have included Barack Obama, Carol Burnett and Robin Williams. The HBO comedy specials “Marc Maron: Panicked” and “From Bleak To Dark” are popular examples of his work.
8 p.m. Nov. 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-$65. statetheatreportland.com.
For five memorable seasons, comic Leslie Jones was a Not Ready for Primetime Player on “Saturday Night Live.” During the 2016 Summer Olympic games, Jones took to what was then called Twitter to offer colorful, comical commentary. NBC recruited her to cover several events, and she offered her spicy takes during a few other summer and winter games. Catch her I’m Hot tour in Portland.
7 p.m. Nov. 7. The Dance Hall, 7 Walker St., Kittery, $28 in advance, $33 day of show. thedancehallkittery.org.
Eddie Pepitone is known as the Bitter Buddha, and is considered by some to be a cross section of Jackie Gleason, Don Rickles and Eckart Tohle. 7 p.m. Nov. 7. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $59-$99. porttix.com.

7:30 p.m. Nov. 14. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $25-$66. jonathansogunquit.com.
Boston comic Jimmy Cash’s shows draw on his experiences of being a janitor for 20 years, as well as a father and someone who maintains long-term sobriety. Cash travels all over the U.S. and Canada, and was Maine comic Bob Marley’s dedicated opener for many years.
7 p.m. Nov. 15. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39.75-$125. porttix.com.
Bert Kreischer brings his Permission to Party tour to Maine, with a mix of his trademark storytelling paired with a huge persona. Kreischer’s latest Netflix special, “Lucky,” premiered in 2025, and his credits include the film “The Machine” and the Netflix series “Free Bert.” As a podcaster, Kreischer hosts “Bertcast” and co-hosts “2 Bears, 1 Cave” with fellow funnyman Tom Segura.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Nov. 20 and 21. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $34.81, $45.36 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Los Angeles-based comic Leah Rudick’s characters include “Wealthy Woman,” “Joannie” and “Love Coach.” With just under 2 million social media followers, Rudick is a hot ticket with her signature “weird girl” brand of comedy.

Paula Poundstone has been making clever observations with her dry yet hilarious delivery for decades. Poundstone is also a longtime panelist on the National Public Radio quiz show “Wait Wait … Don’t Tell Me!”

7 p.m. Jan. 16. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $39.50-$69.50. statetheatreportland.com.
For a midwinter comedy infusion, grab tickets to see award-winning actress and comic Atsuko Okatsuka in Portland. Her exuberant, offbeat brand of stand-up was captured in specials that have aired on Hulu and HBO.
7 p.m. Jan 23. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $33-$55, $199 meet & greet. statetheatreportland.com.
Zarna Garg’s Million Dollar Excuses tour will pack many punches about family life when it comes through Portland. Her Amazon Prime special “One in a Billion” and its Hulu follow-up “Zarna Garg: Practical People Win” both reached wide audiences. As a writer, Zarna published the memoir “This American Woman” about her harrowing ascent from being homeless in Mumbai to an internationally known stand-up comic.
7 p.m. Jan. 23. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $29.50-$69.50. porttix.com.
Brad William’s Big & Small tour will showcase his knack for sharp punchlines and deeply personal storytelling. His latest stand-up special “Live on Short Street” can be streamed on YouTube, as can “Starfish,” which has surpassed 9 million views.
7 p.m. Feb. 6. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., $62-$92. watervillecreates.org.
Canadian comic Samantha Bee is bringing her How to Survive Menopause tour to Waterville. In 2003, Bee started a 12-year run on Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show.” Her own late-night comedy series “Full Frontal with Samantha Bee” debuted on TBS in 2016 and ran for seven seasons.
7 p.m. Feb. 26. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $41.50-$51.50, $152 VIP. statetheatreportland.com.
Justin Willman melds comedy with magic so well, his streaming views surpassed the 1 billion mark. So you can expect the unexpected when his One For the Ages tour comes through Portland. Unlike many comedy shows, this one is suitable for all ages.
4 and 7 p.m. Feb. 27. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39-4109. porttix.com.
Nobody Asked You To Do That is what Taylor Tomlinson is calling her winter tour that includes a late February stop in Portland with late afternoon and evening performances. Head to Netflix to find several specials that emphasize her ability to convert challenging life moments into side-splitting humor.
7 p.m. March 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $29.50-$59.50. statetheatreportland.com.
Estonian-born comic Ari Matti translates his Eastern European roots and globe-trotting experiences into a can’t-miss night of comedy. Matti is a regular on the popular “Kill Tony” podcast and was part of the team that performed “Kill Tony Live” in consecutive years at Madison Square Garden.
8 p.m. March 12. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $49.50-$74.50, 12-plus. porttix.com.
Jo Koy got his start in a Las Vegas coffeehouse and is now, according to Pollstar and Billboard, one of the top 10 grossing stand-up comedians every year. Drawing from his Filipino-American upbringing and his experiences as a parent and son, you can expect nonstop laughs from the lively comic when his Koy Meets World tour comes through Portland at the tail end of winter.
7 and 9:30 p.m. March 18-20. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $34.81 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Los Angeles-based comic, writer and actress Beth Stelling hit paydirt with her latest release on YouTube called “The Landlord Special.” Another one, called “If You Didn’t Want Me Then” is also worth checking out. Stelling’s a veteran comic with a devoted following, thanks to a candid brand of comedy and appearances on Netflix, Comedy Central and late-night shows.
7 p.m. April 1. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
With a friendship that clocks in at just under 20 years, comics Grace Helbig and Mamrie Hart are guaranteed to bring the fun to April Fool’s Day in Portland. Hear them on the weekly podcast “This Might Get Weird.”
6 p.m. May 9. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-$55. statetheatreportland.com.
Ine her act, Maria Bamford is entirely comfortable talking about her acute experiences with mental health, including time spent in a psychiatric facility. She’s an Emmy-nominated comic who also authored the New York Times best-selling memoir “Sure, I’ll Join Your Cult.” Bamford’s Netflix comedy series “Lady Dynamite” was based on her life and ran for two seasons.
9:30 p.m. May 14. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $36-$69. statetheatreportland.com.
The early show is sold out, but you can still grab a ticket if you act fast to see Jeff Arcuri on his Road Trip tour that hits Portland in mid-May. His comedy special “Nice To Meet You” premiered on Netflix in July.

title: After spotting this buck on camera for weeks, a Maine hunter finally got his shot
text:
“This ol boy was taunting me on camera weeks before opening day,” Matthew Overlock wrote.
The Troy hunter saw the buck on opening day at about 28 yards, but thick cover kept him from getting a clear shot. The deer noticed him in his tree stand and walked away.
On his third hunt, he was sitting on the ground when the buck came within about 20 yards. When it looked up and saw him, he took the shot with his crossbow.
The buck ran only 20 to 30 yards before Overlock found it. He tagged it the next morning, when it weighed 199.5 pounds.
It was his first archery deer and his biggest buck yet.

title: After Lewiston shooting, Troy Jackson found the courage to change his mind
text:
In less than half an hour on Maine’s darkest day, a man gunned down 18 people in Lewiston and left at least 13 more injured, some of them grievously.
For me, a former Connecticut journalist, the Oct. 25, 2023 mass shooting brought back memories of the Sandy Hook school shooting in 2012. This is the kind of horror that ought to lead to sweeping policy changes.
Here in America, though, too many people just shrug their shoulders every time bullets fly and innocent people die as a result. They insist there’s nothing we can do about it.
Today, Troy Jackson knows better.
During a rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders in Lewiston on Sunday, Jackson told the crowd supporting his Senate bid that when he “watched this community bury 18 people,” he realized he’d taken the wrong position on some gun-related proposals.
“Eighteen funerals changed me,” Jackson said. “Because sometimes leadership means having the guts to admit that what you believed before isn’t good enough anymore. I couldn’t look at those families and tell them nothing had to change. So I changed.”
Sadly, most politicians looking at the same situation refused to reconsider their positions. But some did.
Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who opted not to run for reelection to Congress this year, backed a ban on assault rifles after the Lewiston mass shooting. He called his earlier position a failure and asked for forgiveness from victims’ families and the community at large.
A more careful Sen. Susan Collins called only for limits on “very high capacity” magazines and suggested she might agree to raise the age limit for buying them from 18 to 21.
“We cannot keep treating these mass shootings like they’re a natural disaster, like some terrible thing that just happens in America and there’s nothing that we can do about it. Because there is,” Jackson said on Sunday. “I learned right here in Lewiston that those 18 people deserve more than our grief. We owe them the courage to change.”
Before the shooting, Jackson earned top marks from pro-gun groups and voted against a number of measures aimed at stemming gun violence, including a proposed 72-hour waiting period for gun purchases, background checks and a ban on devices that allow modification of rifles to allow them to be fired more rapidly.
“I grew up around guns,” Jackson said. “I’m a sportsman — and for a long time I opposed some of the gun laws that people in my own party wanted me to support.”
After the Lewiston shootings, Jackson fought for stronger background checks, a waiting period for gun purchases and a red flag law to allow law enforcement to temporarily confiscate firearms from people considered a threat.
“When a family knows somebody they love is in danger to themselves or others, they ought to be able to do something before it’s too late,” he told the crowd.
To my mind, the 2012 Sandy Hook nightmare that left 20 children blown to bits in their classroom by a high-powered semi-automatic rifle should have been enough to cause every political leader to embrace gun control. But better late than never.
After Lewiston, Jackson and Golden fessed up to their mistaken policy choices. It’s refreshing to see politicians admit they had it wrong.

title: Collins owes Mainers an explanation for vote on West Bank deaths
text:
Brian Garrison is a South Portland resident and advocate for human dignity and equal rights.
Sen. Susan Collins owes Mainers an explanation for voting to block a formal demand for answers about Americans killed in the West Bank.
On Sept. 29, the Senate rejected a motion to discharge S. Res. 852 from the Foreign Relations Committee, 51-47. Sen. Angus King voted to advance it. Collins voted against it. This was a procedural vote, rather than final adoption, but its consequence was clear: the resolution did not move forward.
The distinction matters. So does what senators prevented from advancing.
The resolution would have requested an unclassified State Department statement within 30 days of adoption. It sought evidence and investigation updates concerning nine American deaths involving Israeli forces or settlers, information about Americans in Israeli prisons and an assessment of Palestinian children in military detention, including allegations of torture. It also asked what Washington had done to protect human rights and pursue accountability.
These are questions a responsible Congress should insist on answering.
Forty-four Democrats, independents King and Bernie Sanders and Republican Rand Paul supported advancing the resolution. Fifty Republicans and Democrat John Fetterman opposed it. Republicans Bill Cassidy and Dan Sullivan did not vote. Paul’s vote demonstrated that demanding answers need not be a partisan position.
Protecting Americans abroad should be among the least controversial obligations of their government. Families deserve evidence, meaningful investigations and an explanation of what officials are doing on their behalf. Their right to those answers should never depend on whether the suspected perpetrators belong to an ally.
The resolution also reached beyond citizenship. Palestinian children deserve protection from abuse because they are children. A passport cannot determine whose mistreatment warrants scrutiny. The same commitment to human dignity that requires investigating American deaths requires taking allegations of torture seriously wherever they arise.
There is a legal reason for this scrutiny, too.
The measure invoked Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act. That provision allows Congress to request information about a country’s human rights practices. Failure to provide the requested statement within 30 days triggers restrictions on delivering security assistance, subject to subsequent specific authorization by law, until the statement arrives.
This was therefore an oversight mechanism with consequences. Senators were being asked to advance a process that could make the administration answer publicly for its decisions.
Supporters of Israel may regard such scrutiny as unfair or diplomatically damaging. But an alliance cannot justify exempting a government from examination. If allegations are unsupported, a credible accounting can establish that. If investigations are adequate, the evidence can demonstrate it. If abuses occurred, friendship cannot excuse them.
An inquiry should test allegations. Blocking it leaves the public without the accounting the resolution sought.
There is also money to account for. Track AIPAC, an advocacy group compiling Federal Election Commission data, lists $4,131,569 in career support for Collins from pro-Israel political committees and associated donors, including $565,000 in independent expenditures. That outside spending benefits her candidacy without going to her campaign. These figures do not establish that contributions caused her vote. They do make her explanation, and the independence of her judgment, matters of public interest.
In a July op-ed for this newspaper about deeper U.S.-Israeli military integration, I called on Collins and King to insist on open debate. The principle remains: consequential decisions require public scrutiny.
King deserves credit for supporting this step. He should continue pressing for disclosure. Collins should explain her opposition and identify the alternative she will pursue, with a timetable for obtaining the information these families deserve.
A procedural objection, if that was her concern, would still leave that responsibility intact. Mainers should ask what she will do now.
Our senators represent people who deserve honest government. They should insist that the administration account for American deaths and alleged abuse, regardless of which foreign government is implicated.
When American families are asking how their loved ones died, a senator’s first duty is to demand answers.

title: ”Digger” is a movie that hates itself
text:
Alejandro González Iñárritu, director of surreal meta-commentaries such as “Birdman” and “Babel,” has come out with his latest film, “Digger.” Over the past three days since I saw the movie, I’ve tried to provide a concise synopsis to several friends, yet I always fail to capture what made this movie so captivating. I think almost everyone who sees “Digger” will leave theaters with one of two reactions.
One is that this film is quite possibly a cult classic in the making, perhaps a masterpiece that will stand the test of time and be looked upon in a similar way to how we view Kubrick’s “Dr. Strangelove” today. The other is that this movie may feel to you like an infuriating and tone-deaf sermon, delivered from an ivory pedestal as the Hollywood elite lecture the common man for their shortcomings. “Digger” is currently receiving incredibly divisive reviews, with many viewers falling sharply into one of the two camps I’ve outlined above. I believe both of these opinions are entirely true, and the movie knows it.
Without spoiling anything, this movie can be described as a climate catastrophe film. It is also firmly in the camp of modern political satire, alongside “Eddington,” “Bugonia” and “One Battle After Another.” I believe this film strongly differentiates itself from its contemporaries through the use of subversion. At its core, this movie hates itself.
I got the sense that Iñárritu despised the tactless approach of movies such as “Don’t Look Up,” a movie that, in my opinion, relies on the thin veil of satire and ends up feeling more like a poorly executed lecture than a meaningful statement. Iñárritu is simultaneously making a movie in the same vein as “Don’t Look Up” while also deconstructing the form of this genre and of movies in general. Though this may all sound rather vague, this is a movie best experienced as blindly as possible. You’ll just have to take my word for it.
Beyond the scope of the plot, “Digger” is one of the most visually pleasing movies I have seen in ages. It is absolutely a movie for movie lovers, as Iñárritu and cinematographer Lubezki bring to life some of the most intricate set pieces and visually stunning shots I have seen in the last couple of years. The soundtrack, done by Cosmo Sheldrake, also brings an absolutely dynamic sense of tension and excitement to the film.
One of the highlights of “Digger” was the phenomenal performances by Tom Cruise and the rest of the cast. It is easy to think of Cruise as nothing more than a Scientologist superstar who makes “Mission: Impossible” movies, but every once in a while, I’m reminded why so many people herald him as one of the best actors of his generation. I think this is his best performance since “Magnolia,” and he absolutely embodies the role of Digger. Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sophie Wilde also deliver terrific performances throughout.
I would give this movie an 8/10, truly one of the most unique theatergoing experiences I have ever had. It is an extremely culturally relevant film made by a masterful team of people. I think it will be a long time before another movie comes along like this one. Whether or not you find yourself enjoying this movie, you won’t regret going to see it.

title: ‘He was very wholesome’: Friends mourn high school football player killed in crash
text:
TUPELO, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) — Friends and classmates are mourning the death of a 19-year-old football player who was killed in a crash early Sunday.
According to the Tupelo Police Department, officers responded to a single-vehicle crash a little after 1 a.m. Sunday.
The Lee County Coroner’s Office said Alden Wade was driving a truck when it hit a light pole. He died at the scene.
Tupelo High School students who spoke with WTVA remembered Wade as a genuine and wholesome person.
“It was real hard for the community, his friends and family,” said Tupelo High School student Elijah Bradley. “He was a very wholesome and genuine person you could ever meet, and we’re just sorry for the loss.”
Fellow student Alyviah Hunt said Wade’s death is a reminder of how quickly life can change.
“It’s very sad, and it just makes you think of how quick anything can end,” Hunt said. “And it’s just really sad, and I have prayers for his family.”
An accident reconstruction team responded to the scene to investigate the crash.

title: Bangor marks 89th anniversary of Brady Gang shootout
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Eighty-nine years ago Monday, two members of the Brady Gang were killed and another was captured in Downtown Bangor.
Bangor historian Dick Shaw has dedicated years of his life to researching the full story. He has a personal connection to it, as his mother witnessed the shootout from her classroom above Central Street.
Shaw said Al Brady and the rest of the gang were in Bangor to buy a gun at Dakin’s, not to rob a bank. He said the FBI had sharpshooters ready and had parked cars along both sides of the street the night before to absorb bullets and make the gang double-park.
“The actual shootout lasted less than a minute,” Shaw said. He said the FBI’s setup made the gang “an easier target,” adding that agents were prepared to shoot because the men were “so gun crazy.”
Shaw said the shootout was probably many Americans’ first introduction to Bangor. He spent the morning visiting Brady’s grave at Mount Hope Cemetery.

title: U.S. Senate passes the “Protect College Sports Act”
text:
On Sept. 28, the U.S. Senate approved the “Protect College Sports Act,” a bill that introduces new rules surrounding NIL, the transfer portal and college sports as a whole. The bill still needs approval from the House of Representatives before it can be sent to the president. If it does not complete the legislative process before the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027, lawmakers will have to reintroduce it.
The act follows what has now been years of controversy in the college sports sphere. NIL (name, image and likeness) money has been distributed to athletes as a means to bolster recruitment and compensate players, and has been a topic of conversation among coaches, players and fans since its introduction. There has been debate over how much money college athletes should be eligible to earn and how transfer students should be treated.
For example, PJ Haggerty is a college point guard who started his career at Texas Christian University. After opting for a redshirt season his freshman year, Haggerty transferred to the University of Tulsa before transferring again to the University of Memphis for more opportunity. He became a star there and reportedly received offers worth millions in NIL money to transfer once again, this time going to Kansas State. After one season there, he once again had the opportunity to transfer and now will play at Texas A&M University. Haggerty has attended five schools in five years, with reports of lucrative NIL offers accompanying his transfers. Certain coaches and fans have taken opposition to this kind of transfer behavior.
The proposed bill will put a limit on this type of activity, stating that a student-athlete can only transfer once before having to sit out a year after a second transfer. Many coaches believe that the current rules surrounding transfers make it difficult to build stable rosters or develop programs. This coincides with the NIL budgets of each school. Some schools have more NIL money to give, creating an unfair balance between the top-level schools and those looking to compete from a lower level.
The bill does not only put a limit on transferring. It also outlines that, to compensate for money transferring students would likely lose by constantly transferring, they will be offered benefits instead. These benefits include guarantees of scholarships, five years of post-eligibility sports medical coverage and degree-completion assistance, putting an emphasis on education.
The rate at which athletes are transferring also raises questions about those academics. How much of an education can a student-athlete truly gain if they are constantly switching schools? Most voices in college sports are looking for some sort of compromise between athletes getting the compensation they deserve and regulation of transfers and NIL money.
“We’re an educational institution and we want people to get degrees,” Creighton women’s basketball head coach Jim Flanery said. “When they send that first resume with five schools or six schools on their resume, they’re not getting the job that somebody else is getting who got through in four years at one or two institutions.”
The bill has until early January to be passed before a new Senate is sworn in. If time runs out before that, supporters of the bill will have to restart their efforts to make a change in the rapidly developing landscape of college sports. If the bill does not pass, fans of college sports will likely have to accept that the uncertainty of college athletics will continue to grow.

title: Waterford, school district to hold hearings on elementary school closure
text:
Maine School Administrative District 17 voted in 2025 to permanently close Waterford Memorial School and transfer pre-K through second grade students living in Waterford and Harrison to Harrison Elementary School.
Residents of the two towns can affirm or reverse that decision in a Nov. 3 referendum.
Ahead of the ballot vote, Waterford and SAD 17 have scheduled three public hearings for public comment and inquiry on the school’s future.
Waterford is holding two hearings this month at its municipal headquarters on Valley Road before the Select Board’s regular business meeting. One is Oct. 14 and the second is Oct. 28, both starting at 6 p.m.
People can watch the meeting on Zoom.
SAD 17 has scheduled one public hearing for Oct. 21 at 6 p.m. at Central Office on Main Street in South Paris. The school board will hold its business meeting immediately following.
SAD 17 meetings are broadcast live on Norway Paris Community Television’s cable channel and recorded video may be viewed online within 48 hours.
The referendum question on the Nov. 3 ballot reads: “Do you favor authorizing the School Board of Maine School Administrative District 17 to close Waterford’s elementary school? The additional cost of keeping the school open has been estimated by SAD 17 to be $441,944.41.”
Initial information from district stakeholders and Maine Department of Education communicated that a majority from both towns had to vote “no” to keep the school open, and that the financial burden would completely fall on Waterford taxpayers.
However, Maine DOE has since clarified that a majority of only one town is needed to reopen the school, and the operational cost would be the responsibility of that town.
That means if Harrison residents vote to reopen, it will be up to Harrison to pay for it to reopen. The same is true for Waterford.
If both towns vote to reopen, the cost for each would be calculated based on student enrollments.
If both towns vote yes to permanently close the school, it will pave the way for Waterford to reacquire the school on Valley Road. That decision would by made by residents in a separate vote.
SAD 17 estimates it will save $441,944 from closing the school, based on the budget of the current fiscal year. The operational cost will change every year and require residents to approve it annually.
Waterford Memorial was built in 1949 with a capacity for up to 204 students. It was owned by the town until Waterford joined SAD 17, at which point it was transferred to the school district.
Harrison Elementary was built in 1987 by SAD 17, with a capacity of 213. It has always been owned by the school district.
During the 2024-25 school year, 73 students were enrolled at Waterford Memorial and 107 attended Harrison Elementary.
All elementary students from both towns in grades pre-K through sixth attend school in Harrison.
The two schools are part of a larger state-sanctioned consolidation proposal that calls for a new elementary school that students from Harrison, Waterford and Norway would attend. Voters from all eight of SAD 17’s sending towns will be asked to vote on building a new school, most likely in June of 2027.
After learning Harrison Elementary could potentially close in the future, Harrison voters approved forming a school withdrawal committee during June 2026 state elections.
Its committee does not plan to make any recommendations about remaining with or exiting SAD 17 until after the school district has determined the new elementary school’s location and voters from all eight district towns vote whether to move forward with the proposal.
SAD 17 towns are Harrison, Hebron, Norway, Otisfield, Oxford, Paris, Waterford and West Paris.

title: Patriots QB Drake Maye finds his confidence
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye rediscovered his confidence and production in the Patriots’ dominant 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
And it restored the belief that New England can compete with the AFC’s top teams this season.
It wasn’t just the third-year quarterback’s passing numbers – 26 of 34 for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns – that jumped off the page. It was the calm and deliberate way he commanded the offense that rang the loudest on a day he finished without a turnover for the first time this season.
Equally encouraging was that Maye left the field thinking there was even better football to be played.
“I think that’s what it’s like when we put some things together, and we still have some,” he said. “I mean, it’s crazy to say we’ve still got some left to squeeze.”
It was also a good sign that Maye was able to get multiple players involved.
Playing without wide receivers A.J. Brown (injured reserve/sprained ankle) and Mack Hollins (injured reserve/calf), Maye spread the ball around to nine players.
But it wasn’t all smiles on the sideline after running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) and left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) left the field two plays apart.
It’s a particularly concerning injury for Campbell, who had to go on IR for four games late last season with a right knee injury before returning for the regular-season finale and playoff run.
This is also a recurring issue for Henderson, who dealt with an ankle injury in the preseason that caused him to miss the opener at Seattle.
Campbell was replaced Sunday by rookie Caleb Lomu, who’s expected to fill the role as Maye’s blindside protector for however long Campbell is out.
“I don’t think it was too big for him,” coach Mike Vrabel said of Lomu. “I think he was able to settle down. You didn’t really notice him a lot, so I think that’s probably a good thing.”
What’s working
As well as the Patriots’ offense performed, the defense was just as solid. It limited a Raiders team that came in averaging 28.8 points per game to 5 of 13 on third down. The Patriots also forced a fumble and sacked Kirk Cousins twice. What’s more, New England never allowed the Raiders to get into a groove. After scoring a touchdown early in the first quarter, Las Vegas’ next four drives went punt, punt, missed field goal and punt.
What needs help
Discipline. The Patriots were called for a season-high 12 penalties for 116 yards, a total Vrabel called “ridiculous” postgame. Even with several new combinations of players on the field because of injuries, those are numbers that must be addressed.
Stock up
WR Kyle Williams. The second-year receiver has been waiting to get more opportunities, and Maye linked up with him three times for 91 yards, including a 34-yard TD grab in the third quarter.
Stock down
Secondary. Yes, the group was playing without starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck), but had no answers for Raiders tight end Brock Bowers, who finished with eight catches for 110 yards and a touchdown.
Injuries
The already injury-ravished secondary lost another player when cornerback Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Key number
1 — The number of Patriots quarterbacks (Maye) to complete at least 75% of their passes for at least 300 yards and four touchdowns with no interceptions, along with a rushing touchdown in a single game.
Next steps
The Patriots return to playing an AFC East rival, hosting the New York Jets (2-3) on Sunday.

title: Driver throws water bottle causing crash on interstate highway, troopers say
text:
PHELPS COUNTY, Mo. (KY3/Gray News) - A woman was sent to the hospital after a crash on a Missouri interstate Friday evening.
According to the Missouri State Highway Patrol, the crash happened at the 170-mile marker on Interstate 44 in Phelps County at around 5:25 p.m.
Troopers said a 20-year-old woman from Laquey was driving a Ford Mustang in the westbound lanes when she was hit in the face by a water bottle thrown by another driver. The woman then lost control of the vehicle, went off the road, hit an embankment and overturned.
The woman sustained minor injuries and was brought to a nearby hospital for treatment. The crash report states she was wearing a seatbelt.
No one else was injured.

title: Authorities name the attacker and most of the 8 victims in last week's Erie mass shooting
text:
A coroner on Monday released the names of the gunman and six of the eight people he shot and killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, including seven of his relatives.
The shooter in Friday’s attack was Matthew Stone Sr., 45, according to Erie County coroner Lyell Cook. Stone took his own life at the home, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said.
According to Cook, the adult victims were Michelle Stone, 44; Angelina Stone, 24, who was due to give birth Monday; Jonathan Stone, 19; Matthew Stone, 21, and two women who lived at other addresses: Lora Roberts, 37, and Twila Tanner, 51. He said a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl also died, but that state law prevented him from releasing their names.
At a memorial to the victims, Julius Windham said his daughter Amarianna was the toddler who was killed. The girl’s mother was Angelina Stone, who was also the mother of the boy who died, he said, noting that attacker was a grandfather and the family patriarch.
Family friend Nicole Eller said Roberts frequently went to the house to help during the pregnancy of her niece and neighbor, Angelina Stone.
Roberts, identified by friends as a mother of five who was engaged to be married, was a volunteer and former board member for a community group that helped homeless people. She wrote a July 15 Facebook post decrying recent shootings in Erie.
“Erie we need to do better!!” she wrote. “Life is precious and its heartbreaking to see so much pain and violence. Check on the people you love, and always choose kindness.”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.
Roberts and Tanner, who was the only non-relative, were killed outside the home, Lorah said.
The police chief hasn’t said what the gunman’s possible motives were, but he suggested that his mental health could have been a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.

title: Flock cameras went up without some city councils’ approval. We found out why.
text:
Maryville, Tennessee (InvestigateTV) — When Kyle Skeen moved back to the U.S. after working in London, he said he quickly noticed an abundance of something he hadn’t expected — cameras.
“I was quite surprised when I came back and just saw the scale of what was going on,” he said.
Located just south of Knoxville, the small city of Maryville, Tennessee where Skeen moved in 2024 has 16 Flock Safety automatic license plate readers.
“I cannot leave my neighborhood without passing a Flock camera,” he said. “No matter which way I go, every time I leave my house, it’s put into the database.”
Skeen is more than familiar with the concept of surveillance: his more than 20-year career with the United States Navy culminated in his role as a senior intelligence analyst, and that stint in London was working in intelligence for NATO Maritime Command.
But Skeen said what he found when he started digging into the details — from the nationwide scope of the searching by law enforcement to how his community came to be in business with Flock — still left him shocked.
“The power should lie with the people, and these kind of systems, it tilts the balance,” he said.
Flock’s national network of more than 120,000 cameras is knit together through thousands of contracts the company has signed with communities large and small, with Flock executives touting this as local control.
But as a growing number of communities have reconsidered their relationships with Flock in light of sustained public criticism, the genesis and content of those contracts have drawn scrutiny as well.
“It seems like people are realizing that they’re starting to pop up just everywhere, the sheer volume of them, and they’ve been starting to ask questions,” Skeen said, “and usually when people find the answers to the questions, they get even more concerned.”
Cameras and contracts without a vote
In an April interview with InvestigateTV and in multiple company publications since, Flock has argued that local communities have complete control over their implementation of the technology.
“I think the city council has been democratically elected by the community to go make these sort of decisions,” Flock Chief Communications Officer Josh Thomas said in that April interview. “And if the community doesn’t like the city council’s decision, they should go vote differently. But it is the city council’s job, as a duly elected representative, to go decide how the budget should be spent.”
However, InvestigateTV found numerous instances in communities across the country where cameras were installed and paid for first, with approval from local elected officials sometimes coming later — if at all.
In Maryville, the police chief recently explained during a city council work session that the department began using Flock technology in 2020, but records show the council didn’t vote on the issue until July 2024 when the city needed a right-of-way permit from the state.
“I did not vote for this, and to my knowledge, not a single American voted for this,” Skeen said.
He and others have expressed their concerns about privacy and transparency to local elected officials, including at the public work session, and the city has said it is gathering information.
“We just wanted to hear from everybody and kind of gather information. And to be honest with you, learn more as a council because there’s a lot of things that we learned today from you guys and from the Chief as well,” Maryville Mayor Andy White said at the meeting.
Over the last few months, similar meetings have taken place in hundreds of communities across the country where citizens or elected leaders have questioned the procurement of Flock technology without explicit council or commission approval.
Law enforcement officials have largely defended these actions — with emotions sometimes running high.
“It’s my equipment. I don’t tell you guys when I buy a new gun,” Ron Ambrozaitis, then police chief, said to city leaders during a July public meeting in Chetek, Wisconsin. “You guys want to call and cancel it, go right ahead. I have no problem. But the next time grandma’s missing, or your car got stolen, or you’re missing money, and I can’t ... I can’t help you.”
At the end of August, Ambrozaitis announced his retirement and stepped down from active duty.
Buying under the limit
In Knox County, Tennessee, as local law enforcement looked to expand its Flock portfolio to more than 400 cameras in mid-August, then County Mayor Glenn Jacobs sent a letter to Flock questioning the validity of the county’s contract with the company.
He alleged the payments the Knox County Sheriff’s Office had been making since 2020 appeared to have been outlined to strategically “escape” the county’s contract oversight procedures.
Records show the sheriff’s office purchased Flock cameras in batches of $24,990 — exactly $10 under the $25,000 threshold that would have required a review by the county mayor’s office — as well as in split invoices of $12,500 that combined would have triggered a review.
“If you hit the exact price, minus ten bucks, it’s a red flag to me,” Knox County Commissioner Larsen Jay said during a public meeting the body held after becoming aware of the payments. “[The payment record] to me shows a pattern of buying things right under the threshold again and again and again. That concerns me.”
County Law Director David Buuck, who reviewed the paperwork with the mayor, also didn’t mince words.
“It’s one of the screwiest contracts I ever read because it basically says every time you do another one of these $12,000, $13,000 under-the-limit orders, it automatically renews the contract,” the Buuck said during the meeting.
Now former mayor Jacobs said the deal should never have skipped his desk.
“If it’s a contract: that has to come to commission, that has to come to me,” he said. “That didn’t happen.”
By the time commissioners took up the matter, Knox County’s sheriff’s office had 143 Flock license plate readers active — and according to Jacobs’ letter, more than a quarter of a million taxpayer dollars had been spent.
In light of allegations such as those levied by Knox County leaders, InvestigateTV asked Flock directly if the company works with agencies to avoid budgetary reviews.
“Flock provides public agencies with product information, pricing, and procurement documentation,” a spokesperson said in an emailed response. “Purchasing thresholds, sole-source requirements, and whether council or commission approval is required are governed by each agency’s applicable laws, policies, and procurement procedures.”
Contract questions lead to communities pulling the plug
Knox County ultimately pulled the plug, declaring its own Flock contract invalid and calling for the removal of the cameras. When the company missed a county-imposed deadline to do so, the newly-elected mayor had public works crews cover them. The sheriff’s office has since declared it is no longer using any fixed ALPR systems.
Knox County isn’t the only place that has turned off its cameras — the Institute for Justice has catalogued more than 250 communities that have canceled or will not renew their contract with Flock Safety.
The mayor of Neenah, Wisconsin posted a video to Facebook about how the city terminated its relationship with Flock over security concerns and “mounting evidence” that the company “wasn’t doing what it was supposed to in the contract.”
Ledyard, Connecticut, police got a notification in September from Flock about a security breach involving the system.
The notification appears to have been the final straw for Ledyard Police Chief Ken Creutz, who said he had already had growing concerns about the technology after watching recent congressional hearings.
“The technology may do some things that we were told that it can’t do,” he said in a letter to local elected officials. “The only prudent decision was to take a timeout from the whole Flock situation.”
The department severed its contract with Flock altogether, and the town’s public works department covered all four of the town’s cameras.
Ledyard signed a two-year contract and still owes the company around $12,000. Town leaders have said they are willing to pay the price to get out of the contract, but given the circumstances, some said they want to look into legal recourse because they feel they could have been sold the system on false pretenses.
“If we can display legally that we’ve been misled in this contract, in what we signed up to in terms of the conditions. To me, that’s grounds at least for something,” said Ledyard Town Councilor Tim Ryan. “It makes a statement, right? I don’t want to spend more than we’re already losing.”
The ‘Sole Source’
There are plenty of jurisdictions that are not pulling back.
For example, Dallas is keeping its more than 600 Flock cameras for now, even after Texas Governor Greg Abbott revoked state funding and residents have pressed city leaders on how the system got there in the first place.
City council member Gay Donnell Willis defended the technology’s track record in the city at a public forum hosted by community advocacy groups in mid September.
“Dallas has had 50 homicides solved, where a suspect was identified and arrested since 2023. It’s incredible,” she said in an interview with InvestigateTV.
She also said homicide investigations justify the city’s ALPR data retention period of 365 days.
“It’s important to be able to have that information to pinpoint where a suspect might have been to help catch them and arrest them.”
Stephanie Drenka with the Texas Civil Rights Project, one of the forum host organizations, questioned why Dallas has embraced the technology so fully while nearby cities move the opposite direction.
“Dallas, uniquely, has embraced Flock technology in a way that other cities in Texas are [not],” Drenka said. “They’re rejecting it, and they’re canceling contracts. It’s very puzzling to me why our city, with the views that citizens and residents have been expressing, our leadership does not seem to be listening to that.”
Dallas’ most recent Flock contract, worth $5.7 million, was approved by city council — but exempted from competitive bidding because Flock was listed as the “sole source” for the automated license plate reader technology sought by the city.
Councilmember Willis defended that arrangement, too.
“I think anyone can bid, but there are technologies and proprietary tools that maybe one technology has over another,” she said. “My understanding is that right now, they’ve got the most advanced technology, and until a competitor is able to match that, they’re the only one in the market and they meet the needs that Dallas has for solving crimes, then that might be the reason for a sole source.”
InvestigateTV found dozens of examples of similar sole-source paperwork in other cities and counties across the country — which municipalities used to competitive bidding in an industry that has several competing license plate reader companies.
With examples dating from 2020 to 2026, letters InvestigateTV reviewed were presented to jurisdictions of all sizes, all with nearly identical language.
In response to InvestigateTV’s questions about these “Sole Source Letters” a spokesperson said in a statement:
“Flock provides sole-source letters when public agencies request documentation for their procurement files, purchase orders, invoice processing, renewals, or sole-source justifications. The letters describe Flock’s integrated hardware, software, managed services, and system compatibility so an agency can evaluate whether the solution meets its applicable sole-source criteria. Each public agency is responsible for navigating its own procurement process and complying with the laws, policies, and approval requirements that apply in its jurisdiction.”
Dallas leaders authorized the city’s contracts with Flock, sole-source justification included, through consent agenda votes in 2022 and 2025 with minimal public council discussion, and critics argue the arrangement has left residents with no real say.
“If the grand majority of Dallas was in favor for Flock, then I can respect that. But we never had a vote on this either,” Santiago Diza of the Latino Leaders Coalition, another of the forum host organizations, said. “A product that was sold to the police department and we had no say in it.”
A database, not just a photo
Flock has frequently noted that sharing access to license plate reader data is “optional” for agencies, but in its sole-source letters the company highlights its integrated data network as its premier proprietary offering, calling it “a centralized system that facilitates collaboration across multiple jurisdictions, supporting a more robust and efficient public safety network.”
More than 6,000 jurisdictions are connected to the Flock system, and what the company considers a selling point, Drenka argues is precisely what makes it problematic.
“I think that is why Flock in particular has become such a dangerous entity, almost this monopoly, because of the data sharing and the network that they’re able to build when they have the exclusivity with these agencies,” Drenka said. “Flock has infiltrated communities across the country and we have very limited knowledge about how our data is being accessed and used by those other entities.”
Skeen, the Navy veteran now living in East Tennessee, agrees, and said he thinks the public largely misunderstands what the system actually does.
“This isn’t just one camera on a post on the side of the road. This is a national network,” Skeen said.
He said he’s found the volume of searches against his local cameras to be “staggering” — especially because they’re not all coming from nearby.
“They average about 63,000 searches a day,” Skeen said of cameras in his area. “All the way as far out as California, we’re seeing a massive amount of searches on the cameras here — in Tennessee.”
Jennifer Sanchez of the Texas Civil Rights Project said this functionality has led to distrust.
“Who is accessing this data? Who knows everything about us? Who is watching us? Who is collecting our every move? People have no trust in these cameras. People are scared of these cameras,” Sanchez said.
“If our every move is being recorded and stored in a database for 365 days, that’s scary.”
Flock has refuted that it “tracks” individuals, asserting that its ALPR snapshots are simply point-in-time indications of a vehicle’s location, but Skeen argues that what looks like scattered snapshots ultimately becomes something else entirely once it’s compiled.
“I worked in military intelligence, so I understand the value of information. And once that information by itself is put together, it becomes intelligence,” he said. “I understand when the system like this takes bits of information, like a photo on one street and a photo on another, and then puts that into a database and correlates that, that becomes intelligence.”
Skeen also pushed back on the notion that because the cameras capture license plates that are in public view, there is no invasion of privacy or Fourth Amendment concern.
“Tracking every citizen going around, whether they’re going to the store, to church, to the gun range, or wherever, it’s a lot different than just being seen in public. Being followed in public is a different thing,” he said.
Some vehicles able to ‘opt-out’
But is “every citizen” actually subject to the watchful lenses of Flock’s 120,000-plus cameras?
While digging into the system and how his community utilizes it, Skeen said he discovered the existence of something that further staggered him: a list of vehicles the cameras are built to ignore.
In the same way someone can “whitelist” an e-mail address they trust to allow it to pass through a spam filter, Skeen said he learned that agencies using Flock can designate license plates that effectively pass by the cameras without being flagged.
“It is a list of special plates, or assigned category, which people are suppressed from the system. It means, basically, when you drive around, the camera ignores your car,” Skeen said.
Skeen filed public records requests with agencies in his community, including with Maryville, and the city turned over three license plates on its “whitelist,” set to never expire, but no names attached.
When he asked who decides which vehicles get that kind of permanent exemption, he said the city told him there was no formal process at all.
“They told me there’s no policy and no instruction, and it’s up to a single person there. And they get to decide who goes on the list,” Skeen said.
Maryville’s police chief told InvestigateTV the list exists for a narrow, technical reason — to correct for the system’s own errors, not to grant special treatment: “These entries were whitelisted after our Flock cameras repeatedly generated hotlist alerts because of apparent misreads of similar-looking characters in plate images.”
Flock, for its part, said what Maryville has is what the company calls a “suppressed hit,” separate from a feature called a “Safe List,” which a spokesperson said is now only available to private customers such as homeowners associations and businesses.
“In the past, Flock did offer Safe List functionality to some law enforcement customers that wanted the ability to exclude certain vehicles from their own system. The feature was not widely used by law enforcement agencies and was subsequently removed from the law enforcement product,” a company spokesperson said.
However, in the dozens of Flock sole-source letters for its ALPR system InvestigateTV reviewed, “Privacy controls to enable certain vehicles to ‘opt-out’ of being captured” was listed as a proprietary feature of “the only Law Enforcement Grade ALPR System.”
Asked directly about this, the spokesperson said: “A small number of outdated sole source letters were used in error and referenced an opt-out function that is no longer available to law enforcement customers.”
InvestigateTV found letters from 2020 to 2026, including multiple from March and April of this year, that contained the “opt-out” line, and a version of the letter containing the line was submitted as justification as recently as mid-August by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office — prior to the county canceling its contract in early September.
Skeen said the uncertainty cuts in a troubling direction, since the public has no way to check who benefits from the exemption.
“That’s the huge problem with this, is we don’t have transparency, and we don’t have regulations, and we’re not watching the system,” Skeen said. “We really are just left to guess on what this could be.”
“I don’t believe that these do coincide with the Constitution”
Skeen comes from what he calls a law enforcement family — not an activist background.
“In my family, you went to the military or you went to law enforcement, or a combination,” he said.
But he said the scale of what he uncovered doesn’t square with the oath he took.
“I don’t believe that these do coincide with the Constitution, and that is the biggest issue with these systems,” Skeen said. “Although they might be powerful, they might be preferred, but I do not believe that they hold in standing with the Constitution.”
He said he’s raised those concerns directly with Maryville’s city council, warning of “the dangers of putting in mass surveillance on Americans.”
Skeen said to him, the benefits are not worth the risk.
“This is a great tool. I have to hand it to Flock. It is powerful, it is effective,” Skeen said, “but it’s also something we should not be having here in this country.”

title: Driver throws water bottle causing crash on interstate highway, troopers say
text:
PHELPS COUNTY, Mo. (KY3/Gray News) - A woman was sent to the hospital after a crash on a Missouri interstate Friday evening.
According to the Missouri State Highway Patrol, the crash happened at the 170-mile marker on Interstate 44 in Phelps County at around 5:25 p.m.
Troopers said a 20-year-old woman from Laquey was driving a Ford Mustang in the westbound lanes when she was hit in the face by a water bottle thrown by another driver. The woman then lost control of the vehicle, went off the road, hit an embankment and overturned.
The woman sustained minor injuries and was brought to a nearby hospital for treatment. The crash report states she was wearing a seatbelt.
No one else was injured.

title: 4-year-old boy dies after being found in backyard pool
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) — A 4-year-old boy died Saturday night after being found in a backyard pool, authorities said.
Just before 10 p.m., first responders were called to 67th Avenue and Baseline Road on reports of a boy drowning.
The boy had been pulled from the pool and was unconscious and not breathing when crews arrived, according to the Phoenix Fire Department.
Family members told police the child had been underwater for an unknown amount of time. Firefighters performed CPR and took him to a hospital in critical condition. He later died.
Firefighters said the home did not have a pool fence.

title: Woman arrested after driving recklessly with boyfriend on hood of car, deputies say
text:
LENOIR COUNTY, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - A woman was arrested after she drove nearly five miles with her boyfriend clinging to the hood of her car, according to police.
The Lenoir County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded to reports of a domestic incident on Highway 258 on Saturday.
Janecia Greenfield-Williams, 23, was driving with her boyfriend on the hood of her car. She drove recklessly for 4.6 miles, reaching speeds of up to 60 miles per hour and swerving, according to police.
Authorities said her 3-year-old child was also in the car at the time.
Authorities were able to safely conduct a traffic stop on the car.
The man on the car was assessed and released without injuries, deputies said.
Greenfield-Williams refused to get into the patrol vehicle, but was eventually taken to Lenoir County Jail and faces several charges, including a felony count of assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill, assault with a deadly weapon with a minor present, reckless driving to endanger, resisting a public officer, misdemeanor crime of domestic violence and multiple traffic violations.
