title: Bangor’s service-center role deserves support, accountability, and honest discussion
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Jenn Morin is the mayor of the City of Brewer.
After watching the replay of Bangor’s Government Operations Committee Oct. 5 meeting, I came away concerned about how the relationship between Bangor and its surrounding communities was characterized.
I can imagine the frustration that comes with being a regional service center. People travel to Bangor because that is where many services are located, including healthcare, shelters, substance use treatment, and other assistance. Municipal boundaries do not change where people can find help.
At the same time, it is important to distinguish between helping someone reach an available service and abandoning someone in another community. If there are documented instances of people being dropped off without coordination or an appropriate destination, those situations should be addressed directly. But suggesting that surrounding communities are responsible for Bangor’s broader challenges is neither fair nor productive.
Brewer is part of the regional response, too. Fresh Start identifies three sober living homes in Brewer, and the Bangor Area Recovery Network operates its recovery community center here. People in Brewer are working to provide recovery services and support for those rebuilding their lives.
Bangor and Brewer do not have the same concentration of services or the same financial resources. That difference matters. For example, through the American Rescue Plan Act, Brewer received approximately $955,000 in direct municipal relief funding. Bangor received approximately $20.5 million.
According to the Maine Attorney General’s March 2024 payment estimates, the City of Bangor is projected to receive approximately $3.45 million in opioid settlement payments from 2022 through 2038. In March, Bangor’s city council approved $641,297 in awards to 16 organizations supporting treatment, recovery, and related efforts.
Those resources do not make Bangor’s challenges easy. They do, however, give residents every reason to expect a clear plan, responsible management, and measurable results.
During the committee meeting, a councilor raised concerns about open drug use in the park across the way. In response, Bangor’s police chief outlined several challenges to addressing it, including the need to test needles for evidence of illegal substances.
That raises a reasonable question: Are we allowing the challenges of enforcement to become an excuse for taking no meaningful action? In other words, if gathering sufficient evidence for a drug charge is difficult, what other lawful steps can be taken now to address open drug use and keep public spaces safe?
I trust Brewer’s police chief to determine the appropriate response, and I expect open drug use in our public spaces to be addressed promptly and consistently.
People struggling with addiction deserve access to treatment and recovery services. Residents also deserve safe parks, sidewalks, and neighborhoods. Those goals are not in conflict.
Brewer can approach these issues with both compassion and accountability. We can treat people with dignity while enforcing the law and protecting public spaces.
Every community has a responsibility to help address addiction and homelessness. Regional cooperation requires communication, coordinated referrals, and honest discussion about capacity and costs. It also requires each municipality to take responsibility for the decisions within its control.
Bangor’s role as a service center brings real pressures, but it also brings real responsibility. Brewer is committed to doing its part, and I hope we can move the conversation toward how our communities can work together while recognizing the different services, resources, and responsibilities each brings.
Our region needs cooperation and shared goals, not finger pointing. It needs leadership that can turn available resources into effective services and safer communities. That begins with making sure unacceptable behavior is addressed before it becomes accepted behavior.

title: Goosepecker Trekker Returns Oct. 10
text:
Midcoast Conservancy will host its annual Goosepecker Trekker guided hike at 10 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10 at the new Bolen Hill Trails in Liberty.
The 2.2-mile, moderately challenging hike climbs to the top of Bolen Hill, follows a ridge, and descends a series of switchbacks back to the trailhead. The hike begins at the Bolen Hill Trailhead on Route 3 in Liberty, 1/5 mile west of the state park entrance.
The Bolen Hill Trail network offers 5.5 miles of winding paths through 1,100 acres of conserved land, including parts of Lake St. George State Park. The land spans the Georges River and Sheepscot River watersheds and has more than five miles of frontage on the Sheepscot, which provides spawning and rearing habitat for the southernmost genetically distinct population of Atlantic salmon.

title: Woman with custody of teenager charged after authorities say he shot friend to death
text:
WALHALLA, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A woman who has custody of a teenager accused of accidentally shooting his friend in the head has been arrested.
Davina Jill Browne, 33, was arrested and charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk of harm, according to the Oconee County Sheriff’s Office.
According to the arrest warrant, Browne allowed the 15-year-old to have a Taurus 900 handgun. She allegedly knew the teen had a gun and did not take proper preventative measures.
The 15-year-old boy was charged with involuntary manslaughter after the gun went off while he was handling it, killing 15-year-old Thaddaeus Justice Terezakis, according to the sheriff’s office.
Browne is a family member of the teen and has custody of him.

title: UMaine women’s ice hockey battles No. 3 Minnesota in 4-0 loss
text:
MINNEAPOLIS — The University of Maine women’s ice hockey team suffered a 4-0 loss to No. 3 Minnesota on Friday, Oct. 9, at Ridder Arena. Maine entered the matchup looking to upset one of the nation’s top programs, but the Black Bears struggled to generate enough offense to keep up with the Gophers. Minnesota outshot Maine 43-25 and controlled much of the offensive pressure throughout the game. Despite the loss, Maine’s third-year goalkeeper Kiia Lahtinen delivered a strong performance, recording 39 saves against Minnesota’s offense.
The opening period remained scoreless as both teams looked for an opportunity to take control. Maine managed nine shots on goal during the period, while Minnesota recorded 13 shots. Lahtinen helped keep the Black Bears in the game with several saves, allowing Maine to enter the first intermission tied 0-0.
Minnesota broke through early in the second period with a power-play goal at the 7:45 minute mark. Fourth-year defender Molly Jordan scored off a rebound after graduate student forward Sarah Paul directed a shot toward the net, with third-year forward Julia Schalin also earning an assist. The goal gave the Gophers a 1-0 advantage and shifted momentum in their favor.
Less than three minutes later, Minnesota doubled its lead. Redshirt fourth-year forward Madison Kaiser scored an unassisted goal at 10:30 after forcing a turnover in the neutral zone and driving toward the net. Her finish extended the Gophers’ advantage to 2-0, putting Maine in a difficult position heading into the final period.
The Black Bears tried to respond but could not find a way past Minnesota’s third-year goaltender Hannah Clark. Maine recorded seven shots in the second period, while Minnesota recorded 18, continuing to apply pressure on the Black Bears’ defense. Clark remained a wall in the net, helping Minnesota maintain its two-goal lead.
Minnesota added to its scoring in the third period when Schalin scored at 6:35. Fourth-year forward Emma Kreisz assisted on the play, extending the lead to 3-0 and making Maine’s comeback attempt more challenging. The Gophers continued to limit Maine’s scoring opportunities while maintaining their offensive pressure.
The final goal came with less than a minute remaining. Second-year forward Tereza Plosova scored at 19:11, with Jordan and Paul recording assists, to complete the 4-0 victory. The goal was Plosova’s first of the season and capped off a strong offensive performance by Minnesota.
Maine finished the game with 25 shots, compared to Minnesota’s 43. The Black Bears went 0-for-1 on the power play, while the Golden Gophers converted one of their two opportunities with the man advantage. Lahtinen’s 39 saves were a key bright spot for Maine, as she faced a high volume of shots throughout the game. Minnesota’s Clark finished with 23 saves to earn the shutout.
Despite the score, Maine had several players contribute offensively. Second-year forward Isabelle Michaud led the Black Bears with five shots, while third-year forward Stephanie Jacob and third-year forward Charlotte Wensley recorded four shots each. However, the team was unable to capitalize on its chances against Minnesota’s defense.
The loss dropped Maine to 1-4-0 overall, while Minnesota improved to 3-0-0. The Black Bears were scheduled to continue their season at the East/West Showcase, facing Bemidji State on Saturday, Oct. 10. Maine will aim to improve its offensive execution and build on Lahtinen’s strong performance as it looks to bounce back from the shutout defeat.
Minnesota’s balanced scoring and defensive discipline led the Gophers to victory, while Maine will use the matchup as an opportunity to make adjustments and prepare for its next contest.

title: Emergency help was delayed by confusion after failed execution of Christa Pike, 911 calls reveal
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by The Associated Press.
The recordings show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate. The first call came in at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, and it was about a half an hour before prison officials affirmed it was legitimate and began letting responders through the prison gates.
“Per supervisors here at the DEC (Department of Emergency Communications) we have been informed it is a false call,” one unidentified person says at 9:03 p.m. “There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison.”
Four minutes later, a responder reported: “Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people.”
It wasn’t until 9:11 p.m. that prison officials affirmed the call for help was legitimate, the calls show.
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point, Pike was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance, and she has since been discharged and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
___
Johnson reported from Seattle and Schoenbaum from Salt Lake City.

title: ‘He was very wholesome’: Friends mourn high school football player killed in crash
text:
TUPELO, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) — Friends and classmates are mourning the death of a 19-year-old football player who was killed in a crash early Sunday.
According to the Tupelo Police Department, officers responded to a single-vehicle crash a little after 1 a.m. Sunday.
The Lee County Coroner’s Office said Alden Wade was driving a truck when it hit a light pole. He died at the scene.
Tupelo High School students who spoke with WTVA remembered Wade as a genuine and wholesome person.
“It was real hard for the community, his friends and family,” said Tupelo High School student Elijah Bradley. “He was a very wholesome and genuine person you could ever meet, and we’re just sorry for the loss.”
Fellow student Alyviah Hunt said Wade’s death is a reminder of how quickly life can change.
“It’s very sad, and it just makes you think of how quick anything can end,” Hunt said. “And it’s just really sad, and I have prayers for his family.”
An accident reconstruction team responded to the scene to investigate the crash.

title: How candidates for Maine governor say they’ll fill a projected $1B budget gap
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s next governor will face the early challenge of proposing a balanced state budget, and a projected hole of more than $1 billion may complicate that task.
The periodic fiscal forecast, which state officials released Sept. 30, predicts a General Fund gap of $1.085 billion and a Highway Fund gap of $256.7 million for the next two-year budget running from the middle of 2027 through the middle of 2029. The governor who succeeds Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, must present a balanced budget proposal to state lawmakers by February before the Legislature seeks to pass a plan that kicks in July 1, 2027.
Under state law, the budget bureau within the Department of Administrative and Financial Services completes the Four-Year Revenue and Expenditure Forecast every other year. The projected gap represents how much estimated revenue is falling short of what existing statutes require the state to spend. These mandatory expenditures include maintaining state support for 55% of K-12 education costs, 5% spending on municipal revenue sharing and pensions for retired teachers.
Finance Commissioner Elaine Clark noted that “many of the funding obligations considered in the report are, with Legislative approval, routinely not met” and that the report should only serve as a “starting point” for lawmakers as they begin budget discussions rather than “an accurate reflection of an actual budget shortfall facing State government.”
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the gubernatorial race over Republican Bobby Charles, a lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, and independent Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator.
Here’s what each candidate said when asked during Thursday evening’s debate about how they would fill a budget gap if elected governor. The debate was not the only time the candidates have discussed the budget, with the Portland Press Herald’s Voter Guide among the other places to review their policy plans.
Republican Bobby Charles
Charles, 66, began his budget answer by alluding to how Pingree led the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025, criticizing the Democratic candidate as “the right hand of the governor that put us in all these problem sets.”
“It’s like inviting the arsonist back to put out the fire,” Charles said of electing Pingree.
However, the budget problems are not unique to the outgoing Mills administration. The finance department previously noted that aside from 2022, each report since 2014 had projected a structural gap.
These gaps have occurred under past governors of independent, Republican and Democratic stripes. The projected deficit was also around $1 billion when then-Gov. Angus King, an independent who is now in the U.S. Senate, left office in 2003 and Democratic Gov. John Baldacci took over.
Still, Charles said, the state needs to cut down on its spending. As part of his previously stated plan to ultimately slash $4 billion from the state budget, which is currently near $12 billion, and phase out the income tax, Charles said he would first nix at least $1 billion “by reducing the fraud” as well as eliminating sole source contracts.
He referred to fraud to the tune of $2.1 billion in Maine, though that appeared to reference State Auditor Matt Dunlap’s annual audit in 2024 that noted “deficiencies” and “material weaknesses” involving $2.1 billion in federal spending.
Charles said he would cut 2,000 unfilled state jobs, implement an immediate hiring freeze and order a “top-to-bottom review” of all state agencies while “restructuring” the education and health departments. He would task each commissioner with trimming department costs by 10%.
“None of this, by the way, has any effect on services,” Charles said. “It only makes us more efficient.”
He also argued for ending the process known as the “cascade,” in which unspent surplus General Fund money is transferred at the end of each fiscal year to different areas, such as the Highway Fund.
Charles ended his response with another dig at Pingree. He said he would eliminate the governor’s policy office that oversees housing, climate, economic and other initiatives — which Pingree used to lead.
Democrat Hannah Pingree
Pingree, 49, started her answer by blaming President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war for putting “huge headwinds on our economy,” and she criticized cuts to Medicaid and food benefits in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
She mentioned getting first elected to the Legislature in 2002 and serving on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee when lawmakers and Baldacci faced the roughly $1 billion shortfall. She touted her work with Republicans to pass bipartisan, balanced budgets, including working with then-Republican floor leader Josh Tardy when she was the Maine House speaker from 2008 to 2010.
But Pingree remained light on specifics to fill a budget gap, other than saying she would double the homestead exemption to $50,000 and amend the Maine Constitution to tax second homes that non-Maine residents own in the state at a higher rate.
That second idea from Pingree looks unlikely to pass in the near future, given it would take a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers to amend the Maine Constitution that currently requires all property to be taxed equally per its true value.
Dan Pittman, a Maine Revenue Services lawyer, confirmed to lawmakers last month that such a proposal, or policies like Rhode Island’s “Taylor Swift” tax on empty vacation homes, are not allowed in Maine without a constitutional change.
Charles and Bennett said they disagree with Pingree’s proposal. Pingree acknowledged the hurdles facing her plan but doubled down on pursuing it.
“That is a big thing to do, but we’ve amended our constitution many, many times before, and it would require bipartisan support,” Pingree said. “But I’ll tell you, from Washington County down to southern Maine, people realize that Maine people are having a hard time keeping their home.”
Independent Rick Bennett
Bennett, 63, kicked off his answer by warning about the growth in the state budget over the past decade and how the Mills administration pushed federal money for COVID-19 pandemic relief “out the front door.” He criticized the Legislature for not holding a true public hearing on the continuing services budget that funds baseline services in six years.
“We are spending, in the state government, well beyond the means of Mainers to pay,” Bennett said. “That’s a reality. We need some fiscal prudence.”
If elected, Bennett said, he would put together a finance team the day after the Nov. 3 election to look at every line in the state budget, and he said he would return to the Legislature’s former tradition of passing budgets with at least two-thirds support.
To avoid devoting state dollars to paying back the federal government for potential fiscal issues, Bennett said his office would have an inspector general team that investigates potential misspending or corruption.

title: Are 1 in 5 American adults functionally illiterate?
text:
No.
The claim that a fifth of American adults are functionally illiterate likely confuses low literacy with functional illiteracy.
Functionally illiterate people may struggle to understand basic sentences, find information in short texts or complete simple forms, the U.S. Department of Education says.
The department says adults below Level 1, the lowest proficiency level, may be considered functionally illiterate. In a 2023 international assessment, 12% of U.S. residents ages 16 to 65 fell into that category.
That same assessment found 16% had Level 1 English literacy, which is considered low but more advanced than functional illiteracy. The share at or below Level 1 was 28%, up from 19% — roughly one in five — in 2017.
The rise is partly due to changing methodologies, the department said. Its literacy categories range up to Level 5, with those at Level 1 able to read short passages and find clearly stated information.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

- Irish Central Statistics Office: Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) 2023 (Figure 3.4)

title: After Lewiston shooting, Troy Jackson found the courage to change his mind
text:
In less than half an hour on Maine’s darkest day, a man gunned down 18 people in Lewiston and left at least 13 more injured, some of them grievously.
For me, a former Connecticut journalist, the Oct. 25, 2023 mass shooting brought back memories of the Sandy Hook school shooting in 2012. This is the kind of horror that ought to lead to sweeping policy changes.
Here in America, though, too many people just shrug their shoulders every time bullets fly and innocent people die as a result. They insist there’s nothing we can do about it.
Today, Troy Jackson knows better.
During a rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders in Lewiston on Sunday, Jackson told the crowd supporting his Senate bid that when he “watched this community bury 18 people,” he realized he’d taken the wrong position on some gun-related proposals.
“Eighteen funerals changed me,” Jackson said. “Because sometimes leadership means having the guts to admit that what you believed before isn’t good enough anymore. I couldn’t look at those families and tell them nothing had to change. So I changed.”
Sadly, most politicians looking at the same situation refused to reconsider their positions. But some did.
Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who opted not to run for reelection to Congress this year, backed a ban on assault rifles after the Lewiston mass shooting. He called his earlier position a failure and asked for forgiveness from victims’ families and the community at large.
A more careful Sen. Susan Collins called only for limits on “very high capacity” magazines and suggested she might agree to raise the age limit for buying them from 18 to 21.
“We cannot keep treating these mass shootings like they’re a natural disaster, like some terrible thing that just happens in America and there’s nothing that we can do about it. Because there is,” Jackson said on Sunday. “I learned right here in Lewiston that those 18 people deserve more than our grief. We owe them the courage to change.”
Before the shooting, Jackson earned top marks from pro-gun groups and voted against a number of measures aimed at stemming gun violence, including a proposed 72-hour waiting period for gun purchases, background checks and a ban on devices that allow modification of rifles to allow them to be fired more rapidly.
“I grew up around guns,” Jackson said. “I’m a sportsman — and for a long time I opposed some of the gun laws that people in my own party wanted me to support.”
After the Lewiston shootings, Jackson fought for stronger background checks, a waiting period for gun purchases and a red flag law to allow law enforcement to temporarily confiscate firearms from people considered a threat.
“When a family knows somebody they love is in danger to themselves or others, they ought to be able to do something before it’s too late,” he told the crowd.
To my mind, the 2012 Sandy Hook nightmare that left 20 children blown to bits in their classroom by a high-powered semi-automatic rifle should have been enough to cause every political leader to embrace gun control. But better late than never.
After Lewiston, Jackson and Golden fessed up to their mistaken policy choices. It’s refreshing to see politicians admit they had it wrong.

title: 7 thing to do in central Maine this week include laughs, jazz, ukelele and wolves
text:
LAMBO LAW
Be sure to spend an evening with Lambo Law —Guitar Duet at 7:30 p.m. Friday on the Logan Stage at Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner.
When Neil Lamb and Dave Lawlor first met each had been playing mostly solo jazz guitar. They were introduced by mutual friend, guitar virtuoso Mark Kleinhaut, who said, “You guys know jazz guitar, but you need to play with more people. Jazz is a language meant to be shared.” Following an initial jam it was clear that their different approaches (7 string finger style and 6 string pick style) were complementary. Since then, they have played diverse settings in and outside of northern New England. Their first CD, “Molly Brown” is on the Invisible Music label and was initially aired on Maine Public Radio.
The duo returns to Johnson Hall to perform all new original music that will appear on a new recording slated for release this fall.
Tickets cost $20; johnsonhall.org.
GATSBY SOIRÉE
Lights Up Productions is set to host its first-ever fundraiser — the Gatsby Soirée, planned for 4 p.m. Saturday in The Grand Hall at The Skowhegan, Island Avenue, Skowhegan.
This jazz-age event pairs with the upcoming production of “The Great Gatsby” and helps the organization raise funds for a new stage valence to elevate future performances at the Skowhegan Opera House.
Tickets cost $60 which includes signature “Gatsby” cocktail or mocktail, decadent grazing table, tickets for reserved premium seating at the Saturday performance, a cast meet-and-greet, silent auction and a costume contest.
For more information, visit lightsupskowhegan.org.
BOB MARLEY
Be sure to catch one of comedian Bob Marley’s two shows set for 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. Saturday at the Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville.
The Maine entertainer has put out more than 20 comedy CDs and DVDs. He was inducted into “The Guinness Book of World’s Records” for “the longest stand-up comedy show by an individual” at 40 hours of straight stand-up. He’s been on over 100 TV shows.
Tickets cost $46.50; operahouse.org.
FENG E
The teen uke sensation Feng E, from Taiwan, is scheduled to take the stage at 4 p.m. Sunday at The Waldo Theatre, 916 Main St., Waldoboro.
He gained international fame at 10 years old when his ukulele cover of Tommy Emmanuel’s “Classical Gas” went viral on YouTube. He uses fast-paced, percussive techniques, looping pedals, and harmonics on his small instrument to recreate full-band rock ‘n’ roll sounds.
Tickets are $25 for adults, $15 for youth; thewaldotheatre.org.
NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC LIVE
The Waterville Opera House plans to host National Geographic Live at 2 p.m. Sunday at the opera house at 1 Common St., Waterville.
The topic is Yellowstone National Park, which contains many stories, including one of the best case studies in wildlife conservation. Wildlife biologist and National Geographic Explorer Doug Smith led the project that reintroduced gray wolves in the 1990s. The presentation will show him on assignment in the park to see how the landscape has changed since the wolves arrived, including never-before-seen photos and videos of the quest to bring back this apex predator.
Smith served as a wildlife biologist at the park for nearly three decades and studied everything from beavers to birds.
Tickets are $30-$40; www.watervillecreates.org.
AUDITIONS: ‘LES MISÉRABLES’
The Waterville Opera House has scheduled auditions for “Les Misérables” at 1 p.m. Sunday, 6:30 p.m. Monday, Oct. 19, with callbacks at 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 21, at Studio 1902, 2nd floor, Paul J. Schupf Art Center, 93 Main St., Waterville.
Show times are 7:30 p.m. April 16, 17, 23 and 24; and 2 p.m. April 18 and 25.
For more information visit watervillecreates.org.
CIRQUÉ KALABANTE
Don’t miss the Cirqué Kalabante performance set for 7 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 20, at the Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville.
The WOW (World of Word) show is described as a stage where ancestral African wisdom captivates the audience. Separated by a symbolic line, one group shares its knowledge through powerful storytelling, hypnotic songs and ritual initiation, while the other receives and learns — sometimes with fear, sometimes in resistance.
The exchange begins with the obstacle of spoken language, quickly overtaken by the universal force of gesture, rhythm and sound. The set and its ropes become a language of their own: double Dutch skipping, bungee straps, and rope-based contortion turn into pathways of communication, pulsing with dialogue. Three guiding figures — Trust (W), Respect (O), and Wisdom (W) lead the journey.
Through acrobatic contact and moments of mutual support, the dividing line fades. Bodies merge, blending tradition with contemporary movement. The finale erupts into a choreography of unity and collective awakening: the journey itself becomes a revelation.
Tickets cost $57-$67; operahouse.org.
Looking for more? Check out the online calendar listings for other entertainment offerings.

title: Woman dies after Maine collision
text:
A woman died Sunday after a collision in Poland.
The 40-year-old was driving a 2026 Toyota Camry north on Route 11, also known as Bakerstown Road, where she crossed into the path of a 2019 Ram pickup truck towing a camper, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
The woman succumbed to her injuries at the scene, and her passenger was taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston with minor injuries, the sheriff’s office said.
The Ram’s driver, a 63-year-old Ohio man, was treated at the scene for minor injuries. His passenger wasn’t injured.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: The Latest: Homeland Security agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
text:
Homeland Security agents have searched the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke with The Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
A senior U.S. official said President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
The U.S. Department of Justice meanwhile is investigating whether it was a violation of antitrust law when the White House television press pool collectively halted coverage of Trump last month after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
And a bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia despite a U.S. sanctions law.
The Latest:
Federal agents searched Omar’s home as part of criminal investigation: AP sources
Federal agents have searched Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home as part of a criminal investigation, according to people familiar with the matter.
The people say the search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations agents. The people were not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Details about the investigation are unclear. The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area but provided no other details.
An email seeking comment has been sent to a representative for Omar.
— By Alanna Durkin Richer
Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
DOJ says it’s investigating whether White House TV pool’s coverage halt violated antitrust law
The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the department, said group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” she said.
The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports — a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.
Six senators call for Trump administration to ‘immediately reverse course’ on Russian diesel plan
The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is shown electronically on a pump at a QuikTrip station Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Greenwood Village, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)
A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump and Rubio weigh firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct, AP source says
President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.
In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
— By Matthew Lee

title: 6 events and 1 exhibit to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 25 Lewiston mass shootings
text:
Oct. 25 will mark the three-year anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which killed 18 and wounded 13 at two locations in 2023.
As the anniversary draws closer, the following public tributes have been planned in Lewiston.
Tuesday, Oct. 13
The Maine Resiliency Center is hosting a Community Night at Just-In-Time Recreation, 24 Mollison Way, from 6-8 p.m. The event is free to everyone and will feature food and fun, but organizers say it will also celebrate connection and community. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 17
The Maine Resiliency Center is having a community pumpkin carving from noon-2 p.m. outside Just-In-Time Recreation. There will also be painting and crafts. In the days following the mass shootings, pumpkins were carved with words and symbols of remembrance, love, and hope and left outside the bowling center. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 24
TB Events is hosting the third annual Lewiston Stronger Community Cornhole tournament. There will be two tournaments that day: noon to 4 p.m. and 5-11 p.m. Playing costs $20, with all proceeds going to the Maine Resiliency Center. The organization will raffle off its “Lewiston Stronger” cornhole boards after the tournaments. (facebook.com/TB.Mobile.Events)
Central Maine Healthcare and the American Red Cross are holding a commemorative blood drive from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. to honor the lives of those affected by the mass shootings. It will take place in Conference Room ABC in CMMC in the lower half of 12 High St. (redcrossblood.org)
Sunday, Oct. 25
I Love You Gardens is partnering with the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor to host a community planting and care day from 9 a.m. to noon. It commemorates those whose lives were lost, with attendees planting bulbs and seeds at one of four locations across the Twin Cities: outside the Maine MILL in Lewiston, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Beech streets, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Cross streets, and Auburn’s Bonney Park. Attendees will meet outside the Maine MILL that morning and be sent to one of the four locations. The event is free, and there will be an American Sign Language interpreter. (iloveyougardens.com)
The Maine Resiliency Center is holding a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Memorial Park,46 Beech St., from 6-8 p.m. It will begin at the entrance of the park, with attendees walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.
Ongoing exhibit at Maine MILL
Although the Maine MILL doesn’t have any events in October specific to the third anniversary, the museum has an exhibit dedicated to the Lewiston shootings. The exhibit, “Preserved,” features items in the days following the tragedy, including the doors from Just-In-Time Recreation, which are the exhibit’s entry point, and a light fixture from Schemengees Bar and Grille, with visible bullet holes. The space also features 3D-replicated pumpkins that were carved and left outside by community members at Just-In-Time Recreation.
This display will stay up until October 2027, with a new exhibit in its place to honor the four-year anniversary. For more information, go to mainemill.org.

title: Monday Five and Five: The County's Best and What's Ahead
text:
Monday Five and Five: Big Performances and Big Games Ahead
Another busy week of high school sports across Aroostook County is in the books, and the final stretch of the fall regular season is here.
The Monday Five and Five takes one more look at five of the biggest stories from the past week before counting down five things worth watching in the days ahead.
Five From Last Week
5. Presque Isle Girls Keep Rolling
The Presque Isle girls put together back-to-back shutouts, defeating Orono 4-0 before blanking Ellsworth 2-0 Saturday.
Peyton Boinske scored three goals across the two victories, while goalkeeper Sammi Argraves added two more clean sheets.
The Wildcats enter the new week ranked No. 2 in Class B North at 7-1-2, with 80.842 Heal Points.
4. County Golfers Finish Strong at the State Championships
Aroostook County golfers turned in several strong finishes on the state stage.
Houlton's Beckett Peabody tied for third in Class C with a 76, while Presley Goodwin finished third among the Class C girls with a 92.
Alice Korzekwa added a sixth-place finish in Class B, while Averie Smith was sixth in Class C.
3. County Girls Fill Up the Score Sheet
There was no shortage of offense from County girls last week.
Van Buren's Emily Lapierre delivered one of the biggest individual games of the fall, scoring five goals and adding two assists against MSSM.
Ashland's Sadie Trams finished the week with seven goals, Fort Kent's Reece Doucette scored six, Wisdom's Ellie Cyr recorded four goals and an assist, and Katahdin's Mia McNally added three goals and two assists.
2. County Runners Shine Ahead of Championship Week
Aroostook County runners had another big weekend with the PVC Championships now approaching.
Houlton/GHCA's Malachi Witmer won the Red Riot Challenge in 13:22.20, while Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also picked up individual victories.
Houlton/GHCA added the varsity boys team title at the Red Riot Challenge, along with the JV girls championship.
1. Conor Schmidt Puts Together a Monster Week
Katahdin's Conor Schmidt takes the top spot after one of the biggest offensive weeks of the fall.
Schmidt finished with eight goals and three assists across three Cougar victories.
He scored twice against Ashland, followed with three goals and an assist against East Grand, before closing the week with three goals and two assists against Shead.
That's 11 points in three games.
Five to Watch This Week
5. Penobscot Valley Visits Ashland
Tuesday brings an important Class D North girls matchup when Penobscot Valley travels to Ashland.
Penobscot Valley enters No. 3 at 5-2-3 with 66.071 Heal Points, while Ashland is No. 4 at 8-2-1 with 60.434.
Their first meeting ended in a tie, adding even more importance to the rematch.
4. A Huge Week for Wisdom
Wisdom's girls enter the week ranked No. 1 in North 8-Person at 10-1.
Tuesday brings a rematch with unbeaten Bangor Christian, the only team to defeat Wisdom this season. The Pioneers then host Katahdin Thursday.
The boys matchup Thursday also carries plenty of intrigue. Wisdom is No. 3 at 9-2, while Katahdin is also 9-2 but sits ninth in Heal Points.
3. PVC Cross Country Championships
Championship racing arrives Saturday as County runners head to Old Town for the PVC Championships.
Witmer, Gorneault, Graves and several other County runners enter the meet following strong performances last weekend, giving the area plenty of individual and team storylines to follow.

title: Driver killed after truck strikes train at railroad crossing
text:
SPRINGFIELD TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - A man died after a train and pickup truck collided just before midnight at an Ohio railroad crossing, authorities said.
The crash happened at a railroad crossing on Albon Road near Airport Highway.

Officials said the driver was identified as Michael Jones, 57, of Monclova.
“We’ll have the coroner’s office, we’ll go through our complete investigation, download the vehicle, seeing speed and stuff like that,” said Sgt. Jason Metzger with the Ohio State Highway Patrol. “We’ll do toxicology, see if there’s any factors there.”

title: Sparrows Nest Theater presents: The Gin Game
Hayden Panettiere’s ex Wladimir Klitschko gets legal status to protect their daughter’s inheritance
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal authority by a California court Thursday to protect Panettiere’s property for their 11-year-old daughter after the television star’s accidental overdose death left the girl as her sole heir.
Klitschko had filed the urgent petition last week, saying that pieces of Panettiere’s property were being taken by federal law enforcement agents investigating her death and by an unnamed nonfamily member looking to sell them, with no one in a position to try to recover them for her daughter.
Klitschko, a Ukrainian former world champion boxer, has had full custody of the girl, Kaya, for most of her life, and she has lived with him in Ukraine. The father and daughter appeared in Los Angeles County court remotely via videoconference. They spoke only to introduce themselves at the brief hearing with only Kaya visible on camera, sitting at a table in front of curtains.
Judge Stephanie Santoro granted Klitschko the status of temporary guardian of Kaya’s estate until a long-term administrator can be appointed.
Santoro asked Klitschko’s lawyer, Diane Park, why the matter was urgent. Park said they believed a person described only as a nonrelative had taken items after Panettiere’s death and had tried to sell some of her jewelry at a pawn shop. And she said assets were in danger of going unaccounted for during the death investigation. Court documents said authority was needed to deal with both the pawnshop owner and police agencies. Panettiere’s taxes also need to be filed this month, the lawyer said. Santoro, satisfied with the explanation, approved the move.
Panettiere, the former star of the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 16 at age 36 after paramedics found her unresponsive. A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl. She had been in rehab just weeks before. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.
Park told Santoro that the property, the pawnshop and the nonfamily member were in Los Angeles County, where the judge’s ruling held authority. Park declined to comment outside the courtroom.
Klitschko’s Sept. 24 petition emphasized that his intention is solely to protect his daughter’s future assets until a permanent administrator can be put in place.
“There is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden’s Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated,” the document said.
The filing said that before her death, Panettiere and Klitschko hired security to protect her home because an unnamed person had gained unauthorized access, and it’s expected the same person would continue to try to “misappropriate” her property.
Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, filed a document saying she consented to Klitschko being appointed.
Klitschko, 50, an Olympic gold medalist, held several heavyweight titles between 2000 and 2015. He and Panettiere began dating in 2009 and got engaged in 2013.
His older brother Vitali, also a former champion boxer, is mayor of Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. The two brothers, sons of a Soviet major general, have been prominent public figures in Ukraine during its war with Russia.
In her memoir released earlier this year, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter’s birth in 2014. Kaya went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2. Panettiere’s father told investigators that when she died she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later.

title: Are 1 in 5 American adults functionally illiterate?
text:
No.
The claim that a fifth of American adults are functionally illiterate likely confuses low literacy with functional illiteracy.
Functionally illiterate people may struggle to understand basic sentences, find information in short texts or complete simple forms, the U.S. Department of Education says.
The department says adults below Level 1, the lowest proficiency level, may be considered functionally illiterate. In a 2023 international assessment, 12% of U.S. residents ages 16 to 65 fell into that category.
That same assessment found 16% had Level 1 English literacy, which is considered low but more advanced than functional illiteracy. The share at or below Level 1 was 28%, up from 19% — roughly one in five — in 2017.
The rise is partly due to changing methodologies, the department said. Its literacy categories range up to Level 5, with those at Level 1 able to read short passages and find clearly stated information.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: 6 events and 1 exhibit to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 25 Lewiston mass shootings
text:
Oct. 25 will mark the three-year anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which killed 18 and wounded 13 at two locations in 2023.
As the anniversary draws closer, the following public tributes have been planned in Lewiston.
Tuesday, Oct. 13
The Maine Resiliency Center is hosting a Community Night at Just-In-Time Recreation, 24 Mollison Way, from 6-8 p.m. The event is free to everyone and will feature food and fun, but organizers say it will also celebrate connection and community. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 17
The Maine Resiliency Center is having a community pumpkin carving from noon-2 p.m. outside Just-In-Time Recreation. There will also be painting and crafts. In the days following the mass shootings, pumpkins were carved with words and symbols of remembrance, love, and hope and left outside the bowling center. (maineresiliencycenter.org)
Saturday, Oct. 24
TB Events is hosting the third annual Lewiston Stronger Community Cornhole tournament. There will be two tournaments that day: noon to 4 p.m. and 5-11 p.m. Playing costs $20, with all proceeds going to the Maine Resiliency Center. The organization will raffle off its “Lewiston Stronger” cornhole boards after the tournaments. (facebook.com/TB.Mobile.Events)
Central Maine Healthcare and the American Red Cross are holding a commemorative blood drive from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. to honor the lives of those affected by the mass shootings. It will take place in Conference Room ABC in CMMC in the lower half of 12 High St. (redcrossblood.org)
Sunday, Oct. 25
I Love You Gardens is partnering with the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor to host a community planting and care day from 9 a.m. to noon. It commemorates those whose lives were lost, with attendees planting bulbs and seeds at one of four locations across the Twin Cities: outside the Maine MILL in Lewiston, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Beech streets, at Lewiston’s Oxford and Cross streets, and Auburn’s Bonney Park. Attendees will meet outside the Maine MILL that morning and be sent to one of the four locations. The event is free, and there will be an American Sign Language interpreter. (iloveyougardens.com)
The Maine Resiliency Center is holding a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Memorial Park,46 Beech St., from 6-8 p.m. It will begin at the entrance of the park, with attendees walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.
Ongoing exhibit at Maine MILL
Although the Maine MILL doesn’t have any events in October specific to the third anniversary, the museum has an exhibit dedicated to the Lewiston shootings. The exhibit, “Preserved,” features items in the days following the tragedy, including the doors from Just-In-Time Recreation, which are the exhibit’s entry point, and a light fixture from Schemengees Bar and Grille, with visible bullet holes. The space also features 3D-replicated pumpkins that were carved and left outside by community members at Just-In-Time Recreation.
This display will stay up until October 2027, with a new exhibit in its place to honor the four-year anniversary. For more information, go to mainemill.org.

title: New immunotherapy could offer hope for multiple myeloma patients
text:
(Aging Untold) — It’s been a decade since Susan Lehman was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer that develops in plasma cells in the bone marrow.
“I trust God with my life and with what he has in his plans for me, and so that gave me a sense of peace,” Lehman said. “But it’s still a scary thing.”
Multiple myeloma is treatable but not curable, Lehman said.
The risk increases with age, and the average age at diagnosis is 70, according to WebMD.
Lehman, a 60-year-old mother of four, has been in and out of remission over the years. She has undergone two stem cell transplants and several other treatments.
A new treatment option
Dr. Sumit Madan, an oncologist with Banner Health, had Lehman try something new: CARVYKTI.
“These types of therapies have been revolutionizing the way we treat multiple myeloma now,” Madan said.
Two months into the treatment, Lehman said the immunotherapy has made a big difference.
“I mean, I’m back out hiking,” she said.
CARVYKTI could be an option for multiple myeloma patients when traditional cancer treatments are no longer effective.
Madan said it uses the patient’s own immune cells to act against cancer cells.
Longer-term data shows extended survival
CARVYKTI has been approved for three years, but new, longer-term data from a study shows it doesn’t just slow the progression of the disease — it also helps patients live longer.
“Historically, the outcome of these patients is pretty poor, with the average survival of under a year,” Madan said.
“If you look at the average age of when a patient with multiple myeloma is diagnosed, they’re about 70 years,” Madan said. “And so if I’m able to keep that patient alive for the next 10 to 15 years, and they’re not dying from their cancer, then to me it is a cure.”

title: Maine gas prices continue to rise, GasBuddy says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine (WABI) - Average gasoline prices in Maine have risen in the last week, according to GasBuddy.
GasBuddy reports the average price is $4.38 today.
Prices in Maine are more than 8 cents per gallon higher than a month ago.
The national average price fell 0.4 cents per gallon in the last week, averaging $4.29 today.
The national average price of diesel has decreased 5.9 cents compared to a week ago and stands at $6.25.
“More states saw average gasoline prices decline than rise over the last week, with diesel falling approximately 5 cents per gallon nationally,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “On the policy front, the Trump administration’s proposed diesel deal raises more questions than it answers, and I remain skeptical that it will deliver significant relief to the trucking industry and consumers who depend on diesel. Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias has passed, but we are awaiting updates on two refineries that were in its path, the outcome of which could impact the supply picture in the days ahead. For now, the trend is cautiously in the right direction for motorists, but between hurricane season and continued geopolitical uncertainty, it is far too early to declare the pressure on fuel prices resolved.”

title: NMMC Nurse Speaks Out on Recent Nurse Departures
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FORT KENT, Maine (WAGM) - Six nurses in the Emergency Department at Northern Maine Medical Center left in recent weeks. Several others gave notice. Now, an NMMC nurse is speaking out about why nurses are leaving and how the hospital is dealing with their departures.
Several emergency department nurses have recently left Northern Maine Medical Center. Terry Caron, a nurse at NMMC says it’s affected morale. “With the recent departure of some of our fellow nurses it’s been sad. It’s sad to see them go. It’s a lot of years experience walking out the door and it’s also frustrating because it’s unnecessary. They left not because they truly wanted to. They felt they had no other choice. I think I heard the combined total experience was nearly 70 years and that’s not just clinical expertise that’s also institutional knowledge. That’s also stability. That equals safety. That’s why we unionized to begin with. That was our top priority was patient safety and to lose nearly 70 years experience it’s really disheartening. It’s sad to see them go.”
NMMC’s Board released a statement last week defending the Emergency Department. The Board called it safe, well-staffed, and says it delivers high-quality care. The Board also said that staffing levels are planned around patient volume and acuity and are reviewed every shift.
Caron says the hospital has framed the departures as normal turnover but says that’s not the case. “They’re leaving because they felt they were short staffed. There was a mid-shift nurse they could not staff for which left the busiest part of the shift with only two nurses. If they are working short patient care is at risk. They eliminated a night clerk position which means that the nurse has to step away from the bedside to check in patients and then they are also having nurses rotate shifts from day to night/night to day and then they also changed the way scheduling was handled for no reason. So, all those reasons combined they made that decision that they needed to seek employment elsewhere.”
Caron says she has considered leaving the hospital herself. “I feel like there is very little to no communication. Changes are made. We get no input. We find out about it last minute. Much like the ER nurses were seeing when they eliminated the night desk clerk position. They found out a few days before it happened. I truly love what I do but I would be lying if I said I haven’t thought about it, but I’m also in it for the long haul. I plan on staying and fighting for what is right, and for my community, and for my patients because I’m proud of our little hospital, our little unit, and the nurses I work with. So, I wanna stay right where I am.”
We reached out to NMMC about Caron’s claims. The hospital responded by referring to last week’s statement. Caron says nurses at NMMC will continue doing their best with the resources available. She says the nurses appreciate the support they’ve received from the community, adding no matter what’s going on at the hospital, patient care and safety are their number one priority.

title: The kind of practical response we need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
To the editor:
One of the biggest issues facing Maine families is affordability — and, with winter coming, simply being able to afford to stay warm.
That is why the Mills administration’s announcement this week that thousands of eligible Mainers will automatically receive discounts on their electric bills is such smart policy. Instead of making struggling families navigate another application process, the state will use information it already has through programs such as MaineCare and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, to automatically connect eligible households with assistance. Discounts for some households can exceed 80%.

title: VIDEO: Worker rescued after falling from ladder inside 20-foot deep manhole
text:
VIDEO: Worker who fell from ladder while working in 20-foot deep manhole rescued
A construction worker was pulled to safety after officials said he fell from a ladder while working inside a manhole that was 20 feet deep.
The City of Atlanta Fire Rescue Department shared a video of crews working to hoist the worker back up to the surface, saying the man fell while working in the less-than-four-feet-wide sewer access.
"Rescuers secured the worker in a harness (in the confined space) and used a tripod and rope system to bring him to the surface," the department said in a post on Facebook. "Air was also provided in the space to ensure adequate oxygen levels. The tripod provided the elevated anchor point needed for the lift, while crews monitored the atmosphere and ventilated the space."
Officials did not say if the worker was treated for any serious injuries.

title: A guide to the best leaf-peeping spots in the Lakes Region
text:
Southern Maine is nearing the peak of leaf season, and whether you’re a born and bred New Englander or a tourist just passing through to look at the pretty colors, you probably want to find somewhere to get a picturesque, postcard view. Here are some of the best spots to do so in and around the Sebago Lakes Region, as recommended by three local land trusts.
ROYAL RIVER CONSERVATION TRUST
Royal River Conservation Trust owns 17 preserves in the area of Gray and Yarmouth. Hanae Garrison, the trust’s stewardship director, recommended three areas in the trust’s network with good fall views.
These include Thayer Brook Preserve in Gray, recently in the spotlight as the adoptive home of Rambo the runaway peacock, which has a beaver marsh and beautiful foliage; Knight’s Pond Preserve, an area straddling Cumberland and North Yarmouth centered around a marshy pond with six miles of trail; and Bradbury Mountain State Park in Pownal, which Garrison said has a “short hike to a classic scenic overlook.”
PRESUMPSCOT REGIONAL LAND TRUST
Presumpscot Regional Land Trust owns properties in Gorham, Gray, Standish, Westbrook, and Windham along the Presumpscot River watershed.
Emily Southard, director of development and marketing at Presumpscot Regional Land Trust, recommended visitors go to the Windham Conservation Area, formed recently from a merger between East Windham Conservation Area and Lowell Preserve, to hike to an overlook with views of the White Mountains.
Southard said the main access point for the overlook is Atherton Hill Trailhead, located at 189 Falmouth Road. The overlook is accessible from multiple trails, including the new Universal Access Trail, scheduled to open Oct. 17.
Other recommendations from Southard include Mill Brook Preserve in Westbrook, an area of beautiful and occasionally rugged terrain that she said felt very remote despite its proximity to downtown Westbrook, as well as the Gabo, Cummings, and Rivermeadow preserve along the Presumpscot River.
LOON ECHO LAND TRUST
Based in Bridgton, Loon Echo Land Trust conserves 9,300 acres of land in the northern Lakes Region, stretching from Raymond to Bridgton, including regional landmarks such as Bridgton’s Pleasant Mountain and Casco’s Hackers Hill.
Matt Markot, executive director of Loon Echo Land Trust, recommended four sites in the land trust’s network. These include Bald Pate Mountain Preserve in Bridgton, specifically the 1.5-mile Bob Chase Loop Trail; a pair of 0.6-mile trails the Peabody-Fitch Woods and Pondicherry Park, both of which are located in Bridgton; and a 2-mile loop trail at Sebago Cove Forest in Naples, with views of the Sebago Cove shoreline.

title: Mt. Ararat field hockey beats Skowhegan in Class A North battle of unbeatens
text:
SKOWHEGAN — In a battle of unbeatens, Mt. Ararat made a statement.
Boosted by a quick-strike offensive attack, the Mt. Ararat field hockey team beat Skowhegan 4-1 on Monday in a matchup of two of Class A North’s top teams.
Four players scored for the Eagles (11-0), including freshman Leah Lafrance.
“It’s just a really good game to win and a really good game to play,” said Mt. Ararat senior captain Maddy Sweet, who scored a goal.
It was the first win over Skowhegan for the Eagles since at least 2014, when coach Krista Chase took over the program.
Senior Faith Pease scored for the River Hawks (11-1).
Eagles strike quickly
Mt. Ararat set the tone early, moving the ball with ease up the well-manicured Skowhegan grass field. The Eagles, ranked fourth in the Varsity Maine poll, surprised the second-ranked River Hawks with a goal just over two minutes into the game, when Lafrance was able to swipe a shot past Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams for a 1-0 lead.
“(Lafrance) is a hockey player,” Chase said. “She plays ice hockey on the grass.”
Added Sweet: “(Lafrance) is holding down the fort, we’re really glad to have her. She’s our speed. … We’re so proud of her out there.”
The Eagles extended the lead to 2-0 with 22 seconds remaining in the first half, when Sweet was able to poke a shot in for the score in a scrum in front of the cage.
“They were really hungry and they showed up to play,” Chase said. “I’m really proud of them. It’s been kind of a bumpy year with scheduling, we’re in our games-every-other-day kind of (part) of the season. But we’ve been mentally preparing for this week, a lot of games in eight days.”
The Eagles played Wednesday and Saturday last week, and have games on Wednesday and Friday remaining this week.
Mt. Ararat added two fourth-quarter goals to seal the win. Junior Cali LeClair scored with 14:34 left, then junior Kamryn Chase took a well-placed pass from Avery Elliott and knocked it into the cage with under eight minutes left.
Skowhegan scored with 3:11 left, when Pease was able to knock a shot off a scrum in front of the Mt. Ararat cage.
What does it mean?
Skowhegan entered the game as the No. 1 seed in Class A North, followed by No. 2 Camden Hills (10-1) and Mt. Ararat. With the win, the Eagles swapped places with Camden Hills. The River Hawks, for now, remain the No. 1 seed, because they’ve played one more game than both the Eagles and the Windjammers.
Both the Eagles and the River Hawks face Camden Hills this week, Skowhegan on Wednesday and Mt. Ararat on Friday.
Lesson learned for Skowhegan
While the Eagles dominated possession in the first half, the River Hawks never quit, and turned pressure around on Mt. Ararat in the second half. The River Hawks outshot the Eagles by a 10-6 margin over the final two quarters, and had a 5-0 advantage in penalty corners.
“You’ve got to give respect to your opponent. (Mt. Ararat) played a beautiful game,” Skowhegan coach Gina Davis said. “We’ll be thanking them for that lesson deeper in the season. The goal isn’t to have an undefeated season. You learn your lesson, take your medicine. We’ll bounce back when we play Camden Hills, and how we respond to that will help determine the good versus the great programs.”
Unsung hero
Mt. Ararat junior Jaymie Bergman was outstanding on Monday, making 15 saves, including three saves during a 10-second stretch with 10:15 left in the third quarter.
Milestone win
Krista Chase, who has run the Mt. Ararat program since 2014, earned her 200th career win on Monday. She coached the Cony field hockey program from 2002-09, where she compiled an 88-37-2 record.
“It just means I’ve been around a really long time,” Chase laughed. “I attribute that 200 wins to all of my former teams at Cony and Mt. Ararat. I like that I’ve been around for a long time. I love this game and I love Maine field hockey. I love trying to grow programs, that’s my thing. It’s just a statement of longevity and hard work.”
Chase was gifted a Sea Bag with her name and the number 200 on each side.
