• Skowhegan: Faith Pease (1 goal); Michelle Williams (8 saves)

title: Maine’s energy goals depend on a regulatory process people can trust
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tim Burgess is assistant business manager of IBEW Local 104.
When a severe storm knocks out power in the middle of the night, Mainers don’t think about regulatory dockets — they just look for the flashing lights of utility trucks rolling down their streets. The recent recommendation to deny Central Maine Power’s request for temporary rates has sparked a fierce statewide debate over affordability, spending and the future of our electric system.
These are critical issues that affect every household, but for the men and women who build, maintain and restore our grid, a far more troubling question is emerging.
What happens to the safety and stability of our workforce when participants follow the precise regulatory rules laid out by the state, only to be told at the finish line that the path no longer applies?
Central Maine Power sought temporary rates after the Public Utilities Commission itself
indicated they were available to address the severe financial uncertainty following the dismissal of the company’s long-term grid investment plan. CMP maintains that it followed the direction provided by regulators when it pursued temporary rates, filed the case, presented extensive evidence and all involved parties participated in good faith. 
Everyone assumed that the process established by our regulators was available, stable and reliable. The recommendation currently before the commission calls that fundamental assumption into question.
For most Mainers, utility regulation feels abstract. For those who wear the tool belt and climb the poles, it is anything but. Decisions made in Augusta determine whether local contractors hire apprentices, whether vital grid projects move forward, whether stable work exists next year and whether Maine will possess the skilled workforce necessary to meet its aggressive energy and economic development goals.
Predictable investment, workforce development, apprenticeships and long-term grid reliability are interconnected. Uncertain investment makes it significantly harder for employers to expand their operations, harder for joint apprenticeship programs to grow and harder to prepare the next generation of highly skilled workers. This is not a matter of corporate self-interest. It goes directly to the heart of how safely the infrastructure is built.
Maine’s broader, long-term policy objectives sharpen the point. Our state leaders continue to aggressively promote widespread electrification, economic development, transportation electrification, rapid heat pump adoption and clean energy expansion. Every one of these initiatives drives up the daily demand for electrical infrastructure, heavy-duty service upgrades and overall grid capacity.
Meeting these goals requires a larger workforce and a stronger, more resilient grid. There is an inherent contradiction in encouraging a society-wide dependence on electricity while simultaneously creating deep financial uncertainty around the exact investments that such dependence requires.
The public debate is framed as affordability versus investment. Utility workers understand the strain of affordability as well as anyone; those who build and maintain the grid are local customers and taxpayers, too.
Aging infrastructure continues to age, and its vulnerabilities compound over time. Projects that could have been executed methodically and safely during a planned rollout instead become high-stress emergencies later on. This delays routine progress and forces emergency work at a far greater cost to the customers, all while creating much harder, more hazardous conditions for the people doing the work in storms and sub-zero temperatures.
Witnesses in these proceedings have repeatedly warned that regulatory delay leads directly to higher long-term costs, greater operational challenges and reduced workforce stability. The broader concern is the chilling signal this situation sends across our entire industry. Young lineworker and electrician apprentices count on steady, predictable work to accumulate the thousands of field hours required to become a journeyman, while local contractors need regulatory certainty before investing in heavy equipment or expanding their crews.
Furthermore, major employers looking to bring business to Maine must have absolute confidence that a stable grid will be ready when they plug in. Ultimately, all of these vital
economic decisions rest on a single, fundamental belief: that Maine’s regulatory institutions are predictable, consistent and worthy of trust.
Trust is not built by any single decision, but through a long-term process that participants
believe is transparent, consistent and reliable. When an entity follows the path regulators
indicated was open yet finds that path abruptly closed at the finish line, it is entirely fair to ask whether future participants can truly rely on the process. 
If Maine hopes to build the skilled workforce, modern infrastructure and robust electric system its economic and energy policies require, it must preserve something just as important: a regulatory process people can trust, rely upon and plan their lives around.

title: West Bethel Makerspace grows, offers more resources
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The old Newton Tibbetts wood mill in West Bethel has found new life as a low-cost work center for crafters, small businesses and homeowners with DIY projects. It also serves as a community gathering place.
The workshop is known as the West Bethel Makerspace, modeled on other centers under the worldwide “makerspace” banner.
Such centers provide workspace and both high- and low-tech tools for people at minimal cost, saving them from having to invest in specialized equipment themselves.
West Bethel Makerspace Executive Director Dustin Sysko, a software developer and native of Newry, first became involved in the makerspace while living in the Netherlands, and continued to lend a hand when he returned to the U.S., in Somerville, Massachusetts. He then lived in British Columbia for five years.
Sysko moved back to the Bethel area four years ago, and with other volunteers last year pursued bringing the makerspace here.
“I knew we needed a community workshop,” he said.
They partnered with the mill property owners, Chris Dagdigian and Diana Lamppu, to convert the former machine shop into a community workshop at the 10 Ferry Road site.
Sysko said the couple donated the renovation of the space, a very generous offer that was key to the project. Work on it began last summer. Space for a woodshop, digital fabrication lab, multipurpose assembly/loading bay and community lounge were created. The building was turned over to the local nonprofit Jan. 1 and the work to outfit it began.
Initial equipment included a fully-equipped woodworking shop, computer numerical control router and 3D printers, as well as traditional manual and power tools and work tables. A laser cutter/engraver machine came later this spring.
The makerspace then began to offer classes on use of the equipment and other related skill classes, as well as memberships at a monthly fee. The nonprofit is overseen by a board of five people.
Most of the makerspace users so far are people doing home improvement projects, said Sysko. For example, he said, “They are making planters, shelves, signs, conversion van parts, as well as fabricating parts for home renovations.”
Since opening in late April, the center has expanded its offerings and its plans. Volunteers have made improvements to the facility and acquired many more traditional tools for a tool library. Recent additions included the gift of new laser cutters and an extra-large format 3D printer, donated by friends of the Fay School in Southborough, Massachusetts, Sysko said.
The large printer will not be ready for public use for a while, he said, but plans are in the works to use it to print ceramics using porcelain, earthenware and clay. “I’m excited about it,” he said.
Overall, equipment comes primarily from a combination of donations and items purchased by others and on loan to the makerspace, according to Sysko.
The makerspace is also offering many more classes and events on a wide range of subjects. In addition to basic tool operation, there are CNC wood milling classes, bicycle maintenance classes and themed birthday parties featuring experiments and other learning events. After the annual used ski and snowboard equipment sale at Gould Academy in October, there will be classes “on how to tune equipment, cross-country ski maintenance, and ski and snowboard maintenance,” Sysko said.
Craft offerings include a monthly last-Friday craft event intended to bring families together for crafting projects for all ages. A recent one featured using the laser cutter to cut cardboard into shapes for kids to put together and color however they wish. Sysko said more craft teachers are welcome to get in touch if they would like to offer a class.
Every second Friday there is a workshop with the group Community Mending, which teaches and offers help “on anything that needs to be fixed,” said Sysko. “The Community Mending group offers a place and time for people to get together, where we fix things and share knowledge and ways to reuse otherwise discarded personal items.” They sometimes have a specific topic for the meeting, he said.
The group first started with a focus on clothing and fabric, but then expanded.
The monthly membership fee to use the space is $65. The public may take individual classes without paying the fee. For more on the West Bethel Makerspace go to westbethelmakerspace.org.
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: Tensions run high as Maine men’s ice hockey falls 2-1 to Quinnipiac in home opener
text:
ORONO, Maine — On Friday, Oct. 9, the University of Maine Black Bears lost their home opener 2-1 to the Quinnipiac University Bobcats.
This game marked the first home game for the Black Bears’ 50th season at the Harold Alfond Sports Arena. The packed stands shook as the Black Bears came onto the ice, with energetic fans excited for the game to begin.
To start the first period, the Bobcats won the initial faceoff, but the Black Bears quickly gained possession. Maintaining possession, the Black Bears forced the Bobcats to ice the puck multiple times in quick succession. With the icings UMaine had multiple faceoffs in the offensive zone which led to a Quinnipiac penalty on fourth-year forward Jack Stockfish. Third-year forward Lee Parks took advantage of this opportunity, scoring a goal assisted by second-year forward William Gerrior and fourth-year forward Max Scott.
Just a couple of minutes later, Quinnipiac tied the game following a faceoff win. The goal was scored by fourth-year forward and Bobcats captain Mason Marcellus, assisted by second-year forward Ethan Wyttenbach and third-year defender Elliot Groenewold.
Throughout the period both teams played physically, laying hits against the boards and in open ice. One of these hits by a Black Bear behind Quinnipiac’s net led to a rush opportunity for the Bobcats. The game-winning goal was scored by Wyttenbach.
The second period had plays similar to the first, with scrums almost every time either goalie caught the puck and stopped play. The play this period favored the Bobcats, with better shot attempts and more shots on goal throughout. Despite attempts by both teams, the period remained scoreless.
The third period kept the physicality up, while also giving the Black Bears plenty of opportunities to gain momentum. A little over halfway through the period, Quinnipiac had scored what originally was called a good goal on the ice. However, the net came off its posts, and after review the goal was overturned.
The Black Bears gained a bit of momentum from this with some shots on goal, but nothing hit the back of the net.
With 22 seconds left in the period, Quinnipiac fourth-year forward Andon Cerbone was called for tripping. The Black Bears kept fourth-year goaltender Albin Boija out of the net and took a timeout to plan for a 6-on-4 opportunity to end the period.
Fans were on their feet in anticipation. However, the Black Bears did not get anything going, other than keeping the Bobcats from scoring an empty-net goal.
Despite the loss, the Black Bears played a strong physical game, and when penalties were called they were able to prevent Quinnipiac’s power play unit from scoring. The Black Bears will look to turn their physicality into offense. They will also look to improve their power play after converting just one of their six opportunities.
The Black Bears finished their two-game home series against Quinnipiac on Saturday, Oct. 10. Their next home game is scheduled for Friday, Oct. 23.

title: The growing need for diapers as families face rising costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Diapers are a basic need for many families. Parents already dealing with rising costs for housing, food and transportation can find it hard to keep up with diaper costs.
Volunteers package diapers
Christina and Emily D’Abreo are a mother-daughter volunteer team at the Diaper Bank of North Carolina. Last year, they spent 208 hours volunteering there. They packaged about 29,000 diapers, helping more than 1,000 babies and their families.
“I know that diaper need is a big, something that’s really overlooked in our community,” Emily D’Abreo said.
“It’s really hard when you see a growing family have to choose between food and between diapers,” Christina D’Abreo said. “One in two families cannot afford this.”
Diapers can cost about $100 a month per child. Safety net programs like WIC and SNAP do not cover the cost of diapers.
Demand continues to rise
Jerry Garcia runs the Charlotte branch of the Diaper Bank of North Carolina. He said the need is rising.
Garcia is a father of a 5-year-old daughter and an 18-month-old son. “I’m right in the midst with everybody else experiencing the high cost of diapers, wipes, formula.”
The warehouse distributes 2 million products a year, including baby diapers, adult incontinence underwear and menstrual products.
The products are given out through partnerships with social service organizations and schools.
“When we take a step back, it’s like, wow, that is amazing,” Garcia said. “But also, we see on the flip side of the coin, we see the need. So we’re very fortunate to have the support of our volunteers and support of the community. But I believe we’re barely scratching the surface.”
Garcia said the organization needs more volunteers.
“It’s very meaningful, impactful,” Garcia said. “You come in, you wrap the diapers, you pack them up, and then at the end of the experience, you get to hear how many diapers you wrapped and how many babies you’re going to serve by volunteering those two hours.”
Volunteering as family time
Christina D’Abreo said volunteering became a way to spend time with her daughter.
“You know how it is with high school. There is no, you know, mom time, dad time, but this is our time,” Christina D’Abreo said. “So I made sure that we made it fun. So we would volunteer and then we’d go and grab a bite, you know, hang out together and make it special. And I think that time is invaluable. I’m gonna miss it when she goes to college.”
Emily D’Abreo said she hopes to become a nurse.
“A big part of that for me is like being empathetic and being able to realize the need in our community and just being able to give back is really fulfilling for me,” Emily D’Abreo said.
Christina D’Abreo said she also wanted to set an example for her daughter.
“I wanted to give back to the community and I wanted to show my six-year-old at that time that, I have a full-time job, I have a career, I have a home, but I also have a community,” Christina D’Abreo said.
Multiple studies find that people who give their time report an enriched sense of purpose and lower rates of depression. Regular volunteering is also linked to decreased cognitive decline compared with those who do not volunteer.
A study found that volunteering boosts a person’s chances of gaining employment by 27%.

title: 31 comics coming to Maine to make you laugh into next year
text:
Human beings need to laugh, and that includes Mainers. It’s good for the soul and enables us to take a break and better confront our problems.
A bunch of comedians, from familiar faces to fresh ones — including some with specials you can check out on streaming services — are coming to Maine stages to help provide that humor to soothe our souls. Here is a list of comedy shows at venues across the state over the coming months.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Comic Jason Salmon’s style is described as getting “the best advice you’ve ever gotten … from the dumbest guy you know.” His TV credits include “Orange Is the New Black,” “30 Rock” and “At Home with Amy Sedaris,” along with appearances on HBO and Comedy Central. For a preshow serving of Salmon, view his standup special, “Biscuits and Gravity,” on YouTube.
7 p.m. Sunday. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $20-$45. statetheatreportland.com.
New York City’s Lucas Zelnick has been featured on Comedy Central and has headlined the Netflix is a Joke Festival. Film credits include “Regular” and “Fade to Black.” Be ready to be cracked up by a guy who earned an MBA from Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business.
7:30 p.m. Sunday and Dec. 5. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $42.50-$83.50. jonathansogunquit.com.
Mainer Bob Marley has been cracking people up with his wicked funny humor for decades. Along with the shows in Ogunquit, Marley will be doing his thing Saturday at the Waterville Opera House. Tickets are $46.50 at watervillecreates.org. Marley also has five shows on the calendar at Stone Mountain Arts Center in Brownfield, starting on Dec. 5. Tickets are $36.50 at stonemountainartscenter.com.
7 p.m. Oct. 22. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $24.26, $29.53 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Emma Dalenberg and Sunny Laprade are best friends who are hitting the road together for a co-headlining tour. Expect a wild night from the queer comics, who will be spilling the tea on many topics.
8 p.m. Nov. 5. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $42-$72. statetheatreportland.com.
Writer, actor, radio presenter, podcaster and comic Marc Maron brings his candid brand of humor to the State Theatre with a stop on his Yammering Into The Void tour. As host of the long-running “WFT with Marc Maron” podcast, his galaxy of celebrity guests have included Barack Obama, Carol Burnett and Robin Williams. The HBO comedy specials “Marc Maron: Panicked” and “From Bleak To Dark” are popular examples of his work.
8 p.m. Nov. 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-$65. statetheatreportland.com.
For five memorable seasons, comic Leslie Jones was a Not Ready for Primetime Player on “Saturday Night Live.” During the 2016 Summer Olympic games, Jones took to what was then called Twitter to offer colorful, comical commentary. NBC recruited her to cover several events, and she offered her spicy takes during a few other summer and winter games. Catch her I’m Hot tour in Portland.
7 p.m. Nov. 7. The Dance Hall, 7 Walker St., Kittery, $28 in advance, $33 day of show. thedancehallkittery.org.
Eddie Pepitone is known as the Bitter Buddha, and is considered by some to be a cross section of Jackie Gleason, Don Rickles and Eckart Tohle. His stage presence is described as both calm and chaotic as he walks the line between social rage and self-doubt. Comic, writer and comedy producer Rebecca Donohue will be playing host.
7 p.m. Nov. 7. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $59-$99. porttix.com.
Late-night TV legend and longtime stand-up comic Jay Leno will have you rolling in the aisles when he takes the stage in Portland. Leno has won several awards including an Emmy, the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor and Hasty Pudding Award at Harvard University, among other honors.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 14. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $25-$66. jonathansogunquit.com.
Boston comic Jimmy Cash’s shows draw on his experiences of being a janitor for 20 years, as well as a father and someone who maintains long-term sobriety. Cash travels all over the U.S. and Canada, and was Maine comic Bob Marley’s dedicated opener for many years.
7 p.m. Nov. 15. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39.75-$125. porttix.com.
Bert Kreischer brings his Permission to Party tour to Maine, with a mix of his trademark storytelling paired with a huge persona. Kreischer’s latest Netflix special, “Lucky,” premiered in 2025, and his credits include the film “The Machine” and the Netflix series “Free Bert.” As a podcaster, Kreischer hosts “Bertcast” and co-hosts “2 Bears, 1 Cave” with fellow funnyman Tom Segura.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Nov. 20 and 21. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $34.81, $45.36 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Los Angeles-based comic Leah Rudick’s characters include “Wealthy Woman,” “Joannie” and “Love Coach.” With just under 2 million social media followers, Rudick is a hot ticket with her signature “weird girl” brand of comedy.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 27. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $52.50-$93.50. jonathansogunquit.com.
Paula Poundstone has been making clever observations with her dry yet hilarious delivery for decades. Poundstone is also a longtime panelist on the National Public Radio quiz show “Wait Wait … Don’t Tell Me!”
7 p.m. Dec. 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $37.50-$57.50. statetheatreportland.com.
Spice up your holiday season by hitting comic Becky Robinson’s Holiday Spectacular. With wild characters, including Suzie Chapstick and the Entitled Housewife, Robinson will knock your socks off.
6 p.m. Dec. 6. Aura, 121 Center St., Portland, $52.75-$79, 18-plus. auramaine.com.
Aries Spears brings more than three decades of stand-up experience, and an eight-season run on “MADtv” to Portland. Known for fearless crowd work and uncanny impressions of celebrities including Denzel Washington, Jay-Z and Shaquille O’Neal, Spears isn’t afraid to opine on pop culture, race and relationships.
7 and 9:30 p.m., Dec. 11 and 12. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Jason Cheny is a Taiwanese American stand-up comic out of Los Angeles. His upcoming Hulu half-hour special premieres in January. Cheny is a fixture at upper tier comedy clubs like The Improv and Comedy Cellar, and headlines sold-out shows wherever he goes, both nationally and around the world.
7 p.m. Dec. 26. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39.-75-$69.75. porttix.com.
In one night you can see a pair of big-name comics raise the rafters at Merrill Auditorium. Joe Gatto is best known for TV shows “Impractical Jokers” and “The Misery Index.” His friend Drew Lynch earned a Golden Buzzer on “America’s Got Talent.” When he was 20, Lynch suffered a traumatic brain injury and brought himself back from the brink with an infectious self-deprecating style that continues to win audiences over.
7 p.m. Jan. 16. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $39.50-$69.50. statetheatreportland.com.
For a midwinter comedy infusion, grab tickets to see award-winning actress and comic Atsuko Okatsuka in Portland. Her exuberant, offbeat brand of stand-up was captured in specials that have aired on Hulu and HBO.
7 p.m. Jan 23. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $33-$55, $199 meet & greet. statetheatreportland.com.
Zarna Garg’s Million Dollar Excuses tour will pack many punches about family life when it comes through Portland. Her Amazon Prime special “One in a Billion” and its Hulu follow-up “Zarna Garg: Practical People Win” both reached wide audiences. As a writer, Zarna published the memoir “This American Woman” about her harrowing ascent from being homeless in Mumbai to an internationally known stand-up comic.
7 p.m. Jan. 23. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $29.50-$69.50. porttix.com.
Brad William’s Big & Small tour will showcase his knack for sharp punchlines and deeply personal storytelling. His latest stand-up special “Live on Short Street” can be streamed on YouTube, as can “Starfish,” which has surpassed 9 million views.
7 p.m. Feb. 6. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., $62-$92. watervillecreates.org.
Canadian comic Samantha Bee is bringing her How to Survive Menopause tour to Waterville. In 2003, Bee started a 12-year run on Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show.” Her own late-night comedy series “Full Frontal with Samantha Bee” debuted on TBS in 2016 and ran for seven seasons.
7 p.m. Feb. 26. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $41.50-$51.50, $152 VIP. statetheatreportland.com.
Justin Willman melds comedy with magic so well, his streaming views surpassed the 1 billion mark. So you can expect the unexpected when his One For the Ages tour comes through Portland. Unlike many comedy shows, this one is suitable for all ages.
4 and 7 p.m. Feb. 27. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39-4109. porttix.com.
Nobody Asked You To Do That is what Taylor Tomlinson is calling her winter tour that includes a late February stop in Portland with late afternoon and evening performances. Head to Netflix to find several specials that emphasize her ability to convert challenging life moments into side-splitting humor.
7 p.m. March 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $29.50-$59.50. statetheatreportland.com.
Estonian-born comic Ari Matti translates his Eastern European roots and globe-trotting experiences into a can’t-miss night of comedy. Matti is a regular on the popular “Kill Tony” podcast and was part of the team that performed “Kill Tony Live” in consecutive years at Madison Square Garden.
8 p.m. March 12. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $49.50-$74.50, 12-plus. porttix.com.
Jo Koy got his start in a Las Vegas coffeehouse and is now, according to Pollstar and Billboard, one of the top 10 grossing stand-up comedians every year. Drawing from his Filipino-American upbringing and his experiences as a parent and son, you can expect nonstop laughs from the lively comic when his Koy Meets World tour comes through Portland at the tail end of winter.
7 and 9:30 p.m. March 18-20. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $34.81 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Los Angeles-based comic, writer and actress Beth Stelling hit paydirt with her latest release on YouTube called “The Landlord Special.” Another one, called “If You Didn’t Want Me Then” is also worth checking out. Stelling’s a veteran comic with a devoted following, thanks to a candid brand of comedy and appearances on Netflix, Comedy Central and late-night shows.
7 p.m. April 1. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
With a friendship that clocks in at just under 20 years, comics Grace Helbig and Mamrie Hart are guaranteed to bring the fun to April Fool’s Day in Portland. Hear them on the weekly podcast “This Might Get Weird.”
6 p.m. May 9. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-$55. statetheatreportland.com.
Ine her act, Maria Bamford is entirely comfortable talking about her acute experiences with mental health, including time spent in a psychiatric facility. She’s an Emmy-nominated comic who also authored the New York Times best-selling memoir “Sure, I’ll Join Your Cult.” Bamford’s Netflix comedy series “Lady Dynamite” was based on her life and ran for two seasons.
9:30 p.m. May 14. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $36-$69. statetheatreportland.com.
The early show is sold out, but you can still grab a ticket if you act fast to see Jeff Arcuri on his Road Trip tour that hits Portland in mid-May. His comedy special “Nice To Meet You” premiered on Netflix in July.

title: Paws and reflect: Puppy yoga brings calm and chaos
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Instructors in North Carolina are hosting “puppy yoga” classes that combine traditional yoga practice with puppies.
Jessica Seisay is one of thousands of instructors now hosting the classes, which she said are aimed at bridging two popular interests.
“Everyone loves puppies and everyone loves yoga. It’s a great way to bridge the two,” Seisay said.
Taylor Manley, who tried the class, described the experience as calming.
“Definitely - very Zen, very calm. They’re so sweet. He just came and wanted to sit in my lap the whole time, so I was trying to relax with him, and he was going to make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
Health benefits
Research shows contact with animals lowers cortisol and boosts “feel-good” chemicals like serotonin.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the practice affects the body’s stress response.
“When you’re touching a puppy, looking at a puppy, playing with a puppy, your cortisol lowers, your stress lowers, you get calmer, you get happier… So, your whole emotional system gets uplifted just playing with that puppy,” O’Rourke said.
Socialization benefits
O’Rourke said there is a socialization benefit of the classes as well.
“So, I do yoga. I’ve done yoga with goats. Yoga with puppies, I can’t even imagine the socialization. I’m sitting on my mat. I picture talking to a person on one side and the other side, laughing our heads off. So, you get all that social benefit. You’re creating friends through the puppies and the yoga and the camaraderie of doing yoga together,” O’Rourke said.
Puppy breeder Taylor Terry said the reaction to puppies is consistent.
“Every time you see puppies, you just get happy,” Terry said.

title: Woman dies after hitting a truck pulling a camper in Poland
text:
Woman dies after crashing into oncoming truck pulling a camper in Poland, Maine
A woman is dead after police say she crossed into oncoming traffic and crashed into a pickup truck that was pulling a camper in Poland over the weekend.
On Sunday, the Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office said a 40-year-old woman was driving a 2026 Toyota Camry north on Route 11 (Bakerstown Road) when she crossed the center line and hit the oncoming 2019 Ram pickup truck in the area of 700 Bakerstown Road.
The woman driving the Camry died. A passenger in her car was taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston with what police said were minor injuries.
The driver of the truck, a 63-year-old man from Ohio, was treated for minor injuries at the scene. A passenger in the truck was not hurt.
Police did not release the names of any of the people involved on Sunday because they were still notifying family members.
Part of Route 11 was closed for more than four hours while police investigated.
The cause of the crash was still being determined on Sunday evening.

title: Viral boater explains why he rode out Hurricane Isaias on sailboat
text:
DAUPHIN ISLAND, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — Videos of a man riding out Hurricane Isaias aboard a sailboat off Dauphin Island, Alabama, sparked questions across social media, with many wondering why someone would choose to remain on the water as the storm approached the Gulf Coast.
Ethan Warren said his experience living on the water for six years helped shape his decision to stay aboard his 22-foot sailboat near the east end of Dauphin Island.
Warren, originally from Texas, said he has weathered several major storms along the Gulf Coast.
“I’ve already been through two or three hurricanes that have had 100 mile an hour-plus winds, so I felt confident that my anchoring was going to be secure and so I decided to ride the storm out,” Warren said.
Authorities warned of dangers
Authorities warned Warren about the dangers of remaining on the water as Hurricane Isaias approached, including the threat of hurricane-force winds and dangerous storm surge along the coast.
Warren said he had backup plans in place in case his boat’s anchoring system failed.
“In case things went wrong, I had backup plans. So, I always had, in case the anchor came loose or something, I had another anchor in the back of the boat to throw for safety,” Warren said.
Checks from authorities
Although his decision drew attention online, Warren said he appreciated that authorities checked on him while he remained aboard the sailboat.
“I was still glad someone was there, had my back if anything went wrong,” Warren said.
Warren’s decision to ride out the storm on the water surprised many viewers, but he said his previous hurricane experience, preparations and confidence in his anchoring system factored into his choice.
Emergency officials routinely urge boaters to seek safe shelter before a hurricane arrives because conditions on the water can become dangerous quickly.

title: Robert Granger for District Attorney for Hancock and Washington Counties
text:
This is one of those county races that sometimes you stare at in the voting booth and think, “Who are these people?”
But, even if you or yours do not interact directly with the criminal justice system in the next four years, you need to be informed about this election.
District Attorney is a job with significant power and consequence and it is our responsibility to our communities to elect someone with experience, integrity, respect for the rule of law, and who understands the difference between prosecuting a case to win and prosecuting a case to secure a just outcome. Many years past I worked in that office.
Bob Granger took the helm at a troubled District Attorney’s office four years ago and has worked hard, with considerable success, to move it forward in a positive and productive way.
Bob left a respected decades-long private practice-concentrating in part on criminal law-to step into this. I’d be willing to bet he took a cut in pay to do it.
He has been successful in obtaining increased levels of staffing in the face of an inherited backload of cases. The backload has been substantially reduced even while availability of trial judges in the county has been limited.
He now has a staff with a combined total prosecutorial experience of 155 years.
The deep experience includes areas such as financial crimes, drunk driving, retail theft, child pornography and other computer-related crimes. This level of experience is exceptional in this type of office that is often seen as a stepping-stone for young lawyers. That pipeline is important too, so he has developed a formal internship program for both law students and local college students. He provides important ongoing professional development opportunities for his staff.
He and his staff have obtained numerous significant serious crime convictions.
Bob has been vigilant to ensure the integrity the system of criminal justice in his District. He expects everyone, starting with arresting police officers, to act with honesty. He has personally blocked four officers from testifying in active cases in which he had grounds to believe those standards had been breached.
Bob has earned trust and respect for his work on our behalf and deserves to be re-elected.
Unfortunately, the perennially losing candidate for DA, Steve Juskewitch, is once again on the ballot. If my math is right, a couple years ahead of me in law school, he would now be in his late 70s. This is the seventh time has tried to be elected. Always expressing a very “conservative” political outlook, he first tried running as a Republican. Failing that, he tried running as a Democrat. Not able to find a home in either party, he has settled on running repeatedly as an unenrolled candidate.
Like all times previously, a look at his record of behavior suggests that he is not a suitable candidate.
Mr. Juskewitch writes of himself in glowing terms and is good at putting out signs for himself, but the reality of his capabilities has always been more troubling.
He makes much of his prior National Guard experience and how the leadership skills he learned and employed there still serve him well.
Those of us who have been around a while will remember he was an officer in the Guard decades ago when he was elected to Mount Desert’s school board. He was so singularly disruptive, dismissive of reasonable boundaries, education laws and policies and so damaging to the functioning of the schools that within months of his election the town meet in an unprecedented-and to date unrepeated-special town meeting to remove him from the board. Those unfortunate enough to have witnessed his behavior have to wonder how the lessons of leadership in the National Guard failed him so utterly in such a modest forum as a small town school board but are somehow, all this time later, an asset as he seeks an office of much more consequential impact. And his expressed willingness to flout state education law and local policies is hard to overlook in a candidate for the head of our local criminal justice system.
Mr. Juskewitch’s reputation as both a former prosecutor and a defense lawyer has been far less stellar than he reports. And he has repeatedly been reprimanded by the State Board of Bar Overseers for conduct violative of his duties as a lawyer. The behavior he was sanctioned for suggests that basic traits that led him to fail so spectacularly as a school board member are transferrable skills.
I do not know the current mood in the District Attorney’s office about his candidacy, but in numerous prior races significant percentages of staff, including experienced prosecutors, have explicitly spoken of resigning rather than work for him. A vote for Mr. Juskewitch is a vote to risk weakening the top of the entire criminal justice system in Hancock and Washington Counties.
We should all hope for his sake as well as ours that this is Mr. Juskewitch’s swan song on our ballots.
Gail Marshall is a resident of Mount Desert.

title: Viral boater explains why he rode out Hurricane Isaias on sailboat
text:
DAUPHIN ISLAND, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — Videos of a man riding out Hurricane Isaias aboard a sailboat off Dauphin Island, Alabama, sparked questions across social media, with many wondering why someone would choose to remain on the water as the storm approached the Gulf Coast.
Ethan Warren said his experience living on the water for six years helped shape his decision to stay aboard his 22-foot sailboat near the east end of Dauphin Island.
Warren, originally from Texas, said he has weathered several major storms along the Gulf Coast.
“I’ve already been through two or three hurricanes that have had 100 mile an hour-plus winds, so I felt confident that my anchoring was going to be secure and so I decided to ride the storm out,” Warren said.
Authorities warned of dangers
Authorities warned Warren about the dangers of remaining on the water as Hurricane Isaias approached, including the threat of hurricane-force winds and dangerous storm surge along the coast.
Warren said he had backup plans in place in case his boat’s anchoring system failed.
“In case things went wrong, I had backup plans. So, I always had, in case the anchor came loose or something, I had another anchor in the back of the boat to throw for safety,” Warren said.
Checks from authorities
Although his decision drew attention online, Warren said he appreciated that authorities checked on him while he remained aboard the sailboat.
“I was still glad someone was there, had my back if anything went wrong,” Warren said.
Warren’s decision to ride out the storm on the water surprised many viewers, but he said his previous hurricane experience, preparations and confidence in his anchoring system factored into his choice.
Emergency officials routinely urge boaters to seek safe shelter before a hurricane arrives because conditions on the water can become dangerous quickly.

title: Here’s how Susan Collins secured my vote
text:
My wife is French, holds an EU passport and has multiple advanced degrees in engineering. She applied for a green card to live and work permanently in Maine. Immigration officials instructed us to wait until we received further notice. We heard nothing.
My wife was forced to repeatedly renew her driver’s license and carry a substantial file of immigration documents with her when traveling. We contacted Sen. Susan Collins’ office. Her staff investigated the situation to discover that the paperwork was sent to Portland, Oregon, not Portland, Maine. Their intervention finally moved the process forward.
Today, my wife owns her own engineering LLC and works as an independent contractor on advanced engineering projects in Maine and across the country. She’s contributing her education and professional experience to the U.S. economy — all made possible because of the assistance we received from Sen. Collins and her staff.
That is what effective representation looks like. And that is why Susan Collins has my vote this November.
Mark Zimmer
South Berwick

title: Short but sweet: Word festival keynote to feature short-story masters Shattuck and Link
text:
BLUE HILL — Blue Hill’s literary arts festival, Word, will run from Oct. 22-25, celebrating its 10th anniversary, and for the first time since its founding, the keynote discussion will focus on the short story.
Ben Shattuck and Kelly Link, both masters of the form, will be in conversation at The Bay School on Friday, Oct. 23, at 7 p.m.
Shattuck’s collection “The History of Sound” won the 2025 Mark Twain American Voice in Literature Award. He also wrote the screenplay for the movie based on the collection’s title story, as well as the memoir collection “Six Walks: In the Footsteps of Henry David Thoreau.”
Link is the author of award-winning fantasy stories and the successful debut novel “The Book of Love.” A 2018 MacArthur Fellow, she is the author of five story collections beloved by fantasy fans, a press release said.
On Thursday, Oct. 22, the annual “Word.Art” show will open at the Cynthia Winings Gallery from 5-7 p.m. and be up through the weekend.
The show will feature art created by writers or referencing words or books. Artists include Stu Kestenbaum, Susan Webster, Robert Shetterly, Shanna Compton, Marechal Brown and poet Josh Krugman, who will read at 6 p.m. “Word.Art” will also be shown at the Blue Hill Co-op Café during October.
Programs for youths co-sponsored by the Blue Hill Public Library are planned for Saturday. For the young crowd, Afton Cyrus, founder of The Reader’s Kitchen, will read aloud Eric Carle’s “The Very Hungry Caterpillar” and teach 2-5-year-olds and their caregivers how to make fruit skewers based on the book at 10 a.m.
For teens and tweens, Erich Bensheimer, Nick Berry, Brittany Courtot and Tim Peper will present a workshop on “How to Be a Dungeon Master” from 2-4 p.m.
The annual Saturday Poetry Crawl through Blue Hill from 2:30-5:10 p.m. will feature current Maine Poet Laureate Dawn Porter as well as former state laureate Kestenbaum and Maine poets Maya Stein, Moon Machar and Gibson Fay-LeBlanc.
Word’s Saturday night feature will be a conversation with Michelle Young, author of “The Art Spy: The Extraordinary Untold Tale of WWII Resistance Hero Rose Valland,” honored as a Best Book of 2025 by the New York Public Library and others.
Valland, curator of the Jeu de Paume art museum in Paris during the German occupation, is credited with recovering more than 60,000 artworks the Nazis stole from Jewish owners. Young will speak with journalist Alicia Anstead in the Blue Hill Congregational Church at 7 p.m.
On Sunday at 1 p.m. at BHPL, Caroline Bicks, author of “Monsters in the Archives: My Year of Fear with Stephen King,” will discuss the ideas behind her new book with Laura Miller, Slate books and culture columnist.
Porter will be featured again at a 4 p.m. Sunday celebration combining poetry and dance at The Bay School with Gretchen Berg, Teresa Carson and Gwyneth Jones.
Except for workshops, all author events are free and open to the public.

title: Carolyn Gage to read 'You Don't Know Maine'
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — On Tuesday, Oct. 20, from 5:30-7 p.m., there will be a reading of Carolyn Gage’s play, “You Don’t Know Maine: A Community Conversation,” at the Southwest Harbor Public Library. This program will be presented in-person with online viewing available. Following the reading, Pamela Gagnon da Silva, Licensed Clinical Professional Counselor, will lead a talk-back session.

title: High school robotics students modify 6-volt toy cars for children with mobility challenges
text:
High school robotics students modify battery-powered toy cars for children with challenges
Nearly 100 high school robotics students gathered Saturday morning in Kansas City to adapt toy cars for children with mobility challenges, creating opportunities for independence and play.
"We have a responsibility to make a real change in our community," said Emily Smith, team captain of FRC Team 1939.
The event, called Go Baby Go, was sponsored by Variety KC, which donated the cars for the students to modify.
"The freedom, just the independence. Everybody wants to do something on their own and be able to move and go forward and play with their siblings," said Joanna Long of Variety KC.
The initiative also aimed to teach students valuable lessons.
"I hope they learn how to design with empathy, build things with empathy, and think of other people," said Bree Pusey, Barstow robotics coach.
The students worked to refit small, 6-volt toy cars for mobility, benefiting children like Eliz.
"He doesn't have the opportunity to play like regular kids, so for him to sit here and be able to get a car and play with his siblings and have some sense of independence means a lot to us," said Adriana Johnson, Eliz's mother.
High school robotics students from nine area schools built seven different cars during the event.
"Every kid is unique, and each unique kid has their own unique circumstances," Smith said.
Johnson expressed her excitement about what the modified car would mean for her family.
"They made a life-changing situation independently run over siblings and everything, so it's gonna be a good thing for us. I'm excited," Johnson said.

title: "Massive shellfish die-offs continue" along Maine coast due to red tide
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
"Massive shellfish die-offs continue" along Maine coast due to red tide
The massive algae bloom along the Maine coast is starting to dissipate, at least in some areas, but the severe impacts continue to grow.
The Friends of Casco Bay says it, along with several other groups and the state, has been monitoring the Karenia mikimotoi bloom, commonly known as red tide, in Casco Bay for over a month.
The dense blooms that were present throughout September discolored the water, lowered dissolved oxygen levels, and caused die-offs of marine organisms, particularly soft-shell clams and marine worms.
In late September, testing found high-density blooms near Harpswell. High-density blooms are generally considered those having a density of more than one million cells per liter. Testing in Maine at the time found a density of 20 million cells per liter. Video shared by Harpswell Marine Resources & Harbor Management showed very brown and murky water.
In Casco Bay, the Friends of Casco Bay said on Friday that the bloom is still present but appears to be dissipating. The Maine Department of Marine Resources reports that Karenia cell counts are declining in inner Casco Bay, although some areas continue to have very low oxygen.
"We are still seeing massive shellfish die-offs. Last week, Casco Baykeeper Ivy Frignoca surveyed Maquoit Bay in Brunswick by airboat and found white bacterial mats and extensive soft-shell clam die-offs. Meanwhile, Mike Doan has been keeping an eye on pH and dissolved oxygen levels, both of which are still low," Friends said.
The algae is not dangerous to humans and the state says it is still safe to eat shellfish and fish harvested from Maine waters. However, Maquoit Bay and the eastern side of Middle Bay remain closed to shellfish harvesting, due to concerns about additional stress on the shellfish.
Friends of Casco Bay says its science team plans to collect sediment samples to learn more about what is happening below the surface.
On Sept. 8, sampling confirmed the presence of Karenia mikimotoi in Portland Harbor at levels known to affect fish and shellfish.
On Sept. 10, Harpswell Harbormaster Darcie Couture told Maine's Total Coverage she had received reports of dead and dying clams and worms from clam harvesters.
She said this problem could impact shellfish harvesting in Harpswell for two years.

title: How candidates for Maine governor say they’ll fill a projected $1B budget gap
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s next governor will face the early challenge of proposing a balanced state budget, and a projected hole of more than $1 billion may complicate that task.
The periodic fiscal forecast, which state officials released Sept. 30, predicts a General Fund gap of $1.085 billion and a Highway Fund gap of $256.7 million for the next two-year budget running from the middle of 2027 through the middle of 2029. The governor who succeeds Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, must present a balanced budget proposal to state lawmakers by February before the Legislature seeks to pass a plan that kicks in July 1, 2027.
Under state law, the budget bureau within the Department of Administrative and Financial Services completes the Four-Year Revenue and Expenditure Forecast every other year. The projected gap represents how much estimated revenue is falling short of what existing statutes require the state to spend. These mandatory expenditures include maintaining state support for 55% of K-12 education costs, 5% spending on municipal revenue sharing and pensions for retired teachers.
Finance Commissioner Elaine Clark noted that “many of the funding obligations considered in the report are, with Legislative approval, routinely not met” and that the report should only serve as a “starting point” for lawmakers as they begin budget discussions rather than “an accurate reflection of an actual budget shortfall facing State government.”
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the gubernatorial race over Republican Bobby Charles, a lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, and independent Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator.
Here’s what each candidate said when asked during Thursday evening’s debate about how they would fill a budget gap if elected governor. The debate was not the only time the candidates have discussed the budget, with the Portland Press Herald’s Voter Guide among the other places to review their policy plans.
Republican Bobby Charles
Charles, 66, began his budget answer by alluding to how Pingree led the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025, criticizing the Democratic candidate as “the right hand of the governor that put us in all these problem sets.”
“It’s like inviting the arsonist back to put out the fire,” Charles said of electing Pingree.
However, the budget problems are not unique to the outgoing Mills administration. The finance department previously noted that aside from 2022, each report since 2014 had projected a structural gap.
These gaps have occurred under past governors of independent, Republican and Democratic stripes. The projected deficit was also around $1 billion when then-Gov. Angus King, an independent who is now in the U.S. Senate, left office in 2003 and Democratic Gov. John Baldacci took over.
Still, Charles said, the state needs to cut down on its spending. As part of his previously stated plan to ultimately slash $4 billion from the state budget, which is currently near $12 billion, and phase out the income tax, Charles said he would first nix at least $1 billion “by reducing the fraud” as well as eliminating sole source contracts.
He referred to fraud to the tune of $2.1 billion in Maine, though that appeared to reference State Auditor Matt Dunlap’s annual audit in 2024 that noted “deficiencies” and “material weaknesses” involving $2.1 billion in federal spending.
Charles said he would cut 2,000 unfilled state jobs, implement an immediate hiring freeze and order a “top-to-bottom review” of all state agencies while “restructuring” the education and health departments. He would task each commissioner with trimming department costs by 10%.
“None of this, by the way, has any effect on services,” Charles said. “It only makes us more efficient.”
He also argued for ending the process known as the “cascade,” in which unspent surplus General Fund money is transferred at the end of each fiscal year to different areas, such as the Highway Fund.
Charles ended his response with another dig at Pingree. He said he would eliminate the governor’s policy office that oversees housing, climate, economic and other initiatives — which Pingree used to lead.
Democrat Hannah Pingree
Pingree, 49, started her answer by blaming President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war for putting “huge headwinds on our economy,” and she criticized cuts to Medicaid and food benefits in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
She mentioned getting first elected to the Legislature in 2002 and serving on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee when lawmakers and Baldacci faced the roughly $1 billion shortfall. She touted her work with Republicans to pass bipartisan, balanced budgets, including working with then-Republican floor leader Josh Tardy when she was the Maine House speaker from 2008 to 2010.
But Pingree remained light on specifics to fill a budget gap, other than saying she would double the homestead exemption to $50,000 and amend the Maine Constitution to tax second homes that non-Maine residents own in the state at a higher rate.
That second idea from Pingree looks unlikely to pass in the near future, given it would take a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers to amend the Maine Constitution that currently requires all property to be taxed equally per its true value.
Dan Pittman, a Maine Revenue Services lawyer, confirmed to lawmakers last month that such a proposal, or policies like Rhode Island’s “Taylor Swift” tax on empty vacation homes, are not allowed in Maine without a constitutional change.
Charles and Bennett said they disagree with Pingree’s proposal. Pingree acknowledged the hurdles facing her plan but doubled down on pursuing it.
“That is a big thing to do, but we’ve amended our constitution many, many times before, and it would require bipartisan support,” Pingree said. “But I’ll tell you, from Washington County down to southern Maine, people realize that Maine people are having a hard time keeping their home.”
Independent Rick Bennett
Bennett, 63, kicked off his answer by warning about the growth in the state budget over the past decade and how the Mills administration pushed federal money for COVID-19 pandemic relief “out the front door.” He criticized the Legislature for not holding a true public hearing on the continuing services budget that funds baseline services in six years.
“We are spending, in the state government, well beyond the means of Mainers to pay,” Bennett said. “That’s a reality. We need some fiscal prudence.”
If elected, Bennett said, he would put together a finance team the day after the Nov. 3 election to look at every line in the state budget, and he said he would return to the Legislature’s former tradition of passing budgets with at least two-thirds support.
To avoid devoting state dollars to paying back the federal government for potential fiscal issues, Bennett said his office would have an inspector general team that investigates potential misspending or corruption.

title: Maine should expect an early flu season, experts say
text:
Maine could experience an early peak of influenza cases this flu season, public health experts said, urging residents to not delay getting immunized.
“We are seeing the beginnings of influenza circulating earlier than we have had in recent seasons, said Anna Krueger, an epidemiologist with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
While flu season runs from October to May, typically cases crest in late December, January or February. Cases peaked around the winter holidays during last flu season, with a high of 1,347 reported for the week ending Jan. 3, according to Maine CDC data.
So far this flu season, Maine has recorded 104 cases through Oct. 3, compared to 36 for the same time period in 2025.
During the 2023-24 and 2024-25 flu seasons, cases in Maine peaked in February, while in 2022-23, influenza crested in mid-December. Sometimes, Maine is hit with a second wave of flu cases in March or April. But Krueger said if cases peak early, that does not mean Maine is more likely to get a second wave.
Krueger said with the early uptick in cases, this season’s flu could peak here in November, which is why they are urging people to not wait to get their flu shot. Krueger said they worry that influenza could surge before many people have received their annual shot.
What Maine is seeing coincides with the U.S., which is also expecting an early flu season, experts say. Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, told National Public Radio last week that the nation should anticipate flu to arrive sooner this season.
The flu shot — recommended for everyone 6 months and older — is currently widely available at pharmacies, primary care providers, clinics and many healthcare settings. It is typically free, even for those without insurance.
Krueger said the flu shot appears to be a good match for circulating strains of the virus, which currently is influenza A. That means this year’s shot should be especially effective against the most common strain. Scientists update the flu shot every year, and try to match what they anticipate will be the season’s circulating strains.
Dr. Dora Anne Mills, chief health improvement officer for MaineHealth, advised Maine residents to get their flu shots now because signs are pointing to an early onset of cases.
“I usually wait until mid- to late-October, but I didn’t wait this year. I got my flu shot already,” Mills said.
Mills said a higher-dose flu shot is recommended for those 65 and older.
Mills said it’s also a good idea to get COVID-19 and influenza vaccines during the same appointment. The COVID-19 vaccine is updated every year to match mutations in the virus.
She said some may be afraid of worse side effects if getting both at the same time, but there’s “no evidence” that receiving both vaccines at the same appointment results in more side effects.
COVID-19 levels are currently considered “very low” in Maine, according to state data.

title: Hayden Panettiere’s ex Wladimir Klitschko gets legal status to protect their daughter’s inheritance
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Hayden Panettiere’s ex-fiancé, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal authority by a California court Thursday to protect Panettiere’s property for their 11-year-old daughter after the television star’s accidental overdose death left the girl as her sole heir.
Klitschko had filed the urgent petition last week, saying that pieces of Panettiere’s property were being taken by federal law enforcement agents investigating her death and by an unnamed nonfamily member looking to sell them, with no one in a position to try to recover them for her daughter.
Klitschko, a Ukrainian former world champion boxer, has had full custody of the girl, Kaya, for most of her life, and she has lived with him in Ukraine. The father and daughter appeared in Los Angeles County court remotely via videoconference. They spoke only to introduce themselves at the brief hearing with only Kaya visible on camera, sitting at a table in front of curtains.
Judge Stephanie Santoro granted Klitschko the status of temporary guardian of Kaya’s estate until a long-term administrator can be appointed.
Santoro asked Klitschko’s lawyer, Diane Park, why the matter was urgent. Park said they believed a person described only as a nonrelative had taken items after Panettiere’s death and had tried to sell some of her jewelry at a pawn shop. And she said assets were in danger of going unaccounted for during the death investigation. Court documents said authority was needed to deal with both the pawnshop owner and police agencies. Panettiere’s taxes also need to be filed this month, the lawyer said. Santoro, satisfied with the explanation, approved the move.
Panettiere, the former star of the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 16 at age 36 after paramedics found her unresponsive. A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl. She had been in rehab just weeks before. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.
Park told Santoro that the property, the pawnshop and the nonfamily member were in Los Angeles County, where the judge’s ruling held authority. Park declined to comment outside the courtroom.
Klitschko’s Sept. 24 petition emphasized that his intention is solely to protect his daughter’s future assets until a permanent administrator can be put in place.
“There is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden’s Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated,” the document said.
The filing said that before her death, Panettiere and Klitschko hired security to protect her home because an unnamed person had gained unauthorized access, and it’s expected the same person would continue to try to “misappropriate” her property.
Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, filed a document saying she consented to Klitschko being appointed.
Klitschko, 50, an Olympic gold medalist, held several heavyweight titles between 2000 and 2015. He and Panettiere began dating in 2009 and got engaged in 2013.
His older brother Vitali, also a former champion boxer, is mayor of Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. The two brothers, sons of a Soviet major general, have been prominent public figures in Ukraine during its war with Russia.
In her memoir released earlier this year, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter’s birth in 2014. Kaya went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2. Panettiere’s father told investigators that when she died she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later.

title: Grandmother burned in fire pit explosion dies a day before her 59th birthday
text:
PRESCOTT VALLEY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona grandmother died days after suffering catastrophic burns when her boyfriend allegedly poured gasoline on a fire, causing an explosion.
Tammy Dodson and her boyfriend were sitting around a fire pit Sept. 24 with Dodson’s sister, Tara Carl, in their backyard in Prescott Valley. Carl says the fire pit was a smaller, elevated metal pit.
As the fire began to dwindle, Carl says her sister’s boyfriend grabbed a gas can and poured it on the fire to try to reignite it. She says this caused an explosion that shot the gas can onto a neighbor’s roof and engulfed Dodson in flames.
Dodson spent 10 days intubated at a Phoenix burn center with burns covering her body before she died last Sunday, the day before her 59th birthday.
“I’m very angry. She should not have been taken from us the way she was,” Carl said.
Victim was a mother, grandmother and healthcare worker
Dodson was a mother, grandmother and a beloved healthcare worker, her family says. She leaves behind two children and three young grandchildren, who she adored.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help her family with memorial costs and medical bills associated with the incident.
“Tammy truly was the light of our family. She was vibrant, beautiful, loving, and had a way of bringing so much life wherever she went. She was a mom, a grandma, a sister, and an aunt, and a friend to so many,” the family wrote on GoFundMe.
Dodson’s family says they are traumatized by what happened.
“I don’t want anybody ever to throw gasoline or igniting sources onto fires,” Carl said. “That’s just beyond my comprehension. It’s just beyond it.”
Investigation continues
Prescott Valley Police confirmed the incident allegedly happened while someone tried to reignite a fire pit. They said a man on the property was injured as well but was not taken to the hospital.
The investigation is ongoing.
Dodson’s death was ruled accidental due to “complications of thermal injuries,” according to the Maricopa County Medical Examiner’s Office. However, the report is not yet complete.

title: ‘She’s got a knife!’: Service members save 2 girls whose mother allegedly tried to kill them
text:
PIERCE COUNTY, Wash. (KOMO) - A group of service members is being credited with saving two girls after investigators say their mother tried to kill them on a Washington state interstate.
Army Sgt. 1st Class Jeff Hytower is a practical nursing specialist who helps train other soldiers at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Pierce County. He says the lessons he teaches in the classroom are ones people need to be ready to use.
“I’m a soldier first, but then, I’m a nurse second, too. So, I just want people to be safe, right? I picture people being like my family. So, I want to make sure everyone gets home safe,” he said.
Hytower and another soldier, Sgt. Ricardo Nunez, were driving on Interstate 5 last Monday morning when they saw a serious crash in the opposite direction and stopped to help. The crash involved 35-year-old mother Janieka Ellington and her two daughters, ages 9 and 15.
Sgt. Alexis McKay, a Washington National Guard combat medic, was also among those who stopped to help. She was checking on one of the children when she heard someone screaming that Ellington had a knife and was going after her 15-year-old daughter.
“The most senior of us yells very, very loudly, ‘She’s got a knife!’” McKay said.
Hytower and Nunez quickly stopped Ellington, disarming her and restraining her until help arrived.
“I just jumped up. It was just insane,” Hytower said. “That’s when training kicks in. That’s when everything that we do with soldiers kicks in, and it was more of a reaction than anything.”
Court records state Ellington was reportedly drinking heavily Sunday night before the crash. She allegedly had suicidal thoughts, believed that someone was after the family and that they were going to die. Investigators with the Washington State Patrol say she purposely crashed her car into a concrete barrier on I-5 before trying to kill her teenage daughter.
A judge ordered Ellington to undergo a mental health evaluation as she faces multiple counts of attempted murder and vehicular assault. She is being held without bail and is due back in court later this month.
Both of her daughters were hospitalized with injuries from the crash and the attempted stabbing but have since been released to the care of hospital social workers. Investigators were working to connect with other family members in the area and out of state.
For his part, Hytower says he has no regrets about stepping in.
“Don’t regret it. I would do it two times on Sunday. Just make sure everybody’s OK. Because again, at the end of the day, I just want to make sure everybody’s safe,” he said.
Nunez echoes that sentiment.
“I am glad I was there to help those girls and was just in the right place at the right time. I am also very glad the other two [soldiers] were there and that we were able to work together,” he said.

title: 'Breaking Bad' Star RJ Mitte Dead at 34
text:
‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte Dead at 34 After Championing Disability Awareness
RJ Mitte, the actor best known for playing Walter “Flynn” White Jr. on Breaking Bad, has died. He was 34.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his representative confirmed in a statement to Page Six on Monday (Oct. 12).
Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at age 3 and used his platform to advocate for greater disability awareness and representation.
How Did RJ Mitte Die?
According to TMZ, which first reported the news, Mitte died by suicide on Monday. A county official confirmed to the outlet that the actor died in Texas and that the death investigation is ongoing.
Read More: ‘Breaking Bad’ Named Best TV Show of 21st Century
His representative asked the public to respect the privacy of Mitte’s family and loved ones during this time.
RJ Mitte Was a Disability Rights Advocate
Mitte brought personal experience to his role as Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston’s character on AMC’s acclaimed crime drama Breaking Bad.
Like his character, the actor has cerebral palsy, helping bring authentic representation of the disability to the screen.
Beyond his acting career, Mitte was a passionate advocate for people with disabilities. He served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, as well as a Screen Actors Guild spokesperson for actors with disabilities.
He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives while working to challenge stereotypes and promote inclusion.
Breaking Bad ran for five seasons from 2008 to 2013 and became one of television’s most celebrated dramas.
If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-TALK (8255) or text the Crisis Text Line at 741741.

title: Collins, King join senators opposing Russian diesel purchase plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (WABI) - Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King have joined a bipartisan group of senators in speaking out against plans to purchase diesel from Russia.
The senators are calling on the Trump administration to immediately reverse course on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Bipartisan senators issue joint statement
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” the senators said in a statement. “Congress was clear: The U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies. President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course.”
Collins and King issue separate statements
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia. I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following,” Collins said in a statement to WABI.
King issued his own statement on the plan.
“Americans nationwide are struggling with the cost-of-living – from prices at the pump to the cost of essentials at the grocery story – mostly due to Trump’s unconstitutional war in Iran and his devastating tariffs on our long-standing allies,” King said in the statement. “Instead of pursuing solutions that are consistent with America’s values, President Trump has decided to ease energy sanctions on Russia. In doing so, he chose Putin over the American people, which will ultimately help fuel that autocracy’s bloody, unprovoked war of aggression on Ukraine.”
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. “To put this so-called deal into perspective, it amounts to 300,000 tons of diesel for October and then 500,000 for November – which may sound like a lot, but according to the administration’s own numbers is roughly the amount of diesel the American people use in a single day. This helps Russia far more than it helps the United States.”
“Adding insult to injury, today’s deal is a slap in the face to every member of Congress who voted for the Lindsay Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act just last month which was designed to honor the memory of a strong defender of democracy and punish the leaders of these rogue nations,” King said. “Every member of Congress who voted for this bill – 86 in the Senate, 262 in the House – should be demanding an immediate reversal of this decision.”
“At the end of the day, this deal from the White House is an attempt to boost their short-term political prospects at the true cost of the American people,” King said. “We are helping one adversary (though it’s questionable if the White House considers Putin that) and showing weakness to another due to Iran’s Strait of Hormuz oil blockade. This deal comforts our enemies and will do little for Americans. It’s a fraud.”

title: Trump says he is ‘looking at’ firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday he is “looking at” firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’re not happy.”
His comments came a day after The Associated Press, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and will likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including making an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, but in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations,” they said.
“Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction. We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action,” the lawyers said.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.
