title: Bethel Masonic Lodge grows its community footprint
text:
While the Freemasons may be viewed by some as a secretive fraternal organization, they have long been community minded.
The Bethel Masonic Lodge 30 is no exception, and its current members have greatly expanded their community service in the area in recent years.
The Masons have a long history dating back to the Middle Ages in Europe, where stone masons who worked primarily on cathedrals formed secret guilds to support each other. As cathedral building declined, the organization evolved into one that began accepting other members, and it became known publicly in the early 1700s. Its focus became less about the stone trade and more about the shared values of the members. Many of the secret early rituals and traditions of the members continued, but were given new meaning.
Men joined, then and now, said Bethel Master Gerry Martin, “because we take good men and make them better — better husbands, fathers, brothers and community members.”
Mike Rodney, a member since 2023 and the senior warden of the group, said those values are conveyed “based on symbols and allegory.”
For example, said Martin, two tools of the stone mason trade, a level and a square, are used now to teach how to treat others. The level symbolizes “that we meet on the level, that all are equal,” rather than based on social standing, he said. The square demonstrates “that we treat everyone squarely — fairly, honestly, a ‘square deal.'”
While those are basic concepts associated with the tools, there are many more details of teaching behind them. Those are part of what is kept confidential among members, along with traditional rituals. That confidentiality preserves the close bond and identity among the membership, Martin said, and is not intended to simply hide activities from outsiders.
The Bethel lodge, chartered in 1860, has 105 official members, though some are not active. Martin said about 20 are very active, with the organization having a core of about 10 who handle routine business. There is a wide age range, though many are of retirement age. A recent new young member is Rodney’s son, Aidan, who joined last year.
A man who wishes to join is initiated as an apprentice, taking an oath to keep the rituals and other key traditions in confidence. He progresses through study and discussion to the level of Fellowcraft and finally Master Mason, usually over the course of about three months, Martin said.
COMMUNITY OUTREACH
The Bethel Masons have served the community for years. For example, in August they held their annual public breakfast the morning of MollyOckett Day.
But in recent years they have stepped up their service game.
“Our charitable work is greatly enhanced by the support of the Maine Masonic Charitable Foundation, which grants dollar-for-dollar matching grants to local nonprofits,” said Martin. “Those matching grants are generously funded at up to $5,000 per local lodge.”
He said the lodge is committed to using that to maximize its giving and expand its outreach. The result has been matching grant partnerships with local businesses and organizations.
Most significant so far, said Martin, is their cooperation with the Bethel Rotary Club, for whom they have provided volunteer labor to help with the club’s annual yard sale fundraiser.
That, said Martin, has enabled the Masons to meet the $5,000 matching grant goal.
The organization now supports the following community efforts through the grant funds and volunteer labor: Project Graduation, Mahoosuc Kids Association, NorthStar 4-H Leadership Program, Bethel Area District Exchange and Food Pantry, Meals for Maine, Christmas for Families, Chris’ Haven of Hope, Bikes for Books, and the Magic Lantern 4-H Innovation Center.
“This will be our most ambitious year to date,” said Martin.
For more information on the lodge or how to become a Mason, call Martin at 207-357-9681 or email [email protected], or reach out to any other Mason.
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: ‘Writing on the wall’: New reports highlight history of red flags before toddlers found dead
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — New documents are providing insight into the month leading up to the deaths of two toddlers in South Carolina.
Two-year-old Emory and 1-year-old Harlow Deacon were found starved to death last week at their Ladson home. Their mother, 31-year-old Justine May, was arrested and charged with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
Zachary Deacon—the father of Emory and Harlow—told deputies the writing was on the wall a month before they were found dead.
WCSC has received copies of five additional reports between Aug. 10 and Sept. 29 detailing the calls for concern Deacon made that ultimately led to his arrest.
According to reports, Deacon and May had just ended their eight-year relationship at the beginning of August. The pair had been engaged for the last five of those years and lived together with their two children.
Deputies were called out for a domestic disturbance on Aug. 10.
May accused Deacon of trying to block her car from leaving while Deacon told deputies she was having a mental health episode. No evidence of a mental health crisis was found, according to the reports.
More than two weeks later, Deacon called deputies to do a welfare check, telling them May had been acting unusually and had stopped communicating with family.
He said he discovered disturbing writing on the wall the last time he watched the children days earlier. May told deputies it was Deacon who wrote the disturbing message on the wall. The message itself is redacted from the incident reports.
Authorities found the kids asleep and—again—no evidence of mental health problems.
On Sept. 11, deputies were called again, this time by May’s mother, reporting a mental health crisis in progress. Deputies and the Department of Social Services went to the home and found it clean, the kids happy and “well-fed.”
May then presented deputies with call logs, text messages and screenshots showing Deacon consistently reaching out to her.
Deacon’s messages accused her of “spiraling,” and he told her to “get a grip on reality.” She said Deacon would occasionally patrol the neighborhood as well.
Deputies determined that was enough to issue an arrest warrant for harassment. The next day they met with Deacon and arrested him.
That was Sept. 12, the last day the sheriff’s office said they saw the kids alive.
At some point, deputies were instructed to no longer do welfare checks at May’s home, but they were out there several times between the 12th and the 29th when the kids were discovered.

title: Maine lobstermen’s defamation lawsuit against California aquarium dismissed by appeals court
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BOSTON, Massachusetts (WMTW/WABI) - A federal appeals court has ordered the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit that was brought by the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and four other groups against the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California.
The lawsuit was filed in March 2023 after Seafood Watch, a conservation program operated by the aquarium, placed lobster from the United States and Canada on its do-not-eat “red list” in 2022 because lobster fishing gear poses an entanglement risk to the endangered North Atlantic right whale. The recommendation prompted some retailers, including Whole Foods, to pull lobster from stores.
The lobster fishing industry pushed back against Seafood Watch’s claim, saying it inaccurately portrayed fishing gear as a threat to North Atlantic right whales and constituted defamation that has caused economic harm. The industry claimed that the whales face greater threats from other fishing industries, including the Canadian snow crab fishery.
The Monterey Bay Aquarium made an attempt to have the lawsuit tossed in U.S. District Court in Maine, but Judge John Woodcock ruled in February 2025 that the lawsuit could move forward.
The aquarium then filed an appeal with the Boston-based First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals. During oral arguments held on July 27, one of the appellate judges said that the lawsuit did not strike him as a defamation claim and that he found the case troubling “from a First Amendment perspective.”
“The more you broaden the class of people that fall within this, the more it feels like everybody can sue,” said Judge Seth Aframe.
In a ruling handed down Friday, the First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals reversed the U.S. District Court’s denial of the aquarium’s motion to dismiss. The appeals court said that Seafood Watch’s comments did not target specific members of a group, which is required under the so-called “group defamation rule.” The matter has been remanded to the district court with instructions to dismiss the complaint.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association responded to the decision, saying in part: “The court dismissed our case, but it did not validate the Aquarium’s claims about Maine lobster. Those are two very different things. The ruling did not address MLA’s allegations that the Aquarium’s false claims have harmed Maine’s lobster fishery.”
MLA Executive Director Patrice McCarron went on to say, “Consumers can feel proud choosing Maine lobster, a product brought to market in keeping with a long history of responsible stewardship and a strong commitment to right whale conservation.”
The groups that joined the Maine Lobstermen’s Association in the lawsuit were wholesaler Bean Maine Lobster, the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association, Maine Lobster and Processing, and Maine lobster fishing company Bug Catcher.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home as part of criminal investigation, per report
text:
Omar says she won't 'be silenced’ by search of her home and blasts Trump’s 'intimidation' campaign
Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed scrutiny to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid.
Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called the search of her home the “latest escalation” in President Donald Trump’s "intimidation" campaign.
The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress and raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election.
The Justice Department confirmed in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area in connection with an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The nature and scope of the investigation were unclear, though officials in President Donald Trump's administration have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have repeatedly drawn criticism from Republicans and senior Trump officials.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that there was an “ongoing investigation” related in part to whether Omar lied on her immigration forms and that “something's going to happen.”
Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search of her home took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot for reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” top House Democratic leaders said in a statement. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.
Trump has frequently targeted Omar
Trump and fellow Republicans from the highest ranks of party leadership have repeatedly and publicly criticized the Somali-born Omar over her status as an immigrant to the U.S. and her left-wing views. Trump as recently as this past weekend brought up Omar at a rally in Tennessee, where he attacked her upbringing and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her.
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud — an allegation she has denied — and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate her.
The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area but provided no other details. The street was blocked off Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.
“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the department said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department.
Omar has long been a target for Republicans
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.
In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced recently to 14 months in prison.
Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies.”
“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime.”
In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.”
He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and “trying to look at what the remedies are.”
“That’s the thing that we’re trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she’s committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?”
Omar's office has defended her against past allegations
Omar’s office in March dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
“This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to ‘create stories’ to redirect the media,” Omar’s chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement.
“This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party’s unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers,” McNutt said at the time of the vice president’s allegations and comments.

title: InvestigateTV+: The case for moving school start times
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ examines the fight over the first bell; why experts say early start times can work against the teenage brain and why changing the schedule can be complicated for schools and families.
Plus, a diaper dilemma as soaring prices force some families to choose between necessities and the diaper banks and volunteers working to close the gap.
Shifting school start times could address teen sleep loss
School in many districts across the country begins before sunrise, a schedule doctors say runs counter to how teenage brains are wired to sleep.
School did not always start this early. During the 1950s and 1960s, U.S. schools started between 8:30 and 9 a.m. because most children could walk or bike to a neighborhood school.
With more research linking early start times to teen sleep loss, some communities are trying to move the clock forward.
The need for diapers
Diapers are a basic need for many families. Parents already dealing with rising costs for housing, food and transportation can find it hard to keep up with diaper costs.
According to a 2026 survey by the National Diaper Bank Network, nearly half of families, or one in two, struggled to pay for diapers.
A quarter of parents reported missing work or school because they could not afford the diapers required to leave their baby in childcare.
The virtual need for speed
A new racing simulator center has opened in Portland, giving drivers access to technology used to train professional racers.
Driving a racing simulator is harder than it looks, but in the e-sports industry, people who master sim racing are turning the skill into a career. E-sports, or competitive video gaming, has grown in popularity over the years, with sim racing gaining an engaged fan base.
From janitor to physician
In 2011, Shay Taylor-Allen was working as a janitor at Yale New Haven Hospital when she was 18.
She is now returning years later to the hospital as a resident physician.

title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ has already gotten under Elon Musk’s skin. It goes nationwide this week
text:
VENICE, Italy (AP) — Elon Musk has called filmmaker Alex Gibney a lot of names leading up to the theatrical release of the documentary “Musk,” which is playing in select theaters in New York and Los Angeles and expands nationwide on Friday.
Over the past few weeks, Musk has posted on X that Gibney is an “idiot,” a “horrible human,” a “shill for the far left,” and a “tinfoil hat crackpot” with “zero credibility.” When the documentary was announced three years ago, he called it a “hit piece.”
After its premiere at the Venice Film Festival last month, Musk wrote that dog feces are “worth more respect than Gibney.” The trillionaire has reportedly not yet seen the film and did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press.
Paid advertisements for ‘Musk’ are being rejected by X
The documentary is facing more than a war of words from Musk, however. The film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, has not been able to run paid advertisements on several major social media platforms. As of Sept. 25, YouTube, Meta, TikTok and X had all refused. YouTube, where the trailer had been available through regular channels, and Meta have since reversed course, saying that it had been flagged for “political content.”
There are also concerns about whether “Musk” will eventually land on HBO as originally planned in the aftermath of the Skydance merger, the new entertainment giant created by Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. CEO David Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, is friendly with Musk.
“Would Musk be able to call Larry or David and say, you know, don’t put this doc on? Yeah,” Gibney said in an interview with the AP. “We live in that world now, particularly a world that’s become so transactional in the political realm … it’s literally pay to play.”
There have been threats of lawsuits from Musk’s camp as well. But Gibney is also leaning into it, posting regularly on X from his own account and through a newly created one called @muskfilmfacts, which is actively dispelling false narratives and highlighting suspicions of suppressed content. Recently, Gibney wrote on X that his film is “about a ‘free-speech absolutist’ who has threatened a lawsuit to try to stop the film from being seen.”
The Oscar-winner learned from making his Scientology documentary “Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief” that the best way to fight back is to “not let them get inside your head.”
“We also have a lawyer who’s really, really good,” he said. “Because, of course, we vet this stuff very carefully.”
Musk did not sit for an interview with the filmmakers
Gibney spent nearly four years making the film, a sweeping portrait of the power and influence of the world’s richest man, charting his rise from his early days in Silicon Valley through SpaceX, Tesla and DOGE, the Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency that overhauled the federal workforce last year.
It runs nearly four hours and features on-camera interviews with Musk’s family, including his father Errol Musk, his first wife and another mother of one of his children, as well as journalists, business associates, former friends, colleagues and government officials.
The project became a “runaway story,” said Gibney, who was finalizing a two-hour cut when Musk endorsed Donald Trump following the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania. HBO leadership encouraged Gibney to keep going.
“I started out doing the film because it was about 21st century power,” Gibney said. “I didn’t have a sense at that time that he was literally going to accrete the power of a kind of shadow president. … But that’s what he did, so we had to follow that story where it went.”
Musk did not sit for an interview, so Gibney and his team did something a little unconventional: They made a computer-generated Musk that speaks directly to the camera. The image might be a visual effect, both flattering and a bit uncanny, but the voice and the words it says are all Musk’s own, taken directly from recordings of things he’s said in interviews and at public appearances. Gibney’s team used artificial intelligence to help sync the words to his mouth.
The lasers in space statement comes from a Musk text message
One of the sticking points for Musk and his supporters that has emerged since the film started screening for press and festival audiences has to do with “space lasers” and the 2024 U.S. presidential election.
The source is a text exchange between Musk and Ashley St. Clair, the mother of one of Musk’s children who provided the messages. Musk writes to her about feeling optimistic about Trump’s chances, and how he has “10,000 lasers in space right now.”
Its inclusion in the documentary has provided ammunition for Musk supporters and his lawyers to discredit the film, pointing to an unfounded conspiracy theory about SpaceX’s Starlink satellites interfering in the election. But neither the film, nor St. Clair, make that claim. It simply presents his text messages and lets the audience decide what to make of it.
St. Clair also provides an audio recording of Musk associate Jared Birchall trying to negotiate an NDA with her, on which parental support would be contingent, after she gave birth to their child. She said she turned down some $40 million to maintain her right to speak freely.
Free speech and the benefits of synthesizing information in a film
With attentions fractured in modern life, Gibney hopes there is some benefit in synthesizing information into a narrative. He’s also quick to credit the journalists whose work they draw upon.
The runtime might be longer than your average movie, but it’s an engaging watch. For the first 45 minutes, he said, “you’re kind of rooting for Elon.”
“He’s trying to get those rockets up in the air. Fails three times. He’s got that critical fourth launch, and you see those incredible images of the reusable rockets. It’s Elon at his best,” he said. “But then you have to ask the question, what happened?”
There is also a six-hour version, Gibney said. But they edited it down to stick to the most pressing information, including questions about the data gathered on U.S. citizens during Musk’s DOGE tenure.
“I hope that people will look at some of the stuff that we present in the film and then take it further,” he said. “You know, should there be an investigation in Congress about the data and what happened to the data? And is it sitting in a hard drive in SpaceX or Tesla?”
As for who he thinks the audience might be, he hopes that it’s not just Musk skeptics.
“If you’re in a cult and you assume that he’s your supreme leader, then maybe just like the folks in Scientology, you’ll criticize the film and you won’t see it,” Gibney said. “But if you’re intrigued by the guy, and even if you have some affection and admiration for his accomplishments, I would hope you go see it.”

title: 3 sue owner of Maine schooner after deadly mast break
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Four people have filed separate lawsuits against the owner of the schooner Grace Bailey for injuries they suffered during an October 2023 incident aboard the schooner that claimed the life of a doctor.
Katherine McCann, who now lives in Saint John’s, Newfoundland, filed a lawsuit Oct. 7 in U.S. District Court in Bangor against the schooner Grace Bailey and Grace Bailey Navigation Co. Inc. of Rockland.
Maureen Colvin of Scituate, Massachusetts, filed her lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Portland on Oct. 8.
Christopher and Diane Sarao of Lubec filed his lawsuit in federal court in Portland on Oct. 2. He filed an amended lawsuit on Oct. 9 and also named as defendants the schooner captain Samuel J. Sikkema; former owners Raymond Williamson and Ann Williamson; Michael F. Rogers, individually and doing business as Privateer Boatbuilding and who personally performed, directed or participated in the June 2014 repairs to the Grace Bailey’s mainmast and foremast and the associated assessment of the unrepaired portions of those masts through a repair operation known as Privateer Boatbuilding; and unnamed workers who worked on the vessel.
McCann was hired to perform music for the schooner for its final sail of the season, which was a fall foliage adventure.
On the schooner’s return to Rockland Harbor on Oct. 9, 2023, after a four-day sail, the schooner experienced a catastrophic mainmast failure whereby the mainmast split and collapsed on the deck. The mast struck McCann and four others, including Dr. Emily Mecklenburg, 40, of Rockland, who was declared dead when she was brought ashore by a Coast Guard boat following the accident.
McCann argues in her federal lawsuit that she was a seaman for purposes of the maritime law known as the Jones Act. McCann is a musician and her group Skylark had performed on the vessel.
McCann was brought ashore by the U.S. Coast Guard, and she received urgent/emergency treatment from Rockland Emergency Medical Services, LifeFlight of Maine and Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor. She subsequently received medical treatment from several medical and mental health providers.
Her lawsuit states she has received and continues to require medical treatment for her injuries, and continues to experience pain and suffering as a result of her injuries. McCann has incurred medical bills and expenses as a result of the medical treatment she received. Some of the injuries may have resulted in permanent impairments, according to the lawsuit. She has also missed work and lost earnings.
The lawsuit claims negligence on part of the Grace Bailey and that the vessel was unseaworthy.
McCann is represented by attorney Stephen W. Koerting of Portland.
Colvin and Christopher Sarao were also both injured when the mast struck them. Each is reporting serious injuries that continue.
Diane Sarao heard a loud crack from above, looked up, saw the mast split and begin to fall, screamed, dropped to and struck the deck, and covered her head with her hands. The sudden collapse of the mast and associated rigging onto the occupied deck placed Diane Sarao in immediate risk of traumatic physical harm and caused her reasonably to apprehend such harm, according to the lawsuit.
After the casualty, Diane Sarao remained in shock. Since the casualty, she has experienced recurring distressing dreams about the event and continuing emotional distress, and those symptoms continue to the present, according to the lawsuit.
Colvin is represented by attorney Joseph Orlando of Gloucester, Massachusetts. The Saraos are represented by attorneys Trevor Savage and Sean Murphy of Auburn.
Colvin stated in her lawsuit that when she was struck by the mast she was propelled down 8 feet of stairs. Despite her injuries, she came back up the stairs to assist other injured passengers. She said she saw other passengers attempting to provide CPR to Mecklenburg but that she was beyond recovery.
The captain appeared to be in shock and offered no care or service to passengers, Colvin’s lawsuit claims. She said the Coast Guard took over when they arrived at the vessel.
Sarao was assisting other passengers after he was initially struck and then was struck again, according to his lawsuit.
An exhaustive, nearly two-year investigation by the Coast Guard found that a series of missteps led to the fatal accident. The Coast Guard issued its report in July 2025.
Some of the issues can be traced back 30 years earlier when a prior owner purchased the masts, including the one that snapped because of rot.
“Based on the findings of this investigation, it is not recommended that any administrative or punitive action be taken against any Coast Guard personnel. It is not recommended that suspension or revocation action be taken against any credentialed mariner. Additionally, it is not recommended that criminal prosecution be taken against any person or entity,” the report stated.
The report finds that the problems began when the former owner ordered masts and the supplier provided ones that did not meet the specifications requested. The former owner accepted the masts, however, according to the Coast Guard report.
“In November 1992, the owner personally inspected the material and confirmed these deviations, which included deficiencies in annual growth ring count, sapwood on the upper portion of the mast, and issues with knot size and spacing. Additionally, since air-dried material was unavailable, the material was kiln-dried instead. Despite these discrepancies, the owner proceeded with the purchase and accepted delivery of the masts in May 1993. While some sapwood remained, it should be noted that this condition was limited to minor streaking and was subsequently removed during final mast shaping,” the Coast Guard report stated.
“The mast indeed lacked the specified annual ring count, which is crucial for mechanical strength properties,” the report stated.
The vessel’s prior owner did not have a formally established mast maintenance or inspection program in place from 1993 until the vessel was sold in 2022, the report stated.
“This absence of a structured program meant there was no systematic approach to monitor the condition of the masts. The lack of a formalized routine contributed to unidentified degradation of the mast over time,” the investigation found.
Under the new owner from 2022 to 2023, the operator delegated responsibility for mast and rigging inspections to the mate.
“Although the mate had prior experience, they lacked formal training in mast and wood inspection. This delegation without proper training led to several issues. While the mate conducted inspections monthly, the absence of formal training and adequate guidance likely compromised the thoroughness and accuracy of these assessments. Inspections were conducted visually without the use of sounding hammers or probing tools. This limitation meant that underlying structural issues, such as internal rot or decay, could go undetected, increasing the risk of mast failure,” according to investigators.
The vessel’s mast maintenance and inspection documentation practices were also notably inadequate, according to the Coast Guard.
There was a lack of oversight and formal reporting mechanisms related to the operator’s internal mast inspection processes. Inspections were not adequately documented, and there were no formal expectations set for reporting inspection findings. This lack of oversight most likely contributed to delayed or inadequate responses to emerging issues, allowing hazards to persist and escalate unchecked, the report states.
As with the prior owner, the current owner relied on inspections by the Coast Guard, conducted annually and at 10-year intervals.
The owner also used a marine surveyor, whose inspections focused on areas that were readily accessible without going aloft. Although the surveyor could not directly assess inaccessible parts of the mast, that inspection process allowed for the identification of visible issues with the vessel’s foremast.
The Coast Guard’s Marine Safety Division in Belfast relied on owners, operators and third-party surveyors to identify and report rotted conditions in masts. The masts were last taken down and inspected by the Coast Guard in 2014. The schooner was owned by Ray and Ann Williamson of Camden from 1985 to 2022, according to Grace Bailey’s website.
During interviews with passengers and crew following the October 2023 accident, two passengers reported hearing unusual noises from the mast before its failure. One passenger heard noises about an hour before, and another heard noises about a minute before.
“While both passengers found the noises odd, they did not find them significant enough to report to the crew. Although it was not the passengers’ responsibility to recognize audible warnings as signs of stress or cracking, the lack of reporting was a missed opportunity to detect and address the hazard. A third audible warning, heard by multiple passengers and crew members, immediately preceded the mast collapse. Moments before the collapse, the captain and mate observed signs of failure and warned passengers to get clear of the mainmast. Unfortunately, the warning came simultaneously with the mast’s fall, leaving no time for passengers to get clear of the collapsing rig,” the investigation concluded.
A statement was issued on behalf of the owners of the schooner following the release of the Coast Guard report, from the public relations agency Denterlein in Boston, which advises companies on crisis management.
“The Grace Bailey crew continues to hold Emily closely in our hearts and minds and reflect on that tragic day.
“We have cooperated fully with the U.S. Coast Guard during their investigation of the accident and are grateful to the agency for the extensive research conducted and the thoughtful recommendations they propose in the report for future steps to increase safety for the benefit of all wooden sailing vessels.
“After a thorough overhaul of the Grace Bailey and passing a regular safety inspection by the Coast Guard, the Grace Bailey is back sailing, allowing our passengers to enjoy the beauty of Maine’s coastline,” the statement from the Grace Bailey owners said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.
Correction: An earlier version of this report misstated the number of people suing the owner of the Grace Bailey.

title: 20-year-old dead after drowning in Ellis Pond
text:
ROXBURY, Maine (WMTW) - A 20-year-old man is dead after drowning in Ellis Pond in Roxbury.
Authorities say Shawn Noyes, 20, of Dixfield, was kayaking with family when he fell out of his kayak. He was seen trying to swim to a nearby island. After a few minutes, he disappeared and did not resurface.
The Maine Warden Service began a search Saturday evening. Wardens found his kayak and life jacket. Noyes’ body was recovered mid-afternoon yesterday.
The Maine Warden Service is reminding everyone to wear life jackets when going out on the water.

title: Rapper Soulja Boy teases 2028 presidential bid calling it ‘a new chapter’
text:
(Gray News) - Rapper Soulja Boy teased a presidential bid on Saturday, calling it “a new chapter” and “a bigger vision.”
“SOULJA BOY 2028. A new chapter. A bigger vision. A commitment to creating opportunities for the next generation,” Soulja Boy wrote in an Instagram post.
The rapper, whose real name is DeAndre Cortez Way, said he is focusing on four things: “economic opportunity, criminal justice reform, education and the future of technology and AI.”
“From music to business to technology, I’ve always believed in thinking bigger and challenging what’s possible. Now I’m exploring what it means to bring that same vision to public service. The future starts with a conversation,” he said.
Beyond the four focus areas, the rapper did not elaborate on any specific policies. It is unclear if he plans to formally launch a campaign.

title: New non-profit aims for $1M to buy, preserve local newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine (WABI) - An Ellsworth non-profit has started its mission to help preserve journalism in Hancock County.
The Acadia Newspaper Trust is looking to raise one million dollars by next summer to buy the Ellsworth American, the Bangor Historian, and The Mount Desert Islander from current owner, Reade Brower.
The non-profit was formed back in June and achieved 501(c)(3) status last month.
Ellsworth American Publisher Chris Crockett says a transition to non-profit will help them retain local ownership.
He says the trust is an effort to ensure that local communities do not face the difficulties that come when a paper closes.
“There’s been many studies. Tax mill rates go up, and voter participation goes down when newspapers leave a community. We want to be proactive and really secure the next 175 years for these newspapers,” said Crockett.
Crockett says there has been a lot of community support since their fundraising announcement earlier this month. He also says Brower has been very supportive of the ownership change.
The public is also invited to meet those behind the trust during a community kickoff celebration on October 29th at 5pm at Fogtown Brewing Company in Ellsworth.
To learn more about the Acadia Newspaper Trust, you can visit their website here.

title: The first indigenous peoples’ day film festival held in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The first Indigenous Peoples’ Day Film Festival took place in Bangor Sunday.
It was held at the Unitarian-Universalist Church in Bangor, and showed seven films, all following the theme of Environmental Justice.
Sunlight Media Collective, a group of filmmakers from Wabanakik, produced six of the films, along with one film produced by Bullfrog Films.
The event aimed to show films that asked the question, “What is environmental justice, and why is it so important right now?”
The films covered topics including the Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion, and the proposed AI data center in Passamaquoddy bay.
“These films all fundamentally tell a story that we as Wabanaki people are still here, fighting for and caring for our land and cultures in ways that we’ve been doing for thousands of years,” said Darren Ranco, Professor of Anthropology & Chair of the Native American Program at UMaine.
“Native, non-native people working together in a native framework, is actually one of the key elements of political change and social cultural change that we’re advocating for,” said Ranco.
The film screenings were followed by a “Harvest Potluck Supper” and traditional frybread was served.
For more information about the event, you can email the Peace and Justice Center at peacectr@gmail.com.

title: Sunny and Mild
text:
Showers increase tonight
Showers increase tonight
Skies will be mostly clear along the coast Monday afternoon, while areas closer to the mountains have more clouds and even a few showers. Temperatures will increase into the high 60s and even low 70s. Conditions become cloudier overnight as low pressure tracks into New Hampshire and Maine, bringing shower chances and possible freezing rain to the mountains.
Tuesday will be rainy, with light to moderate showers lasting throughout the day. Showers will be widespread, and areas inland and along the Midcoast are the most likely areas to see rain totals greater than 1 inch. Temperatures will also be cool, with highs in the mid to upper 50s.
Wednesday morning may have a few lingering showers but will otherwise be dry. Thursday will be breezy as the low pressure exits the region, and our next chance for widespread rain will arrive on Friday.

title: Maine’s energy goals depend on a regulatory process people can trust
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tim Burgess is assistant business manager of IBEW Local 104.
When a severe storm knocks out power in the middle of the night, Mainers don’t think about regulatory dockets — they just look for the flashing lights of utility trucks rolling down their streets. The recent recommendation to deny Central Maine Power’s request for temporary rates has sparked a fierce statewide debate over affordability, spending and the future of our electric system.
These are critical issues that affect every household, but for the men and women who build, maintain and restore our grid, a far more troubling question is emerging.
What happens to the safety and stability of our workforce when participants follow the precise regulatory rules laid out by the state, only to be told at the finish line that the path no longer applies?
Central Maine Power sought temporary rates after the Public Utilities Commission itself
indicated they were available to address the severe financial uncertainty following the dismissal of the company’s long-term grid investment plan. CMP maintains that it followed the direction provided by regulators when it pursued temporary rates, filed the case, presented extensive evidence and all involved parties participated in good faith. 
Everyone assumed that the process established by our regulators was available, stable and reliable. The recommendation currently before the commission calls that fundamental assumption into question.
For most Mainers, utility regulation feels abstract. For those who wear the tool belt and climb the poles, it is anything but. Decisions made in Augusta determine whether local contractors hire apprentices, whether vital grid projects move forward, whether stable work exists next year and whether Maine will possess the skilled workforce necessary to meet its aggressive energy and economic development goals.
Predictable investment, workforce development, apprenticeships and long-term grid reliability are interconnected. Uncertain investment makes it significantly harder for employers to expand their operations, harder for joint apprenticeship programs to grow and harder to prepare the next generation of highly skilled workers. This is not a matter of corporate self-interest. It goes directly to the heart of how safely the infrastructure is built.
Maine’s broader, long-term policy objectives sharpen the point. Our state leaders continue to aggressively promote widespread electrification, economic development, transportation electrification, rapid heat pump adoption and clean energy expansion. Every one of these initiatives drives up the daily demand for electrical infrastructure, heavy-duty service upgrades and overall grid capacity.
Meeting these goals requires a larger workforce and a stronger, more resilient grid. There is an inherent contradiction in encouraging a society-wide dependence on electricity while simultaneously creating deep financial uncertainty around the exact investments that such dependence requires.
The public debate is framed as affordability versus investment. Utility workers understand the strain of affordability as well as anyone; those who build and maintain the grid are local customers and taxpayers, too.
Aging infrastructure continues to age, and its vulnerabilities compound over time. Projects that could have been executed methodically and safely during a planned rollout instead become high-stress emergencies later on. This delays routine progress and forces emergency work at a far greater cost to the customers, all while creating much harder, more hazardous conditions for the people doing the work in storms and sub-zero temperatures.
Witnesses in these proceedings have repeatedly warned that regulatory delay leads directly to higher long-term costs, greater operational challenges and reduced workforce stability. The broader concern is the chilling signal this situation sends across our entire industry. Young lineworker and electrician apprentices count on steady, predictable work to accumulate the thousands of field hours required to become a journeyman, while local contractors need regulatory certainty before investing in heavy equipment or expanding their crews.
Furthermore, major employers looking to bring business to Maine must have absolute confidence that a stable grid will be ready when they plug in. Ultimately, all of these vital
economic decisions rest on a single, fundamental belief: that Maine’s regulatory institutions are predictable, consistent and worthy of trust.
Trust is not built by any single decision, but through a long-term process that participants
believe is transparent, consistent and reliable. When an entity follows the path regulators
indicated was open yet finds that path abruptly closed at the finish line, it is entirely fair to ask whether future participants can truly rely on the process. 
If Maine hopes to build the skilled workforce, modern infrastructure and robust electric system its economic and energy policies require, it must preserve something just as important: a regulatory process people can trust, rely upon and plan their lives around.

title: Otter Creek poet and gardener offers free writing workshop
text:
NORTHEAST HARBOR — On Saturday, Oct. 17, at 10 a.m., the Northeast Harbor Library will host a free writing workshop led by poet and gardener for the Land & Garden Preserve, Ben Boegehold.
The workshop is titled “Planting the Writer’s Garden: An Idea About Beginnings,” and will focus on planting the kernels of ideas that have potential to grow into mature works of writing. Participants will leave with a variety of generative tools and strategies for cultivating their future projects.

title: 31 comics coming to Maine to make you laugh into next year
text:
Human beings need to laugh, and that includes Mainers. It’s good for the soul and enables us to take a break and better confront our problems.
A bunch of comedians, from familiar faces to fresh ones — including some with specials you can check out on streaming services — are coming to Maine stages to help provide that humor to soothe our souls. Here is a list of comedy shows at venues across the state over the coming months.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Comic Jason Salmon’s style is described as getting “the best advice you’ve ever gotten … from the dumbest guy you know.” His TV credits include “Orange Is the New Black,” “30 Rock” and “At Home with Amy Sedaris,” along with appearances on HBO and Comedy Central. For a preshow serving of Salmon, view his standup special, “Biscuits and Gravity,” on YouTube.
7 p.m. Sunday. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $20-$45. statetheatreportland.com.
New York City’s Lucas Zelnick has been featured on Comedy Central and has headlined the Netflix is a Joke Festival. Film credits include “Regular” and “Fade to Black.” Be ready to be cracked up by a guy who earned an MBA from Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business.
7:30 p.m. Sunday and Dec. 5. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $42.50-$83.50. jonathansogunquit.com.
Mainer Bob Marley has been cracking people up with his wicked funny humor for decades. Along with the shows in Ogunquit, Marley will be doing his thing Saturday at the Waterville Opera House. Tickets are $46.50 at watervillecreates.org. Marley also has five shows on the calendar at Stone Mountain Arts Center in Brownfield, starting on Dec. 5. Tickets are $36.50 at stonemountainartscenter.com.
7 p.m. Oct. 22. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $24.26, $29.53 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Emma Dalenberg and Sunny Laprade are best friends who are hitting the road together for a co-headlining tour. Expect a wild night from the queer comics, who will be spilling the tea on many topics.
8 p.m. Nov. 5. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $42-$72. statetheatreportland.com.
Writer, actor, radio presenter, podcaster and comic Marc Maron brings his candid brand of humor to the State Theatre with a stop on his Yammering Into The Void tour. As host of the long-running “WFT with Marc Maron” podcast, his galaxy of celebrity guests have included Barack Obama, Carol Burnett and Robin Williams. The HBO comedy specials “Marc Maron: Panicked” and “From Bleak To Dark” are popular examples of his work.
8 p.m. Nov. 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-$65. statetheatreportland.com.
For five memorable seasons, comic Leslie Jones was a Not Ready for Primetime Player on “Saturday Night Live.” During the 2016 Summer Olympic games, Jones took to what was then called Twitter to offer colorful, comical commentary. NBC recruited her to cover several events, and she offered her spicy takes during a few other summer and winter games. Catch her I’m Hot tour in Portland.
7 p.m. Nov. 7. The Dance Hall, 7 Walker St., Kittery, $28 in advance, $33 day of show. thedancehallkittery.org.
Eddie Pepitone is known as the Bitter Buddha, and is considered by some to be a cross section of Jackie Gleason, Don Rickles and Eckart Tohle. His stage presence is described as both calm and chaotic as he walks the line between social rage and self-doubt. Comic, writer and comedy producer Rebecca Donohue will be playing host.
7 p.m. Nov. 7. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $59-$99. porttix.com.
Late-night TV legend and longtime stand-up comic Jay Leno will have you rolling in the aisles when he takes the stage in Portland. Leno has won several awards including an Emmy, the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor and Hasty Pudding Award at Harvard University, among other honors.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 14. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $25-$66. jonathansogunquit.com.
Boston comic Jimmy Cash’s shows draw on his experiences of being a janitor for 20 years, as well as a father and someone who maintains long-term sobriety. Cash travels all over the U.S. and Canada, and was Maine comic Bob Marley’s dedicated opener for many years.
7 p.m. Nov. 15. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39.75-$125. porttix.com.
Bert Kreischer brings his Permission to Party tour to Maine, with a mix of his trademark storytelling paired with a huge persona. Kreischer’s latest Netflix special, “Lucky,” premiered in 2025, and his credits include the film “The Machine” and the Netflix series “Free Bert.” As a podcaster, Kreischer hosts “Bertcast” and co-hosts “2 Bears, 1 Cave” with fellow funnyman Tom Segura.
7 and 9:30 p.m. Nov. 20 and 21. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $34.81, $45.36 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Los Angeles-based comic Leah Rudick’s characters include “Wealthy Woman,” “Joannie” and “Love Coach.” With just under 2 million social media followers, Rudick is a hot ticket with her signature “weird girl” brand of comedy.
7:30 p.m. Nov. 27. Jonathan’s Ogunquit, 92 Bourne Lane, $52.50-$93.50. jonathansogunquit.com.
Paula Poundstone has been making clever observations with her dry yet hilarious delivery for decades. Poundstone is also a longtime panelist on the National Public Radio quiz show “Wait Wait … Don’t Tell Me!”
7 p.m. Dec. 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $37.50-$57.50. statetheatreportland.com.
Spice up your holiday season by hitting comic Becky Robinson’s Holiday Spectacular. With wild characters, including Suzie Chapstick and the Entitled Housewife, Robinson will knock your socks off.
6 p.m. Dec. 6. Aura, 121 Center St., Portland, $52.75-$79, 18-plus. auramaine.com.
Aries Spears brings more than three decades of stand-up experience, and an eight-season run on “MADtv” to Portland. Known for fearless crowd work and uncanny impressions of celebrities including Denzel Washington, Jay-Z and Shaquille O’Neal, Spears isn’t afraid to opine on pop culture, race and relationships.
7 and 9:30 p.m., Dec. 11 and 12. Empire, 575 Congress St., Portland, $29.53, $40.09 preferred seating. empirecomedyme.com.
Jason Cheny is a Taiwanese American stand-up comic out of Los Angeles. His upcoming Hulu half-hour special premieres in January. Cheny is a fixture at upper tier comedy clubs like The Improv and Comedy Cellar, and headlines sold-out shows wherever he goes, both nationally and around the world.
7 p.m. Dec. 26. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39.-75-$69.75. porttix.com.
In one night you can see a pair of big-name comics raise the rafters at Merrill Auditorium. Joe Gatto is best known for TV shows “Impractical Jokers” and “The Misery Index.” His friend Drew Lynch earned a Golden Buzzer on “America’s Got Talent.” When he was 20, Lynch suffered a traumatic brain injury and brought himself back from the brink with an infectious self-deprecating style that continues to win audiences over.
7 p.m. Jan. 16. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $39.50-$69.50. statetheatreportland.com.
For a midwinter comedy infusion, grab tickets to see award-winning actress and comic Atsuko Okatsuka in Portland. Her exuberant, offbeat brand of stand-up was captured in specials that have aired on Hulu and HBO.
7 p.m. Jan 23. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $33-$55, $199 meet & greet. statetheatreportland.com.
Zarna Garg’s Million Dollar Excuses tour will pack many punches about family life when it comes through Portland. Her Amazon Prime special “One in a Billion” and its Hulu follow-up “Zarna Garg: Practical People Win” both reached wide audiences. As a writer, Zarna published the memoir “This American Woman” about her harrowing ascent from being homeless in Mumbai to an internationally known stand-up comic.
7 p.m. Jan. 23. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $29.50-$69.50. porttix.com.
Brad William’s Big & Small tour will showcase his knack for sharp punchlines and deeply personal storytelling. His latest stand-up special “Live on Short Street” can be streamed on YouTube, as can “Starfish,” which has surpassed 9 million views.
7 p.m. Feb. 6. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., $62-$92. watervillecreates.org.
Canadian comic Samantha Bee is bringing her How to Survive Menopause tour to Waterville. In 2003, Bee started a 12-year run on Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show.” Her own late-night comedy series “Full Frontal with Samantha Bee” debuted on TBS in 2016 and ran for seven seasons.
7 p.m. Feb. 26. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $41.50-$51.50, $152 VIP. statetheatreportland.com.
Justin Willman melds comedy with magic so well, his streaming views surpassed the 1 billion mark. So you can expect the unexpected when his One For the Ages tour comes through Portland. Unlike many comedy shows, this one is suitable for all ages.
4 and 7 p.m. Feb. 27. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $39-4109. porttix.com.
Nobody Asked You To Do That is what Taylor Tomlinson is calling her winter tour that includes a late February stop in Portland with late afternoon and evening performances. Head to Netflix to find several specials that emphasize her ability to convert challenging life moments into side-splitting humor.
7 p.m. March 6. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $29.50-$59.50. statetheatreportland.com.
Estonian-born comic Ari Matti translates his Eastern European roots and globe-trotting experiences into a can’t-miss night of comedy. Matti is a regular on the popular “Kill Tony” podcast and was part of the team that performed “Kill Tony Live” in consecutive years at Madison Square Garden.
8 p.m. March 12. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $49.50-$74.50, 12-plus. porttix.com.
Jo Koy got his start in a Las Vegas coffeehouse and is now, according to Pollstar and Billboard, one of the top 10 grossing stand-up comedians every year. Drawing from his Filipino-American upbringing and his experiences as a parent and son, you can expect nonstop laughs from the lively comic when his Koy Meets World tour comes through Portland at the tail end of winter.

title: There’s gnome place like the University of Maine: finding whimsy on campus
text:
Let’s face it. After a couple of months, the University of Maine can be gray. It seems like the color just drains from the sky, and students seem to be left waiting until April to see the sun again. On a lighter note, the meek nature of Orono weather also means the return of UMaine hockey and all the characters that come with it. From the “Naked 5” to the lively security guards, the Alfond has the ability to add a fun light to the lives of students here. To incorporate more whimsy on campus, one student, known as the UMaine gnome, repurposed a Halloween costume from his freshman year to wear to a hockey game, and the rest is history.
The UMaine gnome went out on a whim at the end of his freshman year and showed up at a hockey game in his costume from months prior. After that, his friends “convinced him” to wear it to more games. At his request, I will keep his identity private, but I was able to sit down with the man behind the beard. The gnome told me that while it was somewhat of a dare to wear it to games, he’s “always loved Halloween” and “keeps a folder on his computer” of prospective costumes.
While he started his persona at the end of his freshman year, his friends encouraged him to bring his whimsy to social media at the start of his sophomore year last fall, but he never expected it to take off this way. He said things became real when “the official University of Maine followed [his] Instagram account.” Moreover, he was recently invited to walk in the OronoFest parade by the town council, and that “made things feel real.” On the topic of his content, he said he’s “always loved dancing” and thinks that it’s an easy creative outlet. He further believes that “being good at dancing is subjective” and that “it shows people how easy it is to have fun.”
On the topic of his attendance at events, he said that hockey games are “an accessible way to find community” and that he just “loves to have fun on campus.” While he has amassed quite the following, he enjoys being a mystery. While his friends and family know that it’s him, he said he often has “friends come up to him showing [him] [his] content not even knowing it’s him.” Overall, he just loves to “have fun,” and he continues it “because it brightens people’s day.” He often has people come up to him at games to tell him how much they love his content, and that makes him “feel like he’s making an impact.” While it’s a silly thing, it’s clear that this is a way that he continues to choose joy in his life.
You may be wondering why he keeps his identity secret, and he said it’s because “it’s fun to not have people know it’s you.” While he doesn’t come out and advertise it, he said people sometimes “figure it out from his voice or the way he acts.” Even off campus, people have started to recognize him. While at home, he substitute teaches in his local high school and middle school, and he says “the students have started to figure it out and they always want to talk about it.” While he mentioned that he never expected to have it take off, this just shows another way he brings joy to the people around him.
When asked if he had any advice for students here at UMaine, he started by saying “a lot of people are kinda nervous to go out and be themselves,” and at first “he was scared too,” but he found that “everyone is so supportive.” His overall message is that he “doesn’t think that people should be afraid.” So when things get gray, remember that sometimes the smallest things can be a way to choose joy, and that joy is a ripple effect. You never know what can come from putting yourself out there; take it from the guy in a gnome costume who put himself out there once and is now a joyous staple of the Alfond’s Jumbotron.

title: An aging hunter faces hard truths
text:
As an aging hunter and outdoor writer, I have begun to look inward to get a little introspective. Since I was a kid, I have always been drawn to the hunt. And, truth be known, I have never taken the time to really seriously ponder why that is. I just know that it is apparently the way that I am wired, perhaps some mysterious antediluvian connection with my primitive ancestry?
A psychologist might conclude that, indeed, I have an addiction to deer hunting, in particular. So be it.

title: Teenage caregivers: The hidden generation juggling school and elder care
text:
(Aging Untold) — When you picture a caregiver, you probably imagine a middle-aged adult or a spouse.
But a new study from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health shows that role is starting much earlier — an estimated 1.6 million teens ages 15 to 18 and 2 million young adults ages 19 to 22 are now caregivers in the U.S.
Why so many young people are stepping into caregiving roles
“One of the main drivers is people are waiting to have their children until a much older age,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “You could be a 20-year-old and your parents are in their mid- to late-60s, and that’s unheard of in our generation.”
Cradduck said the strain often doesn’t stop there.
“What’s even worse is when your parents are in that age and maybe needing some assistance, their parents are often still alive,” she said. “So you’ve become a club sandwich. Now you’re not even a sandwich generation with your own kids — you’ve got a whole big feast going on here, because you might be taking care of your grandparents, your parents and raising a child as well while trying to work and provide. This is an astronomical, just huge workload on a human being.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added that earlier onset of chronic conditions among younger generations is compounding the issue.
“Compound this with the younger people who are having these chronic conditions earlier because of the obesity that we’re seeing, the insulin resistance and all this increase in metabolic disorders that’s affecting young people earlier, so now add that on,” Rogers said.
A hidden toll on teenagers’ health
Some teens who are providing care might not even recognize what is happening to them.
“One in 10 teenagers is taking care of someone at home from an early-developed chronic illness,” aging expert Amy O’Rourke said. “They’re going to school, they’re taking care of their mom. They’re anxious or depressed. They’re tired, but they’re not attributing it to the fact that they’re taking care of mom.”
O’Rourke said the impact on their health is often hidden.
Where young caregivers can turn for help
She pointed to specific resources for teens and young adults carrying caregiving responsibilities. (See the list with links below.)
“If you’re one of those teenagers out there, there’s a great organization — actually several resources — that I would turn them to,” she said. “One is Lorenzo’s House, the National Caregiving Alliance group. Go to the school, the school guidance counselors, support at the school, and ask for help, because what you’re doing isn’t really expected until you’re like in your 60s.”
Many young caregivers might not realize the scope of what they’re managing.
“For these young folks, they’re very internet savvy. There are a lot of really cool resources and a lot of help, a lot of support groups available to help caregivers navigate these things. Find your support system,” Cradduck said.
Protecting education, careers and your own future
Cradduck cautioned that young caregivers often sacrifice their own futures to care for others.
“Try really, really hard not to put your own career on the back burner, because that’s going to affect your income and your own retirement and your ability to age healthy and safely with enough resources,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose cautioned young caregivers to ensure that they are getting a good education.
“You’ve got to look out for yourself first so you can even be a caregiver as time goes on and maybe have your own family. It can impact your dating, your future careers, your ability to have a job and child rearing. So it’s very complex. But you don’t want a current crisis to become a generational issue that goes on,” Ambrose added.
O’Rourke also encouraged young caregivers to ask schools and support networks for help directly.
“The American Association of Caregiving Youth — ask for help, because if you’re taking care of somebody, you’re overwhelmed, you can’t think to do all those things,” O’Rourke said. “So you ask somebody, ‘How would I do this? How do I take care of my parents and make sure that my career, my finances aren’t duly affected?’”
Looking for solutions before a crisis hits
Rather than waiting until a caregiving emergency develops, Rogers suggested focusing on prevention.
“Why don’t we look at solutions where we can begin to be preventive, so that we can start to work on those things that we know are affecting us — that foundation, the sleep, inflammation, nutrition — so that we can stop ourselves from getting there,” Rogers said.
Ambrose added that a person’s living situation can play a bigger role than people realize.
“Sometimes a caregiving crisis isn’t necessarily so much a medical problem as it might be a housing problem, where we’re not really in the right environment, and it’s working against the health of the people that maybe need the care,” she said.
O’Rourke also suggested schools could do more to identify students who are quietly managing caregiving at home.
“When a child is interviewed for going to high school, ‘Are you an athlete? Are you into music?’ But they don’t say, ‘Are you a caregiver?’” she said. “That should be added to every interview assessment going into school so that they can get a handle on how many kids in their school need help.”
Cradduck pointed young caregivers toward local government resources that often go overlooked.
“I would point anyone, even our young caregivers, back towards your local adult protective (services), your adult services, aging adult and disabled adult services,” she said. “There’s a lot of grant money that helps with utility bills, transportation assistance, transportation reimbursement. There’s a lot of financial help that can come along with just reaching out to your local county.”
Cradduck said not to think that calling Adult Protective Services is a bad thing — there’s a lot of resources there to help.
“Department of Aging, Area Agency on Aging and your local county, and also mental health associations. That might sound strange, but they can be very well funded and have a lot of diverse programs,” Ambrose added.

Local resources

- Adult services
- Area agency on aging
- Disabled adult services
- Mental health associations
- School guidance counselors
Grant money might be available to help with
- Transportation assistance
- Transportation reimbursement.

title: Miami Vice ’85 Debuts First Look at the New Crockett and Tubbs
text:
Miami Vice ’85 Debuts First Look at the New Crockett and Tubbs as Production Begins
The new Miami Vice movie is going back to the past.
Universal announced today they have officially started production on Miami Vice ’85, a second film based on the iconic ’80s cop series. They also debuted the first images of the movie’s stars, Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler, in costume as the new Crockett and Tubbs.
First here’s Austin Butler as Sonny Crockett:
And here’s Michael B. Jordan as Ricardo Tubbs:
READ MORE: Amazing Practical Horror Effects (And How They Made Them)
The new Miami Vice is directed by Top Gun: Maverick and F1’s Joseph Kosinski, and written by Nightcrawler filmmaker Dan Gilroy. The cast also includes Alden Ehrenreich, Danny Ramirez, John Leguizamo, Edi Gathegi, and Walton Goggins.
The previous Miami Vice movie, simply titled Miami Vice, opened in theaters in 2006 and was directed by the old TV series’ executive producer, Michael Mann. (The show was created by Anthony Yerkovich.) That film had Colin Farrell as Crockett and Jamie Foxx as Tubbs. It underperformed at the box office, barely recouping its $150+ million budget, and it got very mixed reviews at the time. Over the years, though, it’s become one of Mann’s more cultishly beloved titles.
A new director’s cut of Mann’s Miami Vice debuted at film festivals this year and will be available on 4K this holiday season. (Mann has already made one earlier director’s cut of the film. This is the director’s cut’s director’s cut I guess.)
Miami Vice ’85 is scheduled to open in theaters on May 19, 2028. Production on the film is now officially underway.

title: Letter: Susan Collins has proven her worth to Mainers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I am hopeful the voters of this state will have the good sense to reelect Sen. Susan Collins in November. Her track record of working for the people of Maine speaks for itself. I believe without a doubt Collins is the hardest working legislator in Washington, never missing a single vote in the Senate.
Her track record is impressive, from securing funds for Maine’s rural fire and EMS services, to keeping Bath Iron Works viable and competitive, and securing hundreds of millions of dollars for Maine’s hospitals. These are a few of her successes that benefit all Mainers.
I believe that anyone who thinks sending a rookie, freshman senator to Washington to replace Collins is a good idea should rethink their position or get serious help. I think that no freshman senator, regardless of name, would be able to accomplish even one-tenth of what Collins can, given her position in the Senate.
Susan Collins has proven her worth to Mainers through her many years of hard work.
Maine has one of the highest tax burdens in the nation along with some of the highest electricity rates largely because of policies coming from Augusta. Her opponent has been in Augusta for many years presiding over these very policies, and now thinks we should send him to Washington to fight for Mainers. I, for one, have seen all I care to see regarding how Troy Jackson fights for Mainers.
Susan Collins is “Our Senator” and I believe she deserves your vote in November.
Alan Dwelley 
Hermon

title: Pregnant mother who was days away from giving birth among 8 killed in mass shooting
text:
ERIE, Pa. (AP) - A man whose toddler was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, said Sunday that the gunman was a grandfather who never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary.
“I think that was a front for him,” Julius Windham said as he stood at a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting, including his 1-year-old daughter Amarianna, her pregnant mother and the woman’s 5-year-old son and unborn baby.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just — you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.
The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.
Those killed include 2 women outside the home
Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 p.m. Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the women and children and the words, “Forever In My Heart.”
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.
Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the 5-year-old boy and 1-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Police decline to discuss motive as investigation continues
Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”
Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, said they’ve known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything.”
“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.
“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. “What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier. ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”
