title: Flock cameras went up without some city councils’ approval. We found out why.
text:
Maryville, Tennessee (InvestigateTV) — When Kyle Skeen moved back to the U.S. after working in London, he said he quickly noticed an abundance of something he hadn’t expected — cameras.
“I was quite surprised when I came back and just saw the scale of what was going on,” he said.
Located just south of Knoxville, the small city of Maryville, Tennessee where Skeen moved in 2024 has 16 Flock Safety automatic license plate readers.
“I cannot leave my neighborhood without passing a Flock camera,” he said. “No matter which way I go, every time I leave my house, it’s put into the database.”
Skeen is more than familiar with the concept of surveillance: his more than 20-year career with the United States Navy culminated in his role as a senior intelligence analyst, and that stint in London was working in intelligence for NATO Maritime Command.
But Skeen said what he found when he started digging into the details — from the nationwide scope of the searching by law enforcement to how his community came to be in business with Flock — still left him shocked.
“The power should lie with the people, and these kind of systems, it tilts the balance,” he said.
Flock’s national network of more than 120,000 cameras is knit together through thousands of contracts the company has signed with communities large and small, with Flock executives touting this as local control.
But as a growing number of communities have reconsidered their relationships with Flock in light of sustained public criticism, the genesis and content of those contracts have drawn scrutiny as well.
“It seems like people are realizing that they’re starting to pop up just everywhere, the sheer volume of them, and they’ve been starting to ask questions,” Skeen said, “and usually when people find the answers to the questions, they get even more concerned.”
Cameras and contracts without a vote
In an April interview with InvestigateTV and in multiple company publications since, Flock has argued that local communities have complete control over their implementation of the technology.
“I think the city council has been democratically elected by the community to go make these sort of decisions,” Flock Chief Communications Officer Josh Thomas said in that April interview. “And if the community doesn’t like the city council’s decision, they should go vote differently. But it is the city council’s job, as a duly elected representative, to go decide how the budget should be spent.”
However, InvestigateTV found numerous instances in communities across the country where cameras were installed and paid for first, with approval from local elected officials sometimes coming later — if at all.
In Maryville, the police chief recently explained during a city council work session that the department began using Flock technology in 2020, but records show the council didn’t vote on the issue until July 2024 when the city needed a right-of-way permit from the state.
“I did not vote for this, and to my knowledge, not a single American voted for this,” Skeen said.
He and others have expressed their concerns about privacy and transparency to local elected officials, including at the public work session, and the city has said it is gathering information.
“We just wanted to hear from everybody and kind of gather information. And to be honest with you, learn more as a council because there’s a lot of things that we learned today from you guys and from the Chief as well,” Maryville Mayor Andy White said at the meeting.
Over the last few months, similar meetings have taken place in hundreds of communities across the country where citizens or elected leaders have questioned the procurement of Flock technology without explicit council or commission approval.
Law enforcement officials have largely defended these actions — with emotions sometimes running high.
“It’s my equipment. I don’t tell you guys when I buy a new gun,” Ron Ambrozaitis, then police chief, said to city leaders during a July public meeting in Chetek, Wisconsin. “You guys want to call and cancel it, go right ahead. I have no problem. But the next time grandma’s missing, or your car got stolen, or you’re missing money, and I can’t ... I can’t help you.”
At the end of August, Ambrozaitis announced his retirement and stepped down from active duty.
Buying under the limit
In Knox County, Tennessee, as local law enforcement looked to expand its Flock portfolio to more than 400 cameras in mid-August, then County Mayor Glenn Jacobs sent a letter to Flock questioning the validity of the county’s contract with the company.
He alleged the payments the Knox County Sheriff’s Office had been making since 2020 appeared to have been outlined to strategically “escape” the county’s contract oversight procedures.
Records show the sheriff’s office purchased Flock cameras in batches of $24,990 — exactly $10 under the $25,000 threshold that would have required a review by the county mayor’s office — as well as in split invoices of $12,500 that combined would have triggered a review.
“If you hit the exact price, minus ten bucks, it’s a red flag to me,” Knox County Commissioner Larsen Jay said during a public meeting the body held after becoming aware of the payments. “[The payment record] to me shows a pattern of buying things right under the threshold again and again and again. That concerns me.”
County Law Director David Buuck, who reviewed the paperwork with the mayor, also didn’t mince words.
“It’s one of the screwiest contracts I ever read because it basically says every time you do another one of these $12,000, $13,000 under-the-limit orders, it automatically renews the contract,” the Buuck said during the meeting.
Now former mayor Jacobs said the deal should never have skipped his desk.
“If it’s a contract: that has to come to commission, that has to come to me,” he said. “That didn’t happen.”
By the time commissioners took up the matter, Knox County’s sheriff’s office had 143 Flock license plate readers active — and according to Jacobs’ letter, more than a quarter of a million taxpayer dollars had been spent.
In light of allegations such as those levied by Knox County leaders, InvestigateTV asked Flock directly if the company works with agencies to avoid budgetary reviews.
“Flock provides public agencies with product information, pricing, and procurement documentation,” a spokesperson said in an emailed response. “Purchasing thresholds, sole-source requirements, and whether council or commission approval is required are governed by each agency’s applicable laws, policies, and procurement procedures.”
Contract questions lead to communities pulling the plug
Knox County ultimately pulled the plug, declaring its own Flock contract invalid and calling for the removal of the cameras. When the company missed a county-imposed deadline to do so, the newly-elected mayor had public works crews cover them. The sheriff’s office has since declared it is no longer using any fixed ALPR systems.
Knox County isn’t the only place that has turned off its cameras — the Institute for Justice has catalogued more than 250 communities that have canceled or will not renew their contract with Flock Safety.
The mayor of Neenah, Wisconsin posted a video to Facebook about how the city terminated its relationship with Flock over security concerns and “mounting evidence” that the company “wasn’t doing what it was supposed to in the contract.”
Ledyard, Connecticut, police got a notification in September from Flock about a security breach involving the system.
The notification appears to have been the final straw for Ledyard Police Chief Ken Creutz, who said he had already had growing concerns about the technology after watching recent congressional hearings.
“The technology may do some things that we were told that it can’t do,” he said in a letter to local elected officials. “The only prudent decision was to take a timeout from the whole Flock situation.”
The department severed its contract with Flock altogether, and the town’s public works department covered all four of the town’s cameras.
Ledyard signed a two-year contract and still owes the company around $12,000. Town leaders have said they are willing to pay the price to get out of the contract, but given the circumstances, some said they want to look into legal recourse because they feel they could have been sold the system on false pretenses.
“If we can display legally that we’ve been misled in this contract, in what we signed up to in terms of the conditions. To me, that’s grounds at least for something,” said Ledyard Town Councilor Tim Ryan. “It makes a statement, right? I don’t want to spend more than we’re already losing.”
The ‘Sole Source’
There are plenty of jurisdictions that are not pulling back.
For example, Dallas is keeping its more than 600 Flock cameras for now, even after Texas Governor Greg Abbott revoked state funding and residents have pressed city leaders on how the system got there in the first place.
City council member Gay Donnell Willis defended the technology’s track record in the city at a public forum hosted by community advocacy groups in mid September.
“Dallas has had 50 homicides solved, where a suspect was identified and arrested since 2023. It’s incredible,” she said in an interview with InvestigateTV.
She also said homicide investigations justify the city’s ALPR data retention period of 365 days.
“It’s important to be able to have that information to pinpoint where a suspect might have been to help catch them and arrest them.”
Stephanie Drenka with the Texas Civil Rights Project, one of the forum host organizations, questioned why Dallas has embraced the technology so fully while nearby cities move the opposite direction.
“Dallas, uniquely, has embraced Flock technology in a way that other cities in Texas are [not],” Drenka said. “They’re rejecting it, and they’re canceling contracts. It’s very puzzling to me why our city, with the views that citizens and residents have been expressing, our leadership does not seem to be listening to that.”
Dallas’ most recent Flock contract, worth $5.7 million, was approved by city council — but exempted from competitive bidding because Flock was listed as the “sole source” for the automated license plate reader technology sought by the city.
Councilmember Willis defended that arrangement, too.
“I think anyone can bid, but there are technologies and proprietary tools that maybe one technology has over another,” she said. “My understanding is that right now, they’ve got the most advanced technology, and until a competitor is able to match that, they’re the only one in the market and they meet the needs that Dallas has for solving crimes, then that might be the reason for a sole source.”
InvestigateTV found dozens of examples of similar sole-source paperwork in other cities and counties across the country — which municipalities used to competitive bidding in an industry that has several competing license plate reader companies.
With examples dating from 2020 to 2026, letters InvestigateTV reviewed were presented to jurisdictions of all sizes, all with nearly identical language.
In response to InvestigateTV’s questions about these “Sole Source Letters” a spokesperson said in a statement:
“Flock provides sole-source letters when public agencies request documentation for their procurement files, purchase orders, invoice processing, renewals, or sole-source justifications. The letters describe Flock’s integrated hardware, software, managed services, and system compatibility so an agency can evaluate whether the solution meets its applicable sole-source criteria. Each public agency is responsible for navigating its own procurement process and complying with the laws, policies, and approval requirements that apply in its jurisdiction.”
Dallas leaders authorized the city’s contracts with Flock, sole-source justification included, through consent agenda votes in 2022 and 2025 with minimal public council discussion, and critics argue the arrangement has left residents with no real say.
“If the grand majority of Dallas was in favor for Flock, then I can respect that. But we never had a vote on this either,” Santiago Diza of the Latino Leaders Coalition, another of the forum host organizations, said. “A product that was sold to the police department and we had no say in it.”
A database, not just a photo
Flock has frequently noted that sharing access to license plate reader data is “optional” for agencies, but in its sole-source letters the company highlights its integrated data network as its premier proprietary offering, calling it “a centralized system that facilitates collaboration across multiple jurisdictions, supporting a more robust and efficient public safety network.”
More than 6,000 jurisdictions are connected to the Flock system, and what the company considers a selling point, Drenka argues is precisely what makes it problematic.
“I think that is why Flock in particular has become such a dangerous entity, almost this monopoly, because of the data sharing and the network that they’re able to build when they have the exclusivity with these agencies,” Drenka said. “Flock has infiltrated communities across the country and we have very limited knowledge about how our data is being accessed and used by those other entities.”
Skeen, the Navy veteran now living in East Tennessee, agrees, and said he thinks the public largely misunderstands what the system actually does.
“This isn’t just one camera on a post on the side of the road. This is a national network,” Skeen said.
He said he’s found the volume of searches against his local cameras to be “staggering” — especially because they’re not all coming from nearby.
“They average about 63,000 searches a day,” Skeen said of cameras in his area. “All the way as far out as California, we’re seeing a massive amount of searches on the cameras here — in Tennessee.”
Jennifer Sanchez of the Texas Civil Rights Project said this functionality has led to distrust.
“Who is accessing this data? Who knows everything about us? Who is watching us? Who is collecting our every move? People have no trust in these cameras. People are scared of these cameras,” Sanchez said.
“If our every move is being recorded and stored in a database for 365 days, that’s scary.”
Flock has refuted that it “tracks” individuals, asserting that its ALPR snapshots are simply point-in-time indications of a vehicle’s location, but Skeen argues that what looks like scattered snapshots ultimately becomes something else entirely once it’s compiled.
“I worked in military intelligence, so I understand the value of information. And once that information by itself is put together, it becomes intelligence,” he said. “I understand when the system like this takes bits of information, like a photo on one street and a photo on another, and then puts that into a database and correlates that, that becomes intelligence.”
Skeen also pushed back on the notion that because the cameras capture license plates that are in public view, there is no invasion of privacy or Fourth Amendment concern.
“Tracking every citizen going around, whether they’re going to the store, to church, to the gun range, or wherever, it’s a lot different than just being seen in public. Being followed in public is a different thing,” he said.
Some vehicles able to ‘opt-out’
But is “every citizen” actually subject to the watchful lenses of Flock’s 120,000-plus cameras?
While digging into the system and how his community utilizes it, Skeen said he discovered the existence of something that further staggered him: a list of vehicles the cameras are built to ignore.
In the same way someone can “whitelist” an e-mail address they trust to allow it to pass through a spam filter, Skeen said he learned that agencies using Flock can designate license plates that effectively pass by the cameras without being flagged.
“It is a list of special plates, or assigned category, which people are suppressed from the system. It means, basically, when you drive around, the camera ignores your car,” Skeen said.
Skeen filed public records requests with agencies in his community, including with Maryville, and the city turned over three license plates on its “whitelist,” set to never expire, but no names attached.
When he asked who decides which vehicles get that kind of permanent exemption, he said the city told him there was no formal process at all.
“They told me there’s no policy and no instruction, and it’s up to a single person there. And they get to decide who goes on the list,” Skeen said.
Maryville’s police chief told InvestigateTV the list exists for a narrow, technical reason — to correct for the system’s own errors, not to grant special treatment: “These entries were whitelisted after our Flock cameras repeatedly generated hotlist alerts because of apparent misreads of similar-looking characters in plate images.”
Flock, for its part, said what Maryville has is what the company calls a “suppressed hit,” separate from a feature called a “Safe List,” which a spokesperson said is now only available to private customers such as homeowners associations and businesses.
“In the past, Flock did offer Safe List functionality to some law enforcement customers that wanted the ability to exclude certain vehicles from their own system. The feature was not widely used by law enforcement agencies and was subsequently removed from the law enforcement product,” a company spokesperson said.
However, in the dozens of Flock sole-source letters for its ALPR system InvestigateTV reviewed, “Privacy controls to enable certain vehicles to ‘opt-out’ of being captured” was listed as a proprietary feature of “the only Law Enforcement Grade ALPR System.”
Asked directly about this, the spokesperson said: “A small number of outdated sole source letters were used in error and referenced an opt-out function that is no longer available to law enforcement customers.”
InvestigateTV found letters from 2020 to 2026, including multiple from March and April of this year, that contained the “opt-out” line, and a version of the letter containing the line was submitted as justification as recently as mid-August by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office — prior to the county canceling its contract in early September.
Skeen said the uncertainty cuts in a troubling direction, since the public has no way to check who benefits from the exemption.
“That’s the huge problem with this, is we don’t have transparency, and we don’t have regulations, and we’re not watching the system,” Skeen said. “We really are just left to guess on what this could be.”
“I don’t believe that these do coincide with the Constitution”
Skeen comes from what he calls a law enforcement family — not an activist background.
“In my family, you went to the military or you went to law enforcement, or a combination,” he said.
But he said the scale of what he uncovered doesn’t square with the oath he took.
“I don’t believe that these do coincide with the Constitution, and that is the biggest issue with these systems,” Skeen said. “Although they might be powerful, they might be preferred, but I do not believe that they hold in standing with the Constitution.”
He said he’s raised those concerns directly with Maryville’s city council, warning of “the dangers of putting in mass surveillance on Americans.”
Skeen said to him, the benefits are not worth the risk.
“This is a great tool. I have to hand it to Flock. It is powerful, it is effective,” Skeen said, “but it’s also something we should not be having here in this country.”

title: 1 killed, several injured in incident at Six Flags Over Georgia
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — One person was killed and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, according to the Cobb County Police Department.
Police have not said what happened, but witnesses said a man fell to his death from the Goliath roller coaster.
Several riders were stuck on the coaster after the deadly incident late Monday afternoon. First Alert Chopper captured footage of the Goliath roller coaster stuck on the tracks and riders being helped to the ground.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement. “The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Police and Six Flags officials have not identified anyone involved or provided details about the extent of the injuries.
Six Flags shut down over the incident and guests were told to leave. Others were left stranded on Goliath’s steep incline, watching emergency crews rush past them below and wondering what went wrong.
“We saw mechanics and paramedics running down there. We realized something bad had happened,” said Ben Edwards, who was among nearly 20 people trapped on Goliath’s two-hundred-foot incline when the coaster suddenly stopped shortly before 4 p.m., stranding many for at least an hour way above the ground.
“Very tragic – the first thing you think about is the people you’re on the ride with,” said Edwards, who is visiting from Canada.
Edwards tried calming those around him, unsure when help would arrive. With each passing minute, frustration grew as trapped passengers looked down, waiting for a way off.
The real panic was in the car ahead of Edwards, where the deadly incident occurred.
The victim who died was found on a nearby roof, footage shows.
Edwards called for changes following the incident.
“Being stuck up there, some people are really scared of that stuff,” he said. “They need to do better.”
Goliath tops out at 70 miles per hour with an elevation of 200 feet and two drops, one of 170 feet and another of 175 feet. Considered a hypercoaster – a roller coaster that’s at least 200 feet tall – the ride was developed by Bolliger & Mabillard and uses restraints that sit across riders’ laps, not over-the-shoulder restraints.
Similar coasters exist throughout the Six Flags chain.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities,” the chain said.
The incident comes less than a month after Six Flags closed the famous X2 roller coaster at Magic Mountain in California after lawsuits revealed more than 100 people had suffered brain injuries while riding.
Cobb County Chairwoman Lisa Cupid called the incident “a terrible tragedy.”
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Cupid said in a statement.
Cupid added that the county is working closely with the amusement park “and other appropriate partners” as the investigation proceeds.
“Six Flags Over Georgia is a significant part of our tourism landscape, drawing visitors from across our county, our state, and the Southeast. I look forward to learning more as the investigation unfolds,” Cupid said. “In the meantime, please keep in your thoughts the family of the deceased, those who were injured, the employees and leadership of Six Flags, and our community. We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories.”

title: Appeals court dismisses Maine lobstermen defamation case against California aquarium
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A federal appeals court has sided with the California-based Monterey Bay Aquarium, which faced a defamation lawsuit from Maine lobstermen and groups representing the state’s industry.
The lobstermen sued three years ago, after the aquarium’s Seafood Watch program stripped the U.S. and Canadian lobster fisheries of their sustainability certifications and urged consumers not to buy lobster.
The aquarium said the fishery poses a threat to the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale.
Maine lobstermen argued that the aquarium made defamatory statements against the lobster fishery that caused them economic harm. The plaintiffs also included Bean Maine Lobster Inc., the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association.
But Friday an appeals court disagreed with a district court’s interpretation of the group defamation rule and said that the Maine lobstermen cannot prove harm to their individual businesses.
The justices said the case should return back to a lower court to be dismissed.
Maine lobstermen said their gear has been tied to just a few documented right whale entanglements in recent decades.
But conservationists and federal biologists argue the vast majority of entanglements are undocumented, and tracing entanglements back to a specific fishery is often difficult.
Entanglements from fishing gear and ship strikes are the two biggest threats to the right whale population. There are roughly 380 right whales remaining.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Church deacon, teacher arrested for reportedly kicking children off bus, leaving them on side of road
text:
ALBANY, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — A deacon for a church in Georgia, who is also a teacher, is facing charges after allegedly kicking a group of young kids off his bus and leaving them on the side of the road.
According to the incident report from the Albany Police Department, officers were called on Sunday, Oct. 11, to Oakridge Baptist Church. When officers got there, they talked to a woman who said her three children (ages 12, 11, and 9) and their 10-year-old friend who they had invited to church, had been kicked off the church bus.
She reported that her mother called her and told her the church deacon, Erin Menefee, had called and said he had put the kids off the bus because they were cursing.
The mom said she was told Menefee left the kids at an intersection about three miles away. She said it was too far for the kids to walk home. The mom says she got in her car and went looking for her kids, but couldn’t find them. She did, however, spot the church bus on the road and tried to flag it down.
According to police, the mom spoke with Menefee, who said he’d left the kids down the road. At that point, the mom went to the church to speak with the pastor and got a call from someone telling her the kids had been brought home by a stranger.
In the report, the grandmother claimed she was told the children were put off the bus because they were cursing and hitting each other and the bus driver, “Don’t play that.”
Officers spoke with Menefee about these accusations. Menefee reportedly told officers he had about 20 kids on the bus and this particular group of kids was being disruptive, and he needed to put them off the bus for his safety. Police asked Menefee how he thought the kids were going to get home, and he claimed he called their grandmother.
Police say Menefee acknowledged he should’ve waited for someone to come pick them up.
At this point, officers arrested Menefee. He was charged with multiple counts of reckless conduct. According to the incident report, Menefee is also a teacher at Mitchell County High School.

title: Tired of complaints about Susan Collins
text:
I’m tired of hearing that Sen. Susan Collins is responsible for the Supreme Court.
Look at the actual record. Yes, she voted to confirm Republican nominees. She also voted to confirm Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, every one of the court’s three liberal justices. No other Republican serving today can claim that.
Collins’ standard has never changed: a president of either party is entitled to qualified nominees, and each one gets judged on the merits, not on who sits in the White House. The only Supreme Court nominee she ever voted against was Amy Coney Barrett — because the confirmation was rushed through days before a presidential election. Collins said the same rule should apply no matter which party held the Senate, and she meant it.
People who blame Collins for the Supreme Court’s rulings are really just angry that she doesn’t vote the way they would, every single time. But that’s exactly the point of an independent. Someone who agrees with us on everything isn’t independent; they’re just on our team.
The same people demanding Sen. Collins reject every Republican nominee would be furious if a Democratic senator took marching orders from the other side. Consistency is a fair thing to ask for, yet Collins has delivered it for nearly 30 years.
People can disagree with a vote here or there. But the moment anyone looks at the “yes” votes, idea that Collins is a reliable partisan on the courts collapses.
Maine deserves a senator who thinks for herself. We have one.
Maeann Bush
Belgrade

title: This former Gardiner athlete succeeded on one kidney. Now, she’s in a battle for her life
text:
Kylie Boardman has been fighting the odds since the day she was born.
Boardman, a Gardiner native, has solitary dysplastic kidney disease, which means she was born with one kidney that will never reach full development. Before she was born, doctors told her parents, Bill and Jennifer Boardman, that she had a less than one percent chance to survive.
The doctor’s advice? Terminate the pregnancy.
“It was a day that my wife and I will never forget,” Bill Boardman said. “It wasn’t in our nature (to do it). We went home and were like, ‘If we get one hour with her, great. If we get two hours, that’s even better.’ We learned to put a catheter in our daughter at 2 days old. We’d do all this at home to survive as long as she could. We were told she’d need a transplant in her teens or early 20s, and here we are.”
Kylie Boardman defied those odds and played four sports (field hockey, volleyball, girls hockey and softball) at Gardiner Area High School. She also played women’s hockey at Central Maine Community College in Auburn, recording eight goals and 22 assists in two seasons.
“In retrospect, I really shouldn’t even be here,” Kylie Boardman said. “I feel so blessed that I’m here in the first place and that I’ve been able to do as many things as I’ve been doing. I’m not someone who just sits at home.”
Now 21, Boardman is in need of a kidney transplant. She also has fluid pressing against her ocular nerves, and may need a shunt in her brain to prevent her from going blind. She is exhausted all the time. At a time in life when she would normally be out with her friends, she rests at home, because simple acts expend more energy.
“I wake up and feel like I slept a good two hours, even though I normally get 10,” Boardman said. “I have shortness of breath, because there’s fluid around the lungs as well. … Putting up my ponytail is like running 5 miles. It’s a very hard adjustment going from an active sports lifestyle to this.”
Battling the odds
As a standout athlete at Gardiner, Kylie Boardman earned Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference honors in volleyball and was a member of the 2022 Class B softball state championship team. She was most at home on the ice as a tough and skilled defenseman on the girls hockey team, for which she also served as a team captain.
It was never obvious that Boardman was playing with one functioning kidney, and the family made a point not to publicly disclose it.
“It’s not something we shared. We never used as an excuse,” Bill Boardman said. “What she did was kind of remarkable, considering what she was going through.”
According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the global odds of a child being born with kidney dysplasia is 1 in 4,300. The kidneys are a filtration system for the human body, helping clean blood, and filter waste and extra fluid into urine. It also controls sodium and potassium levels and helps produce hormones.
One effect of kidney dysplasia is a lower than normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR), or how quickly the kidney can filter waste and extra fluid from the blood. It also makes Boardman’s bones more fragile. When she was freshman in high school, she broke her pelvis, which effected the remainder of her playing career.
“It never fully healed, I re-injured it two different times,” Boardman said. “I couldn’t play my sophomore season of volleyball, which was fine, because (it was the COVID season). Because there’s less calcium, it never fully healed, so I played with this broken bone inside of me.”
Last year, during her final season with the CMCC women’s hockey team, she began to notice the fast decline of the remaining kidney.
“My quality of life has definitely gone down. As I’ve grown more, my kidney is trying to do more,” Boardman said. “I hit that point where it’s just not able to pump anymore for me.”
A needed getaway
Bragoli Gym at Gardiner Area High School is rocking with pop music and laughs at the tail end of a practice for the Gardiner volleyball team.
Bill Boardman gathers the team for final instructions before a match the following day against Medomak Valley. He’s in his third season as the head coach of the Tigers, and led them to the Class C final last season.
Boardman was up front at the beginning of the season, with the team and parents, about Kylie’s need for a kidney transplant — and that when it happens, he’ll take a leave of absence, if it’s during the season. He constantly travels with Kylie to her medical appointments.
“The fact that he’s here for us and loves us, we’re just all so grateful,” said Gardiner senior Joely Cote. “It’s also important that we’re giving him that support while he’s going through this. We love him, and we want to look out for him the same way he looks out for us.
Coaching is a needed escape from the concerns a father has for his daughter.
“He is so devoted to that team and he loves coaching that team,” Kylie Boardman said. “It’s refreshing to see him coach and coach with such passion. It’s not an easy process (for him), because he comes to most of my appointments. That balance is key for everybody.”
Light at the end of the tunnel
The Boardman family has been more open about Kylie’s battle now that she needs a new kidney. A website (kidney4kylie.com) has been created to help find a donor.
The Boardmans received good news in late August. Insurance was approved for a kidney transplant, placing Kylie on the transplant list. She also received a voucher through the National Kidney Registry, which she received from the organization when someone donated a kidney in her name. Through the voucher program, it allows Kylie’s case to be prioritized.
There’s a possibility she could receive her new kidney by the end of the year.
“At this point, it’s just a waiting game for me,” Boardman said. “It’s a very quiet waiting game to hopefully get a new and better chance at life. Every day, I just pray it’s out there.”
Another effect of Boardman’s condition is vision loss, which began within the past year.
“I started to notice that my vision would go away and go black, in certain situations,” Boardman said. “I thought it was a symptom from a med, because I take 15 different meds every day. My optical nerves are swollen because of IIH.”
IIH is Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. According to the Cleveland Clinic, it occurs when cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the spinal cord and brain, builds up in the skull, causing pressure on the optic nerves.
“I’ve been told if this pressure doesn’t come down, it will cause vision loss,” Boardman said.
Boardman’s doctors will soon discuss whether she needs the shunt now, or can wait until after her kidney donation takes place.
Kylie Boardman now lives in Poland, with her boyfriend, Jack Keefe. Despite her current condition, she works four days per week at Serendipity Creek Childcare Center in Gray, while still making her appointments, as she waits for a donor and a new kidney.
“I’ve never been scared. I don’t get scared of much,” Boardman said. “It’s just hard. I see people planning for their future right now, and I can’t do that because I have this massive surgery that I have to plan for, and plan, for a year, to be out of everything. It’s kind of frustrating. But I’m at peace with it. I have such a good support system around me that I’m OK with the fact that it’s going to happen. And I’m OK because I have so many people around me.”

title: Maine gas prices continue to rise, GasBuddy says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine (WABI) - Average gasoline prices in Maine have risen in the last week, according to GasBuddy.
GasBuddy reports the average price is $4.38 today.
Prices in Maine are more than 8 cents per gallon higher than a month ago.
The national average price fell 0.4 cents per gallon in the last week, averaging $4.29 today.
The national average price of diesel has decreased 5.9 cents compared to a week ago and stands at $6.25.
“More states saw average gasoline prices decline than rise over the last week, with diesel falling approximately 5 cents per gallon nationally,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “On the policy front, the Trump administration’s proposed diesel deal raises more questions than it answers, and I remain skeptical that it will deliver significant relief to the trucking industry and consumers who depend on diesel. Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias has passed, but we are awaiting updates on two refineries that were in its path, the outcome of which could impact the supply picture in the days ahead. For now, the trend is cautiously in the right direction for motorists, but between hurricane season and continued geopolitical uncertainty, it is far too early to declare the pressure on fuel prices resolved.”

title: Actress Selma Blair arrested, accused of attacking flight staff
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) - Actress Selma Blair was arrested after allegedly trying to open an airplane door mid-flight and injuring two flight attendants, TMZ and Variety confirmed.
Blair, 54, was aboard a Delta Air Lines Flight to New York City from Los Angeles on Sunday night, according to the New York Port Authority.
While in flight, Blair allegedly tried to open the plane’s door, then allegedly hit one flight attendant and bit another.
A representative for Blair told TMZ and Variety that she experienced a medical emergency that caused the alleged conduct.
“Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first,” a representative from Delta Air Lines wrote.
Officers from the Port Authority Police Department were called out to the plane around 11 p.m., where it was parked at the gate.
Blair was taken into custody and then to the hospital for evaluation, Port Authority officials said. They went on to confirm one of the flight attendants was also taken to an area hospital.
The FBI, which investigates all alleged assaults on board aircrafts, is investigating what may have happened.
What charges Blair will face was not immediately clear at the time of publication.

title: 2 charged after child allegedly suffers burns on feet at daycare
text:
LAFAYETTE COUNTY, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - Two people, including a 17-year-old, were arrested after an investigation into alleged child abuse at a Mississippi daycare, authorities said.
The Lafayette County Sheriff’s Office said deputies received a report on Sept. 22 about a child who sustained burns to the feet, allegedly at a daycare in the county.
Investigators initiated an investigation into the allegations and later obtained for two women: Rhina Delgado, 20, and a 17-year-old girl, both from Oxford.

title: Former wedding videographer repurposing event florals to spread joy, cheer
text:
Former wedding videographer repurposing event florals to spread joy, cheer
Nora McCormack-Bowen is the founder of After Party, a Portland-based nonprofit organization saving event florals from being thrown out. She previously worked in the wedding industry as a videographer for more than a decade.
"I worked a particular wedding where I watched them throw out literally hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of flowers in two dumpsters behind the venue, and I snapped," McCormack-Bowen said.
She captured the sweetest moments in a couple's love story, but behind the scenes, she watched them leave behind so much waste.
"It just kind of crushed my soul to see all of these beautiful flowers being wasted," McCormack-Bowen said.
It pushed her to leave the industry. She hiked the Appalachian Trail and then came home to Portland to start her nonprofit organization.
"There is this problem that I had noticed for, you know, over a decade and I just figured I could actually do something about it rather than just keep complaining about it," she said.
She accepts financial donations in exchange for sending someone to the event venue to collect the flowers. Volunteers then rearrange them into smaller bouquets that are donated to nearby hospitals, care centers, and group homes.
"My favorite part of this whole process so far has been seeing the joy that these flowers can provide to people," McCormack-Bowen said. "Especially in times when they might need that extra lift."
She and the volunteers work together to recycle as many flowers as possible. Whatever they don't use is composted. Many of the glass vases or jars they use are donated and reused. Sustainability is a priority for After Party, and so is spreading cheer and joy.
McCormack-Bowen recalled being thanked after a recent delivery to Florence House, a supportive housing facility managed by Preble Street.
"You're our neighbor. You’re a part of our community, and your joy matters just as much as somebody else's," she said.
She believes something as simple as a flower can change someone's day. That's her goal moving forward. McCormack-Bowen would like to reach even more people for collections and donations in the years ahead.

title: New life revving up at old Bessey Motors in South Paris
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A year after going on the market, the former Bessey Motors at 209 Main St. in South Paris has a new owner, Shawn Holbrook, who operates Midtown Motors next door at 217 Main St.
Joining him as partners and co-owners are Rob Kahkonen and Richie Kimball, who are closing their business, R/K Automotive on Beal Street in Norway, and moving to the new site.
“Richie and Rob will be bringing their experience, dedication and commitment to their customers right along with them,” according to Holbrook.
Holbrook, who also owns Meineke Car Care Center in Auburn, purchased the Main Street building and the lot behind it.
Within a day or two of receiving the keys, crews were ripping at the facade of the building. The three expect to open as an auto dealer/service center by the end of this year.
Kimball and Kahkonen have been partners for years, first working on vehicles at Kimball’s home garage and then opening the Beal Street shop together about five years ago.
“We have great customers and we’re extremely busy,” Kimball said during an Oct. 8 interview. “We book a month out right now. At the new place we’ll have the space to add a couple of technicians” and a service writer.
Along with their individual clients, the pair are also the fleet techs for local businesses Valley View Pies, Flanders Electric and Midtown Motors.
It was a casual conversation with Holbrook that led to a partnership among the three of them.
“That’s where good ideas come from,” Kimball continued. “We were just talking and he asked about our plans. My answer was, ‘the question is, what’s next?’”
With R/K’s business bursting at the seams and Midtown Motors splitting its parking lot with Twin Town Glass, the answer to Kimball’s question was to join forces and put the empty commercial space back in use.
The partnership combines sales with service. Kimball said there will be seven bays in the garage, six for regular automotive service and one for classic vehicle conditioning, an in-demand part of his and Kahkonen’s business.
Both men have longstanding connections to auto repair around Oxford Hills. Kahkonen worked at Bessey Motors for more than 20 years; Kimball previously worked at A-1 Auto in Mechanic Falls and Trafford Truck Equipment in New Gloucester.
Both admit to having a penchant for collecting vehicles.
Kimball recently drove his 1956 Chevy Bel Air to work, and has two others, plus pickup trucks.
Doing quick math in his head, Kahkonen said he has nine trucks.
“Shawn has great plans for this,” Kimball said of the business venture. “He wants to get involved in the Christmas for Kids, and be part of the parades that they have around here. We used to build the floats at Bessey’s.
“We’re going to support local sports, we’re going to be part of the community, just like it used to be,” he said.

title: LaGrange Shooting Leads To Arrests Of Two Convicted Felons In Penobscot County
text:
Deputies Arrest LaGrange Men On Firearms Charges After Weapons Were Discharged Earlier This Week
Deputies in Penobscot County arrested two men from LaGrange Thursday afternoon, following reports that a weapon had been discharged in the area.
Read More: Maine Man Charged After Allegedly Breaking Into Ex's Home In Passadumkeag
According to the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office, 37-year-old Guy Shurman and 44-year-old Daniel Turner were arrested, with help from the Maine State Police, and without incident, and taken to the Penobscot County Jail, following reports from folks in town that a shooting had taken place near or around a residence in the area.
"During the investigation, deputies determined that gunfire had crossed the roadway and struck a residence located across the street, creating a potentially dangerous situation for nearby residents. As the investigation progressed, deputies obtained a search warrant for the suspects’ residence. Investigators confirmed that both individuals were convicted felons and prohibited from possessing firearms."
Authorities say this is a great example of "see something, say something" (or, in this case, "hear something") in action.
Read More: Maine Man Shot And Killed In Indian Township, Suspect Arrested
Authorities arrested both men and charged them with Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person.
In the state of Maine, prohibited people include felons, those involved with domestic violence cases, mental illness cases, and juvenile offenders.
Convicted felons like Turner and Shurman, who are found guilty of possession of a firearm, could face up to 10 years in prison and up to $20,000 in fines.
Others might only face up to 5 years in prison and a fine of up to $5,000. In either case, the minimum jail sentence is at least 2 years for felons, and 1 year for others found guilty of firearm possession by a prohibited person.

title: 7 Maine events include ‘Arcadia’ at Portland Stage and Biddeford Art Walk
text:
7:30 p.m. Wednesday, 2 and 7:30 p.m. Thursday, 7:30 p.m. Friday, 3:30 and 8 p.m. Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday. Through Oct. 25. Portland Stage, 25A Forest Ave., $35-$77. portlandstage.org.
Tom Stoppard’s “Arcadia” moves between 1809 and the present day as scholars delve into the history of an idyllic English locale. At Coverly Estate in 1809, young Thomasina learns math and science with her tutor, Septimus, who is also caught up in an affair with a married woman while facing a looming duel. Almost two centuries later, two researchers try to uncover what really happened. Science, sex, literature and love overlap, along with timelines.
7 p.m. Thursday, 7:30 p.m. Friday, 2 and 7:30 p.m. Saturday. Through Oct. 31. Footlights Theatre, 190 US Route 1, Falmouth, $28. thefootlightstheatre.com.
Agatha Christie’s thrilling tale, “Miss Marple: Murder at the Vicarage” runs through Halloween night in Falmouth. When the unpopular Colonel Protheroe is murdered in the village vicarage, there is no shortage of suspects and motives. Can investigator Miss Marple see through the lies and gossip to uncover the truth? There’s one way to find out.
6:30 p.m. Friday, 11:30 a.m. and 6:30 p.m. Saturday, 1:30 p.m. Sunday. Cross Insurance Arena, Portland, $20.25-$71. crossarenaportland.com.
Be ready for Hot Wheels Monster Trucks coming to life, including the incredible Mega Wrex, Tiger Shark, HW 5-Alarm, Bone Shaker, Bigfoot and Skelesaurus. Plus you’ll see riders performing crazy stunts while you shriek at a fire-breathing car and car-crushing robot dinosaur. Not only that, this year’s extravaganza features the new Rhinomite, a rhino-themed truck. If none of this makes sense, just ask a kid, or someone with a wild imagination and love for all things Hot Wheels-related.
5-8 p.m. Friday. Main Street, and surrounding streets, downtown Biddeford. artofbiddeford.org/artwalk.
This is the final Third Friday Biddeford Art Walk of the year. The vibe is cheerful and positive, and downtown is lined with artists and makers selling their wares. You might also find a pop-up performance as you walk around and visit galleries, studios, shops and public spaces.
Friday and Saturday. Maine Jewish Museum, 267 Congress St., Portland, $81.88 Friday event, $59.47 Saturday event. mainejewishmuseum.org.
Ari’el Stachel is a Tony and Grammy award-winning actor and writer, known for his role in the musical “The Band’s Visit.” You’ve got two chances to engage with him this weekend at the Maine Jewish Museum. Friday’s event is At the Table with Ari’el Stachel: A Yemenite-Inspired Shabbat. The pescetarian Yemenite-inspired meal will be accompanied by family stories, heritage and conversation. An Evening with Ari’el Stachel, on Saturday, draws from his autobiographical work “Other” and features an ensemble of characters from his life in a performance that is funny, poignant and richly human. This includes a post-show dessert reception.
7:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday, 2:30 p.m. Sunday, 2:30 p.m. Wednesday-Oct. 22, 7:30 p.m. Oct. 23-24, 2:30 p.m. Oct. 25. Saco River Theatre, 29 Salmon Falls Road, Buxton, pay-what-you-can, $25 suggested. sacorivertheatre.org.
The Originals presents a play set in 1669, when women were at long last allowed to take the stage in England after enduring decades of Puritan rule. “Playhouse Creatures” is a funny and poignant look at five pioneering women who figure out fame, love and the world of Restoration actresses on the forefront of England’s theatrical revolution.
9:30 a.m.-6 p.m. Saturday, 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. Sunday. Portland Expo, 239 Park Ave., $15, $20 for early entry at 9 a.m., free for 12 and under. northeastcardexpo.com/maine-2026.
The Northeast Sports Card Expo will feature more than 225 vendor tables covered with sports cards, memorabilia, Pokémon, Funko Pops and other collectibles. James Spence Authentication will be on-site for autograph authentication and celebrity guests include former Red Sox pitcher Dennis “Oil Can” Boyd and former Boston Bruins player and head coach Steve Kasper, among several others. The first 200 attendees on both days will receive the official Northeast Sports Card Expo poster, designed by Maine-based artist Max Erwin.

title: Quentin Tarantino's first stage play will debut in London with Sacha Baron Cohen as star
text:
Quentin Tarantino's first stage play will debut in London with Sacha Baron Cohen as star
The latest project from Quentin Tarantino is a swashbuckling stage comedy featuring “Borat” star Sacha Baron Cohen.
Sony Pictures Entertainment and Sonia Friedman Productions announced Sunday that the Oscar-winning filmmaker’s first stage play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” will open in London’s West End in March.
It’s set in 1830s Europe, and the producers call it “a rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen.”
The play will be directed by Tarantino and marks the West End debut of Baron Cohen, creator of comic characters Borat and Ali G.
“When the best director in the world calls, you don’t ask questions,” Baron Cohen said.
“The Popinjay Cavalier” begins previews Feb. 23 and opens March 18 at London’s Phoenix Theatre.
Tarantino, best known for films including “Reservoir Dogs,” “Pulp Fiction” and “Inglourious Basterds,” hasn’t directed a feature film since “Once Upon a Time ... in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019.
He wrote the screenplay for a sequel, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” due for release in November. David Fincher is directing, with Brad Pitt returning in the title role of a former Hollywood stuntman.
Tarantino wrote a novelization of “Once Upon a Time ... in Hollywood” as well as one for the new film, which will be published Dec. 8 by Harper, an imprint of HarperCollins.

title: Elon Musk quietly becomes biggest known donor in midterm contests as he tries to save Republicans
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Elon Musk, the world’s only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress.
The numbers, first reported by the New York Times ahead of this week’s federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk’s super PAC.
The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history.
Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump in 2024.
Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton.
It’s a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough,” he said at the time.
Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared on stage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president’s second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency.
He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week.
Musk’s net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.
Republican have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts — a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president’s performance, stubbornly high prices and the unpopular war with Iran.

title: Understands firsthand
text:
To the editor:
Though we are saddened to see our dedicated and talented House District 48 Rep. Holly Stover leave the field, it is heartwarming that a similarly committed and capable candidate, Charlotte Nutt, D-Edgecomb, has stepped up to succeed Holly as our representative.
When I first met Charlotte I loved learning that, though she grew up on the Boothbay peninsula, she and her siblings also spent part of their young years sailing the world with her boatbuilder father and mother, a physician. Having had a similar experience in my own childhood, I know how significant overseas learning can be, not just about other cultures, but, most importantly, about our own unique American experience and how precious it is.

title: 24-year-old hiker missing in Great Smoky Mountains found dead after dayslong search
text:
BLOUNT COUNTY, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A 24-year-old man was hiking in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park when his phone became untraceable, setting off a dayslong search that ended in tragedy.
Sahil Jilani, 24, went missing while hiking in the Great Smoky Mountains. Park officials say he was last seen around 8 p.m. last Monday at the Riverstone Campground in Townsend. His car was found at the Abrams Falls trailhead Wednesday.
The next day, divers found Jilani’s body in the water at Abrams Falls, according to his family. His phone, keys and clothes were also found near the falls.
While waiting for official reports, Jilani’s family believes he drowned after getting caught in powerful currents near the waterfall.
“With heavy hearts, we share the loss of our beloved brother, Sahil Jilani... Sahil was a pure, kind, generous soul who always cared for others. He dreamed of helping Mom retire, taking on her bills and helping Dad with dental procedures. A new uncle, he couldn’t wait to spoil his niece and teach her martial arts and self-defense. His absence leaves an irreplaceable void,” said Jilani’s sister, Asma Jilani Bustamante.
Bustamante says the family asked for help the day Jilani went missing due to the fact that their mother felt something was “terribly wrong.”
“He never went hours without checking in, but his location sharing stopped in a dead zone. We requested a welfare check from rangers the next day, but were told hikers often lose service. We kept requesting help as our fear grew,” Bustamante said.
Jilani’s family is now asking for help through donations, prayers and sharing their story, as they work to get his body back to Houston, Texas, and cover other bills related to the incident. Among these is getting care for Jilani’s mother, who was hospitalized “after losing her precious son,” according to Bustamante.
The family also hopes to raise awareness about water safety in honor of Jilani.
“I am determined to honor Sahil by helping save lives. If his story saves even one life, his memory will continue to protect others,” Bustamante said.
She is urging others to be aware of their surroundings, even when engaging in something beautiful like a waterfall.
“Beauty can turn deadly in an instant. Please heed warning signs, especially where lives have been lost. Share travel plans, prepare for cellular dead zones and consider carrying a satellite communication device in remote areas,” Bustamante said. “An upset or disappointed loved one who turns back from dangerous water is infinitely better than a deceased one.”
Official reports about the incident are pending.

title: ProPublica report, outrageous? Yes it is, senator.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Confronted with credible accusations that Sen. Susan Collins received large contributions from someone seeking a lucrative contract with the federal government, the senator and her campaign responded by calling it “outrageous.”
I agree. It certainly is outrageous that such payments appear to have been accepted under those circumstances. It’s also outrageous that we have an electoral system that allows such payments under any circumstances, and an economy so dominated by a wealthy few who are able to virtually control our governing institutions.
Troy Jackson doesn’t seek or accept contributions like that. In truth, I doubt they would be offered anyway, because when Troy gets to Washington he will work with fellow progressives to fix our corrupt political system and promote a more equal and fair economy.
I can’t wait.
Mike Roland
Bowdoinham

title: Penobscot County Deputies Locate Passadumkeag Burglary Suspect On Island In the River
text:
Maine Burglary Suspect is Apprehended After Fleeing in a Kayak
A Chester man is accused of breaking into his ex's Passadumkeag home before fleeing to an island.
Chester, Maine Man Charged With Burglary After Alleged Passadumkeag Break-in
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office has identified the suspect as Nicholas Violette, 25, of Chester.
He's charged with burglary and violation of conditional release after an incident Saturday night in Passadumkeag.
READ MORE: Are You Aware of the 100-Foot Law in Maine?
Dispatchers received a report at approximately 10:45 pm of an alleged burglary in that town.
Passadumkeag, Maine Burglary Suspect Fled From the Police in a Kayak
The caller told authorities that her ex-boyfriend had allegedly broken into the Main Road residence through a window and then fled.
Her ex-boyfriend, Violette, has active bail conditions that prohibit him from being at the home or having contact with the victim.
When deputies arrived, they heard movement in the woods and began tracking the suspect.
Officials located Violette and a kayak on an island in the river.
Multiple Maine Law Enforcement Agencies Worked Together to Apprehend a Burglary Suspect
Deputies tried to make verbal contact with Violette, but he didn't respond or comply with commands to surrender.
Officials requested a drone from the Lincoln Police Department and a K9 from the Old Town Police Department.
Maine Wardens also responded with a boat and game wardens.
As the drone flew overhead, Violette surrendered to authorities, who crossed the small waterway and took him into custody without incident.
This incident remains under investigation.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Put my life on the line
text:
To the editor:
A large number of the homeless in the United States are veterans who live in tents and cardboard boxes. I see veterans in Togus missing limbs and using guide dogs to help with mental disorders.
Shouldn’t we be giving them a tax exemption for real estate taxes so they can remain in their own homes? I built a small kit log cabin 25 years ago. My taxes have gone up dramatically in that period of time.

text:
North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, adding to streak of weapons tests
North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters, South Korea’s military said, adding to a recent streak of weapons demonstrations that has heightened tensions during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were fired from an area around the North Korean capital of Pyongyang, where the country has used its airport as a major launch site in recent years. The joint chiefs did not immediately specify how many missiles they detected or how far they flew. Japan’s Defense Ministry said it detected at least two missiles and assessed that the weapons landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone.
The launch came days after South Korea on Friday flight-tested its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, which President Lee Jae Myung described as an important step in strengthening the South’s conventional defense capabilities.
While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an Oct. 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.
North Korea has also conducted other missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.
Tensions were further worsened after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South’s military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology.
Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described the neighbor as a permanent enemy during a prolonged stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. He has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts. Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea’s conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States. Washington unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with South Korea in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim.
___
AP writer Mari Yamaguchi contributed from Tokyo.

title: InvestigateTV+: The case for moving school start times
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ examines the fight over the first bell; why experts say early start times can work against the teenage brain and why changing the schedule can be complicated for schools and families.
Plus, a diaper dilemma as soaring prices force some families to choose between necessities and the diaper banks and volunteers working to close the gap.
Shifting school start times could address teen sleep loss
School in many districts across the country begins before sunrise, a schedule doctors say runs counter to how teenage brains are wired to sleep.
School did not always start this early. During the 1950s and 1960s, U.S. schools started between 8:30 and 9 a.m. because most children could walk or bike to a neighborhood school.
With more research linking early start times to teen sleep loss, some communities are trying to move the clock forward.
The need for diapers
Diapers are a basic need for many families. Parents already dealing with rising costs for housing, food and transportation can find it hard to keep up with diaper costs.
According to a 2026 survey by the National Diaper Bank Network, nearly half of families, or one in two, struggled to pay for diapers.
A quarter of parents reported missing work or school because they could not afford the diapers required to leave their baby in childcare.
The virtual need for speed
A new racing simulator center has opened in Portland, giving drivers access to technology used to train professional racers.
Driving a racing simulator is harder than it looks, but in the e-sports industry, people who master sim racing are turning the skill into a career. E-sports, or competitive video gaming, has grown in popularity over the years, with sim racing gaining an engaged fan base.
From janitor to physician
In 2011, Shay Taylor-Allen was working as a janitor at Yale New Haven Hospital when she was 18.
She is now returning years later to the hospital as a resident physician.

title: Maine lobstermen’s defamation lawsuit against California aquarium dismissed by appeals court
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BOSTON, Massachusetts (WMTW/WABI) - A federal appeals court has ordered the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit that was brought by the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and four other groups against the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California.
The lawsuit was filed in March 2023 after Seafood Watch, a conservation program operated by the aquarium, placed lobster from the United States and Canada on its do-not-eat “red list” in 2022 because lobster fishing gear poses an entanglement risk to the endangered North Atlantic right whale. The recommendation prompted some retailers, including Whole Foods, to pull lobster from stores.
The lobster fishing industry pushed back against Seafood Watch’s claim, saying it inaccurately portrayed fishing gear as a threat to North Atlantic right whales and constituted defamation that has caused economic harm. The industry claimed that the whales face greater threats from other fishing industries, including the Canadian snow crab fishery.
The Monterey Bay Aquarium made an attempt to have the lawsuit tossed in U.S. District Court in Maine, but Judge John Woodcock ruled in February 2025 that the lawsuit could move forward.
The aquarium then filed an appeal with the Boston-based First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals. During oral arguments held on July 27, one of the appellate judges said that the lawsuit did not strike him as a defamation claim and that he found the case troubling “from a First Amendment perspective.”
“The more you broaden the class of people that fall within this, the more it feels like everybody can sue,” said Judge Seth Aframe.
In a ruling handed down Friday, the First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals reversed the U.S. District Court’s denial of the aquarium’s motion to dismiss. The appeals court said that Seafood Watch’s comments did not target specific members of a group, which is required under the so-called “group defamation rule.” The matter has been remanded to the district court with instructions to dismiss the complaint.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association responded to the decision, saying in part: “The court dismissed our case, but it did not validate the Aquarium’s claims about Maine lobster. Those are two very different things. The ruling did not address MLA’s allegations that the Aquarium’s false claims have harmed Maine’s lobster fishery.”
MLA Executive Director Patrice McCarron went on to say, “Consumers can feel proud choosing Maine lobster, a product brought to market in keeping with a long history of responsible stewardship and a strong commitment to right whale conservation.”
The groups that joined the Maine Lobstermen’s Association in the lawsuit were wholesaler Bean Maine Lobster, the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association, Maine Lobster and Processing, and Maine lobster fishing company Bug Catcher.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: Homicide agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting
text:
MIMS, Fla. (WESH) — A Florida sheriff’s office agent died Saturday night after a wrong-way driver hit his vehicle head-on on Interstate 95, according to authorities.
What happened
The Brevard County Sheriff’s Office said a 26-year-old woman from Kissimmee was driving back from a beachside wedding. Authorities said she made a U-turn near a rest stop and began traveling the wrong way on I-95 north.
Florida Highway Patrol received calls about the wrong-way driver and had law enforcement en route, but troopers could not reach her before the crash occurred.
“That vehicle traveled from the rest area down south of 46, where it hit Kevin head-on,” Brevard County Sheriff Wayne Ivey said.
Agent Kevin Morris was headed to respond to a shooting in Mims at the time of the crash. Both vehicles caught fire after the collision.
Investigation underway
The female driver’s name has not been released. FHP said a toxicology test will be conducted on the driver.
“There will be a toxicology on the driver. We don’t know what that is right now,” said Lt. Channing Taylor of Florida Highway Patrol.
“No matter what the outcome, our thoughts, our prayers go out to that family,” Ivey said.
Morris remembered by colleagues, friend
The sheriff’s office said Morris previously served with the Palm Bay Police Department, left to work in a church, then returned to law enforcement with the Brevard County Sheriff’s Office in 2021. He served as a deputy, field training officer, agent in the homicide unit and a polygraph examiner.
“Our agency, our community, family of Kevin are absolutely devastated,” Ivey said. “There’s so many things you could say about Kevin. If you were going to, you would start with he was just absolutely an amazing guy.”
Ashley Hughes, who knew Morris, said he officiated her wedding.
“He was a treasured friend, but most importantly, he was our pastor,” Hughes said. “I was in shock when I learned about it. If you needed help with something, he was there, and he was always there for my husband and I.”
Ivey said he will remember the response effort at the scene.
“What I saw was everybody fighting, working as hard as they could to save both of the people in those cars,” Ivey said.

DONCASTER, U.K. (Gray News) - A wildlife park in the United Kingdom reportedly said it will not euthanize a tiger that mauled a man to death after he entered its enclosure.
A man who has not been identified entered the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday.
Police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury.” The man was pronounced dead at the scene. The tiger was not injured and stayed inside the enclosure during the incident, according to police.
The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park said its “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” are with the family of the man who lost his life. The park also said Altai, the tiger, is “safe and well and will not be euthanized,” according to The Guardian.
