title: UMF presents 20th annual Constitution Day U.S. Supreme Court Case Review, Oct. 14
What happens to Maine’s economy without congressional clout?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am not voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson because I support either candidate. I am voting against Donald Trump. But Maine should also think carefully about what happens after this election, when we no longer have a senator with Collins’ seniority and appropriations power.
Bath Iron Works is not just another employer. Its future depends on a steady Navy workload and continued investment in the yard. BIW has historically competed against Huntington Ingalls Industries in Mississippi for DDG-51 destroyers, and Maine’s congressional delegation has repeatedly fought to preserve ship allocations and funding that sustain the workforce and industrial base.
The contrast with Portsmouth Naval Shipyard is important. Portsmouth is one of the Navy’s four public shipyards and benefits directly from the Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program, or SIOP, which has funded major modernization there. BIW, as a privately owned shipyard, does not have that same direct federal recapitalization path.
That makes congressional influence especially important. A sustained loss of destroyer work could mean not only thousands of jobs, but erosion of the engineering, design, integration and skilled-trades capacity needed to build complete warships.
We have seen that kind of decline before. Once-major yards such as the Brooklyn Navy Yard and Quincy Shipyard lost workload, shed skilled workers and capabilities and ultimately ceased shipbuilding altogether. The lesson is that industrial capacity can disappear gradually before the final closure makes headlines.
Whatever our politics this November, Maine needs a serious plan for preserving BIW’s shipbuilding capability after today’s senior delegation is gone.
Kay Aikin
Portland

title: Haunted hikes in Maine for spooky fun this Halloween
text:
This story was originally published in October 2016.
The state of Maine has long been known as a place of ghost stories and otherworldly happenings. Perhaps it’s the landscape that inspires such tales. What makes the state beautiful — its jagged coastline, fog-socked harbors, mossy woods and old quaint towns — can also appear spooky and ethereal. Or maybe — just maybe — Maine truly is a hotspot for the supernatural.
Whatever the reason, Maine is home to some of the nation’s oldest and most elaborate ghost tales, as well as host of modern spectres. Most of these stories take place in old homes, inns and theaters. But there are a few ghosts that prefer to haunt Maine’s great outdoors.
So for those who would like to mix recreation with spectral lore, here are a few haunted Maine trails that you can visit this Halloween season, in the spirit of all that goes bump in the night.
To locals, this mountain is known as “Catherine’s Hill,” home of a particularly spooky ghost known as Headless Catherine. While there are several versions of this ghosts story floating around out there, all stories agree that this particular ghost is that of a woman who died in a vehicle accident nearby. She has been seen walking along Blackwoods Road between the towns of Cherryfield and Franklin, and is said to also haunt the banks of nearby Fox Pond and the slopes of Catherine Mountain.
Rising 942 feet above sea level, the sparsely wooded top of Catherine Mountain offers spectacular views of the surrounding mountains, lakes and ponds of eastern Maine. The top can be reached by a moderately difficult hiking trail that includes a few steep, rocky sections. Up and back, the hike is about 1.4 miles long.
How to get there: From Route 1 and Route 182 in Franklin, turn east on Route 182 (Blackwoods Scenic Byway) and turn right onto Dynamite Brook Road, a dirt road marked with a blue public reserved land sign. Drive a short distance and park in the first small parking area on the left. The trailhead — marked with a boulder and painted blue blaze — is farther down the road on the left, just before the narrow bridge. A short distance into the trail will be a sign that reads “Caribou Mt. Trail.” This trail will lead you to a juncture, where you will turn left to hike Catherine Mountain (right to hike Caribou Mountain).
The Old Narrow Gauge Trail in Randolph
This public path for walkers and bicyclists was constructed along the former Kennebec Central Railroad, which from the 1890s to 1920s transported passengers and goods to the nation’s first veterans hospital at Togus. And for years, area residents have been sharing stories about scary experiences they’ve had while on the trail, which some people believe to be haunted.
One theory is that the trail is haunted by the spirit of Bicycle Larry, a Randolph man who disappeared from the town in fall 2004 and was never found. However, some people in the town claim that the Old Narrow Gauge Volunteer Trail and the woods it passes through was haunted long before then. Ghost stories associated with this trail include shadow people, disembodied voices and glowing orbs floating through the forest.
Passing through a thin strip of woods with residential houses on either side, the trail then crosses Route 226 and enters a quieter, older forest. In addition to following the old railroad bed, the trail follows a brook.
How to get there: The trail starts beside Googins IGA on Route 27 in Randolph.
Located in a 67-acre park on the shore of Silver Lake, this trail network totals about 2 miles of walking and is said to be haunted by the ghost of Sarah Ware, who died in 1898.
As the story goes, Sarah Ware was a Bucksport resident whose murderer was never brought to justice. This is the painfully short version of the story, which is rehashed in the book “In Search of Sarah Ware: Reinvestigating Murder and Conspiracy in a Maine Village” by local historian Emeric Spooner.
Silver Lake Trails are six intersecting trails that lead downhill to the shores of Silver Lake. The trails are wide and well-marked with various colors of paint, making it hard to get lost in the reportedly haunted woods. Watch your footing on sections of the trail that are rocky and covered with tangled tree roots.
How to get there: From Main Street in Bucksport, turn onto Central Street (beside Stowaways Town Tavern and across from Fort Knox Park Inn). Follow Central Street approximately 1.8 miles and turn left into the parking area of Bucksport Public Works (362 Central St.). Follow signs for Silver Lake Trails to the left of the blue buildings and down a dirt drive to the parking area for the trail network. A kiosk with a trail map marks the trailhead.
Rising 800 feet above Megunticook Lake, Maiden Cliff is one of the most popular hiking destinations of Midcoast Maine. It also happens to be the location of a tragic accident, which has led some people to believe it to be haunted.
In May 7, 1864, a young girl fell to her death from Maiden Cliff. Her story can be read on a memorial plaque at the top of the cliff, where a large, metal cross was erected in her memory.
Today, visitors can climb to the cliff on a 1-mile hiking trail that is steep and rocky. The trail ends at the cross, memorial plaque and a spectacular view of the lake and nearby hills.
How to get there: From the intersection of Route 1 and Route 52 in Camden, turn onto Route 52 and travel north for about 2.8 miles. The parking area for Maiden Cliff will be on the right.
Pott’s Point Preserve in Harpswell
It’s not that the preserve that is haunted; it’s the body of water the preserve overlooks: Merriconeag Sound leading into Harpswell Harbor. In the 1800s, this waterway was known to be visited by a ghost ship that some believed to the Dash, a Freeport-built privateer that disappeared in January 1815 with 60 men aboard. Appearing often at Lookout Point or Pott’s Point, the ghost ship — on which no sailors are seen aboard — was said to indicate a local death was imminent. The last sighting of the ship was 1880, but the story lives on in the 1866 poem “The Dead Ship of Harpswell” by John Greenleaf Whittier.
Pott’s Point Preserve is owned and maintained by the Harpswell Heritage Trust and includes nice secluded beaches and tidal pools. While there are no official hiking trails on this small preserve, visitors must walk from the parking lot about 0.25 mile along the private Pott’s Point Rd to reach the preserve, where can continue your walk along the water.
How to get to Pott’s Point Preserve: From the intersection of Route 123 and Bath Road in Brunswick, follow Route 123 south 13.9 miles to the end of Route 123. Park by the side of the road, but do not block the pier or town landing. Walk along private Pott’s Point Road to the preserve. You may also walk along the shore below the high tide line.

title: 3 lawsuits filed against owners of Maine schooner years after fatal incident
text:
Three lawsuits were filed early this month in the U.S. District Court of Maine against the owners of a schooner involved in a fatal incident in 2023.
Dr. Emily Mecklenburg, 40, of Rockland, was killed when the top of the rear mast of the Rockland-based Grace Bailey split and fell on Oct. 9, 2023. Three others who were injured are now suing Grace Bailey Navigation Co. Inc. and the schooner.
The two-masted schooner, built in 1882 and restored in 1990, was about a mile east of Rockland Harbor at about 10 a.m. when the mast fell. A report released by the U.S. Coast Guard last year determined that the inside of the main mast had rotted.
The boat had been involved in other accidents, but this was its first fatality, the Press Herald reported at the time.
Two separate lawsuits that name Grace Bailey Navigation Inc. Co. and the schooner as defendants were filed last week on behalf of Maureen Colvin, of Scituate, Massachusetts, and Katherine McCann, who lived in Montville at the time of the incident but currently resides in Newfoundland, Canada.
A lawsuit on behalf of Christopher Sarao, of Lubec, was filed on Oct. 2 against the company and vessel. It was amended on Friday to include his wife, Diane Sarao, who was also on board, as a plaintiff. The amended suit also added numerous additional defendants, including members of the crew, the former owners of the Grace Bailey, and people and companies responsible for repairs and examinations of the vessel in the years leading up to the incident.
Colvin, a passenger, was “abruptly impacted from above” by the sail and was “propelled down approximately eight feet of stairs, resulting in a violent and painful impact with the floor deck below,” her suit says, but went on to aid other passengers.
McCann, who was a hired musician for the voyage, was injured and eventually transported by LifeFlight to a hospital, according to her suit, and has since received treatment from several providers and continues to do so.
Christopher Sarao, also a passenger, was assisting those injured in the “initial collapse” when “a fallen spar shifted and struck his forehead,” the suit states. Diane Sarao has suffered emotional distress, according to the suit, including “recurring distressing dreams about the event.”
All three lawsuits bring counts related to negligence and unseaworthiness against Grace Bailey Navigation and seek monetary relief. McCann’s lawsuit tacks on a count of “maintenance and cure” as the musician was “in service” of the vessel, while the Sarao suit tacks on counts of negligence against its additional defendants.
Grace Bailey Navigation did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.

title: Monday Five and Five: The County's Best and What's Ahead
text:
Monday Five and Five: Big Performances and Big Games Ahead
Another busy week of high school sports across Aroostook County is in the books, and the final stretch of the fall regular season is here.
The Monday Five and Five takes one more look at five of the biggest stories from the past week before counting down five things worth watching in the days ahead.
Five From Last Week
5. Presque Isle Girls Keep Rolling
The Presque Isle girls put together back-to-back shutouts, defeating Orono 4-0 before blanking Ellsworth 2-0 Saturday.
Peyton Boinske scored three goals across the two victories, while goalkeeper Sammi Argraves added two more clean sheets.
The Wildcats enter the new week ranked No. 2 in Class B North at 7-1-2, with 80.842 Heal Points.
4. County Golfers Finish Strong at the State Championships
Aroostook County golfers turned in several strong finishes on the state stage.
Houlton's Beckett Peabody tied for third in Class C with a 76, while Presley Goodwin finished third among the Class C girls with a 92.
Alice Korzekwa added a sixth-place finish in Class B, while Averie Smith was sixth in Class C.
3. County Girls Fill Up the Score Sheet
There was no shortage of offense from County girls last week.
Van Buren's Emily Lapierre delivered one of the biggest individual games of the fall, scoring five goals and adding two assists against MSSM.
Ashland's Sadie Trams finished the week with seven goals, Fort Kent's Reece Doucette scored six, Wisdom's Ellie Cyr recorded four goals and an assist, and Katahdin's Mia McNally added three goals and two assists.
2. County Runners Shine Ahead of Championship Week
Aroostook County runners had another big weekend with the PVC Championships now approaching.
Houlton/GHCA's Malachi Witmer won the Red Riot Challenge in 13:22.20, while Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also picked up individual victories.
Houlton/GHCA added the varsity boys team title at the Red Riot Challenge, along with the JV girls championship.
1. Conor Schmidt Puts Together a Monster Week
Katahdin's Conor Schmidt takes the top spot after one of the biggest offensive weeks of the fall.
Schmidt finished with eight goals and three assists across three Cougar victories.
He scored twice against Ashland, followed with three goals and an assist against East Grand, before closing the week with three goals and two assists against Shead.
That's 11 points in three games.
Five to Watch This Week
5. Penobscot Valley Visits Ashland
Tuesday brings an important Class D North girls matchup when Penobscot Valley travels to Ashland.
Penobscot Valley enters No. 3 at 5-2-3 with 66.071 Heal Points, while Ashland is No. 4 at 8-2-1 with 60.434.
Their first meeting ended in a tie, adding even more importance to the rematch.
4. A Huge Week for Wisdom
Wisdom's girls enter the week ranked No. 1 in North 8-Person at 10-1.
Tuesday brings a rematch with unbeaten Bangor Christian, the only team to defeat Wisdom this season. The Pioneers then host Katahdin Thursday.
The boys matchup Thursday also carries plenty of intrigue. Wisdom is No. 3 at 9-2, while Katahdin is also 9-2 but sits ninth in Heal Points.
3. PVC Cross Country Championships
Championship racing arrives Saturday as County runners head to Old Town for the PVC Championships.
Witmer, Gorneault, Graves and several other County runners enter the meet following strong performances last weekend, giving the area plenty of individual and team storylines to follow.
2. Madawaska Meets Central Aroostook
Tuesday's Madawaska-Central Aroostook doubleheader carries major Class D North implications.
On the boys side, it's No. 1 Madawaska at 9-1 against No. 2 Central Aroostook at 9-2.
Central Aroostook also holds the No. 1 spot in the girls standings at 10-2, while Madawaska enters No. 5 at 8-2.
One doubleheader could have an impact near the top of both Class D North races.
1. Presque Isle and John Bapst Meet Twice
Presque Isle and John Bapst meet twice in six days, with important Class B North positioning at stake on both sides.
The Presque Isle girls enter No. 2 in Class B North at 7-1-2 with 80.842 Heal Points, while unbeaten John Bapst sits right behind at No. 3.
On the boys side, John Bapst is No. 2 at 9-0-1, while Presque Isle is No. 4 at 6-3-1 with 59.668 Heal Points.
The teams meet Monday in Presque Isle before doing it all over again Saturday at John Bapst.
With the regular season winding down, those four games could play a major role in where both Wildcat teams land when the Class B North tournament begins.
Another Big Week Ahead
The regular season is running out, tournament positioning is becoming clearer, and every result carries a little more weight.
We'll continue following the scores, standings, standout performances and championship action throughout another busy week of high school sports across Aroostook County.

title: Bipartisan group of senators condemns Trump's energy deal with Russia
text:
Bipartisan group of senators condemns President Trump's energy deal with Russia
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to reverse a deal with Russia to purchase diesel, citing concerns over its alignment with U.S. sanctions and lack of congressional consultation.
Bipartisan group of senators condemns President Trump's energy deal with Russia
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to reverse a deal with Russia to purchase diesel, citing concerns over its alignment with U.S. sanctions and lack of congressional consultation.
A bipartisan group of senators is urging President Donald Trump to reverse a deal with Russia to purchase diesel, which was announced Friday as part of an effort to address high fuel prices in the United States.
Four Republican and two Democratic senators released a statement Sunday protesting the deal, stating that the administration failed to consult Congress or provide an explanation to justify the decision.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.
"If President Trump wants to end the strain of energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran and, number two, recognize that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, said.
The Republicans who signed the letter include Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
The deal Trump announced contrasts sharply with a Russia sanctions law he signed last month, which was aimed at restricting oil and gas revenues that fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the deal, calling it a birthday gift to Putin.
"Because it gives Putin money and he spends money only on this war to kill us, kill our children," Zelenskyy said.
Trump also announced Sunday that there is an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. While Zelenskyy welcomed the development, he said Russia continues to target energy infrastructure in the region.

title: RJ Mitte, ‘Breaking Bad’s Walter White Jr., Dies at 34
text:
‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte Dies at 34
Terrible news from the world of television today. RJ Mitte, best known as Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad, has died. He was only 34 years old.
Mitte appeared on all five seasons of Breaking Bad as the son of Bryan Cranston’s Walter White. His death was reported by TMZ, who wrote they confirmed with officials that Mitte passed away in Texas on Monday. They also wrote that they were “told he died by suicide.”
They also included this statement from Mitte’s representatives:
It is with profound sadness we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte. RJ Mitte was best known for his role as Walter 'Flynn' White Jr. on AMC’s critically acclaimed, award-winning series Breaking Bad. Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion. Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s.
Born in Mississippi in 1992, Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy as a young child. He moved to Los Angeles in the 2000s and began taking acting classes. He was cast in Breaking Bad in 2007.
In addition to his key role on all five seasons of Breaking Bad, Mitte also appeared on the TV show Switched at Birth and starred in the 2021 film Triumph, about a young man with cerebral palsy who wants to compete for his high school wrestling team.
In an interview conducted during Breaking Bad’s original run on AMC, Mitte was asked how he liked working on the show.
“I love it,” he said. “I get to work with some of the best actors in the business, Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul ... we are a really tight cast, like family.”

title: Trump officials say Maine ignores Medicaid fraud. Cases are sitting with his prosecutors
text:
While President Donald Trump’s administration hammers Maine over alleged Medicaid fraud, state prosecutors are frustrated by federal delays in two cases involving nearly $2 million in potential losses to taxpayers.
Attorney General Aaron Frey’s office has made “multiple inquiries” about the cases and was “awaiting an update,” according to a September report the office mistakenly sent to multiple news outlets Thursday. The federal investigators who once worked these cases are gone. A key Scarborough office closed by 2024, a Bangor Daily News review found.
The stalled cases and shrinking federal presence undercut the Trump administration’s monthslong campaign casting Maine as the next Minnesota, where federal prosecutors have charged dozens in sprawling Medicaid fraud schemes. But some of the state’s own fraud cases now depend on federal prosecutors deciding whether to act.
In a July letter to Frey, the agency’s inspector general, T. March Bell, faulted Maine for a drop in Medicaid fraud prosecutions, from four in fiscal year 2024 to none in 2025. He conceded “staffing limitations and vacancies in Maine” were part of the problem, although he said many of his investigators have good relationships with states where they have no presence.
A spokesperson for the inspector general’s office declined to comment.
On Friday, the Trump administration announced an audit of MaineCare. The stakes are significant for Maine. The federal government pays roughly 60% of the $4.7 billion MaineCare program, yet federal prosecutors have not filed a criminal healthcare fraud case in the state since 2019, according to court records reviewed by the BDN.
The inspector general’s Maine presence dates back to at least 2007, when the federal government leased space in a Scarborough office building, according to a lease agreement with the building’s management company on file with the town.
Blueprints from 2007 and 2017 identify it as the agency’s Maine field office. Agents worked there until at least 2023, federal court records show. In 2024, the town issued a new certificate of occupancy for the space to a business, according to Scarborough code enforcement records.
It is unclear when the last agent assigned to Maine left. One of them, Brian Pellerin, departed in 2023 to become chief deputy of the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office.
The attorney general’s erroneously released report describes the two stalled investigations as part of a larger group of cases with similar allegations that federal prosecutors are weighing for possible civil or criminal action. It does not say how many cases are in that group or when they were referred and the office declined to comment.
The office of Maine U.S. Attorney Andrew Benson, a Trump appointee, also declined to comment on the cases. Federal regulations restrict state authorities from independently pursuing cases that may be of federal interest until state action has been approved.
The sharp federal criticism of Maine dates back at least to February, when Dr. Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, wrote to Gov. Janet Mills asking how the state was addressing fraud. In a video, Oz warned that Maine could become “another Minnesota,” referring to the widespread fraud cases there.
Vice President JD Vance blamed Mills for failing to crack down during a May visit to Bangor. In August, Oz said 90% of Maine’s Medicaid billing was fraudulent without citing a source. Maine’s rate of improper payments, which include documentation errors and are not the same as fraud, is 2.4%, less than half the national average of 6.1%, according to the state.
Mills has dismissed criticism as political and said her administration pursues fraud in coordination with federal authorities. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services said it refers credible allegations to law enforcement, including the attorney general’s office.
The two stalled investigations involve southern Maine companies that bill MaineCare. The report describes allegations, not charges. The BDN is not naming the companies in the leaked memo because it has not independently confirmed they are under investigation.
The report alleges phony billing, billing for services MaineCare does not cover, services by at least one provider whose certification had lapsed, and progress notes that did not match what was billed.
MaineCare spending has grown by 21% since the end of the 2023 fiscal year. There’s been a particular expansion in its largest program: providing in-home care for people with disabilities. In response to federal scrutiny, the state highlighted nine providers, most of them home-care agencies, that it had recently cut off from MaineCare payments over allegations of fraud or patient safety concerns.
In 2024, a new tenant moved into the Scarborough space the inspector general’s office once called its Maine office. It’s a home health care agency, which has not faced those allegations.

title: Maine Hospital Association, EMMC sue HRSA, RFK Jr. over 340B rebate model
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Hospital Association, Eastern Maine Medical Center sue HRSA, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over 340B rebate model
The Maine Hospital Association (MHA) and Eastern Maine Medical Center (EMMC) are part of a legal effort to stop a rebate pilot program for the 340B drug pricing program from taking effect.
The MHA, EMMC, American Hospital Association and three other hospitals filed a federal lawsuit Friday in Maine against the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and HRSA Administrator Tom Engels.
The lawsuit challenges a proposed rebate system for the 340B program, which helps hospitals serving low-income and rural communities afford care and medications.
The plaintiffs estimate costs under the rebate pilot program, which is set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, could top $1 billion per year — which is nearly double the federal government's estimate of $537 million.
In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs argue that the HRSA violated administrative law by failing to adequately account for the costs the rebate model would impose on 340B covered entities. The lawsuit also states that the HRSA dismissed concerns raised by hospitals while accepting drug manufacturers' assertions without sufficient scrutiny. According to the lawsuit, this unequal treatment of stakeholder input is legally improper.
The MHA website states that the nonprofit association represents 33 community-governed hospitals in Maine. According to the legal filing, 26 of the MHA's member hospitals participate in the 340B program, including EMMC in Bangor.
The AHA is a nonprofit trade association representing hospitals, healthcare systems, networks and other providers of care across the country, including EMMC and the other three hospitals that are plaintiffs in the lawsuit: Nathan Littauer Hospital and Nursing Home in Gloversville, New York; Unity Medical Center in Grafton, North Dakota; and Dallas County Medical Center in Fordyce, Arkansas.
The U.S. District Court in Maine had previously blocked the HRSA's original 340B rebate pilot in late 2025, leading the agency to withdraw that version and develop a revised program. On Oct. 1, the HRSA approved 10 manufacturer rebate pilot plans.

title: This former Gardiner athlete succeeded on one kidney. Now, she’s in a battle for her life
text:
Kylie Boardman has been fighting the odds since the day she was born.
Boardman, a Gardiner native, has solitary dysplastic kidney disease, which means she was born with one kidney that will never reach full development. Before she was born, doctors told her parents, Bill and Jennifer Boardman, that she had a less than one percent chance to survive.
The doctor’s advice? Terminate the pregnancy.
“It was a day that my wife and I will never forget,” Bill Boardman said. “It wasn’t in our nature (to do it). We went home and were like, ‘If we get one hour with her, great. If we get two hours, that’s even better.’ We learned to put a catheter in our daughter at 2 days old. We’d do all this at home to survive as long as she could. We were told she’d need a transplant in her teens or early 20s, and here we are.”
Kylie Boardman defied those odds and played four sports (field hockey, volleyball, girls hockey and softball) at Gardiner Area High School. She also played women’s hockey at Central Maine Community College in Auburn, recording eight goals and 22 assists in two seasons.
“In retrospect, I really shouldn’t even be here,” Kylie Boardman said. “I feel so blessed that I’m here in the first place and that I’ve been able to do as many things as I’ve been doing. I’m not someone who just sits at home.”
Now 21, Boardman is in need of a kidney transplant. She also has fluid pressing against her ocular nerves, and may need a shunt in her brain to prevent her from going blind. She is exhausted all the time. At a time in life when she would normally be out with her friends, she rests at home, because simple acts expend more energy.
“I wake up and feel like I slept a good two hours, even though I normally get 10,” Boardman said. “I have shortness of breath, because there’s fluid around the lungs as well. … Putting up my ponytail is like running 5 miles. It’s a very hard adjustment going from an active sports lifestyle to this.”
Battling the odds
As a standout athlete at Gardiner, Kylie Boardman earned Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference honors in volleyball and was a member of the 2022 Class B softball state championship team. She was most at home on the ice as a tough and skilled defenseman on the girls hockey team, for which she also served as a team captain.
It was never obvious that Boardman was playing with one functioning kidney, and the family made a point not to publicly disclose it.
“It’s not something we shared. We never used as an excuse,” Bill Boardman said. “What she did was kind of remarkable, considering what she was going through.”
According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the global odds of a child being born with kidney dysplasia is 1 in 4,300. The kidneys are a filtration system for the human body, helping clean blood, and filter waste and extra fluid into urine. It also controls sodium and potassium levels and helps produce hormones.
One effect of kidney dysplasia is a lower than normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR), or how quickly the kidney can filter waste and extra fluid from the blood. It also makes Boardman’s bones more fragile. When she was freshman in high school, she broke her pelvis, which effected the remainder of her playing career.
“It never fully healed, I re-injured it two different times,” Boardman said. “I couldn’t play my sophomore season of volleyball, which was fine, because (it was the COVID season). Because there’s less calcium, it never fully healed, so I played with this broken bone inside of me.”
Last year, during her final season with the CMCC women’s hockey team, she began to notice the fast decline of the remaining kidney.
“My quality of life has definitely gone down. As I’ve grown more, my kidney is trying to do more,” Boardman said. “I hit that point where it’s just not able to pump anymore for me.”
A needed getaway
Bragoli Gym at Gardiner Area High School is rocking with pop music and laughs at the tail end of a practice for the Gardiner volleyball team.
Bill Boardman gathers the team for final instructions before a match the following day against Medomak Valley. He’s in his third season as the head coach of the Tigers, and led them to the Class C final last season.
Boardman was up front at the beginning of the season, with the team and parents, about Kylie’s need for a kidney transplant — and that when it happens, he’ll take a leave of absence, if it’s during the season. He constantly travels with Kylie to her medical appointments.
“The fact that he’s here for us and loves us, we’re just all so grateful,” said Gardiner senior Joely Cote. “It’s also important that we’re giving him that support while he’s going through this. We love him, and we want to look out for him the same way he looks out for us.
Coaching is a needed escape from the concerns a father has for his daughter.
“He is so devoted to that team and he loves coaching that team,” Kylie Boardman said. “It’s refreshing to see him coach and coach with such passion. It’s not an easy process (for him), because he comes to most of my appointments. That balance is key for everybody.”
Light at the end of the tunnel
The Boardman family has been more open about Kylie’s battle now that she needs a new kidney. A website (kidney4kylie.com) has been created to help find a donor.
The Boardmans received good news in late August. Insurance was approved for a kidney transplant, placing Kylie on the transplant list. She also received a voucher through the National Kidney Registry, which she received from the organization when someone donated a kidney in her name. Through the voucher program, it allows Kylie’s case to be prioritized.
There’s a possibility she could receive her new kidney by the end of the year.
“At this point, it’s just a waiting game for me,” Boardman said. “It’s a very quiet waiting game to hopefully get a new and better chance at life. Every day, I just pray it’s out there.”
Another effect of Boardman’s condition is vision loss, which began within the past year.
“I started to notice that my vision would go away and go black, in certain situations,” Boardman said. “I thought it was a symptom from a med, because I take 15 different meds every day. My optical nerves are swollen because of IIH.”
IIH is Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. According to the Cleveland Clinic, it occurs when cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the spinal cord and brain, builds up in the skull, causing pressure on the optic nerves.
“I’ve been told if this pressure doesn’t come down, it will cause vision loss,” Boardman said.
Boardman’s doctors will soon discuss whether she needs the shunt now, or can wait until after her kidney donation takes place.
Kylie Boardman now lives in Poland, with her boyfriend, Jack Keefe. Despite her current condition, she works four days per week at Serendipity Creek Childcare Center in Gray, while still making her appointments, as she waits for a donor and a new kidney.
“I’ve never been scared. I don’t get scared of much,” Boardman said. “It’s just hard. I see people planning for their future right now, and I can’t do that because I have this massive surgery that I have to plan for, and plan, for a year, to be out of everything. It’s kind of frustrating. But I’m at peace with it. I have such a good support system around me that I’m OK with the fact that it’s going to happen. And I’m OK because I have so many people around me.”

title: Actress Selma Blair arrested, accused of attacking flight staff
text:
NEW YORK (Gray News) - Actress Selma Blair was arrested after allegedly trying to open an airplane door mid-flight and injuring two flight attendants, TMZ and Variety confirmed.
Blair, 54, was aboard a Delta Air Lines Flight to New York City from Los Angeles on Sunday night, according to the New York Port Authority.
While in flight, Blair allegedly tried to open the plane’s door, then allegedly hit one flight attendant and bit another.
A representative for Blair told TMZ and Variety that she experienced a medical emergency that caused the alleged conduct.
“Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first,” a representative from Delta Air Lines wrote.
Officers from the Port Authority Police Department were called out to the plane around 11 p.m., where it was parked at the gate.
Blair was taken into custody and then to the hospital for evaluation, Port Authority officials said. They went on to confirm one of the flight attendants was also taken to an area hospital.
The FBI, which investigates all alleged assaults on board aircrafts, is investigating what may have happened.
What charges Blair will face was not immediately clear at the time of publication.

title: Carefully consider health care when deciding who to vote for in Maine’s 2nd District
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Steve Bien is a privately practicing family physician in Farmington. He has been in practice there since 1982.
The health and healthcare of Second Congressional District voters are on the line in this election so we should choose carefully. Due to federal health funding cuts, a financial tsunami is poised to hit patients, providers, and our hospitals.
Maine’s health care system is already stressed. Staff retention is problematic at all levels, several major practices have closed recently, and a number of hospitals are on the verge of shuttering. This is the backdrop for the coming loss of federal Medicaid funds to Maine. In my 40 years in medicine, I have never seen resources so thinly stretched.
No issue will be more important to our two congressional candidates, Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage. Their responses will impact every Mainer.
The tsunami is the catastrophic reduction in healthcare funding scheduled to hit our state next year because of President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill. To fund tax cuts for the wealthy, the Republican Congress took $1 trillion from Medicaid. Our state’s hit is predicted to be $345 million per year.
Medicaid funds health care for about 30% of Maine residents and represents approximately 18% of state hospital incomes. In some 2nd District communities MaineCare provides as much as 60% of facilities’ budgets.
How does that gap get closed when many hospitals are operating on less than a 5% profit margin. The answer is it doesn’t. Katie Fullam Harris, chief government affairs officer at MaineHealth, recently said: “Maine’s healthcare infrastructure is teetering on the edge of real challenge right now … There’s no room to absorb additional costs.”
Already we have seen primary care offices close in Houlton, Presque Isle, Waterville, Fairfield, Oakland, Castine and Manchester. Downeast Ob-Gyn in Bangor shut down because they could not retain and recruit physicians. Twelve Maine birthing centers have closed in the last decade. Routine care for pregnant women in those areas now requires an average of 45 minutes of travel.
There are 24 rural hospitals in Maine and 10 are at risk of closing. Four are at risk of closing in the next three years (Presque Isle, Ellsworth, Caribou, and Calais). MaineCare covers nearly 40% of all births in Maine, so the access to care for women and infants will only get much worse.
My patients commonly wait six months or longer for referrals to rheumatology, dermatology, cardiology and gastroenterology, if those referrals are accepted at all.
How will our two congressional candidates face this crisis?
Paul LePage was no fan of MaineCare during his tenure as governor. He dismissed it as “welfare” and resisted any effort to expand it. He now says that its expansion is the source of our state’s health care finance woes, not part of any solution. In response to the hospital funding crisis he faced during his second term as governor, LePage said “we definitely have too many hospitals.”
None of our state’s hospital administrators seem to agree with him and all are alarmed by the prospect of the coming cuts, which will create a financial hole they cannot fill.
Candidate Matt Dunlap pledges to do what he can to restore federal funding so that we can preserve what we have. Beyond that, Medicare for all, meaning an expansion of publicly funded health care, is the centerpiece of his campaign.
I believe Medicare for all is the ideal solution to the MaineCare problem we are facing. Medicare, since it serves everybody over 65, is widely respected and supported by politicians across the spectrum. The public correctly sees Medicare as an essential benefit to ensure appropriate care for the elderly. In contrast, cuts to Medicaid, which undermine care for the less politically powerful low-income population, came right out of a cynical political playbook. I believe Medicare for all would be a step toward better care for all Mainers regardless of age or income.
The axe falling on MaineCare funding is timed to fall after the midterm elections. We need to be aware of the impending cuts and keep them uppermost in our minds when we vote in this election.

title: Scott Wyman (1963-2026)
Homicide agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting
text:
MIMS, Fla. (WESH) — A Florida sheriff’s office agent died Saturday night after a wrong-way driver hit his vehicle head-on on Interstate 95, according to authorities.
What happened
The Brevard County Sheriff’s Office said a 26-year-old woman from Kissimmee was driving back from a beachside wedding. Authorities said she made a U-turn near a rest stop and began traveling the wrong way on I-95 north.
Florida Highway Patrol received calls about the wrong-way driver and had law enforcement en route, but troopers could not reach her before the crash occurred.
“That vehicle traveled from the rest area down south of 46, where it hit Kevin head-on,” Brevard County Sheriff Wayne Ivey said.
Agent Kevin Morris was headed to respond to a shooting in Mims at the time of the crash. Both vehicles caught fire after the collision.
Investigation underway
The female driver’s name has not been released. FHP said a toxicology test will be conducted on the driver.
“There will be a toxicology on the driver. We don’t know what that is right now,” said Lt. Channing Taylor of Florida Highway Patrol.
“No matter what the outcome, our thoughts, our prayers go out to that family,” Ivey said.
Morris remembered by colleagues, friend
The sheriff’s office said Morris previously served with the Palm Bay Police Department, left to work in a church, then returned to law enforcement with the Brevard County Sheriff’s Office in 2021. He served as a deputy, field training officer, agent in the homicide unit and a polygraph examiner.
“Our agency, our community, family of Kevin are absolutely devastated,” Ivey said. “There’s so many things you could say about Kevin. If you were going to, you would start with he was just absolutely an amazing guy.”
Ashley Hughes, who knew Morris, said he officiated her wedding.
“He was a treasured friend, but most importantly, he was our pastor,” Hughes said. “I was in shock when I learned about it. If you needed help with something, he was there, and he was always there for my husband and I.”
Ivey said he will remember the response effort at the scene.
“What I saw was everybody fighting, working as hard as they could to save both of the people in those cars,” Ivey said.

title: “Verity” is a dark Hallmark movie in disguise
text:
Picture this: you’re a struggling writer played by Dakota Johnson. You’re slinging short stories for peanuts and giving lame book readings at local bookstores when you get “the call.” It’s your lawyer, and it’s the big one: a big book deal is incoming and they wanna meet you. You’re on your way to the meeting, but, oh no! A pedestrian gets obliterated right before your eyes, and now you’re covered in blood! A handsome man you don’t know, who looks suspiciously like Josh Hartnett, ushers you away and helps you clean up, even giving you his shirt. When you leave him and arrive at the meeting, you learn that the man who helped you earlier is also the one who wants to hire you.
This contrived and hokey but otherwise perfectly adequate opener is what you can expect from Michael Showalter’s 2026 film “Verity,” which I distinctly remember wanting to see without actually knowing a single thing about it. Who knew this psychological thriller also featured a healthy amount of soft-core erotica? Certainly not me. I only know what the trailers tell me, much like when I first watched “The Housemaid.” Compared with the 2025 film featuring Sydney Sweeney and Brandon Sklenar, however, “Verity” does not quite measure up.
Of course, I will say that this film was, in fact, adapted from a 2018 novel of the same name, much like “The Housemaid” was, and “The Housemaid” was a very good film! It was well put together, with a shocking twist at the end, especially for someone who has never read the book. But if the two films don’t quite compare well, then what makes “Verity” worth your money and, more importantly, your time?
Well, not a whole lot, if I am being perfectly honest. The phrase “dark Hallmark movie” came to mind as I watched this film because it certainly seemed to, in some cases, contain a lot of the same elements. This woman is a loser in the big city who meets a guy from a small place who sweeps her off her feet, but adds a more chilling twist that seems compelling at first but then falls apart the minute you think about it, and blammo! You ladies and germs have yourselves your very own “dark Hallmark movie.”
I hate to say it, too, because I did really expect more from this film. I mean, Anne Hathaway played the film’s namesake character, Verity Crawford, and did a spectacular job. Josh Hartnett, as her husband Jeremy, wasn’t bad either, but I can only describe Dakota Johnson’s performance as the film’s protagonist, ghostwriter Lowen Ashleigh, as about as interesting as a limp piece of lettuce. I think I remember more about the performance of the actor playing their son, Crew Crawford, than Miss Johnson’s.
You’ve got the unsuspecting victim stumbling upon an incapacitated writer’s deep-seated inner thoughts only to realize that maybe that incapacitation is all a ruse and there is something darker going on. The twist revealed at the end is short-lived when you look back at the plot and realize that you have to give it too much of the benefit of the doubt before it all simply crumbles apart.
Better luck next time, I suppose, but hey, it’s not all doom and gloom this Halloween! We still have “Other Mommy.” There is some hope for something spine-chilling.

title: Mexico property assessments could mean loss of state revenue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MEXICO — For residents and others wondering where their property tax bill is, you haven’t missed it. The town of Mexico has not mailed them yet.
Town Manager Amy Bernard, who started her role in early July, told the Select Board on Oct. 6, “I wish I had better news.”
“Right now, our certified assessment ratio is 55% of state valuation, which presents a significant challenge for this year’s (tax) commitment,” she said.
A certified ratio is the ratio of assessed value to fair market value within a municipality, as determined by the State Tax Assessor, according to Cumberland County Regional Assessing. It is applied to exemptions so municipalities with lower ratios will not receive a greater proportional benefit than those with higher ratios. Maine requires that certified ratios fall between 70% and 110%.
Last year, she said, the certified assessment ratio went from 95% to 76% of state valuation, resulting in Mexico losing $400,000 in state revenue-sharing. It has now dropped to 55%, meaning assessments are 55% of what the state considers fair market value.
“So, when you lose $400,000 in revenue sharing, your (tax) rate is going up, pretty significantly. You can’t overcome that,” she said. “So, I’m trying to find a way to prevent us from certifying at 55%.”
Bernard said the last property revaluation for Mexico was about 20 years ago.
Bernard said she is working with consultant Amy Dunn, a certified Maine assessor, “to find a way for us to do some kind of ratio percentage to increase our values. Our values are very, very low compared to the state’s sales data.
She said the town’s revenue-sharing, the homestead exemption, veterans exemption and others will all be affected.
“So, we’ve got to do some kind of adjustment, or we’ve got to find a way to increase our assessments somehow,” she said. “You absolutely are going to have to seriously consider doing a revaluation of the town. There’s just no other way.”
The town is relying on the consultants to offer the best options to soften the blow heading into the next year, she added. Bernard also said she is in conversations with the state to see what options are available to address the low ratio.
“With that being said, we have to commit the taxes,” she said. “The taxes are supposed to be due on Nov. 28 and you have to give them four weeks. You have to give them 30 days after we commit. And it’s probably going to take me four days just to get them in the mail to somebody. So, we’re really not looking at taking tax dollars in until the middle of November.”
A special board meeting was scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 15, at 4 p.m. to review FY 2027 tax commitment calculations, considering the assessor’s recommendations and CPA review, establish the appropriate property tax rate, commit the taxes and establish the due date. The meeting will take place downstairs in the Town Office.
The property tax rate for the 2025-26 fiscal year is $29.40 per $1,000 of assessed value.
When Select Board member Calvin Burgess asked if the town had enough money to pay its bills, Bernard said, “We have enough money so far. But I wouldn’t go much further than next week because we’re going to have cash flow issues come the middle of November, because when you start paying for plowing, sand, diesel, home heating oil, it’s going to catch up to us pretty quickly.”
Bernard said she did find an assessor “who’s willing to take us on.”
She said the town’s assessor is working with the town to finalize the information necessary to complete the FY 2027 tax commitment. Once the preliminary commitment calculations are completed, the information will be forwarded to accountant Mark Roy for an independent review to help ensure the calculations and commitment documents are accurate before they are presented to the Select Board.

title: Driver killed after truck strikes train at railroad crossing
text:
SPRINGFIELD TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - A man died after a train and pickup truck collided just before midnight at an Ohio railroad crossing, authorities said.
The crash happened at a railroad crossing on Albon Road near Airport Highway.
The Ohio State Highway Patrol said the pickup drove southbound through the downed gates before hitting the westbound train. The driver was not wearing a seat belt and was killed in the collision.
Officials said the driver was identified as Michael Jones, 57, of Monclova.
“We’ll have the coroner’s office, we’ll go through our complete investigation, download the vehicle, seeing speed and stuff like that,” said Sgt. Jason Metzger with the Ohio State Highway Patrol. “We’ll do toxicology, see if there’s any factors there.”

title: Shalom House plants hope garden to inspire positivity, community in Portland
text:
Shalom House plants hope garden to inspire positivity, community in Portland
Shalom House, a community-based mental health provider, now has a new hope garden. In partnership with the national Yellow Tulip Project, 250 tulip bulbs were planted Thursday in the lawn of Shalom House's residential property on Clark Street.
Emily Mitchell, the development and communications manager, explained, "This is a highly supportive housing property for adults living with severe mental illnesses, with 24-hour staff support for individuals who need rehabilitative and intensive support services. This is a long-term program that offers a home-like environment with extensive skill-building opportunities." 
The planting event fell during national Mental Illness Awareness Week, which is observed annually during the first full week of October. Shalom House staff intend for the garden to spark positivity and inspiration for the residents when it blooms in the spring.
Executive director Abby Spadone said, "We have a lot of clients who really struggle with severe and persistent mental illness. On a day-to-day basis, it's really hard for them to have hope just for recovery, so a big part of what we do is just hold some of that hope for the clients that we have."
Spadone was joined in the garden by board members and other staff, but noticeably missing was Marlene McNeill, a program manager killed by a resident in May 2026 at a Shalom House property on Woodford Street. McNeill was described by Shalom House as kind, compassionate, deeply respected, and an irreplaceable part of the organization.
During a break from planting, Spadone said, "We've had a rough year this year, and to bring people together to do something that is just a vein of positivity is a really nice thing to do."
She went on to say they look forward to planting more of these hope gardens at their other properties throughout the city, and she encourages other groups to do the same.

title: 1 killed, several injured in incident at Six Flags Over Georgia
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — One person was killed and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, according to the Cobb County Police Department.
Police have not said what happened, but witnesses said a man fell to his death from the Goliath roller coaster.
Several riders were stuck on the coaster after the deadly incident late Monday afternoon. First Alert Chopper captured footage of the Goliath roller coaster stuck on the tracks and riders being helped to the ground.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement. “The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Police and Six Flags officials have not identified anyone involved or provided details about the extent of the injuries.
Six Flags shut down over the incident and guests were told to leave. Others were left stranded on Goliath’s steep incline, watching emergency crews rush past them below and wondering what went wrong.
“We saw mechanics and paramedics running down there. We realized something bad had happened,” said Ben Edwards, who was among nearly 20 people trapped on Goliath’s two-hundred-foot incline when the coaster suddenly stopped shortly before 4 p.m., stranding many for at least an hour way above the ground.
“Very tragic – the first thing you think about is the people you’re on the ride with,” said Edwards, who is visiting from Canada.
Edwards tried calming those around him, unsure when help would arrive. With each passing minute, frustration grew as trapped passengers looked down, waiting for a way off.
The real panic was in the car ahead of Edwards, where the deadly incident occurred.
The victim who died was found on a nearby roof, footage shows.
Edwards called for changes following the incident.
“Being stuck up there, some people are really scared of that stuff,” he said. “They need to do better.”
Goliath tops out at 70 miles per hour with an elevation of 200 feet and two drops, one of 170 feet and another of 175 feet. Considered a hypercoaster – a roller coaster that’s at least 200 feet tall – the ride was developed by Bolliger & Mabillard and uses restraints that sit across riders’ laps, not over-the-shoulder restraints.
Similar coasters exist throughout the Six Flags chain.
“Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities,” the chain said.
The incident comes less than a month after Six Flags closed the famous X2 roller coaster at Magic Mountain in California after lawsuits revealed more than 100 people had suffered brain injuries while riding.
Cobb County Chairwoman Lisa Cupid called the incident “a terrible tragedy.”
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Cupid said in a statement.
Cupid added that the county is working closely with the amusement park “and other appropriate partners” as the investigation proceeds.
“Six Flags Over Georgia is a significant part of our tourism landscape, drawing visitors from across our county, our state, and the Southeast. I look forward to learning more as the investigation unfolds,” Cupid said. “In the meantime, please keep in your thoughts the family of the deceased, those who were injured, the employees and leadership of Six Flags, and our community. We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories.”

title: When hunting moose, help is always available
text:
A flatbed truck hauling a bull moose slowed as it approached our group of four pickups, nine guys and one gal holding an infant parked in a turnoff on a remote gravel road. The driver offered a friendly wave and a brief, “how you doing?” before starting to turn.
“You want some chicken wings?” shouted one of our hunting party who was dutifully tending the grill on his tailgate.
“Sure,” replied the driver who, along with his father, joined our party for an hour of eating and swapping stories.
That’s not an unusual occurrence in the North Woods during moose season. More than any other pursuit, moose hunting in Maine is a very social experience. Sure, deer camp is social, but most of the socializing occurs at camp, after each day’s hunt. Turkey hunting tends to be more enjoyable when done with a partner, but two’s company and three’s a crowd.
A moose hunting crew might consist of two or three folks per truck, and possibly several trucks. Many eyes are handy, but many bodies are handier still when you’ve got 800-1,000 pounds of moose on the ground. The help often extends beyond individual hunting parties.
We were parked at the bottom of a dead-end road one morning, awaiting shooting light, when we noticed lights on the road below us and went down to investigate. A gentleman hunting with his 10-year-old son had a flat tire. Our crew of five, several of whom just happen to be mechanics, eagerly jumped in, and we had the father and son on their way in time for both groups to make our destination before sun-up.
Two years prior, we were just finishing up field dressing a moose when two truckloads of hunters stopped to investigate. When they saw we had a bull down, they all eagerly volunteered to help us load it into the truck.
And the willingness to help doesn’t end there.
Most hunters get only six days to fill their tag. Some need all six, while others tag out early. The latter are in the North Woods with time to kill, and many will eagerly jump in with another crew to help them find their bull.
As a side note, Maine guides typically book one hunter for a week-long hunt. If their hunter tags out early, that means they are free and available. For someone who decided to go the DIY route but is struggling, it might be worth making a few phone calls or checking social media toward the end of the week.
Even, and perhaps especially, if you start with a guide, you’ll find the same ethic. Everyone in camp wants to be part of the hunt. Guides and their tagged-out hunters are often eager to join others in camp to help out in any way they can.
I’ve been fortunate to fall in with a group of guys who love to hunt moose and are good at it. Our forces were spread a little thin this year because three among us drew tags. That won’t be the case next year, but some among us will have a friend or relative who pulls a permit, and we’ll rally our resources to see they have all the help they need. For all of us, even those who live near and work in the North Woods, it’s a chance to get away into the woods for a week and be hunters.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Campaign finance reform needs to be our top priority
text:
Beth Franklin of Cumberland worked on Capitol Hill for a Mississippi congressman and has lived in Maine for the last 32 years.
Given the eye-popping revelations about Sen. Susan Collins’ involvement with a pay-to-play arrangement with a campaign donor, it may be time to reexamine how Collins and her opponent, Troy Jackson, are funding their campaigns.
A quick check of Federal Election Commission contribution reports reveals who is giving
money to Collins in her bid to retain the Senate seat she has held since 1997.
The biggest donors in the last several months include the following people: Matthew Steinmetz of Illinois, attorney, whose practice focuses on leveraged buyouts ($100,000); Konstantine Sokolov of Illinois, private equity investor ($100,000); Edward C. Levy Jr. of Michigan, owner of a construction materials company and former president of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee ($250,000); Adam Freede of California, investor ($100,000); Michelle and David Kroin of New York, lawyer and investor ($400,000); Gary Rosenthal of Texas, private equity investor ($50,000); Michael Kassen of Connecticut, investor and former president of the American Israel Political Action Committee ($100,000); J. Blair Frank of Utah, equity portfolio manager and philanthropist ($200,000); Barry MacLean, president of a manufacturing company in Illinois ($50,000).
The most recent entries on the FEC campaign report show that only 24 of the last 100 donors who gave directly to Susan Collins gave under $10,000. All the rest gave what some might refer to as “real money.”
This doesn’t include the donations to the Pine Tree Results Political Action Committee
supporting Sen. Collins. 
Of the most recent donors this year, the top giver to Pine Tree Results was Kenneth Griffin, CEO of Citadel, LLC, a multinational hedge fund based in Florida ($2.5 million). Second runner-up was Stephen Schwarzman, CEO of the Blackstone Group in New York, the world’s largest alternative asset manager ($1 million). Next were Jude and Christopher Reyes, co-chairs of Reyes Holdings in Florida ($1 million, or $500,000 each). More than 20 of the most recent 100 donors to Pine Tree Results gave $100,000 or more.
So, what about Troy Jackson? Given his recent entry into the race, his first FEC report won’t be coming out until October. A quick search of various news outlets painted a different picture of the kinds of donations received by the Jackson campaign.
One report stated that Troy Jackson had 58,000 unique donors in the first few days following his nomination. Another report stated that while Jackson had received a “massive” small donor influx, it was dwarfed by the large sums that continued to pour into the Collins camp.
You don’t have to believe these reports; just watch the evening news. The ads are beginning to all look alike and surely voters are tuning them out. The negative ads about Jackson are double the number that you see about Collins. And if you listen to the fast talk at the end, all those negative ads about Troy Jackson are funded by Pine Tree Results.
What does this say about our candidates? There is no question that Susan Collins’ campaign is being financed by large corporations and investment interests. Does that make her beholden to them? Recent reports about Collins’ alleged “pay-to-play” arrangement with Navatek suggest it may.
But this also points to the broader problem of how campaigns are financed. “Elon Musk-like” money does not always win, but negative ads can sway enough voters to help wealthy interests get the candidates and outcomes they paid for. It’s only when the public makes campaign finance reform their highest priority that this will change.

title: What to know about the search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
text:
Federal agents searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on Monday, only three weeks before the frequent target of President Donald Trump’s criticism stands for reelection in her congressional district in Minnesota.
Here’s what to know:
Is this political retribution?
Trump has not been shy about wanting to use federal law enforcement to target his perceived political enemies. He’s pushed prosecutions of former FBI Director James Comey and New York’s Democratic Attorney General, Letitia James, following earlier probes the two launched against him. Omar, a left-wing firebrand, has been a longtime target of Trump and Republicans in general.
Omar was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen. Trump has especially targeted Somali immigrants in Minnesota, posting on social media last week that the people of the state must “fight back” against them. The state has reeled from several federal fraud cases sometimes involving Somali-run nonprofits in Minnesota. Many of those cases were filed by former President Joe Biden’s Department of Justice. Omar is not involved in them.
Omar has long criticized Trump, and the president has likewise gone after her repeatedly over the years. Trump late last week alluded to possible action against the congresswoman. At a rally in Tennessee on Saturday, Trump referred pejoratively to Omar as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her.
Justice Department protocol has long been to avoid legal action against politicians in the final weeks before their election. The Trump administration’s violation of that added to Democratic criticism that this is simply political payback.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement issued from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats.
“Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
Asked about the search, Trump deferred to the Justice Department, saying “that has nothing to do with me.”
“I’ve always found her to be very crooked, personally,” he said.
Is this about immigration?
The agents who searched Omar’s home, pursuant to a federal search warrant, were Homeland Security investigators, indicating the investigation regards immigration issues. Several Trump officials have suggested that is how they intend to pursue Omar.
Vance has suggested before that Omar committed immigration fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud on her family’s immigration paperwork.
“Something’s going to happen,” he said at the time.
The Department of Justice on Monday was typically tight-lipped, giving few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.
Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17 years old, five years after she arrived with her family after obtaining asylum in the United States.
What happens next?
The election is in 20 days. Omar’s district in Minneapolis is deep blue and she’s in little actual peril on Nov. 3.
We don’t know enough about the next steps in the investigation. It’s likely, however, that conservatives will continue slamming Omar. Now, however, she has one more way to hit back — by arguing she’s being persecuted by her political opponents.
In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
