title: A rare climb of remote Burnt Jacket Mountain west of Jackman
text:
During the summer, I paddled Little Big Wood Pond located in a remote, mountainous area west of Jackman for the first time. Accompanied by my wife, Nancy, and our son, Adam, we marveled at the picturesque beauty of the mountain tarn bordered on the south and west by extensive Burnt Jacket Mountain. Not lost on us were their unique names.
Based on my research, the origin of Burnt Jacket’s name has been lost in time. However, Little Big Wood Pond is the smaller companion of nearby and much larger Big Wood Pond. Both names reflect their location in the heavily forested Jackman region.
Our map indicated a trail along the south shore of the pond led to Burnt Jacket Mountain. During our circumnavigation, we searched for and finally found the elusive trail. Adam and I resolved to return for an overnight trip that included climbing the mountain and further exploration of the pond.
Unlike our maiden voyage on the pond when it was mirror calm, northwest winds were gusting when Adam and I launched from the badly eroded landing on the far eastern end in September. Whitecapped waves broke over the decks of our kayaks as we hurriedly paddled toward the north shore seeking partial shelter from the powerful gale.
Once next to the shoreline, we paddled west along the largely undeveloped, secluded pond. About two-thirds of the way down, we found a good location to camp.
After erecting tents, we traversed the gusty pond to the south shore. With a strong tailwind behind us, we navigated easily east until locating a path that leads to an old logging road. After hiking to the logging road, we walked east for a short distance and entered narrow Burnt Jacket Mountain Trail on the right.
We hiked on a gradual incline that traveled circuitously up a mixed hardwood and conifer forest for a long mile. The path then steepened as it transitioned to a sparse spruce growth. After a prolonged climb, we encountered a series of steep ledges that led to the summit of the eastern-most peak on the mountain. From that vantage point, we enjoyed spectacular views of the mountains of Quebec in the north and peaks surrounding Attean Pond in the south.
We contemplated what appeared to be an arduous bushwhack to the more distant western peaks in the massif but were poorly equipped and lacked time for such a substantial endeavor. Alas, that’s an adventure that awaits more favorable circumstances.
After returning to our kayaks, we struggled mightily against a powerful headwind when paddling west. The waves and winds were too treacherous for an open crossing, so we continued to the western terminus and rode a welcome tailwind east along the north shore to our campsite.
After a very pleasant night, we awoke to light winds and calm waters. Our plan for the day was to explore Wood Stream on both ends of the pond.
First on the agenda was locating where Wood Stream enters the pond. We found the elusive mouth of the stream amidst tall swamp grass in the southwestern corner and began kayaking upstream.
We were surprised to find a fairly deep, wide flow that was easily kayaked. As we progressed upstream, the waterway narrowed, the depth diminished and the downstream current increased. After about 2 miles, an accumulation of fallen branches and shallow water marked the end of navigation.
When we returned to the pond, gusty winds were blowing from the west. The strong tailwind helped propel us rapidly east to a narrow channel leading to the Wood Stream outlet.
A few cottages populate the shore at the beginning of the stream. However, further downstream exploration ended when a shallow, unnavigable rapid was encountered. We speculated that during periods of high water a multiday trip could be completed from the headwaters of Wood Stream to Big Wood Pond in Jackman.
The most challenging paddling of the trip was encountered when kayaking west into a robust headwind while leaving the outlet. After turning east into a wide cove where 2- and 3-foot waves were breaking, we literally surfed to the takeout completing a very entertaining hiking and paddling adventure.
Read about more overnight paddling expeditions; including surf and turf exploits on Moosehead Lake and Donnell Pond in my book “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine.”
The author of “The Great Mars Hill Bank Robbery” and “Mountains for Mortals – New England,” Ron Chase resides in Topsham. His latest book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine” is available at North Country Press and through online retailers. Visit his website at ronchaseoutdoors.com or he can be reached at [email protected].

title: Some Bangor residents are skeptical of Jonathan Bush's spending on City Council race
text:
About 20 people gathered in Bangor’s West Market Square Monday morning for an event kicking off Jonathan Bush’s advertising campaign around this year’s city council race.
Some were there to support the wealthy tech entrepreneur and other Republicans who spoke about getting more conservative candidates elected, while others were skeptical of the introduction of outside money and influence to what’s officially a nonpartisan local election.
The influx of cash could have a significant impact on a race that doesn’t typically see much attention from outside the Bangor area.
Bush, a Cape Elizabeth resident and cousin of former President George W. Bush who made an unsuccessful bid for the Republican gubernatorial nomination in Maine this year, announced last week that he plans to pour $100,000 into local elections in Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville through his nonprofit, Maine for Keeps.
The group has already rolled out more than 10 social media ads, according to the Meta ad library, mostly targeting issues like rising taxes and crime. Residents can also expect to see the group’s ads on streaming services, according to Bush.
In a speech Monday, Bush criticized harm reduction and the Yellen Pines housing development in Bangor and emphasized the need for economic growth in Maine.
“I think that Maine for Keeps should be spending its money on the place where it can get the most leverage, and that to me is in city councils,” he said. Bush previously told the Bangor Daily News he chose the three target cities because he didn’t think it was feasible for his preferred candidates to win in Portland.
He noted Monday that while he thinks most Bangor city councilors mean well, he’s worried by their approach to the city’s issues.
Jim Deyermond, chair of the Maine Republican Party and a Sanford resident, was harsher in his criticism of the councilors, painting a bleak picture of the city.
“I’m here today to support Mr. Bush and all the friends around that I see here today to take back this city council, to get rid of the crazy people that are in charge of the city and to put sane Republicans, conservatives on this city council,” Deyermond said, pointing to issues like syringe litter and policing. “People have to be arrested many times, and have to be put in custody and then forced to go to rehab,” he said.
He blamed addiction issues on Democrats, saying, “The Democrats made it a political issue by doing nothing to help this. They’re making it worse, and you need to take back your cities or there will be no cities to take back in America.”
MaryAnn Larson, a resident who attended the event, said she was unhappy with that rhetoric, which she saw as an “oversimplification of the drug issue,” pointing out that none of the speakers mentioned the Sackler family or the larger opioid epidemic.
While multiple speakers criticized the Yellen Pines housing development, which will house 30 chronically homeless residents when it opens, Larson said she appreciates the project because it means that “we’re doing something. For so long, nothing’s been done.”
On the other hand, some residents were excited to see the attention on Bangor’s election.
“This is fantastic,” Irv Masters, owner of the Bangor Letter Shop, said after the event, sporting a red Bobby Charles hat.
Masters said his business on Washington Street has had several encampments right outside, and that he’s frustrated by the “inaction of the city council” on issues like homelessness and addiction. He said he’s been knocking doors for council candidates Joseph Pratt and Terry Dinkins.
His excitement encapsulated a growing frustration among many residents, particularly business owners, with the Bangor City Council over its inability to address persistent challenges like the city’s homelessness crisis. Meetings have been packed in recent months, and a record 12 candidates are running for three open seats.
Although Maine for Keeps doesn’t plan to endorse council candidates, Bush has said he will do so personally, and he was joined at the event by Philip Henry, whose political action committee has endorsed Pratt and Dinkins, as well as Anthony Cote.
Henry also criticized Yellen Pines in a speech and talked about public drug use and understaffing in the Bangor Police Department. The local real estate investor and principal officer for the Concerned Citizens of Bangor PAC said he moved to Bangor because of its safety, affordable housing and good schools but now worries that his children won’t be able to enjoy those things in the city.
Several candidates running for council have denounced Bush’s involvement in the race.
Candidate John King attended Monday and said he thinks the focus should be on residents, not outside political influences or partisanship.
“This is just proving that it’s now become a partisan election,” King said.
Andrei Yermakov also attended and expressed similar concerns, as did Dawson Nevells in a Facebook post this weekend. Both are also running for council.
“I believe that the people of Bangor should decide the future of Bangor,” Nevells said. “Not political parties, not outside political interests, and not whoever has the deepest pockets.”
Jonathan Bush is known for co-founding Athenahealth in the 1990s and has had a growing presence in Maine politics since moving to Cape Elizabeth in 2021.
Vincent Harris, a strategist for the Charles campaign who’s also worked for Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and a pro-Trump SuperPAC, is overseeing the Maine for Keeps local election project.

title: How candidates for Maine governor say they’ll fill a projected $1B budget gap
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s next governor will face the early challenge of proposing a balanced state budget, and a projected hole of more than $1 billion may complicate that task.
The periodic fiscal forecast, which state officials released Sept. 30, predicts a General Fund gap of $1.085 billion and a Highway Fund gap of $256.7 million for the next two-year budget running from the middle of 2027 through the middle of 2029. The governor who succeeds Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, must present a balanced budget proposal to state lawmakers by February before the Legislature seeks to pass a plan that kicks in July 1, 2027.
Under state law, the budget bureau within the Department of Administrative and Financial Services completes the Four-Year Revenue and Expenditure Forecast every other year. The projected gap represents how much estimated revenue is falling short of what existing statutes require the state to spend. These mandatory expenditures include maintaining state support for 55% of K-12 education costs, 5% spending on municipal revenue sharing and pensions for retired teachers.
Finance Commissioner Elaine Clark noted that “many of the funding obligations considered in the report are, with Legislative approval, routinely not met” and that the report should only serve as a “starting point” for lawmakers as they begin budget discussions rather than “an accurate reflection of an actual budget shortfall facing State government.”
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the gubernatorial race over Republican Bobby Charles, a lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, and independent Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator.
Here’s what each candidate said when asked during Thursday evening’s debate about how they would fill a budget gap if elected governor. The debate was not the only time the candidates have discussed the budget, with the Portland Press Herald’s Voter Guide among the other places to review their policy plans.
Republican Bobby Charles
Charles, 66, began his budget answer by alluding to how Pingree led the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025, criticizing the Democratic candidate as “the right hand of the governor that put us in all these problem sets.”
“It’s like inviting the arsonist back to put out the fire,” Charles said of electing Pingree.
However, the budget problems are not unique to the outgoing Mills administration. The finance department previously noted that aside from 2022, each report since 2014 had projected a structural gap.
These gaps have occurred under past governors of independent, Republican and Democratic stripes. The projected deficit was also around $1 billion when then-Gov. Angus King, an independent who is now in the U.S. Senate, left office in 2003 and Democratic Gov. John Baldacci took over.
Still, Charles said, the state needs to cut down on its spending. As part of his previously stated plan to ultimately slash $4 billion from the state budget, which is currently near $12 billion, and phase out the income tax, Charles said he would first nix at least $1 billion “by reducing the fraud” as well as eliminating sole source contracts.
He referred to fraud to the tune of $2.1 billion in Maine, though that appeared to reference State Auditor Matt Dunlap’s annual audit in 2024 that noted “deficiencies” and “material weaknesses” involving $2.1 billion in federal spending.
Charles said he would cut 2,000 unfilled state jobs, implement an immediate hiring freeze and order a “top-to-bottom review” of all state agencies while “restructuring” the education and health departments. He would task each commissioner with trimming department costs by 10%.
“None of this, by the way, has any effect on services,” Charles said. “It only makes us more efficient.”
He also argued for ending the process known as the “cascade,” in which unspent surplus General Fund money is transferred at the end of each fiscal year to different areas, such as the Highway Fund.
Charles ended his response with another dig at Pingree. He said he would eliminate the governor’s policy office that oversees housing, climate, economic and other initiatives — which Pingree used to lead.
Democrat Hannah Pingree
Pingree, 49, started her answer by blaming President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war for putting “huge headwinds on our economy,” and she criticized cuts to Medicaid and food benefits in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
She mentioned getting first elected to the Legislature in 2002 and serving on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee when lawmakers and Baldacci faced the roughly $1 billion shortfall. She touted her work with Republicans to pass bipartisan, balanced budgets, including working with then-Republican floor leader Josh Tardy when she was the Maine House speaker from 2008 to 2010.
But Pingree remained light on specifics to fill a budget gap, other than saying she would double the homestead exemption to $50,000 and amend the Maine Constitution to tax second homes that non-Maine residents own in the state at a higher rate.
That second idea from Pingree looks unlikely to pass in the near future, given it would take a two-thirds majority vote in both chambers to amend the Maine Constitution that currently requires all property to be taxed equally per its true value.
Dan Pittman, a Maine Revenue Services lawyer, confirmed to lawmakers last month that such a proposal, or policies like Rhode Island’s “Taylor Swift” tax on empty vacation homes, are not allowed in Maine without a constitutional change.
Charles and Bennett said they disagree with Pingree’s proposal. Pingree acknowledged the hurdles facing her plan but doubled down on pursuing it.
“That is a big thing to do, but we’ve amended our constitution many, many times before, and it would require bipartisan support,” Pingree said. “But I’ll tell you, from Washington County down to southern Maine, people realize that Maine people are having a hard time keeping their home.”
Independent Rick Bennett
Bennett, 63, kicked off his answer by warning about the growth in the state budget over the past decade and how the Mills administration pushed federal money for COVID-19 pandemic relief “out the front door.” He criticized the Legislature for not holding a true public hearing on the continuing services budget that funds baseline services in six years.
“We are spending, in the state government, well beyond the means of Mainers to pay,” Bennett said. “That’s a reality. We need some fiscal prudence.”
If elected, Bennett said, he would put together a finance team the day after the Nov. 3 election to look at every line in the state budget, and he said he would return to the Legislature’s former tradition of passing budgets with at least two-thirds support.
To avoid devoting state dollars to paying back the federal government for potential fiscal issues, Bennett said his office would have an inspector general team that investigates potential misspending or corruption.

title: 2 Penobscot County men allegedly shot across the road and hit a house
text:
The Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office on Thursday arrested two men from the town of LaGrange who were allegedly shooting guns illegally and recklessly.
Police were called to a report of guns being fired in LaGrange. In their investigation, deputies determined that the gunfire had crossed the roadway and struck a residence located across the street, the sheriff’s office said.
The two men suspected of doing the shooting are both convicted felons who were prohibited from possessing firearms, according to the sheriff’s office.
Guy Shurman, 37, and Daniel Turner, 44, both of LaGrange, were arrested and taken to Penobscot County Jail. Both are charged with possession of a firearm by a prohibited person.

title: Patriots QB Drake Maye finds his confidence
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye rediscovered his confidence and production in the Patriots’ dominant 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
And it restored the belief that New England can compete with the AFC’s top teams this season.
It wasn’t just the third-year quarterback’s passing numbers – 26 of 34 for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns – that jumped off the page. It was the calm and deliberate way he commanded the offense that rang the loudest on a day he finished without a turnover for the first time this season.
Equally encouraging was that Maye left the field thinking there was even better football to be played.
“I think that’s what it’s like when we put some things together, and we still have some,” he said. “I mean, it’s crazy to say we’ve still got some left to squeeze.”
It was also a good sign that Maye was able to get multiple players involved.
Playing without wide receivers A.J. Brown (injured reserve/sprained ankle) and Mack Hollins (injured reserve/calf), Maye spread the ball around to nine players.
But it wasn’t all smiles on the sideline after running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) and left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) left the field two plays apart.
It’s a particularly concerning injury for Campbell, who had to go on IR for four games late last season with a right knee injury before returning for the regular-season finale and playoff run.
This is also a recurring issue for Henderson, who dealt with an ankle injury in the preseason that caused him to miss the opener at Seattle.
Campbell was replaced Sunday by rookie Caleb Lomu, who’s expected to fill the role as Maye’s blindside protector for however long Campbell is out.
“I don’t think it was too big for him,” coach Mike Vrabel said of Lomu. “I think he was able to settle down. You didn’t really notice him a lot, so I think that’s probably a good thing.”
What’s working
As well as the Patriots’ offense performed, the defense was just as solid. It limited a Raiders team that came in averaging 28.8 points per game to 5 of 13 on third down. The Patriots also forced a fumble and sacked Kirk Cousins twice. What’s more, New England never allowed the Raiders to get into a groove. After scoring a touchdown early in the first quarter, Las Vegas’ next four drives went punt, punt, missed field goal and punt.
What needs help
Discipline. The Patriots were called for a season-high 12 penalties for 116 yards, a total Vrabel called “ridiculous” postgame. Even with several new combinations of players on the field because of injuries, those are numbers that must be addressed.
Stock up
WR Kyle Williams. The second-year receiver has been waiting to get more opportunities, and Maye linked up with him three times for 91 yards, including a 34-yard TD grab in the third quarter.
Stock down
Secondary. Yes, the group was playing without starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck), but had no answers for Raiders tight end Brock Bowers, who finished with eight catches for 110 yards and a touchdown.
Injuries
The already injury-ravished secondary lost another player when cornerback Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Key number
1 — The number of Patriots quarterbacks (Maye) to complete at least 75% of their passes for at least 300 yards and four touchdowns with no interceptions, along with a rushing touchdown in a single game.
Next steps
The Patriots return to playing an AFC East rival, hosting the New York Jets (2-3) on Sunday.

title: Irate about government-funded Trump ads
text:
I was watching “CBS Sunday Morning” last weekend and was shocked to see President Donald Trump in an ad for himself. What was more shocking was seeing the notation at the end that it was paid for by the U.S. government. I understand it was also on during some NFL games.
Sen. Susan Collins, to my knowledge, has not said one word about this. I have called and written to her office and received no response. Other Republican senators have spoken out against it. How is government funding being used for this; who appropriated it?
Needless to say, I am outraged.
Susan Rephan
Portland

title: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
text:
(AP) — President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP.
“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.
___
Associated Press reporters Collin Binkley and Ali Swenson contributed.

title: Pentagon clears the way for Bath Iron Works to build destroyer
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Pentagon officials have cleared the way for a Navy destroyer to be built by Bath Iron Works this fiscal year.
Members of Maine’s congressional delegation had urged the Trump administration to fund an additional Arleigh Burke-class guided missile destroyer in the 2027 fiscal year after the administration proposed just one, which would be built at a competing shipyard.
After a review of the Bath shipyard, the Pentagon determined that BIW had made significant improvements and was equipped to build the additional destroyer, should Congress secure funding, Sen. Susan Collins announced in a news release Monday.
Collins, who heads the appropriations committee, said that the results of the review show the hard work of shipbuilders at BIW, one of the state’s largest employers.
“I have advocated for a second destroyer to be included in this year’s budget, and I worked with the administration during its careful review and repeated visits to BIW to verify the ability of the shipyard to construct another ship while continuing to complete its current workload,” Collins said. “This certification will help keep our Navy strong and support BIW as a steady source of good-paying Maine jobs. I will continue to work to ensure our shipbuilders have the resources to meet the Navy’s needs at a time when China is relentlessly expanding its fleet.”
Following her announcement Monday, BIW President Charles Krugh thanked Collins for advocating for funding for Maine shipbuilding.
“At a time when our nation urgently needs more surface combatants and is even looking to shipyards overseas, this American shipyard is answering that call, delivering each destroyer to the Navy faster than the last. The announcement makes it clear that we are succeeding in our efforts to improve shipbuilding and that is leading to more work — which is good for the business and good for each and every one of us who works here,” Krugh said in a prepared statement.
The senator met with Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg in July to urge the department to fund a BIW-built destroyer. A Pentagon team then traveled to Bath to conduct the review, according to Collins’ office.
Feinberg said in a press release Monday that BIW had proven it has the capacity to respond to “demands for increased speed and volume” of shipbuilding.
“While the operational improvements we have seen at BIW are a significant step in the right direction, the shipyard must continue this momentum to fully resolve legacy production challenges — sustained performance is essential,” he said. “The department will continue to partner with contractors who prioritize execution, accountability, and the rapid modernization of our forces.”
Krugh said the company has made improvements in its building process, production schedule and the “stability and skill of our shipbuilders.”
“Together these improvements are accelerating delivery of ships to the U.S. Navy, where they perform their critical role protecting our country and our families. We appreciate this clear and consistent demand signal, which will help propel our accelerated performance,” Krugh said.

title: Woman dies in head-on collision in Poland
text:
A 40-year-old woman died in a head-on crash in Poland on Sunday, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
Authorities say the woman was driving a 2026 Toyota Camry northbound on Route 11 when it crossed into the southbound lane, hitting a 2019 Ram pickup truck towing a camper.
The woman was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the sheriff’s office. The other driver, a 63-year-old man from Ohio, suffered minor injuries.
The stretch of road in the 700 block of Route 11, also known as Bakerstown Road, was closed for several hours while emergency personnel responded to the crash.
The Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office is not releasing the name of the woman pending notification of her family. The crash investigation is ongoing.

title: ‘Writing on the wall’: New reports highlight history of red flags before toddlers found dead
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — New documents are providing insight into the month leading up to the deaths of two toddlers in South Carolina.
Two-year-old Emory and 1-year-old Harlow Deacon were found starved to death last week at their Ladson home. Their mother, 31-year-old Justine May, was arrested and charged with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
Zachary Deacon—the father of Emory and Harlow—told deputies the writing was on the wall a month before they were found dead.
WCSC has received copies of five additional reports between Aug. 10 and Sept. 29 detailing the calls for concern Deacon made that ultimately led to his arrest.
According to reports, Deacon and May had just ended their eight-year relationship at the beginning of August. The pair had been engaged for the last five of those years and lived together with their two children.
Deputies were called out for a domestic disturbance on Aug. 10.
May accused Deacon of trying to block her car from leaving while Deacon told deputies she was having a mental health episode. No evidence of a mental health crisis was found, according to the reports.
More than two weeks later, Deacon called deputies to do a welfare check, telling them May had been acting unusually and had stopped communicating with family.
He said he discovered disturbing writing on the wall the last time he watched the children days earlier. May told deputies it was Deacon who wrote the disturbing message on the wall. The message itself is redacted from the incident reports.
Authorities found the kids asleep and—again—no evidence of mental health problems.
On Sept. 11, deputies were called again, this time by May’s mother, reporting a mental health crisis in progress. Deputies and the Department of Social Services went to the home and found it clean, the kids happy and “well-fed.”
May then presented deputies with call logs, text messages and screenshots showing Deacon consistently reaching out to her.
Deacon’s messages accused her of “spiraling,” and he told her to “get a grip on reality.” She said Deacon would occasionally patrol the neighborhood as well.
Deputies determined that was enough to issue an arrest warrant for harassment. The next day they met with Deacon and arrested him.
That was Sept. 12, the last day the sheriff’s office said they saw the kids alive.
At some point, deputies were instructed to no longer do welfare checks at May’s home, but they were out there several times between the 12th and the 29th when the kids were discovered.

title: Why CMP is suing the state of Maine over a new revenue blocking law
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Power sued Maine regulators Friday to stop the implementation of a new state law that would block the utility from collecting a $4.6 million boost in investment return.
The law, LD 2038, requires transmission line owners in Maine — CMP, Versant and the utility-owned Maine Electric Power Co. — to join a regional group that operates the lines and manages the flow of electricity.
CMP, MEPCO and Versant are already voluntary members of that group, called ISO New England — which means they are eligible for a federal profit incentive that goes to companies that choose to participate in such collectives. By requiring the utilities to participate, lawmakers hoped to eliminate that federal incentive.
Maine regulators and consumer advocates asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to block utilities from collecting that incentive on Sept. 1. CMP, meanwhile, wants to get the state law thrown out.
The lawsuit comes amid an ongoing fight between CMP and regulators over the utility’s proposed rate hike — and again puts the CMP’s allowed investment profit center stage.
MEPCO joined CMP’s lawsuit against the Maine Public Utilities Commission, public advocate and Department of Energy Resources; Versant did not.
Here’s what to know about the incentive, the state law and the arguments on either side.
THE ‘ADDER’
A 2005 federal law spells it out: For voluntarily joining ISO New England and allowing it to operate CMP’s transmission lines, federal regulators allow CMP to earn an extra 0.5% return on equity — the profit it can make on its built infrastructure.
That 0.5% is an “adder,” as FERC puts it. Utilities all around the country benefit from it.
For CMP, that adder is worth about $4.6 million this year, the Office of the Public Advocate said in March testimony on the bill. Combined, Versant and MEPCO earned $1.35 million.
In 2024, Maine ratepayers paid about $700,000 extra on their bills for this 0.5% “adder,” according to a Sept. 1 complaint from the OPA and Maine regulators. Ratepayer costs are split between New England states.
Congress intended for the incentive to compensate utilities for “surrendering operational control of their facilities” and for maintaining the lines, CMP and MEPCO said in the lawsuit. Without the adder, the company may not be able to afford to keep up its infrastructure and attract outside investment, the lawsuit says.
The adder also helps “handle growing demand for electricity from changing weather patterns due to climate change, the construction of data centers, and the rapid electrification of cars, heating and cooling, home appliances, and other consumer products,” the companies wrote.
CMP, by its own account, is hurting financially. After Maine regulators denied a $7 per month rate increase this month, the company said that it would need to defer upgrades to grid infrastructure, pause hiring and “consider workforce reductions.” CMP’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in its rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
A spokesperson for CMP declined to comment.
THE STATE LAW
Maine’s LD 2038, passed mostly along party lines this spring, followed the lead of Maryland and Connecticut, which approved similar legislation this year and brought their case to federal regulators shortly thereafter.
California and Ohio have similar laws or rules, too — FERC recently denied the adder for utilities in those states. Federal appeals courts backed up FERC’s decisions last year.
The law was always meant to be the first of two steps, Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in January testimony in favor of the bill.
Like the other states, officials in Maine planned to petition federal regulators to remove the adder for Maine utilities as soon as the law was implemented. Maine did so Sept. 1, and three other New England states joined the complaint three weeks later.
“It is long past time to eliminate this ROE adder, which adds millions of dollars to customer bills,” former Public Utilities Commission Chair Philip Bartlett said in a September news release. “Maine has joined other states in the region in requiring transmission owner participation in ISO-New England, providing a clear pathway to reducing this inflated return on equity.”
Maine’s law, like the others, was born out of a concern for affordability and high electricity rates. By most measures, Maine’s rates rank in the top five most expensive in the country, and the effort, when combined with Connecticut’s new law, was estimated to save Maine customers $2 million per year — $5 million if all New England states enacted the same law.
“Given the urgency of electricity affordability issues, this is a simple and easy solution that will have immediate impact,” Sanborn told legislators.
Sanborn declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation. A spokesperson for the PUC did not respond to a request for comment.
CMP argued in its lawsuit that Maine attempted to supersede federal law, in violation of the Constitution, by interrupting transmission rates that had already been approved by FERC.
CMP also said the new law violated its contractual right to withdraw from ISO New England — a scenario the public advocate called “highly unlikely” in its bill testimony. It also argued that the law essentially made it so it no longer owned its transmission property.
The utility also blasted the new Maine law in a response to the Sept. 1 complaint. CMP said the Maine lawmakers enacted an “unlawful state statute in a naked attempt to interfere with FERC’s authority” over transmission rates.
WHAT NOW?
A federal judge will review the case in the coming weeks, and FERC will continue to consider the complaint from the public advocate and PUC.
CMP’s state-level rate case will continue in the meantime, too. Maine regulators recently rejected a $7 per month increase — but the larger rate hike, worth about $18 per month to the average household, will remain under consideration until the spring.

title: Credit union employee accused of stealing more than $28,000 from dead people
text:
BETTENDORF, Iowa (KWQC/Gray News) - An employee at an Iowa credit union is facing charges after police say she stole more than $28,000 from seven people, six of whom were dead.
Amanda N. Tincher, a 38-year-old employee at IH Mississippi Valley Credit Union, was booked on several felony charges Friday after Bettendorf Police say she stole money from the accounts of six dead people and one living person.
A credit union official contacted police July 2 about an employee who had made multiple suspicious transactions on the account of someone who had died, according to court documents.
Police say Tincher made multiple withdrawals from the person’s account and created cashier’s checks in her name, transferred money to a CashApp in her name and made multiple cash withdrawals. She stole $21,279.51 from the account, officials say.
Police met with Tincher at the credit union July 3 and asked her about the suspicious transactions.
“It’s pretty clear what was done,” Tincher reportedly said.
Officials say Tincher denied taking money from other accounts, but the credit union later found she had made similar transactions on six more accounts. Court documents show six of the seven accounts belonged to someone who was dead. She took a total of $28,326.28 from the accounts.
Police say Tincher transferred money from the one living person’s account to the account of a dead person to cover money she took when the beneficiaries noticed the money was missing.
Tincher is facing the following charges:
- First-degree theft, a felony
- Ongoing criminal conduct, unlawful activity, a felony
- First-degree fraudulent practice, a felony
- Second-degree theft, a felony
- Second-degree fraudulent practice, a felony
- Four counts of third-degree theft, an aggravated misdemeanor
- Four counts of third-degree fraudulent practice, an aggravated misdemeanor
- Fifth-degree theft, a simple misdemeanor
- Fifth-degree fraudulent practice, a simple misdemeanor
Tincher was released on bond last Friday afternoon. She has a preliminary hearing scheduled this coming Friday.

title: What does Amazon think about you? Here’s how to find out
text:
(CNN) - Amazon’s “About You” feature is drawing attention after users reported comical entries. The feature was unveiled in May.
A Threads account claims a customer found the words “has flat buttocks” in her section.
A TikTok creator said her section states that she kayaks regularly, though she says she has never done so.
Customers cannot delete the section, but they can review and revise it.
In the Amazon app, select the profile icon, choose “Account,” scroll down and select “About You.”
On the web, select “Accounts and Lists” in the upper-right corner and find the section.

title: Political groups invest in Bangor City Council race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Political groups are spending money on Bangor City Council races, with speakers at a Monday event citing public safety, police staffing, needle exchanges and homelessness among their concerns.
Jonathan Bush, a former gubernatorial candidate and founder of Maine for Keeps, said he hopes the group’s investment in local races across Maine — including Waterville, Lewiston and Bangor — will reach six figures.
“I gave, as you know, 50,000 bucks, which is all I had left in Maine for Keeps,” Bush said. “And I’m hoping to get another 50 from the other folks that are concerned.”
Bush said Maine for Keeps focuses on voter education and policy advocacy rather than endorsing candidates. He said city councils are a place where he believes his group can have the most influence.
Bangor group backs three candidates
Concerned Citizens of Bangor is supporting three of the 12 declared candidates running for City Council, said Philip Henry, a member of the group.
“We have a PAC set up. We have funding coming in from the local Bangor community. And so, we are supporting three candidates,” Henry said. “We don’t want the vote to get diluted.”
Henry said the group wants transparency and metrics on efforts to fully staff the Police Department. He said there is bipartisan support for the group’s calls for change.
Maine Republican Party Chairman Jim Deyermond urged voters to support Republicans, saying the goal was to “put sane Republicans and conservatives on this city council.” Bush said his group was fully committed to the three races in Bangor, Waterville, and Lewiston.
Organizer criticizes election spending
Bangor resident and progressive organizer Mitchell Cooper criticized the spending, calling it an attempt by wealthy people to influence an election. He said the money should instead go toward solutions, including needle return boxes, a needle bounty program and funding to fully staff the Police Department.

title: Orono’s live band scene might be the best thing since sliced bread
text:
OPINION: It’s no secret that the University of Maine’s party scene is frat-based. On an average Saturday, you can drive through Frat Row and see numerous houses opening their doors to well-hydrated students in search of another reason to sit through five days of school every week. Delta, TKE, Kap Sig, Beta, ATO, ASig and more are frequent student destinations, typically featuring a mix of house music from an amateur DJ and a plethora of pong and die players, sardined in a pseudo-rave room full of freshmen shouting “SO WHAT’S YOUR MAJOR?” It is quintessential and I wouldn’t have it any other way.
However, an alternative to the traditional frat party has begun to take hold of the UMaine houses hosting parties this semester. In lieu of Bluetooth speakers and LED disco lights, actual rock bands are beginning to take center stage. The bands themselves are nothing new to UMaine. Houses like Bulkhead and Radon (RIP) have been hosting concerts for a while now. Radon, in particular, set the bar for what a band house should look like — skate magazines all over the wall, a stage that’s both level with and accessible to the crowd and bands that actually love doing what they do. My first Radon concert featured Snake Lips, Gunshot Glitter and Care For, all of whom were fantastic.
This semester, it seems like live concerts are becoming increasingly popular. Sept. 25, in particular, was a monumental night for Orono-based bands, with ATO hosting an outdoor charity show featuring And Then Some, Fishscale, Common Earth Worms and Free Beer (the band), and TKE hosting Park Street Band for their first show of the year.
Playing guitar for PSB has been the highlight of my semester so far, and the crowds have been electric. Having nearly 300 people watch you screw up “Bark At The Moon” is mildly infuriating, but it beats being sandwiched in a wall of sweaty teenagers while Rhianna’s “S&M” plays through a JBL in the corner of the room. Original songs be damned, I will play “Santeria” a hundred times if the people keep singing with us.
As someone who loves frat parties as much as any other 19-year-old guy on campus, I think there is something untouchable about a live band. For me, it is the human element, both in the shared experience of a crowd witnessing live music and in every mistake a band can make. Bands can reach out to their audience, receive feedback and generally have just as much fun as the crowd.
It evokes what I thought college would look like as a kid: hundreds of people partying, not caring about the assignment due that night and the class scheduled tomorrow. Am I arguing that a live band is definitively better than the traditional frat party? I would say no. Like most things, there is a right time and place, and I feel that right now is the right time and place for the live band scene.

title: October is Pedestrian Safety Month
text:
October is pedestrian safety month, a time to remember that everyone is a pedestrian at some point. Whether walking to work or school, running errands, exercising, or enjoying Maine’s beautiful fall foliage, pedestrians and drivers share the responsibility for keeping Maine’s roadways safe.
The Maine Bureau of Highway Safety urges drivers to slow down, stay alert, and watch carefully for pedestrians. Pedestrians are encouraged to remain alert, watch for vehicles, and take steps to make themselves as visible as possible.

title: Super PAC buys Troy Jackson attack ad in Portland, Oregon
text:
A Republican-supporting Super PAC purchased about $25,000 in attack ads against Maine’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson in the Portland, Oregon, region.
The ads, paid for by the Defending Maine Street Super PAC, ran in more than 260 zip codes in Oregon between Oct. 8 and 11, according to the Google Ads Transparency Center. It was updated on Monday to cover Maine.
“The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend,” a spokesperson for Defending Main Street said in an email Monday. “No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error.”
They were shown more than 1.2 million times, according to the center. Approximately $25,000 was spent on the ads.
The PAC’s spokesperson also included a statement from its vendor, the 1903 Group, which said: “This was 100% a Cross Screen Media error.” Cross Screen Media is a political and public affairs advertising company that is owned by the 1903 Group, a holding company.
“Susan Collins’ allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map,” Dan Gottlieb, a spokesperson for Jackson’s campaign, said in a written statement. “Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in.”
A spokesperson for Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.

title: What happens to Maine’s economy without congressional clout?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am not voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson because I support either candidate. I am voting against Donald Trump. But Maine should also think carefully about what happens after this election, when we no longer have a senator with Collins’ seniority and appropriations power.
Bath Iron Works is not just another employer. Its future depends on a steady Navy workload and continued investment in the yard. BIW has historically competed against Huntington Ingalls Industries in Mississippi for DDG-51 destroyers, and Maine’s congressional delegation has repeatedly fought to preserve ship allocations and funding that sustain the workforce and industrial base.
The contrast with Portsmouth Naval Shipyard is important. Portsmouth is one of the Navy’s four public shipyards and benefits directly from the Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program, or SIOP, which has funded major modernization there. BIW, as a privately owned shipyard, does not have that same direct federal recapitalization path.
That makes congressional influence especially important. A sustained loss of destroyer work could mean not only thousands of jobs, but erosion of the engineering, design, integration and skilled-trades capacity needed to build complete warships.
We have seen that kind of decline before. Once-major yards such as the Brooklyn Navy Yard and Quincy Shipyard lost workload, shed skilled workers and capabilities and ultimately ceased shipbuilding altogether. The lesson is that industrial capacity can disappear gradually before the final closure makes headlines.
Whatever our politics this November, Maine needs a serious plan for preserving BIW’s shipbuilding capability after today’s senior delegation is gone.
Kay Aikin
Portland

title: Teenage caregivers: The hidden generation juggling school and elder care
text:
(Aging Untold) — When you picture a caregiver, you probably imagine a middle-aged adult or a spouse.
But a new study from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health shows that role is starting much earlier — an estimated 1.6 million teens ages 15 to 18 and 2 million young adults ages 19 to 22 are now caregivers in the U.S.
Why so many young people are stepping into caregiving roles
“One of the main drivers is people are waiting to have their children until a much older age,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “You could be a 20-year-old and your parents are in their mid- to late-60s, and that’s unheard of in our generation.”
Cradduck said the strain often doesn’t stop there.
“What’s even worse is when your parents are in that age and maybe needing some assistance, their parents are often still alive,” she said. “So you’ve become a club sandwich. Now you’re not even a sandwich generation with your own kids — you’ve got a whole big feast going on here, because you might be taking care of your grandparents, your parents and raising a child as well while trying to work and provide. This is an astronomical, just huge workload on a human being.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added that earlier onset of chronic conditions among younger generations is compounding the issue.
“Compound this with the younger people who are having these chronic conditions earlier because of the obesity that we’re seeing, the insulin resistance and all this increase in metabolic disorders that’s affecting young people earlier, so now add that on,” Rogers said.
A hidden toll on teenagers’ health
Some teens who are providing care might not even recognize what is happening to them.
“One in 10 teenagers is taking care of someone at home from an early-developed chronic illness,” aging expert Amy O’Rourke said. “They’re going to school, they’re taking care of their mom. They’re anxious or depressed. They’re tired, but they’re not attributing it to the fact that they’re taking care of mom.”
O’Rourke said the impact on their health is often hidden.
Where young caregivers can turn for help
She pointed to specific resources for teens and young adults carrying caregiving responsibilities. (See the list with links below.)
“If you’re one of those teenagers out there, there’s a great organization — actually several resources — that I would turn them to,” she said. “One is Lorenzo’s House, the National Caregiving Alliance group. Go to the school, the school guidance counselors, support at the school, and ask for help, because what you’re doing isn’t really expected until you’re like in your 60s.”
Many young caregivers might not realize the scope of what they’re managing.
“For these young folks, they’re very internet savvy. There are a lot of really cool resources and a lot of help, a lot of support groups available to help caregivers navigate these things. Find your support system,” Cradduck said.
Protecting education, careers and your own future
Cradduck cautioned that young caregivers often sacrifice their own futures to care for others.
“Try really, really hard not to put your own career on the back burner, because that’s going to affect your income and your own retirement and your ability to age healthy and safely with enough resources,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose cautioned young caregivers to ensure that they are getting a good education.
“You’ve got to look out for yourself first so you can even be a caregiver as time goes on and maybe have your own family. It can impact your dating, your future careers, your ability to have a job and child rearing. So it’s very complex. But you don’t want a current crisis to become a generational issue that goes on,” Ambrose added.
O’Rourke also encouraged young caregivers to ask schools and support networks for help directly.
“The American Association of Caregiving Youth — ask for help, because if you’re taking care of somebody, you’re overwhelmed, you can’t think to do all those things,” O’Rourke said. “So you ask somebody, ‘How would I do this? How do I take care of my parents and make sure that my career, my finances aren’t duly affected?’”
Looking for solutions before a crisis hits
Rather than waiting until a caregiving emergency develops, Rogers suggested focusing on prevention.
“Why don’t we look at solutions where we can begin to be preventive, so that we can start to work on those things that we know are affecting us — that foundation, the sleep, inflammation, nutrition — so that we can stop ourselves from getting there,” Rogers said.
Ambrose added that a person’s living situation can play a bigger role than people realize.
“Sometimes a caregiving crisis isn’t necessarily so much a medical problem as it might be a housing problem, where we’re not really in the right environment, and it’s working against the health of the people that maybe need the care,” she said.
O’Rourke also suggested schools could do more to identify students who are quietly managing caregiving at home.
“When a child is interviewed for going to high school, ‘Are you an athlete? Are you into music?’ But they don’t say, ‘Are you a caregiver?’” she said. “That should be added to every interview assessment going into school so that they can get a handle on how many kids in their school need help.”
Cradduck pointed young caregivers toward local government resources that often go overlooked.
“I would point anyone, even our young caregivers, back towards your local adult protective (services), your adult services, aging adult and disabled adult services,” she said. “There’s a lot of grant money that helps with utility bills, transportation assistance, transportation reimbursement. There’s a lot of financial help that can come along with just reaching out to your local county.”
Cradduck said not to think that calling Adult Protective Services is a bad thing — there’s a lot of resources there to help.
“Department of Aging, Area Agency on Aging and your local county, and also mental health associations. That might sound strange, but they can be very well funded and have a lot of diverse programs,” Ambrose added.

title: Zelenskyy says Russia has already violated Trump’s surprise energy ceasefire
text:
Zelenskyy says Russia has already violated Trump’s surprise energy ceasefire
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia had already violated the surprise energy ceasefire announced by U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend.
Related video: Bipartisan group of senators condemning President Trump's energy deal with Russia
Trump announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to what he described as an “energy ceasefire,” a development that Zelenskyy said Kyiv did not know about in advance, and one that Moscow has remained tight-lipped about in the hours since.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump said on social media Sunday morning.
Shortly after Trump’s announcement, Russia “launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system,” Zelenskyy said. Despite the fresh attacks, the Ukrainian leader vowed to abide by the new agreement, if Russia does too.
“We agree if they agree, and we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning, but at midnight, a Russian jet-powered Shahed struck a gas production facility in Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, where he spoke via video link.
CNN has reached out to the White House for information on how the agreement was reached and what the next steps may be.
When asked about Trump and Zelenskyy’s comments on Monday, the Kremlin said that “contacts are ongoing,” without providing any further details. “I have nothing to add on this subject,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
After the announcement, Zelenskyy wrote on X that he had talked to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte about the news.
“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side,” Zelenskyy wrote Sunday. “For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace.”
Trump’s U.S.-Russia diesel deal comes under fire
The announcement comes days after Trump spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and the two announced a controversial deal to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel.
That deal induced bipartisan blowback, with lawmakers warning that the administration was defying a federal law meant to crack down on Russia after its invasion of Ukraine.
Seven senators, including four Republicans, released a statement over the weekend asking the administration to “reverse course” and strike its plan to supply markets with Russian diesel.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” the statement read. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies.”
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” it continued.
Talks with top Ukrainian and U.S. officials, including Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, got underway in Miami as the diesel deal was announced Friday, but Zelenskyy criticized the diesel news, saying the move would prolong the war.
Trump responded by suggesting Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.”
Asked about these comments on Monday, Zelenskyy ruled out fresh elections in Ukraine while the war continues. “From a security standpoint, that’s completely impossible. We have attacks day and night,” he said.
It was not immediately clear what led to the Sunday announcement. In an interview earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy also called for a ceasefire.
“OK, if they want energy ceasefire, we are open for this,” Zelenskyy said about Russia during an interview with ABC News. “Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it’s fair, fair deal.”
Energy infrastructure has been one of the key targets of Russian attacks since the first months of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukraine later began targeting Russian oil refining facilities using domestically made drones to strike deep inside Russia. In recent months, both sides have escalated the aerial war as front lines remain largely stagnant.
Trump has expressed frustration about Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy sites. But there have still been several in the past week, with Kyiv viewing them as an essential part of the Kremlin’s war machine.
Ukraine seeking further clarity
Zelenskyy said Sunday that Russia continued to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, including a power plant in Kyiv and energy facilities in the Kharkiv region.
“And all of this happened AFTER the President of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire,” he posted on X.
The Ukrainian leader repeated that assertion on Monday, saying “there were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump.”
“It is clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” he added.
A source close to Zelenskyy told CNN that Ukraine was not attacking Russian oil refineries while it waits for further clarity about the ceasefire from the U.S. side.
This story has been updated with additional information.
Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Mark Carney is the Prime Minister of Canada.

title: Maine’s energy goals depend on a regulatory process people can trust
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tim Burgess is assistant business manager of IBEW Local 104.
When a severe storm knocks out power in the middle of the night, Mainers don’t think about regulatory dockets — they just look for the flashing lights of utility trucks rolling down their streets. The recent recommendation to deny Central Maine Power’s request for temporary rates has sparked a fierce statewide debate over affordability, spending and the future of our electric system.
These are critical issues that affect every household, but for the men and women who build, maintain and restore our grid, a far more troubling question is emerging.
What happens to the safety and stability of our workforce when participants follow the precise regulatory rules laid out by the state, only to be told at the finish line that the path no longer applies?
Central Maine Power sought temporary rates after the Public Utilities Commission itself
indicated they were available to address the severe financial uncertainty following the dismissal of the company’s long-term grid investment plan. CMP maintains that it followed the direction provided by regulators when it pursued temporary rates, filed the case, presented extensive evidence and all involved parties participated in good faith. 
Everyone assumed that the process established by our regulators was available, stable and reliable. The recommendation currently before the commission calls that fundamental assumption into question.
For most Mainers, utility regulation feels abstract. For those who wear the tool belt and climb the poles, it is anything but. Decisions made in Augusta determine whether local contractors hire apprentices, whether vital grid projects move forward, whether stable work exists next year and whether Maine will possess the skilled workforce necessary to meet its aggressive energy and economic development goals.
Predictable investment, workforce development, apprenticeships and long-term grid reliability are interconnected. Uncertain investment makes it significantly harder for employers to expand their operations, harder for joint apprenticeship programs to grow and harder to prepare the next generation of highly skilled workers. This is not a matter of corporate self-interest. It goes directly to the heart of how safely the infrastructure is built.
Maine’s broader, long-term policy objectives sharpen the point. Our state leaders continue to aggressively promote widespread electrification, economic development, transportation electrification, rapid heat pump adoption and clean energy expansion. Every one of these initiatives drives up the daily demand for electrical infrastructure, heavy-duty service upgrades and overall grid capacity.
Meeting these goals requires a larger workforce and a stronger, more resilient grid. There is an inherent contradiction in encouraging a society-wide dependence on electricity while simultaneously creating deep financial uncertainty around the exact investments that such dependence requires.
The public debate is framed as affordability versus investment. Utility workers understand the strain of affordability as well as anyone; those who build and maintain the grid are local customers and taxpayers, too.
Aging infrastructure continues to age, and its vulnerabilities compound over time. Projects that could have been executed methodically and safely during a planned rollout instead become high-stress emergencies later on. This delays routine progress and forces emergency work at a far greater cost to the customers, all while creating much harder, more hazardous conditions for the people doing the work in storms and sub-zero temperatures.
Witnesses in these proceedings have repeatedly warned that regulatory delay leads directly to higher long-term costs, greater operational challenges and reduced workforce stability. The broader concern is the chilling signal this situation sends across our entire industry. Young lineworker and electrician apprentices count on steady, predictable work to accumulate the thousands of field hours required to become a journeyman, while local contractors need regulatory certainty before investing in heavy equipment or expanding their crews.
Furthermore, major employers looking to bring business to Maine must have absolute confidence that a stable grid will be ready when they plug in. Ultimately, all of these vital
economic decisions rest on a single, fundamental belief: that Maine’s regulatory institutions are predictable, consistent and worthy of trust.
Trust is not built by any single decision, but through a long-term process that participants
believe is transparent, consistent and reliable. When an entity follows the path regulators
indicated was open yet finds that path abruptly closed at the finish line, it is entirely fair to ask whether future participants can truly rely on the process. 
If Maine hopes to build the skilled workforce, modern infrastructure and robust electric system its economic and energy policies require, it must preserve something just as important: a regulatory process people can trust, rely upon and plan their lives around.

title: Ingrained in state culture, beloved atlases are a must for Mainers
text:
This column was originally published in March 2021.
Every Mainer receives two things at birth: a name, and a Delorme’s Maine Atlas.
The atlas is so ingrained in Maine culture that a car feels empty without one. Sure, nowadays there are GPS devices and apps that modernize direction-finding, but there’s still a comfort in leafing through the pages of an old-fashioned atlas. Torn pages and coffee stains testify that its owner has actually gone somewhere.
Each atlas page has secrets. Tiny symbols invite exploration of recreation areas, family outing opportunities, and unique natural features. And there are ghosts on these pages — ghosts of places that once were — places where only the name survives.
Many of the ghosts have funny names. A drive from Rockwood to Jackman takes motorists through Taunton & Raynham Academy Grant, which is just north of Misery Gore.
When Maine became a state in 1820, part of the separation agreement with Massachusetts required that the two states divide up any land that hadn’t already been granted to someone. Massachusetts could then sell its share of the land and pay off its debts for the War of 1812. In reality, a lot of Maine land had already been sold while the state was still part of Massachusetts, helping to pay off debts incurred during the American Revolution.
Historically, the act of fighting the British moved a lot of Maine real estate.
Several grants around Moosehead Lake were made to fund educational institutions. Taunton is so old, it was founded by the original Pilgrims. This southern Massachusetts town is closer to Providence than Boston. The original Taunton & Raynham Academy is barely a footnote in history, but the name survives, printed on the Maine map just west of Rockwood.
Likewise, Sandwich Academy Grant was given to a school founded in 1804 on Cape Cod in Sandwich, Massachusetts. The academy is long gone, but its namesake ghost is on the Maine map, just west of the Taunton & Raynham Academy ghost.
Days Academy in Wrentham, Massachusetts was founded in 1806. It disappeared 64 years later, but its ghost survives. The Days Academy Grant Township sits at the entrance to Mt. Kineo on the east side of Moosehead Lake.
Bowdoin College was a Massachusetts institution for 26 years before Maine gained statehood. The Massachusetts legislature considered it important enough to double the usual donation. In 1812, it gifted the college with two townships, now on the map as Bowdoin College Grant West and Bowdoin College Grant East. They lie just east of Greenville.
Some of the land was sold to subsidize other Bay State priorities. In the 18th Century, canals moved large quantities of goods. Erie Canal may be the most famous, but the Middlesex Canal lasted half a century, connecting Boston to the Merrimack River. To help fund this early Big Dig, two parcels of Maine land were granted, one on each side of Moosehead Lake’s north end. Little remains of the Middlesex Canal, but its name still lingers on the Maine map.
Massachusetts Gore is a small piece of land just beneath Coburn Gore, along the New Hampshire border in Franklin County. The first part of its name is a relic of the fact that Massachusetts retained the timber rights. The latter part means the parcel was a mistake. All of Maine is divided into townships. Southern Maine towns tend to be irregularly shaped, corresponding to historic settlements. Northern Maine townships are evenly square, six miles on a side. Early surveying was good, but with different companies in the woods doing different survey work, sometimes lines didn’t exactly match up. Gore is an Old English word for such mistakes. Rather than resurvey, gores were simply marked on the map and given a name.
Misery Gore in Somerset County is 17 miles long, but just a half mile wide. Hibbert’s Gore in Lincoln County is a tiny sliver of a mistake — totaling just 640 acres, in the shape of a flagpole. Altogether, there are eight gores on the Maine map.
Most unorganized townships are simply designated by letters and numbers. T2 R3 corresponds to Township 2, Range 3. But the map is full of anomalies. A northbound trip to Rangeley travels through Township E. Although Township D lies just west of it, and Township C is west of D, there is no Township A or B. And how does one explain E Township in Aroostook County, 175 miles away as the confused crow flies? The Maine Atlas: a book of ghosts and mysteries.

title: Chester man faces burglary charges after land-and-water chase
text:
PASSADUMKEAG, Maine (WABI) - A Chester man is facing burglary and other charges after authorities say he led them on a chase on land and in the water.
Deputies with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office were called to Main Road in Passadumkeag Saturday night.
A caller reported her ex-boyfriend, 25-year-old Nicholas Violette, had broken into the home through a window. He took off before authorities arrived. Violette was not supposed to have contact with the woman.
When deputies arrived, they heard movement in the woods. They say Violette was ultimately located across the river on an island. He apparently used a kayak to cross the water.
Authorities say Violette refused to surrender to them.
Lincoln Police provided a drone and the Old Town Police Department provided a canine unit to help take Violette into custody. The Maine Warden Service also responded with a boat and game wardens.
As the drone flew overhead, authorities say Violette surrendered. An arrest team crossed the river and took Violette into custody.

title: Patriots QB Drake Maye finds his confidence
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye rediscovered his confidence and production in the Patriots’ dominant 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
And it restored the belief that New England can compete with the AFC’s top teams this season.
It wasn’t just the third-year quarterback’s passing numbers – 26 of 34 for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns – that jumped off the page. It was the calm and deliberate way he commanded the offense that rang the loudest on a day he finished without a turnover for the first time this season.
Equally encouraging was that Maye left the field thinking there was even better football to be played.
“I think that’s what it’s like when we put some things together, and we still have some,” he said. “I mean, it’s crazy to say we’ve still got some left to squeeze.”
It was also a good sign that Maye was able to get multiple players involved.
Playing without wide receivers A.J. Brown (injured reserve/sprained ankle) and Mack Hollins (injured reserve/calf), Maye spread the ball around to nine players.
But it wasn’t all smiles on the sideline after running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) and left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) left the field two plays apart.
It’s a particularly concerning injury for Campbell, who had to go on IR for four games late last season with a right knee injury before returning for the regular-season finale and playoff run.
This is also a recurring issue for Henderson, who dealt with an ankle injury in the preseason that caused him to miss the opener at Seattle.
Campbell was replaced Sunday by rookie Caleb Lomu, who’s expected to fill the role as Maye’s blindside protector for however long Campbell is out.
“I don’t think it was too big for him,” coach Mike Vrabel said of Lomu. “I think he was able to settle down. You didn’t really notice him a lot, so I think that’s probably a good thing.”
What’s working
As well as the Patriots’ offense performed, the defense was just as solid. It limited a Raiders team that came in averaging 28.8 points per game to 5 of 13 on third down. The Patriots also forced a fumble and sacked Kirk Cousins twice. What’s more, New England never allowed the Raiders to get into a groove. After scoring a touchdown early in the first quarter, Las Vegas’ next four drives went punt, punt, missed field goal and punt.
What needs help
Discipline. The Patriots were called for a season-high 12 penalties for 116 yards, a total Vrabel called “ridiculous” postgame. Even with several new combinations of players on the field because of injuries, those are numbers that must be addressed.
Stock up
WR Kyle Williams. The second-year receiver has been waiting to get more opportunities, and Maye linked up with him three times for 91 yards, including a 34-yard TD grab in the third quarter.
Stock down
Secondary. Yes, the group was playing without starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck), but had no answers for Raiders tight end Brock Bowers, who finished with eight catches for 110 yards and a touchdown.
Injuries
The already injury-ravished secondary lost another player when cornerback Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Key number
1 — The number of Patriots quarterbacks (Maye) to complete at least 75% of their passes for at least 300 yards and four touchdowns with no interceptions, along with a rushing touchdown in a single game.
Next steps
The Patriots return to playing an AFC East rival, hosting the New York Jets (2-3) on Sunday.

title: Are 1 in 5 American adults functionally illiterate?
text:
No.
The claim that a fifth of American adults are functionally illiterate likely confuses low literacy with functional illiteracy.
Functionally illiterate people may struggle to understand basic sentences, find information in short texts or complete simple forms, the U.S. Department of Education says.
The department says adults below Level 1, the lowest proficiency level, may be considered functionally illiterate. In a 2023 international assessment, 12% of U.S. residents ages 16 to 65 fell into that category.
That same assessment found 16% had Level 1 English literacy, which is considered low but more advanced than functional illiteracy. The share at or below Level 1 was 28%, up from 19% — roughly one in five — in 2017.
The rise is partly due to changing methodologies, the department said. Its literacy categories range up to Level 5, with those at Level 1 able to read short passages and find clearly stated information.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Pro-Susan Collins ads accidentally run in Portland, Oregon
text:
A Political Action Committee aiming to boost the reelection campaign of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine saw its ads mistakenly run in Portland, Oregon, instead of in the Maine city of the same name.
NBC reported the error on Monday saying the Republican group, Defending Main Street SuperPAC Inc., spent $20,000 to $25,000 to run ads branding Collins’ Democratic challenger “taxin’ Troy Jackson.”
Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the SuperPAC, told NBC she’s “absolutely furious” about the “ridiculous” error, adding that the Oregon ad is “down now and they’re running it in Portland, Maine.”
