A spokesperson from Cross Screen Media, the company that placed the ad in the Oregon market, admitted to the mistake, chalking it up to working on thousands of campaigns.
The spokesperson told NBC that Cross Screen Media refunded the money to the SuperPAC.

title: Tired of complaints about Susan Collins
text:
I’m tired of hearing that Sen. Susan Collins is responsible for the Supreme Court.
Look at the actual record. Yes, she voted to confirm Republican nominees. She also voted to confirm Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, every one of the court’s three liberal justices. No other Republican serving today can claim that.
Collins’ standard has never changed: a president of either party is entitled to qualified nominees, and each one gets judged on the merits, not on who sits in the White House. The only Supreme Court nominee she ever voted against was Amy Coney Barrett — because the confirmation was rushed through days before a presidential election. Collins said the same rule should apply no matter which party held the Senate, and she meant it.
People who blame Collins for the Supreme Court’s rulings are really just angry that she doesn’t vote the way they would, every single time. But that’s exactly the point of an independent. Someone who agrees with us on everything isn’t independent; they’re just on our team.
The same people demanding Sen. Collins reject every Republican nominee would be furious if a Democratic senator took marching orders from the other side. Consistency is a fair thing to ask for, yet Collins has delivered it for nearly 30 years.
People can disagree with a vote here or there. But the moment anyone looks at the “yes” votes, idea that Collins is a reliable partisan on the courts collapses.
Maine deserves a senator who thinks for herself. We have one.
Maeann Bush
Belgrade

title: Chester man faces burglary charges after land-and-water chase
text:
PASSADUMKEAG, Maine (WABI) - A Chester man is facing burglary and other charges after authorities say he led them on a chase on land and in the water.
Deputies with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office were called to Main Road in Passadumkeag Saturday night.
A caller reported her ex-boyfriend, 25-year-old Nicholas Violette, had broken into the home through a window. He took off before authorities arrived. Violette was not supposed to have contact with the woman.
When deputies arrived, they heard movement in the woods. They say Violette was ultimately located across the river on an island. He apparently used a kayak to cross the water.
Authorities say Violette refused to surrender to them.
Lincoln Police provided a drone and the Old Town Police Department provided a canine unit to help take Violette into custody. The Maine Warden Service also responded with a boat and game wardens.
As the drone flew overhead, authorities say Violette surrendered. An arrest team crossed the river and took Violette into custody.

title: Windham holds grand opening for sewage facility
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WINDHAM — Officials cut the ribbon for the ceremonial opening of the North Windham Wastewater Treatment plant on Oct. 8, bringing the long-gestating project to a close two years after it broke ground.
The official opening of the plant, which began operations in August, marked the conclusion of a project half a decade in the making. Work on the project began in 2021, when the town entered into an agreement with the Portland Water District to put a sewer site together. The following year, the town voted overwhelmingly in favor of a revolving loan, and construction on the treatment plant, located next to Manchester School, began in 2023.
Prior to the construction of the new wastewater system, Windham largely relied on septic systems, which limited opportunities for business, housing and community development, while increasing nitrate levels in the town’s aquifers.
The facility is based around membrane bio-reactor technology and is the first in Maine to employ the technology at such a large scale. According to a press release from the Portland Water District, which is responsible for the plant’s operations, in MBR technology, microorganisms break down organic matter and nutrients before the water passes through microscopic membrane pores that separate remaining solids, bacteria and other contaminants.
The result, according to the water district, is high-quality treated water that will be sent through an advanced drip dispersal system beneath the athletic fields at Manchester School, which were built in conjunction with the plant.
Former Town Manager Barry Tibbetts, who led the town for much of the project’s development, said it was exciting to see the plant completed. He said it will open up benefits for the community by allowing for additional business growth while also cleaning up local water sources, noting that the water released by the plant is clean enough to drink.
The plant is designed to handle 160,000 gallons of waste per day, with the potential to expand to 320,000 gallons per day. It is permitted to discharge 154,000 gallons per day of treated effluent. The plant will operate largely autonomously, with operators working at the plant for a couple of hours on weekdays.
According to Windham Town Council Chair Mark Morrison, the project was funded with a mixture of $2 million from the federal government, around $3 million each from the town of Windham and Cumberland County, and $42 million from the clean water state revolving loan. The $50 million investment, he said, will lead to a projected $160 million in economic growth for the town.
In addition to the wastewater treatment plant, the town is currently building a connection between the plant and the new Windham Middle School, due to open next school year. RSU 14 Superintendent Chris Howell also said the new wastewater treatment plant will allow the district’s Windham Center Campus wastewater treatment facility, built in the 1960s, to be retired.

title: The growing need for diapers as families face rising costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Diapers are a basic need for many families. Parents already dealing with rising costs for housing, food and transportation can find it hard to keep up with diaper costs.
According to a 2026 survey by the National Diaper Bank Network, nearly half of families, or one in two, struggled to pay for diapers.
A quarter of parents reported missing work or school because they could not afford the diapers required to leave their baby in childcare.
Volunteers package diapers
Christina and Emily D’Abreo are a mother-daughter volunteer team at the Diaper Bank of North Carolina. Last year, they spent 208 hours volunteering there. They packaged about 29,000 diapers, helping more than 1,000 babies and their families.
“I know that diaper need is a big, something that’s really overlooked in our community,” Emily D’Abreo said.
“It’s really hard when you see a growing family have to choose between food and between diapers,” Christina D’Abreo said. “One in two families cannot afford this.”
Diapers can cost about $100 a month per child. Safety net programs like WIC and SNAP do not cover the cost of diapers.
Demand continues to rise
Jerry Garcia runs the Charlotte branch of the Diaper Bank of North Carolina. He said the need is rising.
Garcia is a father of a 5-year-old daughter and an 18-month-old son. “I’m right in the midst with everybody else experiencing the high cost of diapers, wipes, formula.”
The warehouse distributes 2 million products a year, including baby diapers, adult incontinence underwear and menstrual products.
The products are given out through partnerships with social service organizations and schools.
“When we take a step back, it’s like, wow, that is amazing,” Garcia said. “But also, we see on the flip side of the coin, we see the need. So we’re very fortunate to have the support of our volunteers and support of the community. But I believe we’re barely scratching the surface.”
Garcia said the organization needs more volunteers.
“It’s very meaningful, impactful,” Garcia said. “You come in, you wrap the diapers, you pack them up, and then at the end of the experience, you get to hear how many diapers you wrapped and how many babies you’re going to serve by volunteering those two hours.”
Volunteering as family time
Christina D’Abreo said volunteering became a way to spend time with her daughter.
“You know how it is with high school. There is no, you know, mom time, dad time, but this is our time,” Christina D’Abreo said. “So I made sure that we made it fun. So we would volunteer and then we’d go and grab a bite, you know, hang out together and make it special. And I think that time is invaluable. I’m gonna miss it when she goes to college.”
Emily D’Abreo said she hopes to become a nurse.
“A big part of that for me is like being empathetic and being able to realize the need in our community and just being able to give back is really fulfilling for me,” Emily D’Abreo said.
Christina D’Abreo said she also wanted to set an example for her daughter.
“I wanted to give back to the community and I wanted to show my six-year-old at that time that, I have a full-time job, I have a career, I have a home, but I also have a community,” Christina D’Abreo said.
Multiple studies find that people who give their time report an enriched sense of purpose and lower rates of depression. Regular volunteering is also linked to decreased cognitive decline compared with those who do not volunteer.
A study found that volunteering boosts a person’s chances of gaining employment by 27%.

title: 20-year-old father of 2 killed in railcar derailment, officials say
text:
DURANT, Okla. (KXII/Gray News) - A 20-year-old father of two was identified as the rail crew worker who died after a railcar derailed in Oklahoma on Wednesday morning.
The Bryan County Communications Center received a call Wednesday morning about a railroad incident involving a railcar. Several agencies responded, including the Durant Police Department.
Family members identified the worker as Axcell Hernandez. They told KXII that Hernandez was a hard worker and loving father to a toddler and a newborn.
Hernandez was part of a crew loading and moving railcars that were not connected or being moved by an engine.
Durant police Sgt. Nick Spencer said officers “did in fact locate the railcar that was overturned and had witnesses on scene that confirmed that a male employee of a local business had been trapped underneath.”
Spencer said a derailer, “a device known as a derailer was in place and was designed to prevent anything rolling onto an active railway.”
Investigators say the accident happened at the Hardy Farms plant. The plant has so far declined comment.
Specialized equipment was needed for rescue and recovery operations, and Hernandez’s body was recovered during the operation.
Spencer said the department is working to complete a thorough investigation.
“It’s our mission to make sure that we give a thorough investigation to contribute to go along with a much broader investigation. At this time, we’re treating this as a workplace accident,” Spencer said.
The National Transportation Safety Board is also investigating.

title: New immunotherapy could offer hope for multiple myeloma patients
text:
(Aging Untold) — It’s been a decade since Susan Lehman was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer that develops in plasma cells in the bone marrow.
“I trust God with my life and with what he has in his plans for me, and so that gave me a sense of peace,” Lehman said. “But it’s still a scary thing.”
Multiple myeloma is treatable but not curable, Lehman said.
The risk increases with age, and the average age at diagnosis is 70, according to WebMD.
Lehman, a 60-year-old mother of four, has been in and out of remission over the years. She has undergone two stem cell transplants and several other treatments.
A new treatment option
Dr. Sumit Madan, an oncologist with Banner Health, had Lehman try something new: CARVYKTI.
“These types of therapies have been revolutionizing the way we treat multiple myeloma now,” Madan said.
Two months into the treatment, Lehman said the immunotherapy has made a big difference.
“I mean, I’m back out hiking,” she said.
CARVYKTI could be an option for multiple myeloma patients when traditional cancer treatments are no longer effective.
Madan said it uses the patient’s own immune cells to act against cancer cells.
Longer-term data shows extended survival
CARVYKTI has been approved for three years, but new, longer-term data from a study shows it doesn’t just slow the progression of the disease — it also helps patients live longer.
“Historically, the outcome of these patients is pretty poor, with the average survival of under a year,” Madan said.
“If you look at the average age of when a patient with multiple myeloma is diagnosed, they’re about 70 years,” Madan said. “And so if I’m able to keep that patient alive for the next 10 to 15 years, and they’re not dying from their cancer, then to me it is a cure.”

title: How these simulation racing centers help drivers train for professional races
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) — A new racing simulator center has opened in Portland, giving drivers access to technology used to train professional racers.
Driving a racing simulator is harder than it looks, but in the e-sports industry, people who master sim racing are turning the skill into a career. E-sports, or competitive video gaming, has grown in popularity over the years, with sim racing gaining an engaged fan base.
The newly opened Northwest Sim Racing is hosting some of its fastest drivers.
Callum Read is the co-owner of the center.
“So they’re actually racing against five other sim centers, so 25 other people, right now across the country,” Read said.
One reason sim racing has become more popular is that the technology has improved, allowing for more affordable options. Racing enthusiasts now have access to the same equipment professional drivers train on.
“A lot of the people that come through my place, they have rigs at home, but nothing like what I’m offering, right? They don’t have motion and don’t have triple monitors,” Read said.
Between home rigs and racing centers, accessibility is changing who can get into the industry.
“Racing is probably the most expensive sport to get into, so it’s not really available to most people,” said Ryan Henifin, a sim race. “It’s real-life racing in a video game that’s much cheaper than real-life racing.”
From hobby to real-world opportunity
Sim racing can save thousands of dollars in car repairs, track time and other costs. While it’s mostly a hobby for Henifin, others want to see where the sport takes them, like Brydon Thomas.
“Sim racing and racing in general is something I want to do. It’s been a dream since I’ve been a kid. And I mean, there’s a bunch of different opportunities within the sim world, but the sim world can also lead to opportunities in the real world,” Thomas said.
Racing sims available at NW Sim include iRacing from NASCAR and others that mimic the performance of different types of cars, down to specific details like tires and brakes, in addition to using advanced scanning systems to replicate tracks from around the world.
“Whereas in Montreal or Miami or Circuit of the Americas or Atlanta, like all these big tracks, they’re all right there. I can go to every single one of those tracks on a simulator and to the point where you memorize it so much,” said Cameron Root, a sim racer.
Racing sims give local racers like Root, the 2023 Ferrari Challenge winner, a competitive edge.
Big racing brands including NASCAR, McLaren and Red Bull have also gotten into sim racing.

title: ‘She’s got a knife!’: Service members save 2 girls whose mother allegedly tried to kill them
text:
PIERCE COUNTY, Wash. (KOMO) - A group of service members is being credited with saving two girls after investigators say their mother tried to kill them on a Washington state interstate.
Army Sgt. 1st Class Jeff Hytower is a practical nursing specialist who helps train other soldiers at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Pierce County. He says the lessons he teaches in the classroom are ones people need to be ready to use.
“I’m a soldier first, but then, I’m a nurse second, too. So, I just want people to be safe, right? I picture people being like my family. So, I want to make sure everyone gets home safe,” he said.
Hytower and another soldier, Sgt. Ricardo Nunez, were driving on Interstate 5 last Monday morning when they saw a serious crash in the opposite direction and stopped to help. The crash involved 35-year-old mother Janieka Ellington and her two daughters, ages 9 and 15.
Sgt. Alexis McKay, a Washington National Guard combat medic, was also among those who stopped to help. She was checking on one of the children when she heard someone screaming that Ellington had a knife and was going after her 15-year-old daughter.
“The most senior of us yells very, very loudly, ‘She’s got a knife!’” McKay said.
Hytower and Nunez quickly stopped Ellington, disarming her and restraining her until help arrived.
“I just jumped up. It was just insane,” Hytower said. “That’s when training kicks in. That’s when everything that we do with soldiers kicks in, and it was more of a reaction than anything.”
Court records state Ellington was reportedly drinking heavily Sunday night before the crash. She allegedly had suicidal thoughts, believed that someone was after the family and that they were going to die. Investigators with the Washington State Patrol say she purposely crashed her car into a concrete barrier on I-5 before trying to kill her teenage daughter.
A judge ordered Ellington to undergo a mental health evaluation as she faces multiple counts of attempted murder and vehicular assault. She is being held without bail and is due back in court later this month.
Both of her daughters were hospitalized with injuries from the crash and the attempted stabbing but have since been released to the care of hospital social workers. Investigators were working to connect with other family members in the area and out of state.
For his part, Hytower says he has no regrets about stepping in.
“Don’t regret it. I would do it two times on Sunday. Just make sure everybody’s OK. Because again, at the end of the day, I just want to make sure everybody’s safe,” he said.
Nunez echoes that sentiment.
“I am glad I was there to help those girls and was just in the right place at the right time. I am also very glad the other two [soldiers] were there and that we were able to work together,” he said.

title: Donations from April telethon still stocking Aroostook County food pantries
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) -Donations sent in by viewers during the Operation Hunger telethon in April are still making a difference as the need for food assistance continues to grow.
Every month, five truckloads of food arrive at Catholic Charities, which distributes the food to pantries across Aroostook County. Those pantries put the food on the tables of friends, family and neighbors. The Operation Hunger telethon in April brought in more than $35,000 to help make that possible.
“And I want to say, if I remember right, we were around, it was about 23 or $2,500 a month goes into that effort to buy food for us, which is a good chunk,” said Jon Blanchard, director of Hunger and Relief Services.
Need for pantries has grown
Blanchard has been part of Catholic Charities Hunger and Relief Services for five years. He said the number of people turning to food pantries has steadily increased during that time.
“Pretty much the whole time I’ve been with Catholic Charities, it seems like it’s been on a slow march uptick for folks making use of pantry services. You know, it always seems like there’s something going on, which is tough, but hey, that’s why we’re here and we’re trying to serve the county the best we possibly can,” Blanchard said.
Funds directed toward new freezer
October’s food order has already been made. Blanchard said they are prioritizing some of their funds toward filling a new freezer in Monticello, particularly with protein-rich frozen foods.
“We need to fill this freezer at this point. Donations are going to go a long way, but we also need to have that regular flow of incoming food every single month because it goes out of here every single month. So it’s incredibly important. We can’t do it without donations. That’s literally how we make the machine work here,” Blanchard said.
About $17,500 in telethon donations have been spent, according to Blanchard, who said the rest of the funds will go out in even increments over the next five months. The next Operation Hunger telethon is scheduled for April. Until then, Catholic Charities says donations along with support from its thrift shops help keep food moving into local pantries and onto tables across Aroostook County.

title: Trump says he is ‘looking at’ firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday he is “looking at” firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’re not happy.”
His comments came a day after The Associated Press, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and will likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including making an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, but in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations,” they said.
“Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction. We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action,” the lawyers said.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

title: How Mainers can navigate wood’s role in sustainable home construction
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Earlier this fall, we saw that low-carbon concrete can reduce the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, sea levels, and storm intensity. Likewise, building with solid-wood products can make for “cleaner” residential construction. However, they are not invariably the most sustainable choice.
Acquiring untreated wood secondhand supports sustainability by preserving trees and landfill space. Additionally, unless stained or painted — potentially with lead paint if predating 1978 — such wood is chemical-free. Beams, flooring, boards, windows, doors, and cabinetry reclaimed from dismantled structures are available at architectural salvage stores in Midcoast Maine, and ReStores stock a similar range of surplus materials.
In contrast, using untreated virgin products may actually harm the environment. Some forest managers do not prioritize maintaining wildlife habitat, biodiversity, and long-term viability. Moreover, harvesting, cutting, and transporting lumber depletes natural resources. To reduce a home’s climate impact, therefore, look for wood stamped with independent forest-certification labels like FSC, SFI, or PEFC, which identify lumber from forests managed with demonstrably sustainable management practices. Additionally, source certified wood as close to home as possible to minimize the distance it has traveled in fossil-fuel-burning ships and trucks.
Pressure-treated lumber is infused with chemicals to improve its longevity. Used in such residential constructs as decks and retaining walls, it is subject to the same certification and sourcing factors as have been described. Additionally, if measured solely based on durability, treated wood is more sustainable than virgin lumber because it lasts longer. However, the chemicals that ward off rot from insects and mold cast doubt on its eco-friendliness.
Older treated wood can be especially problematic because until 2004, lumber for the residential market was typically treated with a known carcinogen, chromated copper arsenate. The copper compounds commonly used thereafter, including ACQ, CA, and MCA, are considered less toxic. Nevertheless, they can leach into nearby soil and groundwater, eventually to be absorbed by the roots of plants eaten by people and animals. How dangerous these chemicals are depends on whom one asks. Ultimately, since both working with treated wood if not masked and burning it are considered unsafe, then perhaps one should assume it poisons the environment too.
Since wood is a renewable resource that originates in carbon sinks, we can reduce our carbon footprint by building with it. However, some wood products are more eco-friendly than others, so let’s choose them carefully.
David Conwell belongs to the nationwide advocacy organization Citizens’ Climate Lobby and is a former member of Brunswick’s Sustainability Committee.

title: Nearly a third of Americans admit to shoplifting, survey finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As prices climb, more Americans say they are willing to risk a criminal record to cover basic necessities.
A new LendingTree survey of 2,000 Americans found 30% admit to shoplifting, up from 23% just a couple of years ago. Most respondents who shoplifted blame inflation and financial strain.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said the actual number is likely even higher than reported.
“The truth is that the numbers are actually probably higher than what we state, because there’s certainly some people who have done it who aren’t going to admit that even anonymously in a survey,” Schulz said.
Schulz said the findings are troubling for retailers and help explain why more stores are scaling back self-checkout options. He said the willingness to risk the consequences of shoplifting reflects how financially strained many households currently are.
“What our numbers showed is that most people are doing this out of necessity, and they’re not stealing things like diamond necklaces from jewelry stores,” Schulz said. “It’s more likely to be a loaf of bread and a pound of ground beef from your local grocery store.”
Schulz said the survey also revealed a generational gap, with younger Americans far more likely to report having shoplifted.
Schulz said there are better options available than stealing, including local groups, food banks and community organizations that can offer assistance to those facing financial hardship.

title: Water, stone and color: A foliage drive through Oxford Hills
text:
Fall is fleeting in Maine, but it is not too late to enjoy the foliage sights between the Crooked and Little Androscoggin rivers in Oxford Hills.
The Crooked River starts at Songo Pond in Oxford County and winds around Routes 35, 118 and 117 into Harrison before emptying into Sebago Lake in Cumberland County.
You can follow the Little Androscoggin along Route 26 from Bryant Pond into Oxford. From there it flows toward Auburn and into the Androscoggin River.

title: Bangor marks 89th anniversary of Brady Gang shootout
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Eighty-nine years ago Monday, two members of the Brady Gang were killed and another was captured in Downtown Bangor.
Bangor historian Dick Shaw has dedicated years of his life to researching the full story. He has a personal connection to it, as his mother witnessed the shootout from her classroom above Central Street.
Shaw said Al Brady and the rest of the gang were in Bangor to buy a gun at Dakin’s, not to rob a bank. He said the FBI had sharpshooters ready and had parked cars along both sides of the street the night before to absorb bullets and make the gang double-park.
“The actual shootout lasted less than a minute,” Shaw said. He said the FBI’s setup made the gang “an easier target,” adding that agents were prepared to shoot because the men were “so gun crazy.”
Shaw said the shootout was probably many Americans’ first introduction to Bangor. He spent the morning visiting Brady’s grave at Mount Hope Cemetery.

title: Sen. Bernie Sanders campaigns with US Senate Candidate Troy Jackson in 'Solidarity Forever Tour'
text:
Sen. Bernie Sanders campaigns with US Senate Candidate Troy Jackson in 'Solidarity Forever Tour'
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-VT, spent the weekend in Maine campaigning with U.S. Senate Democratic candidate Troy Jackson.
The pair was joined by Congresswoman Chellie Pingree, candidate for CD1, to close out the weekend in Biddeford.
All three spoke on a range of issues but focused largely on ICE reform.
"This activity has to stop," said Pingree. "And ICE has to get out of Maine, and we have to abolish ICE."
It comes after Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by an ICE agent earlier this year in Biddeford.
"Immigrants aren't deciding whether you can afford health care, gas or groceries, and immigrants sure as hell aren't the reason that working people have been getting screwed in this country my whole damn life," stated Jackson.
Sanders and Jackson held events in Bangor on Saturday and earlier on Sunday in Lewiston.
Sanders largely emphasized Democratic control of the Senate, stating the race between Troy Jackson and Republican Sen. Susan Collins holds incredible importance to a Democratic majority.
"If you want to hold Donald Trump and his disastrous policies accountable, the only way to do that is by electing a Democratic Senate," added Sanders.
According to Collins' campaign team, she spent the weekend cheering on UMaine's hockey team, focusing the efforts of the campaign on Mainers. Rather than, they said, on whom the Democratic Socialists of America want in Washington.

title: She was a janitor at this hospital. Now she’s returning as a physician
text:
NEW HAVEN, Conn. (InvestigateTV) — In 2011, Shay Taylor-Allen was working as a janitor at Yale New Haven Hospital when she was 18. She is now returning years later to the hospital as a resident physician.
Taylor-Allen said she took the janitor job after finishing high school because her mother told her she needed to either work or go to school.
“And that’s when I got a call back that I got a job as a janitor,” Taylor-Allen said.
Taylor-Allen said her mother, Shema, became sick, and doctors did not have answers. She said a doctor asked her a question that changed her outlook.
“The doctor pulled me to the side and was like, ‘Does your mother have a history of mental illness?’ And I’m like, ‘Why’d you ask me that?’” Taylor-Allen said.
Taylor-Allen said she began researching health care disparities. She then emailed the hospital’s CEO.
“I am the janitor that cleans your office. And this is what my mom is going through and I don’t think is right. Is there any way that you can help us?” Taylor-Allen said. “Within that day, she emailed me back. They ended up switching her team and they found out that she had vocal cord dysfunction, and I just got to see advocacy happen so fast. And I was very motivated by that.”
Taylor-Allen said that experience led her to want to work as a doctor. She knew that she wanted to help people and “be that doctor that my mom didn’t have at the time.”
“It was very personal to me,” Taylor-Allen said.
At 28, Taylor-Allen enrolled at Howard University College of Medicine in Washington, D.C. She said she had no mentorship and did not know anyone in her family who was a doctor.
During that time, she met Kenton Allen, who became her husband.
“She doesn’t take no for an answer. She wakes up every single day and she’s like, ‘I need to get this done,’ and she always accomplishes it,” Kenton Allen said.
Taylor-Allen, now 32, graduated from Howard University College of Medicine in May 2026. She is returning to Yale New Haven Hospital as a resident physician specializing in anesthesiology.
Black women make up 2.8% of physicians in the United States, according to a study published in The Lancet.
“I had people who say, you pushed me to go get my masters at 50 years old,” Taylor-Allen said. “I think the biggest lesson is that the sky’s the limit. I think a lot of people love this story because it’s the American dream that we always want, right? You work hard, you can eventually get what you want.”
Her husband, Kenton Allen, is heading to Georgetown University to earn his master’s degree in AI management.

title: The Best Cosplay at New York Comic-Con 2026
text:
The Coolest Cosplay at New York Comic-Con 2026
The cosplayers were out in full force at New York Comic-Con over the weekend. We expected nothing less, of course. Every year, attendees at the Big Apple’s biggest con astound us with their creativity, their fearlessness, and their sewing and makeup skills. 2026 was no exception. FDA: Baby supplement sold online recalled after testing discovers undeclared alcohol
text:
Parents urged to stop use of baby supplement sold online after testing found undeclared alcohol
A dietary supplement for babies, advertised to help "better sleep," has been recalled after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said testing identified three different types of alcohol that were not declared on the product's label.
Related video: How to stay ahead of recalls
Pacific Health Sciences, the FDA said, voluntarily recalled one lot of Babies' Magic Tea brand Baby Sleep Gripe Water, a dietary supplement sold in 4-ounce amber-colored bottles. The product is found inside a blue cardboard box with an oral syringe.
The recall affects Lot 25122bw, which has a best-before date of December 2028. Officials said the product was distributed to Secrets of Tea to then be sold on its website and on Amazon.
The FDA said testing found the recalled product contained "approximately 8.3% ethanol, 0.35% methanol and 0.48% isopropanol," none of which were listed on the label.
"These substances were not listed on the label," the FDA said in a recall notice posted on Oct. 7. "Their presence may pose a risk depending on the amount consumed and the age and body weight of the person using the product."
According to the recall notice, infant ethanol exposure has been linked to long-term developmental consequences. The notice says exposure to higher amounts can "increase risk of respiratory depression and other serious adverse health consequences."
Pacific Health Sciences has not received any reports of health impacts from the associated lot.
Parents and caregivers should stop use of the product from the recalled lot. The FDA said consumers should either discard it or return it for a refund.
Anyone who experiences symptoms after using the product should seek medical attention and contact Pacific Health Sciences.

title: Harmonie Universelle opens new Evening Music season at St. Saviour's
text:
BAR HARBOR — Evening Music, the series of chamber-music concerts presented by the Friends of Music at St. Saviour’s, will open its new season on Saturday, Oct. 17, with a concert at 4 p.m. in the church. The concert will feature the period-instrument ensemble Harmonie Universelle, playing music from the mid-18th century by Franz Xaver Richter, Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach, and Johann Christoph Friedrich Bach.
The music on this program dates from the decades between 1740 and 1760. During this time the philosophical movement known as the Enlightenment was taking hold in European culture. At the same time music was evolving from the mature Baroque style, exemplified in the work of Johann Sebastian Bach, into the Classical style that we associate with Haydn and Mozart. Two of the composers represented in this concert were children (and students) of Bach. Richter was an Austrian contemporary of C. P. E. Bach; and J. C. F. Bach was an exact contemporary of Haydn.

title: How these simulation racing centers help drivers train for professional races
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) — A new racing simulator center has opened in Portland, giving drivers access to technology used to train professional racers.
Driving a racing simulator is harder than it looks, but in the e-sports industry, people who master sim racing are turning the skill into a career. E-sports, or competitive video gaming, has grown in popularity over the years, with sim racing gaining an engaged fan base.
The newly opened Northwest Sim Racing is hosting some of its fastest drivers.
Callum Read is the co-owner of the center.
“So they’re actually racing against five other sim centers, so 25 other people, right now across the country,” Read said.
One reason sim racing has become more popular is that the technology has improved, allowing for more affordable options. Racing enthusiasts now have access to the same equipment professional drivers train on.
“A lot of the people that come through my place, they have rigs at home, but nothing like what I’m offering, right? They don’t have motion and don’t have triple monitors,” Read said.
Between home rigs and racing centers, accessibility is changing who can get into the industry.
“Racing is probably the most expensive sport to get into, so it’s not really available to most people,” said Ryan Henifin, a sim race. “It’s real-life racing in a video game that’s much cheaper than real-life racing.”
From hobby to real-world opportunity
Sim racing can save thousands of dollars in car repairs, track time and other costs. While it’s mostly a hobby for Henifin, others want to see where the sport takes them, like Brydon Thomas.
“Sim racing and racing in general is something I want to do. It’s been a dream since I’ve been a kid. And I mean, there’s a bunch of different opportunities within the sim world, but the sim world can also lead to opportunities in the real world,” Thomas said.
Racing sims available at NW Sim include iRacing from NASCAR and others that mimic the performance of different types of cars, down to specific details like tires and brakes, in addition to using advanced scanning systems to replicate tracks from around the world.
“Whereas in Montreal or Miami or Circuit of the Americas or Atlanta, like all these big tracks, they’re all right there. I can go to every single one of those tracks on a simulator and to the point where you memorize it so much,” said Cameron Root, a sim racer.
Racing sims give local racers like Root, the 2023 Ferrari Challenge winner, a competitive edge.
Big racing brands including NASCAR, McLaren and Red Bull have also gotten into sim racing.

title: What happens to Maine’s economy without congressional clout?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am not voting for Susan Collins or Troy Jackson because I support either candidate. I am voting against Donald Trump. But Maine should also think carefully about what happens after this election, when we no longer have a senator with Collins’ seniority and appropriations power.
Bath Iron Works is not just another employer. Its future depends on a steady Navy workload and continued investment in the yard. BIW has historically competed against Huntington Ingalls Industries in Mississippi for DDG-51 destroyers, and Maine’s congressional delegation has repeatedly fought to preserve ship allocations and funding that sustain the workforce and industrial base.
The contrast with Portsmouth Naval Shipyard is important. Portsmouth is one of the Navy’s four public shipyards and benefits directly from the Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program, or SIOP, which has funded major modernization there. BIW, as a privately owned shipyard, does not have that same direct federal recapitalization path.
That makes congressional influence especially important. A sustained loss of destroyer work could mean not only thousands of jobs, but erosion of the engineering, design, integration and skilled-trades capacity needed to build complete warships.
We have seen that kind of decline before. Once-major yards such as the Brooklyn Navy Yard and Quincy Shipyard lost workload, shed skilled workers and capabilities and ultimately ceased shipbuilding altogether. The lesson is that industrial capacity can disappear gradually before the final closure makes headlines.
Whatever our politics this November, Maine needs a serious plan for preserving BIW’s shipbuilding capability after today’s senior delegation is gone.
Kay Aikin
Portland

title: As Jay lot rent vote nears, residents face rising housing costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — With voters preparing to decide whether to limit mobile home park lot rent increases Nov. 3, an organizer working with local residents says some households have already faced increases of $50 to $200 per month, adding hundreds or thousands of dollars to annual housing costs.
Lorri Nandrea, a field organizer with the Maine Labor Climate Council, said rising rents and corporate ownership are putting pressure on residents who typically own their homes but rent the land beneath them, making relocation difficult or financially impossible.
“Rent raises put them at risk of losing their own homes, in which they have invested their savings,” Nandrea said.
The proposed ordinance would generally limit annual lot rent increases to changes in the Northeast Consumer Price Index, while allowing park owners to petition the Planning Board for larger increases under extraordinary circumstances, capped at 10%. It would also permit increases of up to 5% when a lot becomes vacant.
Nandrea began working with Jay residents last fall after three mobile home parks — Hidden Circle, Pine Haven and Lambert Street — were placed on the market. Residents successfully organized support for a temporary rent moratorium, which voters approved in April.
Hidden Circle residents subsequently formed a cooperative and purchased their park in June, while Pine Haven and Lambert Street were acquired by Guardian Communities, according to Nandrea.
She said the company owns 11 parks in the surrounding area, including properties in Farmington, Wilton, Mexico and Livermore Falls, raising concerns about reduced competition and additional rent increases.
“Manufactured home communities are one of Maine’s last and most important sources of unsubsidized affordable housing,” Nandrea said. She said lot rent is only part of residents’ housing expenses, which can also include mortgages, property taxes, insurance, utilities and maintenance. Some residents have also reported additional fees and reduced services, increasing their financial burden.
At a Sept. 14 public hearing, six people spoke in favor of the proposed ordinance, including three park residents and Nandrea. No one spoke against it, according to Nandrea.
The ordinance would take effect upon voter approval and includes provisions intended to apply rent restrictions retroactively to Dec. 8, 2025. Cooperative-owned parks where rent decisions are controlled by residents would be exempt.
Nandrea said that although Maine has adopted additional protections for manufactured housing residents, state law does not establish a general cap on lot rent increases.
Jay voters will decide the ordinance as Article 2 on the Nov. 3 ballot. Voting will take place from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Jay Community Building.

title: Finding the right running shoe is the first step to avoiding injury
text:
(Aging Untold) — Whether it’s a lunch-break jog or training for a marathon, an injury can stop a runner’s progress.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said proper footwear is the foundation for avoiding injury.
“Your shoes are supporting your feet, which is supporting your body. So, you want to make sure that you’re getting the right shoes so that you’re walking properly. You’re not creating an injury, which can happen if you’re not wearing the right shoes. You do not want to underestimate that,” O’Rourke said.
Feet change over time
O’Rourke said feet change over time, meaning a shoe size worn five years ago might not be the right size today.
“Well, if you’re wearing the wrong shoe, you can start walking differently. You could just create an injury from compensating on the wrong side. You could be off balance. You could create dizziness. You could create all kinds of neurological problems stemming from your feet,” O’Rourke said.
Shoes lose their support after 300 to 400 miles.
Experts suggest visiting a specialty store for a gait analysis to see how a foot strikes the ground.
“So if you have the wrong fitting shoe, and by wrong fitting, I mean it’s too tight or it’s too wide or your toes are pushing up against the front of the shoe, if there’s any discomfort, walk around the store for a long time to make sure that it’s really comfortable,” O’Rourke said.
Fit is individual
Your friend’s favorite shoe brand might not work for a different foot type.
“The thing that you want to look for is, do you have any pain whatsoever in any part of your body, your foot, your knee, your hip, anywhere in your body that you’re feeling pain or discomfort? Get a new pair,” O’Rourke said.

title: Tired of complaints about Susan Collins
text:
I’m tired of hearing that Sen. Susan Collins is responsible for the Supreme Court.
Look at the actual record. Yes, she voted to confirm Republican nominees. She also voted to confirm Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, every one of the court’s three liberal justices. No other Republican serving today can claim that.
Collins’ standard has never changed: a president of either party is entitled to qualified nominees, and each one gets judged on the merits, not on who sits in the White House. The only Supreme Court nominee she ever voted against was Amy Coney Barrett — because the confirmation was rushed through days before a presidential election. Collins said the same rule should apply no matter which party held the Senate, and she meant it.
People who blame Collins for the Supreme Court’s rulings are really just angry that she doesn’t vote the way they would, every single time. But that’s exactly the point of an independent. Someone who agrees with us on everything isn’t independent; they’re just on our team.
The same people demanding Sen. Collins reject every Republican nominee would be furious if a Democratic senator took marching orders from the other side. Consistency is a fair thing to ask for, yet Collins has delivered it for nearly 30 years.
People can disagree with a vote here or there. But the moment anyone looks at the “yes” votes, idea that Collins is a reliable partisan on the courts collapses.
Maine deserves a senator who thinks for herself. We have one.
Maeann Bush
Belgrade

Burglary suspect fled from police to Penobscot River island
text:
A Chester man allegedly burglarized his ex’s Passadumkeag home and then fled from police onto an island in the Penobscot River.
Nicholas Violette, 25, has been charged with burglary and violating his conditions of release, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
Violette allegedly broke into his ex’s Main Road home through a window about 10:45 p.m. Saturday.
He fled from the home before deputies arrived, but the deputies heard him in the woods and Violette was tracked to a nearby island on the Penobscot River, the sheriff’s office said Sunday.
Violette allegedly didn’t comply with commands to surrender, prompting deputies to call in reinforcements, including a drone from the Lincoln Police Department.
When the drone flew over him, Violette surrendered to police, who crossed the river and took him into custody.
Violette was taken to the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor, where he remained Monday morning, according to the jail’s website.

title: Paws and reflect: Puppy yoga brings calm and chaos
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Instructors in North Carolina are hosting “puppy yoga” classes that combine traditional yoga practice with puppies.
Jessica Seisay is one of thousands of instructors now hosting the classes, which she said are aimed at bridging two popular interests.
“Everyone loves puppies and everyone loves yoga. It’s a great way to bridge the two,” Seisay said.
Taylor Manley, who tried the class, described the experience as calming.
“Definitely - very Zen, very calm. They’re so sweet. He just came and wanted to sit in my lap the whole time, so I was trying to relax with him, and he was going to make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
Health benefits
Research shows contact with animals lowers cortisol and boosts “feel-good” chemicals like serotonin.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the practice affects the body’s stress response.
“When you’re touching a puppy, looking at a puppy, playing with a puppy, your cortisol lowers, your stress lowers, you get calmer, you get happier… So, your whole emotional system gets uplifted just playing with that puppy,” O’Rourke said.
Socialization benefits
O’Rourke said there is a socialization benefit of the classes as well.
“So, I do yoga. I’ve done yoga with goats. Yoga with puppies, I can’t even imagine the socialization. I’m sitting on my mat. I picture talking to a person on one side and the other side, laughing our heads off. So, you get all that social benefit. You’re creating friends through the puppies and the yoga and the camaraderie of doing yoga together,” O’Rourke said.
Puppy breeder Taylor Terry said the reaction to puppies is consistent.
“Every time you see puppies, you just get happy,” Terry said.

title: Super PAC buys Troy Jackson attack ad in Portland, Oregon
text:
A Republican-supporting Super PAC purchased about $25,000 in attack ads against Maine’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson in the Portland, Oregon, region.
The ads, paid for by the Defending Maine Street Super PAC, ran in more than 260 zip codes in Oregon between Oct. 8 and 11, according to the Google Ads Transparency Center. It was updated on Monday to cover Maine.
“The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend,” a spokesperson for Defending Main Street said in an email Monday. “No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error.”
They were shown more than 1.2 million times, according to the center. Approximately $25,000 was spent on the ads.
The PAC’s spokesperson also included a statement from its vendor, the 1903 Group, which said: “This was 100% a Cross Screen Media error.” Cross Screen Media is a political and public affairs advertising company that is owned by the 1903 Group, a holding company.
“Susan Collins’ allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map,” Dan Gottlieb, a spokesperson for Jackson’s campaign, said in a written statement. “Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in.”
A spokesperson for Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.

title: Letter: Don’t let Susan Collins vote for any more Supreme Court justices

title: Memories of Bowdoin’s Searles Hall remind me that physics is about the future
text:
Mark Hineline is a visiting scholar in the Department of Communication at the University of California San Diego. He formerly taught at Bowdoin College.
Just around this time, give or take a month, the then chair of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Bowdoin College gave me a tour of the physics building, Searles Hall, as it was in 1992 when I started teaching “Physics of the Twentieth Century.”
This wouldn’t be much of a story if I were a physicist. I wasn’t then, and I’m still not. I’m a historian of science, and the science I was studying for a doctorate in was geology, not physics. The reasoning behind hiring me is ancient history, not all that interesting. Suffice to say that I was a good fit for what the department needed that year and the next. Historians of science in that era needed to know their physics cold, and I fit the bill.
In the two years I was there, I was made to feel — by all of the faculty — as though I were one of them. That I, in fact, was not, only showed up as a matter of concern exactly once, and then it vanished with the speed of light. It was when I asked to have the key to the machine shop. The chair informed me that outsiders often asked for the key — and then he stopped himself in his tracks. I was back to being an insider again.
But without a key.
Back to that tour. During the war, Bowdoin College had an agreement with the U.S. Navy to provide a sort of attic space in the Victorian building as the site where navigators learned their craft. In this upstairs room were tables covered with nautical charts, dividers and parallel rules. When the war was over, the door to the room was closed to trainees for a last time, all the apparatus in place, only to be seen by insiders like myself.
I was duly impressed by this and other relics of bygone days, like the “geyser” apparatus in the cellar for a demonstration of geophysical thermodynamics. Or, a way to give undergraduates in the lecture theater a good soaking.
I was more impressed by the collection of lantern slides, in the anteroom of the lecture theater. Still waiting for someone to lecture with them, these were the precursors of carousel slides, themselves replaced by PowerPoints. I was especially interested in them because I was studying a Harvard geologist who held other scientists to strict standards in providing the best lantern slides they could muster for lectures and for scientific meetings. I hadn’t actually held one in my hand until I got to teach at Bowdoin.
Searles Hall, its treasures and the students who learned there were the scene of recurring dreams until I returned there a decade ago and found that the site of my dreams was all but gone. Searles Hall was gutted and updated. I didn’t ask what became of the geyser, the slides or the nautical charts. After teaching for other institutions for many years, sometimes even in departments of history, where I more or less belonged, this was none of my business.
Was I nostalgic about what was gone? I was. Was I concerned, or disappointed, to find it all missing and replaced? Not at all.
Physics is a progressive science. While it builds on its history, as a science it is about the future — the next advancement, the next so-called paradigm. And I don’t feel that way only about physics. It’s good that academic institutions should have deep memory-pockets.
But memory is there to inform the future. Historians have a derisive term for overglorifying the past while looking at their discipline in a rearview mirror. They call it “antiquarianism.’
There’s nothing wrong with antiquarianism. It’s just not good science or scholarship.
Physics is about the future in the same way that everything at the college, at all academic institutions, is about the future. That includes the Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museum at Bowdoin. Bowdoin is there to train future leaders, even the mayor of New York City.
And so I see those maps and lantern slides right where they belong — in my memory, where I treasure the occasion of looking at them. And share what I saw with others who didn’t get the chance.

title: Pope will be admitted to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery, Vatican says
text:
Pope will be admitted to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery, Vatican says
The Vatican said Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to the hospital on Tuesday in the late morning, ahead of surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests.
Related video: Conjoined twins successfully separated after high-risk surgery
The Vatican press office didn't say when the operation itself would take place, but it was expected in the first days of the week, with a weeklong recovery.
Leo revealed the discovery of the nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors’ advice to have it removed. The Vatican press office said Monday that no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted Leo to undergo the checkup.
On Monday, it was business as usual at the Vatican. The 71-year-old Leo presided over an audience with members of a Rome-based charity, the Circolo San Pietro, and received a donation from them. He spoke in a strong, clear voice, praising their service and sacrifice. The crowd gave him a rousing round of applause afterward.
He had six other private audiences, made three appointments and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals, thanking him for his service. The letter was signed on Sunday.
In the afternoon, he was expected to continue his audiences and, if time, rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.
A first medical event for the papacy
Leo's surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing, with thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope's health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
Leo's decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended to ascertain whether it is cancerous since performing a lung biopsy by needle can be difficult.
Oncologists say if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
Unlike his predecessor Pope Francis, whose decade-long respiratory problems made him speak in a whisper, Leo tends to project his voice and frequently sings his prayers.
___
Barry reported from Milan

title: Collins owes Mainers an explanation for vote on West Bank deaths
text:
Brian Garrison is a South Portland resident and advocate for human dignity and equal rights.
Sen. Susan Collins owes Mainers an explanation for voting to block a formal demand for answers about Americans killed in the West Bank.
On Sept. 29, the Senate rejected a motion to discharge S. Res. 852 from the Foreign Relations Committee, 51-47. Sen. Angus King voted to advance it. Collins voted against it. This was a procedural vote, rather than final adoption, but its consequence was clear: the resolution did not move forward.
The distinction matters. So does what senators prevented from advancing.
The resolution would have requested an unclassified State Department statement within 30 days of adoption. It sought evidence and investigation updates concerning nine American deaths involving Israeli forces or settlers, information about Americans in Israeli prisons and an assessment of Palestinian children in military detention, including allegations of torture. It also asked what Washington had done to protect human rights and pursue accountability.
These are questions a responsible Congress should insist on answering.
Forty-four Democrats, independents King and Bernie Sanders and Republican Rand Paul supported advancing the resolution. Fifty Republicans and Democrat John Fetterman opposed it. Republicans Bill Cassidy and Dan Sullivan did not vote. Paul’s vote demonstrated that demanding answers need not be a partisan position.
Protecting Americans abroad should be among the least controversial obligations of their government. Families deserve evidence, meaningful investigations and an explanation of what officials are doing on their behalf. Their right to those answers should never depend on whether the suspected perpetrators belong to an ally.
The resolution also reached beyond citizenship. Palestinian children deserve protection from abuse because they are children. A passport cannot determine whose mistreatment warrants scrutiny. The same commitment to human dignity that requires investigating American deaths requires taking allegations of torture seriously wherever they arise.
There is a legal reason for this scrutiny, too.
The measure invoked Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act. That provision allows Congress to request information about a country’s human rights practices. Failure to provide the requested statement within 30 days triggers restrictions on delivering security assistance, subject to subsequent specific authorization by law, until the statement arrives.
This was therefore an oversight mechanism with consequences. Senators were being asked to advance a process that could make the administration answer publicly for its decisions.
Supporters of Israel may regard such scrutiny as unfair or diplomatically damaging. But an alliance cannot justify exempting a government from examination. If allegations are unsupported, a credible accounting can establish that. If investigations are adequate, the evidence can demonstrate it. If abuses occurred, friendship cannot excuse them.
An inquiry should test allegations. Blocking it leaves the public without the accounting the resolution sought.
There is also money to account for. Track AIPAC, an advocacy group compiling Federal Election Commission data, lists $4,131,569 in career support for Collins from pro-Israel political committees and associated donors, including $565,000 in independent expenditures. That outside spending benefits her candidacy without going to her campaign. These figures do not establish that contributions caused her vote. They do make her explanation, and the independence of her judgment, matters of public interest.
In a July op-ed for this newspaper about deeper U.S.-Israeli military integration, I called on Collins and King to insist on open debate. The principle remains: consequential decisions require public scrutiny.
King deserves credit for supporting this step. He should continue pressing for disclosure. Collins should explain her opposition and identify the alternative she will pursue, with a timetable for obtaining the information these families deserve.
A procedural objection, if that was her concern, would still leave that responsibility intact. Mainers should ask what she will do now.
Our senators represent people who deserve honest government. They should insist that the administration account for American deaths and alleged abuse, regardless of which foreign government is implicated.
When American families are asking how their loved ones died, a senator’s first duty is to demand answers.

title: Mt. Ararat field hockey beats Skowhegan in Class A North battle of unbeatens
text:
SKOWHEGAN — In a battle of unbeatens, Mt. Ararat made a statement.
Boosted by a quick-strike offensive attack, the Mt. Ararat field hockey team beat Skowhegan 4-1 on Monday in a matchup of two of Class A North’s top teams.
Four players scored for the Eagles (11-0), including freshman Leah Lafrance.
“It’s just a really good game to win and a really good game to play,” said Mt. Ararat senior captain Maddy Sweet, who scored a goal.
It was the first win over Skowhegan for the Eagles since at least 2014, when coach Krista Chase took over the program.
Senior Faith Pease scored for the River Hawks (11-1).
Eagles strike quickly
Mt. Ararat set the tone early, moving the ball with ease up the well-manicured Skowhegan grass field. The Eagles, ranked fourth in the Varsity Maine poll, surprised the second-ranked River Hawks with a goal just over two minutes into the game, when Lafrance was able to swipe a shot past Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams for a 1-0 lead.
“(Lafrance) is a hockey player,” Chase said. “She plays ice hockey on the grass.”
Added Sweet: “(Lafrance) is holding down the fort, we’re really glad to have her. She’s our speed. … We’re so proud of her out there.”
The Eagles extended the lead to 2-0 with 22 seconds remaining in the first half, when Sweet was able to poke a shot in for the score in a scrum in front of the cage.
“They were really hungry and they showed up to play,” Chase said. “I’m really proud of them. It’s been kind of a bumpy year with scheduling, we’re in our games-every-other-day kind of (part) of the season. But we’ve been mentally preparing for this week, a lot of games in eight days.”
The Eagles played Wednesday and Saturday last week, and have games on Wednesday and Friday remaining this week.
Mt. Ararat added two fourth-quarter goals to seal the win. Junior Cali LeClair scored with 14:34 left, then junior Kamryn Chase took a well-placed pass from Avery Elliott and knocked it into the cage with under eight minutes left.
Skowhegan scored with 3:11 left, when Pease was able to knock a shot off a scrum in front of the Mt. Ararat cage.
What does it mean?
Skowhegan entered the game as the No. 1 seed in Class A North, followed by No. 2 Camden Hills (10-1) and Mt. Ararat. With the win, the Eagles swapped places with Camden Hills. The River Hawks, for now, remain the No. 1 seed, because they’ve played one more game than both the Eagles and the Windjammers.
Both the Eagles and the River Hawks face Camden Hills this week, Skowhegan on Wednesday and Mt. Ararat on Friday.
Lesson learned for Skowhegan
While the Eagles dominated possession in the first half, the River Hawks never quit, and turned pressure around on Mt. Ararat in the second half. The River Hawks outshot the Eagles by a 10-6 margin over the final two quarters, and had a 5-0 advantage in penalty corners.
“You’ve got to give respect to your opponent. (Mt. Ararat) played a beautiful game,” Skowhegan coach Gina Davis said. “We’ll be thanking them for that lesson deeper in the season. The goal isn’t to have an undefeated season. You learn your lesson, take your medicine. We’ll bounce back when we play Camden Hills, and how we respond to that will help determine the good versus the great programs.”
Unsung hero
Mt. Ararat junior Jaymie Bergman was outstanding on Monday, making 15 saves, including three saves during a 10-second stretch with 10:15 left in the third quarter.
Milestone win
Krista Chase, who has run the Mt. Ararat program since 2014, earned her 200th career win on Monday. She coached the Cony field hockey program from 2002-09, where she compiled an 88-37-2 record.
“It just means I’ve been around a really long time,” Chase laughed. “I attribute that 200 wins to all of my former teams at Cony and Mt. Ararat. I like that I’ve been around for a long time. I love this game and I love Maine field hockey. I love trying to grow programs, that’s my thing. It’s just a statement of longevity and hard work.”
Chase was gifted a Sea Bag with her name and the number 200 on each side.
Statitical leaders
• Mt. Ararat: Leah Lafrance (1 goal, 1 assist); Maddy Sweet (1 goal); Cali LeClair (1 goal); Kamryn Chase (1 goal); Jaymie Bergman (15 saves)
• Skowhegan: Faith Pease (1 goal); Michelle Williams (8 saves)

title: A simple impeachment
text:
To the Editor:
The framers of the U.S. Constitution saw emoluments as such a major danger that they made their prohibition the very first article of that document.
The simplest way to impeach President Trump clearly is to use the Foreign Emoluments Clause of that Article. The DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel and two courts have already considered its use favorably.
Known gifts to the president and his family amount to many billions of dollars. But impeachment can be based on one or a limited number of small transferred amounts or gifts that directly caused a favorable action by Trump on behalf of the gift giver.
The most publicized is the $400 million luxury aircraft given to Trump for his post-retirement use, for which the Qataris have received very substantial aid packages. But it may be easier to prove that the UAE’s $263 million purchase of half the Trump family’s interest in the cryptocurrency enterprise World Liberty Financial is a forbidden emolument. Also, Trump businesses received $38 million in licensing fees from Gulf Nations getting U.S. aid from President Trump. Then there were Ivanka Trump’s trademark approvals by China, and many more.
To justify impeachment the prosecution must show: the existence of a money or gift transfer; specific foreign policy decisions tied to that transfer; reasonably close timing between those occurrences; and evidence that a senior representative of a foreign government was involved. Specific Trump actions have to be shown to be attributable to the transfers.
This is based on evaluations of evidence by members of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate. The House indicts and the Senate convicts if, in the opinion of both Houses, impeachment is justified.
The evidence regarding Trump’s many transgressions is extremely voluminous. Congressional judgment is paramount.
Ray Tillman
Westbrook
