title: New Gloucester variety store closed by fire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Link’s Variety in New Gloucester has been shut down indefinitely after a fire early Sunday morning, but its owners are vowing to rebuild.
New Gloucester Fire Rescue was dispatched to a structure fire at the store at 2:08 a.m. The fire was fully extinguished five hours later and no one was injured.
Investigators with the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal believe the fire originated “in or around the furnace area, where multiple boxes were located,” Maine Department of Public Safety spokesperson Shannon Moss said in a news release Monday night. However, the cause has yet to be determined, and the investigation is ongoing.
Link’s Variety posted that the building had suffered “significant damage,” and would be shut down until it could be rebuilt. The post discouraged residents from going near the building.
“We will rebuild. We will be back,” wrote the owners of Link’s, thanking everyone in the community who reached out to them in the aftermath of the fire.
Both New Gloucester Fire Rescue and Link’s Variety praised a passerby, who identified herself in the comments as Sarenna Collins, who was the first to report the fire to emergency services. Without Collins, who remained on scene as the fire was being extinguished, the building would have been completely engulfed, Link’s said.
New Gloucester received mutual aid from Gray, Auburn, Raymond, Durham, Yarmouth and North Yarmouth, with Windham providing station coverage.
The owners of Link’s could not be immediately reached for comment.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Judge orders Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded TV ads
text:
Judge orders Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting political message
President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
Related video above: Public service announcements or propaganda? Experts weigh in on new Trump ads
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws.
“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, the nonprofit legal organization that represents them. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”
In a court declaration Saturday, senior DHS official Holly Mehringer wrote that the money came from funds appropriated by Congress that are “available for, among other things, ‘commemorating efforts and events related to border security.’”
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration’s capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
The use of public funds to pay for the ads drew heavy criticism — including from some in the GOP.
"It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters.
The Democratic National Committee has separately sued the Republican administration over the ads.
Amid the backlash, Trump said he would start paying for the ads with a campaign account. A White House official said there were no immediate plans to reimburse the government for money already spent.
___
Associated Press reporters Collin Binkley and Ali Swenson contributed

title: Meet the Candidates offers two opportunities to connect with Ellsworth candidates
text:
ELLSWORTH — Ellsworth residents will have two opportunities to meet candidates for local office this month as Meet the Candidates returns with a City Council forum Oct. 13 and a new gathering for school board and library trustee candidates Oct. 21.
Presented by Heart of Ellsworth in partnership with The Ellsworth American, Ellsworth Public Library and the City of Ellsworth, the annual nonpartisan event helps residents learn about the people seeking to represent them ahead of the November election. Events like these connect community members with opportunities to participate in local democracy.
The City Council forum will take place at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 13 at The Grand, where four candidates running for two seats will be featured. Robert Grant Sr., Casey Hanson, Tiffany Gaspar and Nancy Smith will take the stage alongside Cyndi Wood, managing editor of The Ellsworth American, who will moderate. The forum is free and open to the public, with a livestream and recording available on the City of Ellsworth’s YouTube channel. Residents may submit questions for possible inclusion by emailing news@ellsworthamerican.com or completing an index card at the event.
New this year, candidates for the Ellsworth School Board and Ellsworth Public Library Board of Trustees will gather at 5 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 21 at the Ellsworth Public Library. The informal, conversational setting will give residents an opportunity to introduce themselves, share their questions and learn more about the people interested in serving their schools and library.
By including school board and library trustee candidates, Meet the Candidates builds on its commitment to nonpartisan voter education, offering a welcoming space to share priorities and make informed decisions.
For more information about both events, visit heartofellsworth.org/meet-the-candidates.

title: Grandmother burned in fire pit explosion dies a day before her 59th birthday
text:
PRESCOTT VALLEY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona grandmother died days after suffering catastrophic burns when her boyfriend allegedly poured gasoline on a fire, causing an explosion.
Tammy Dodson and her boyfriend were sitting around a fire pit Sept. 24 with Dodson’s sister, Tara Carl, in their backyard in Prescott Valley. Carl says the fire pit was a smaller, elevated metal pit.
As the fire began to dwindle, Carl says her sister’s boyfriend grabbed a gas can and poured it on the fire to try to reignite it. She says this caused an explosion that shot the gas can onto a neighbor’s roof and engulfed Dodson in flames.
Dodson spent 10 days intubated at a Phoenix burn center with burns covering her body before she died last Sunday, the day before her 59th birthday.
“I’m very angry. She should not have been taken from us the way she was,” Carl said.
Victim was a mother, grandmother and healthcare worker
Dodson was a mother, grandmother and a beloved healthcare worker, her family says. She leaves behind two children and three young grandchildren, who she adored.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help her family with memorial costs and medical bills associated with the incident.
“Tammy truly was the light of our family. She was vibrant, beautiful, loving, and had a way of bringing so much life wherever she went. She was a mom, a grandma, a sister, and an aunt, and a friend to so many,” the family wrote on GoFundMe.
Dodson’s family says they are traumatized by what happened.
“I don’t want anybody ever to throw gasoline or igniting sources onto fires,” Carl said. “That’s just beyond my comprehension. It’s just beyond it.”
Investigation continues
Prescott Valley Police confirmed the incident allegedly happened while someone tried to reignite a fire pit. They said a man on the property was injured as well but was not taken to the hospital.
The investigation is ongoing.
Dodson’s death was ruled accidental due to “complications of thermal injuries,” according to the Maricopa County Medical Examiner’s Office. However, the report is not yet complete.

title: Agents search Rep. Omar’s Washington home in criminal probe as she vows she won’t ‘be silenced’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid.
The search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican’s “political enemies.”
The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. “Something’s going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search.
In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
At a political rally in Ohio later Monday, Trump attacked Omar’s Somali origins, saying, “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” The crowd responded by shouting, “Deport.”
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump’s perceived adversaries.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
Trump says he had “nothing to do” with search
The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security.
A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The street around Omar’s home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”
The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ.”
Trump suggested he didn’t know what was happening with the investigation even as he seemed to suggest that Omar was engaged in suspect behavior.
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.
Omar has long been a target for Republicans
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.
In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.
According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.”
Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”
“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody’s entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we’re going to investigate it. We’re going to take a look at it. If we think there’s a crime, we’re going to prosecute that crime. And that’s something the Department of Justice is looking at right now.”
In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance’s comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something’s going to happen.”
He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family’s immigration paperwork.
“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It’s actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there’s no expiration to that.”

title: ‘Thousands’ of dead fish discovered along Androscoggin River
text:
Local environmental advocates say scores of river herring were killed in the turbines of the Brunswick-Topsham dam while attempting to move down the Androscoggin River recently.
Free the Andro, a local group that has been advocating for better fish passage at the dam during its federal relicensing period, has reported thousands of dead herring “lining the shores” along the river. Many of these dead fish are visible along Water Street in Brunswick.
The group said the young fish were killed while attempting to move downriver through dam turbines.
“This fish kill is, unfortunately, not a surprise,” said Free the Andro founder Chip Spies. “These occurrences are the reason we founded Free the Andro and are working to create safe and effective upstream and downstream fish passage requirements for the Brunswick dam by (the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission). This is one more, very obvious example of what is wrong with the existing facility and how it impacts migratory species that rely on the Androscoggin to complete their life cycles.”
A spokesperson for the dam owner, Brookfield Renewable, said Monday evening that the company is aware of the weekend’s fish mortality event. The hydroelectric dam has been offline since Saturday to prevent further deaths, said spokesperson David Heidrich.
“(Brookfield White Pine Hydro) had been notified of an anticipated outmigration associated with water level changes upstream and, as is the protocol for such circumstances, implemented overnight operational shutdowns at the Brunswick Project to facilitate the safe passage of out-migrating fish,” Heidrich said in an email. “After project personnel observed fish mortality downstream of the dam on Saturday morning, we expanded those measures and shut down generation completely while we assessed conditions and coordinated with resource agencies.”
Another local environmental nonprofit, Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, issued a complaint to FERC, which is currently considering relicensing the dam, on Monday. In its complaint, FOMB wrote that the only way for migratory fish to pass downstream is through a pipe immediately next to turbines.
The fish observed in Brunswick were killed by decapitation, direct concussive strikes and the sudden difference in pressure, FOMB said.
Heidrich said fish protection is an “important operational priority” for Brookfield.
“We are continuing to review the circumstances and will work closely with state and federal resource agencies to better understand what occurred,” he said.
Spies, of Free the Andro, began hearing about the fish kill Sunday morning, he said.
The dam owner’s license expires in 2029. In the coming years, FERC will determine whether to renew the license for another 50 years and what conditions should be imposed. This could include a new fish passage system or even dam removal.
Most fish are not making it through the current fish ladder at the Brunswick dam, en route to their historic breeding grounds, according to counts conducted by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
“This recurring kill emphasizes that all potentially safe passage possibilities must be thoroughly vetted, including and especially dam removal; since any time safe passage is dependent on human intervention, a certain amount of failure is inevitable,” Friends of Merrymeeting Bay wrote in its complaint to FERC.

title: Aging Untold: Teens are the hidden generation juggling school and elder care
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore the hidden weight carried by millions of teens and young adults stepping into caregiving roles for aging family members.
We break down the causes, warning signs and prevention strategies for painful kidney stones.
Finally, volunteers with a global nonprofit help seniors with limited mobility rediscover the outdoors through shared scenic bike rides.
Millions of teens and young adults in the United States are caregivers, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. .
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said many young caregivers are going to school while taking care of a parent and the impact on the teen’s health is often hidden.
“They’re anxious or depressed. They’re tired, but they’re not attributing it to the fact that they’re taking care of mom,” she said.
There are organizations that teens can turn to for help.
Resources
Local resources
- Adult protective services
- Adult services
- Area agency on aging
- Disabled adult services
- Mental health associations
- School guidance counselors
Grant money might be available to help with:
- Transportation assistance
- Transportation reimbursement.
- Utility bills
A kidney stone is very painful and there are some things that you can do to help lower your risk.
Hydration, diet and certain medical conditions can all affect your risk for developing painful kidney stones, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Susan Lehman was diagnosed a decade ago with multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer that develops in plasma cells in the bone marrow.
The 60-year-old mother of four has been in and out of remission over the years. She has undergone two stem cell transplants and several other treatments. Then an oncologist with Banner Health had Lehman try something new: CARVYKTI.
Two months into the treatment, Lehman said the immunotherapy has made a big difference.
Volunteers with a nonprofit are giving older adults the feeling of wind in their hair, no matter their mobility.
The nonprofit, Cycling Without Age, has 3,500 chapters across the world.
The rides are on trishaws, bicycles equipped with a passenger seat, as volunteers pedal.

title: UMaine administrators address budget concerns at UMSG meeting
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine General Student Government (UMSG) met on Sept. 29 in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union, where university administrators addressed concerns about UMaine’s budget deficit, potential program changes and the future of student services.
President Joan Ferrini-Mundy, Vice President for Finance and Administration and Chief Business Officer Jenny Boyden and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs and Provost Gabriel Paquette spoke with senators about the university’s financial situation and answered questions about how administrators plan to address the deficit.
Boyden began the discussion with a presentation on the university’s budget, explaining its different sources of funding and the distinction between restricted and unrestricted funds. Approximately 67% of the university’s budget goes toward compensation and benefits, while other recurring expenses include facilities, fuel, utilities and technology.
Boyden said expenses are increasing faster than university revenue, making changes necessary to prevent the budget gap from continuing to grow.
Ferrini-Mundy said financial challenges are not unique to UMaine, noting that colleges and universities nationwide are facing rising costs and limited or declining revenue. She said the university is considering both short and long-term strategies, including increasing enrollment among out-of-state, returning and graduate students.
“The University of Maine has been here for a long time and will continue to be,” Ferrini-Mundy said.
Paquette addressed concerns about academic programs and potential program closures. He said the university has a responsibility to students who enroll in a program to continue offering that course of study until they graduate.
He added that programs regularly change based on student demand. The University of Maine System (UMS) Board of Trustees, for example, recently voted to eliminate a Romance Languages degree that currently has no enrolled students. Paquette described the creation and elimination of programs as part of the university’s normal academic planning process.
Senators questioned the administrators about enrollment, tuition, student services and how decisions about cuts would be made.
Paquette said the university hopes to increase enrollment by approximately 1% across several categories, including first-year, transfer, returning and graduate students. Administrators also hope to reach former students who earned college credits but never completed their degrees.
Sen. Braun asked whether student support services, including advising, counseling, disability services and financial aid, would be protected from staffing cuts.
Ferrini-Mundy described those services as vital but said the university could not guarantee that any particular area would be protected. Paquette said the university is currently making investments in those areas rather than cutting them.
Sen. Drost also asked whether students should expect another tuition increase following a 4% increase already approved by the UMS.
Ferrini-Mundy said specific guidance was not yet available but that tuition increases are “inevitable.” She said keeping UMaine comparatively affordable remains a priority. Boyden said additional budget assumptions would likely become available within the next month.
Administrators also addressed how potential staffing and academic cuts would be determined. Ferrini-Mundy said decisions would be based on factors including demand and use, while Paquette said academic program reviews examine where resources could better meet student demand.
When asked about potential layoffs, Ferrini-Mundy said the process would be guided in part by collective bargaining agreements and described layoffs as only one part of the university’s efforts to address its financial situation.
Club business
Outside of the budget discussion, the Senate granted preliminary recognition to the UMaine Chess Club and Student Maine Education Association.
The Chess Club currently has 20 members and meets on Saturdays in the Memorial Union. The Student Maine Education Association aims to build a community for students interested in education and connect students with the Maine Education Association.
Funding requests
The Senate also approved two major funding requests.
The Non-Traditional, Commuter and Transfer Students Committee received $4,264 for First Friday Bagels and Tasty Treat Tuesday. Sen. Olivia Barthelemy said the events are intended to bring students into the Wade Center, where they can learn about other resources and opportunities available to them.
The Society of Women Engineers received $10,973 to help send 37 students to a conference in Boston. Club representatives said the conference is expected to include more than 14,000 professionals and students and over 300 employers, providing networking, internship and employment opportunities.
The estimated total cost of the trip is $20,329, with additional funding coming from engineering departments and the Maine College of Engineering and Computing.
New business
During new business, senators also discussed the possibility of creating a representative board focused on student mental health and wellness. Sen. St. Lawrence proposed the idea as a way to provide students with more direct input on health-related issues.
Senators discussed how such a board could interact with the existing Holistic Health and Wellness Committee and other university resources. No final action was taken on the proposal.
The Senate approved a separate policy establishing a structured process for student organizations to request storage space.

title: Native athlete pride: Shiyazh Pete recognized on Indigenous Peoples Day
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — Shiyazh Pete’s time with the Dallas Cowboys was brief, but his NFL debut gave fellow Navajo citizens a moment to remember. When the rookie offensive lineman took the field for a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals in August, thousands of fans who had traveled from across the Navajo Nation erupted in cheers, waving tribal flags and exclaiming “yéego,” an affirmation that translates roughly to “with great effort, do it.”
Pete played just six snaps, but returned to the sideline to a standing ovation — a powerful show of support for the first member of the Navajo Nation to sign with an NFL team.
Now a free agent after being waived by the Cowboys, Pete has returned home to the Navajo Nation, where he has been thanking fans for their support as he looks for his next NFL opportunity. He surprised students at his alma mater, Shiprock High School, with an appearance at their homecoming pep rally and served as grand marshal of the Northern Navajo Nation Fair Parade.
On Monday, Pete will meet and greet fans at an Indigenous Peoples Day event in Albuquerque, New Mexico.
Pete joins a long list of Native athletes who have broken barriers in sports, inspired pride in their communities and become role models for Native children. From Olympic champions to professional basketball players, these athletes have helped shape sports history while opening doors for those who follow.
Native athletes stood on Olympic podium
Still widely considered the greatest athlete of all time, Jim Thorpe, of the Sac and Fox Nation in Oklahoma, won the decathlon and pentathlon in the 1912 Olympics. He also played six seasons in Major League Baseball and 12 in professional football, including in the American Professional Football Association, the precursor to the National Football League.
A track and field teammate of Thorpe’s at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, Louis Tewanima carried on the Hopi spiritual practice of running to gain recognition at the repressive institution. He finished ninth in the marathon at the 1908 Olympics in London and second in the 10,000 meters at the 1912 Olympics in Stockholm, setting an American record in the event.
Modern surfing traces its history to Native Hawaiian Duke Kahanamoku. His international demonstrations between winning gold and silver swimming medals at the 1912, 1920 and 1924 Olympics made surfing widely known. Kahanamoku helped establish surfboards as standard ocean lifeguarding equipment. He acted in movies and served from 1935 to 1961 as sheriff of Honolulu.
Native runners set the pace through the 20th century
Marathoner Ellison Myers “Tarzan” Brown, of the Narragansett Tribe in Rhode Island, won the Boston Marathon in 1936 and 1939 and competed for the U.S. in the 1936 Olympics in Berlin. Brown was to run the marathon in the 1940 Olympics, but the games were canceled due to World War II.
Oglala Lakota runner Billy Mills was the first non-European to win Olympic gold in the 10-kilometer run with his upset, Olympic-record race at the 1964 Olympics in Tokyo. The run was the best U.S. medal finish in that Olympic event since Tewanima’s silver more than half a century earlier — and Mills’ 10K gold has yet to be equaled by a U.S. Olympian.
The first American woman to finish a marathon under 2 hours, 30 minutes, Patti Catalano Dillon, is of Mi’kmaw descent and grew up in Massachusetts. Dillon was runner-up in the 1980 New York Marathon and in the 1979, 1980 and 1981 Boston marathons. Dillon held world records in the half marathon and 30-kilometer and 20-kilometer runs.
Indigenous players gained recognition in pro sports, too
Ryneldi Becenti was the first Native American WNBA athlete, playing for the Phoenix Mercury in the 1997 season. Becenti grew up playing fast-paced “rez ball” on the Navajo Nation and was a top player for Scottsdale Community College and Arizona State University before going pro as a player in Europe.
Los Angeles Sparks player Aaliyah Nye is a citizen of the Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi in Michigan. A top scorer in high school, then for Alabama, Nye joined the WNBA in 2025 as a Las Vegas Aces draft pick. In 2026, she was drafted and waived by the Toronto Tempo and Atlanta Dream before being claimed by the Sparks.
Golfer Notah Begay III notched four PGA Tour wins in 1999 and 2000. A Native American with Navajo, San Felipe and Isleta heritage, Begay established a foundation to promote Native American health and wellness through soccer and golf programs. He is a TV golf analyst. ___ Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.
___
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Memories of Bowdoin’s Searles Hall remind me that physics is about the future
text:
Mark Hineline is a visiting scholar in the Department of Communication at the University of California San Diego. He formerly taught at Bowdoin College.
Just around this time, give or take a month, the then chair of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Bowdoin College gave me a tour of the physics building, Searles Hall, as it was in 1992 when I started teaching “Physics of the Twentieth Century.”
This wouldn’t be much of a story if I were a physicist. I wasn’t then, and I’m still not. I’m a historian of science, and the science I was studying for a doctorate in was geology, not physics. The reasoning behind hiring me is ancient history, not all that interesting. Suffice to say that I was a good fit for what the department needed that year and the next. Historians of science in that era needed to know their physics cold, and I fit the bill.
In the two years I was there, I was made to feel — by all of the faculty — as though I were one of them. That I, in fact, was not, only showed up as a matter of concern exactly once, and then it vanished with the speed of light. It was when I asked to have the key to the machine shop. The chair informed me that outsiders often asked for the key — and then he stopped himself in his tracks. I was back to being an insider again.
But without a key.
Back to that tour. During the war, Bowdoin College had an agreement with the U.S. Navy to provide a sort of attic space in the Victorian building as the site where navigators learned their craft. In this upstairs room were tables covered with nautical charts, dividers and parallel rules. When the war was over, the door to the room was closed to trainees for a last time, all the apparatus in place, only to be seen by insiders like myself.
I was duly impressed by this and other relics of bygone days, like the “geyser” apparatus in the cellar for a demonstration of geophysical thermodynamics. Or, a way to give undergraduates in the lecture theater a good soaking.
I was more impressed by the collection of lantern slides, in the anteroom of the lecture theater. Still waiting for someone to lecture with them, these were the precursors of carousel slides, themselves replaced by PowerPoints. I was especially interested in them because I was studying a Harvard geologist who held other scientists to strict standards in providing the best lantern slides they could muster for lectures and for scientific meetings. I hadn’t actually held one in my hand until I got to teach at Bowdoin.
Searles Hall, its treasures and the students who learned there were the scene of recurring dreams until I returned there a decade ago and found that the site of my dreams was all but gone. Searles Hall was gutted and updated. I didn’t ask what became of the geyser, the slides or the nautical charts. After teaching for other institutions for many years, sometimes even in departments of history, where I more or less belonged, this was none of my business.
Was I nostalgic about what was gone? I was. Was I concerned, or disappointed, to find it all missing and replaced? Not at all.
Physics is a progressive science. While it builds on its history, as a science it is about the future — the next advancement, the next so-called paradigm. And I don’t feel that way only about physics. It’s good that academic institutions should have deep memory-pockets.
But memory is there to inform the future. Historians have a derisive term for overglorifying the past while looking at their discipline in a rearview mirror. They call it “antiquarianism.’
There’s nothing wrong with antiquarianism. It’s just not good science or scholarship.
Physics is about the future in the same way that everything at the college, at all academic institutions, is about the future. That includes the Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museum at Bowdoin. Bowdoin is there to train future leaders, even the mayor of New York City.
And so I see those maps and lantern slides right where they belong — in my memory, where I treasure the occasion of looking at them. And share what I saw with others who didn’t get the chance.

title: Penobscot County Deputies Locate Passadumkeag Burglary Suspect On Island In the River
text:
Maine Burglary Suspect is Apprehended After Fleeing in a Kayak
A Chester man is accused of breaking into his ex's Passadumkeag home before fleeing to an island.
Chester, Maine Man Charged With Burglary After Alleged Passadumkeag Break-in
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office has identified the suspect as Nicholas Violette, 25, of Chester.
He's charged with burglary and violation of conditional release after an incident Saturday night in Passadumkeag.
READ MORE: Are You Aware of the 100-Foot Law in Maine?
Dispatchers received a report at approximately 10:45 pm of an alleged burglary in that town.
Passadumkeag, Maine Burglary Suspect Fled From the Police in a Kayak
The caller told authorities that her ex-boyfriend had allegedly broken into the Main Road residence through a window and then fled.
Her ex-boyfriend, Violette, has active bail conditions that prohibit him from being at the home or having contact with the victim.
When deputies arrived, they heard movement in the woods and began tracking the suspect.
Officials located Violette and a kayak on an island in the river.
Multiple Maine Law Enforcement Agencies Worked Together to Apprehend a Burglary Suspect
Deputies tried to make verbal contact with Violette, but he didn't respond or comply with commands to surrender.
Officials requested a drone from the Lincoln Police Department and a K9 from the Old Town Police Department.
Maine Wardens also responded with a boat and game wardens.
As the drone flew overhead, Violette surrendered to authorities, who crossed the small waterway and took him into custody without incident.
This incident remains under investigation.

title: Agents search Rep. Omar’s Washington home in criminal probe as she vows she won’t ‘be silenced’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid.
The search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican’s “political enemies.”
The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. “Something’s going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search.
In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
At a political rally in Ohio later Monday, Trump attacked Omar’s Somali origins, saying, “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” The crowd responded by shouting, “Deport.”
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump’s perceived adversaries.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
Trump says he had “nothing to do” with search
The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security.
A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The street around Omar’s home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”
The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ.”
Trump suggested he didn’t know what was happening with the investigation even as he seemed to suggest that Omar was engaged in suspect behavior.
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.
Omar has long been a target for Republicans
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.
In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.
According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.”
Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”
“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody’s entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we’re going to investigate it. We’re going to take a look at it. If we think there’s a crime, we’re going to prosecute that crime. And that’s something the Department of Justice is looking at right now.”
In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance’s comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something’s going to happen.”
He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family’s immigration paperwork.
“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It’s actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there’s no expiration to that.”

title: This former Gardiner athlete succeeded on one kidney. Now, she’s in a battle for her life
text:
Kylie Boardman has been fighting the odds since the day she was born.
Boardman, a Gardiner native, has solitary dysplastic kidney disease, which means she was born with one kidney that will never reach full development. Before she was born, doctors told her parents, Bill and Jennifer Boardman, that she had a less than one percent chance to survive.
The doctor’s advice? Terminate the pregnancy.
“It was a day that my wife and I will never forget,” Bill Boardman said. “It wasn’t in our nature (to do it). We went home and were like, ‘If we get one hour with her, great. If we get two hours, that’s even better.’ We learned to put a catheter in our daughter at 2 days old. We’d do all this at home to survive as long as she could. We were told she’d need a transplant in her teens or early 20s, and here we are.”
Kylie Boardman defied those odds and played four sports (field hockey, volleyball, girls hockey and softball) at Gardiner Area High School. She also played women’s hockey at Central Maine Community College in Auburn, recording eight goals and 22 assists in two seasons.
“In retrospect, I really shouldn’t even be here,” Kylie Boardman said. “I feel so blessed that I’m here in the first place and that I’ve been able to do as many things as I’ve been doing. I’m not someone who just sits at home.”
Now 21, Boardman is in need of a kidney transplant. She also has fluid pressing against her ocular nerves, and may need a shunt in her brain to prevent her from going blind. She is exhausted all the time. At a time in life when she would normally be out with her friends, she rests at home, because simple acts expend more energy.
“I wake up and feel like I slept a good two hours, even though I normally get 10,” Boardman said. “I have shortness of breath, because there’s fluid around the lungs as well. … Putting up my ponytail is like running 5 miles. It’s a very hard adjustment going from an active sports lifestyle to this.”
Battling the odds
As a standout athlete at Gardiner, Kylie Boardman earned Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference honors in volleyball and was a member of the 2022 Class B softball state championship team. She was most at home on the ice as a tough and skilled defenseman on the girls hockey team, for which she also served as a team captain.
It was never obvious that Boardman was playing with one functioning kidney, and the family made a point not to publicly disclose it.
“It’s not something we shared. We never used as an excuse,” Bill Boardman said. “What she did was kind of remarkable, considering what she was going through.”
According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the global odds of a child being born with kidney dysplasia is 1 in 4,300. The kidneys are a filtration system for the human body, helping clean blood, and filter waste and extra fluid into urine. It also controls sodium and potassium levels and helps produce hormones.
One effect of kidney dysplasia is a lower than normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR), or how quickly the kidney can filter waste and extra fluid from the blood. It also makes Boardman’s bones more fragile. When she was freshman in high school, she broke her pelvis, which effected the remainder of her playing career.
“It never fully healed, I re-injured it two different times,” Boardman said. “I couldn’t play my sophomore season of volleyball, which was fine, because (it was the COVID season). Because there’s less calcium, it never fully healed, so I played with this broken bone inside of me.”
Last year, during her final season with the CMCC women’s hockey team, she began to notice the fast decline of the remaining kidney.
“My quality of life has definitely gone down. As I’ve grown more, my kidney is trying to do more,” Boardman said. “I hit that point where it’s just not able to pump anymore for me.”
A needed getaway
Bragoli Gym at Gardiner Area High School is rocking with pop music and laughs at the tail end of a practice for the Gardiner volleyball team.
Bill Boardman gathers the team for final instructions before a match the following day against Medomak Valley. He’s in his third season as the head coach of the Tigers, and led them to the Class C final last season.
Boardman was up front at the beginning of the season, with the team and parents, about Kylie’s need for a kidney transplant — and that when it happens, he’ll take a leave of absence, if it’s during the season. He constantly travels with Kylie to her medical appointments.
“The fact that he’s here for us and loves us, we’re just all so grateful,” said Gardiner senior Joely Cote. “It’s also important that we’re giving him that support while he’s going through this. We love him, and we want to look out for him the same way he looks out for us.
Coaching is a needed escape from the concerns a father has for his daughter.
“He is so devoted to that team and he loves coaching that team,” Kylie Boardman said. “It’s refreshing to see him coach and coach with such passion. It’s not an easy process (for him), because he comes to most of my appointments. That balance is key for everybody.”
Light at the end of the tunnel
The Boardman family has been more open about Kylie’s battle now that she needs a new kidney. A website (kidney4kylie.com) has been created to help find a donor.
The Boardmans received good news in late August. Insurance was approved for a kidney transplant, placing Kylie on the transplant list. She also received a voucher through the National Kidney Registry, which she received from the organization when someone donated a kidney in her name. Through the voucher program, it allows Kylie’s case to be prioritized.
There’s a possibility she could receive her new kidney by the end of the year.
“At this point, it’s just a waiting game for me,” Boardman said. “It’s a very quiet waiting game to hopefully get a new and better chance at life. Every day, I just pray it’s out there.”
Another effect of Boardman’s condition is vision loss, which began within the past year.
“I started to notice that my vision would go away and go black, in certain situations,” Boardman said. “I thought it was a symptom from a med, because I take 15 different meds every day. My optical nerves are swollen because of IIH.”
IIH is Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. According to the Cleveland Clinic, it occurs when cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the spinal cord and brain, builds up in the skull, causing pressure on the optic nerves.
“I’ve been told if this pressure doesn’t come down, it will cause vision loss,” Boardman said.
Boardman’s doctors will soon discuss whether she needs the shunt now, or can wait until after her kidney donation takes place.
Kylie Boardman now lives in Poland, with her boyfriend, Jack Keefe. Despite her current condition, she works four days per week at Serendipity Creek Childcare Center in Gray, while still making her appointments, as she waits for a donor and a new kidney.
“I’ve never been scared. I don’t get scared of much,” Boardman said. “It’s just hard. I see people planning for their future right now, and I can’t do that because I have this massive surgery that I have to plan for, and plan, for a year, to be out of everything. It’s kind of frustrating. But I’m at peace with it. I have such a good support system around me that I’m OK with the fact that it’s going to happen. And I’m OK because I have so many people around me.”

title: It’s time to make Election Day an academic holiday
text:
EDITORIAL: This year’s midterm elections has put the spotlight on Maine.
With the Senate race being razor-thin between Democrats and Republicans, and the control of Congress hanging in the balance, the race between Democratic candidate Troy Jackson and Republican Sen. Susan Collins is one the whole nation is watching.
It cannot be emphasized enough how important the results of elections like the Maine Senate race are to the future of this country. With such high stakes, we believe that every citizen eligible to vote should have ample time and access to exercise their right to decide the future leadership of this country.
This year’s Election Day is happening on Nov. 3, which falls on a Tuesday. Despite the importance of this election, and every federal and state election, there is no change to the day’s schedule. It’s just another Tuesday filled with work or classes, or in some cases, both. This is something that needs to change.
With an average range of between 40% and 60% of eligible voters casting their ballots in federal elections in recent years, the federal government should remove all barriers for citizens voting. The simple solution is to make Election Day a national holiday.
A change like that is not likely to come from Washington, but it can start to appear in a more local form. Universities, like our own, could exercise their power to declare Election Day an academic holiday. This would allow students who reside in Maine to vote or travel to where they are eligible to cast their ballots.
While the university does things that make it easier to vote, like hosting a voting center in the Collins Center for the Arts (CCA), it fails to go all the way with its efforts. While shortening proximity to a place you can vote is helpful, it does not get rid of all the time constraints that come with being a student and citizen.
Giving students the day off of classes and homework would go a long way in creating opportunities for students to let their voices be heard at the voting booth. Not only will it give students who don’t work more time to wait in line and register to vote if they haven’t beforehand, but it will give students who work a job a window to vote before or after work.
Out of all the age demographics that vote, voters ages 18-29 historically do not show up like older voters do. With this being the case, it is even more important that universities give students the opportunity and encouragement to be involved in the election process.
The future of this country is as uncertain as it ever has been. With huge issues like the war in Iran, the economy, AI regulation and data centers, abortion rights, immigration policy and many others up in the air, it is paramount that as many voters as possible show up at the polls. So we need to call on our governments and institutions to make changes that encourage voter turnout.

title: Wabanaki Alliance celebrates Indigenous Peoples Day in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Native peoples and their allies gathered Monday in Augusta for a celebration of Indigenous Peoples Day.
The event, hosted by the Wabanaki Alliance, included music, dancing, films and demonstrations of Wabanaki culture.
“We have all the tribes represented here. We have drumming and dancing. We have an ash basket demonstration,” said Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance. “I’m just always so excited when everyday Mainers get to come together with Wabanaki people because we are all neighbors and friends.”
Holiday replaced Columbus Day in 2019
The holiday replaced Columbus Day in Maine in 2019, a change organizers say reflects an ongoing effort to recognize Indigenous history and sovereignty, rather than Christopher Columbus’ history of exploiting Indigenous peoples.
“It got to a point where I didn’t even want to talk about Columbus anymore. Why go there?” said Barry Dana, former chief of the Penobscot Nation. “It’s Indigenous Peoples Day. We’re going to focus on Indigenous people, our survival traits and who we are.”
Organizers focus on education
For organizers, the gathering was also a chance to bring people together around Indigenous education outside of the legislature.
“It feels good to connect around a celebration and it feels good to just focus on education,” Bryant said. “Why not do some education and some cultural things as well?”
The Wabanaki Alliance says it hopes to make the gathering an annual event.

We appreciate this clear and consistent demand signal, which will help propel our accelerated performance. text:

We break down the causes, warning signs and prevention strategies for painful kidney stones.
Finally, volunteers with a global nonprofit help seniors with limited mobility rediscover the outdoors through shared scenic bike rides.

Susan Lehman was diagnosed a decade ago with multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer that develops in plasma cells in the bone marrow.

title: Finding the right running shoe is the first step to avoiding injury
text:
(Aging Untold) — Whether it’s a lunch-break jog or training for a marathon, an injury can stop a runner’s progress.
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said proper footwear is the foundation for avoiding injury.
“Your shoes are supporting your feet, which is supporting your body. So, you want to make sure that you’re getting the right shoes so that you’re walking properly. You’re not creating an injury, which can happen if you’re not wearing the right shoes. You do not want to underestimate that,” O’Rourke said.
Feet change over time
O’Rourke said feet change over time, meaning a shoe size worn five years ago might not be the right size today.
“Well, if you’re wearing the wrong shoe, you can start walking differently. You could just create an injury from compensating on the wrong side. You could be off balance. You could create dizziness. You could create all kinds of neurological problems stemming from your feet,” O’Rourke said.
Shoes lose their support after 300 to 400 miles.
Experts suggest visiting a specialty store for a gait analysis to see how a foot strikes the ground.
“So if you have the wrong fitting shoe, and by wrong fitting, I mean it’s too tight or it’s too wide or your toes are pushing up against the front of the shoe, if there’s any discomfort, walk around the store for a long time to make sure that it’s really comfortable,” O’Rourke said.
Fit is individual
Your friend’s favorite shoe brand might not work for a different foot type.
“The thing that you want to look for is, do you have any pain whatsoever in any part of your body, your foot, your knee, your hip, anywhere in your body that you’re feeling pain or discomfort? Get a new pair,” O’Rourke said.

title: Pentagon clears Bath Iron Works to build another destroyer
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Improvements at Bath Iron Works have created the capacity and stability needed to build another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer should Congress secure the funding, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office and the Pentagon announced Monday morning.
The announcement followed a push from Collins, independent U.S. Sen. Angus King, and Democratic U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden after the proposed 2027 defense budget included only a single destroyer from the Maine shipyard.
The decision marks a reversal by the Trump administration as it faces pushback over a costly and unpopular war in Iran, while coming as welcome news for Collins, a five-term Republican who’s made bringing federal investment home a centerpiece of her reelection campaign against Democrat Troy Jackson.
The U.S. Navy has been exploring new ship designs, including nuclear-powered battleships bearing President Donald Trump’s name, as well as potentially building vessels in Japan and South Korea. The budget request of a lone destroyer, combined with shifts in Navy plans, sparked concerns about the shipyard’s future even with 11 destroyers on contract. In May, when the BIW announced it had begun fabrication of a new destroyer, the future USS J. William Middendorf, at least 10 BIW-built destroyers were in the Middle East.
“Our national security requires an industrial base that can respond to demands for increased speed and volume,” Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg said in a statement. “After a rigorous review, Bath Iron Works has proven it has the capacity and stability to support construction of a second destroyer.”
The Pentagon’s review evaluated production throughput, schedule adherence, quality assurance benchmarks, supply chain resilience and workforce optimization. Defense leaders believe Bath Iron Works showed “significant operational and managerial improvements” over the last several months, but Feinberg said the shipyard “must continue this momentum to fully resolve legacy production challenges.”
Collins said in a statement that the decision validates Bath Iron Works’ capacity and the work of its 6,800 employees.
“I have advocated for a second destroyer to be included in this year’s budget, and I worked with the administration during its careful review and repeated visits to BIW to verify the ability of the shipyard to construct another ship while continuing to complete its current workload,” she said.
The Navy’s own shipbuilding plan acknowledged the Bath-built destroyer “is the most capable surface combatant anywhere at sea,” but said the U.S. has “reached the limits of its capacity.” The plan came a few months after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited BIW and said the Pentagon intended to “max out” production of the DDG 51 destroyers.
On Monday, the Pentagon said clearing BIW for a second destroyer was part of the administration’s “aggressive campaign” to revitalize the maritime industrial base and “outmatch global pacing threats.”
The Maine congressional delegation, which has long supported General Dynamics’ Bath Iron Works, has been pressing the Navy for long-term multiship contracts. Collins said she’d continue to work to ensure shipbuilders have the resources to meet the Navy’s needs, particularly “at a time when China is relentlessly expanding its fleet.”

title: Maine should expect an early flu season, experts say
text:
Maine could experience an early peak of influenza cases this flu season, public health experts said, urging residents to not delay getting immunized.
“We are seeing the beginnings of influenza circulating earlier than we have had in recent seasons, said Anna Krueger, an epidemiologist with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
While flu season runs from October to May, typically cases crest in late December, January or February. Cases peaked around the winter holidays during last flu season, with a high of 1,347 reported for the week ending Jan. 3, according to Maine CDC data.
So far this flu season, Maine has recorded 104 cases through Oct. 3, compared to 36 for the same time period in 2025.
During the 2023-24 and 2024-25 flu seasons, cases in Maine peaked in February, while in 2022-23, influenza crested in mid-December. Sometimes, Maine is hit with a second wave of flu cases in March or April. But Krueger said if cases peak early, that does not mean Maine is more likely to get a second wave.
Krueger said with the early uptick in cases, this season’s flu could peak here in November, which is why they are urging people to not wait to get their flu shot. Krueger said they worry that influenza could surge before many people have received their annual shot.
What Maine is seeing coincides with the U.S., which is also expecting an early flu season, experts say. Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, told National Public Radio last week that the nation should anticipate flu to arrive sooner this season.
The flu shot — recommended for everyone 6 months and older — is currently widely available at pharmacies, primary care providers, clinics and many healthcare settings. It is typically free, even for those without insurance.
Krueger said the flu shot appears to be a good match for circulating strains of the virus, which currently is influenza A. That means this year’s shot should be especially effective against the most common strain. Scientists update the flu shot every year, and try to match what they anticipate will be the season’s circulating strains.
Dr. Dora Anne Mills, chief health improvement officer for MaineHealth, advised Maine residents to get their flu shots now because signs are pointing to an early onset of cases.
“I usually wait until mid- to late-October, but I didn’t wait this year. I got my flu shot already,” Mills said.
Mills said a higher-dose flu shot is recommended for those 65 and older.
Mills said it’s also a good idea to get COVID-19 and influenza vaccines during the same appointment. The COVID-19 vaccine is updated every year to match mutations in the virus.
She said some may be afraid of worse side effects if getting both at the same time, but there’s “no evidence” that receiving both vaccines at the same appointment results in more side effects.
COVID-19 levels are currently considered “very low” in Maine, according to state data.

title: Collins owes Mainers an explanation for vote on West Bank deaths
text:
Brian Garrison is a South Portland resident and advocate for human dignity and equal rights.
Sen. Susan Collins owes Mainers an explanation for voting to block a formal demand for answers about Americans killed in the West Bank.
On Sept. 29, the Senate rejected a motion to discharge S. Res. 852 from the Foreign Relations Committee, 51-47. Sen. Angus King voted to advance it. Collins voted against it. This was a procedural vote, rather than final adoption, but its consequence was clear: the resolution did not move forward.
The distinction matters. So does what senators prevented from advancing.
The resolution would have requested an unclassified State Department statement within 30 days of adoption. It sought evidence and investigation updates concerning nine American deaths involving Israeli forces or settlers, information about Americans in Israeli prisons and an assessment of Palestinian children in military detention, including allegations of torture. It also asked what Washington had done to protect human rights and pursue accountability.
These are questions a responsible Congress should insist on answering.
Forty-four Democrats, independents King and Bernie Sanders and Republican Rand Paul supported advancing the resolution. Fifty Republicans and Democrat John Fetterman opposed it. Republicans Bill Cassidy and Dan Sullivan did not vote. Paul’s vote demonstrated that demanding answers need not be a partisan position.
Protecting Americans abroad should be among the least controversial obligations of their government. Families deserve evidence, meaningful investigations and an explanation of what officials are doing on their behalf. Their right to those answers should never depend on whether the suspected perpetrators belong to an ally.
The resolution also reached beyond citizenship. Palestinian children deserve protection from abuse because they are children. A passport cannot determine whose mistreatment warrants scrutiny. The same commitment to human dignity that requires investigating American deaths requires taking allegations of torture seriously wherever they arise.
There is a legal reason for this scrutiny, too.
The measure invoked Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act. That provision allows Congress to request information about a country’s human rights practices. Failure to provide the requested statement within 30 days triggers restrictions on delivering security assistance, subject to subsequent specific authorization by law, until the statement arrives.
This was therefore an oversight mechanism with consequences. Senators were being asked to advance a process that could make the administration answer publicly for its decisions.
Supporters of Israel may regard such scrutiny as unfair or diplomatically damaging. But an alliance cannot justify exempting a government from examination. If allegations are unsupported, a credible accounting can establish that. If investigations are adequate, the evidence can demonstrate it. If abuses occurred, friendship cannot excuse them.
An inquiry should test allegations. Blocking it leaves the public without the accounting the resolution sought.
There is also money to account for. Track AIPAC, an advocacy group compiling Federal Election Commission data, lists $4,131,569 in career support for Collins from pro-Israel political committees and associated donors, including $565,000 in independent expenditures. That outside spending benefits her candidacy without going to her campaign. These figures do not establish that contributions caused her vote. They do make her explanation, and the independence of her judgment, matters of public interest.
In a July op-ed for this newspaper about deeper U.S.-Israeli military integration, I called on Collins and King to insist on open debate. The principle remains: consequential decisions require public scrutiny.
King deserves credit for supporting this step. He should continue pressing for disclosure. Collins should explain her opposition and identify the alternative she will pursue, with a timetable for obtaining the information these families deserve.
A procedural objection, if that was her concern, would still leave that responsibility intact. Mainers should ask what she will do now.
Our senators represent people who deserve honest government. They should insist that the administration account for American deaths and alleged abuse, regardless of which foreign government is implicated.
When American families are asking how their loved ones died, a senator’s first duty is to demand answers.
