text:
Maine's Bath Iron Works cleared to build Navy's second destroyer for FY27, Pentagon says
The U.S. Department of War [Department of Defense] announced Monday that it has determined General Dynamics Bath Iron Works (BIW) has the ability to build a guided-missile destroyer, the Navy's second allocated for the current fiscal year.
The department said it conducted a thorough review that evaluated production throughput, schedule adherence, quality assurance benchmarks, supply chain resilience and workforce optimization at the shipyard in Bath, Maine.
Through its review, the department determined that BIW made significant operational and managerial improvements, and found that building another Arleigh Burke-class (DDG 51) destroyer at the shipyard is possible — should Congress secure the necessary funding. The department also found that building a destroyer at BIW is "strategically advantageous for the Navy's fleet."
"After a rigorous review, Bath Iron Works has proven it has the capacity and stability to support construction of a second destroyer," Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg said in a statement. "While the operational improvements we have seen at BIW are a significant step in the right direction, the shipyard must continue this momentum to fully resolve legacy production challenges —sustained performance is essential."
In May, Senate Appropriations Committee chair Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, called on Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to maintain a stable DDG 51 procurement demand of no fewer than two ships per year in the Navy's Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) budget and send a steady production signal to shipyards, including BIW.
A spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee said Collins met with Feinberg in July and as a result, he sent his team to BIW ahead of schedule to verify that improvements had been made at the shipyard. In early October, Feinberg called Collins to tell her that BIW was capable of taking on the work and that a second destroyer for FY27 — which began on Oct. 1 — would be requested.
"(Monday's) decision by the Department of War validates the capacity of Bath Iron Works and the hard work of its highly skilled 6,800 employees who build the best ships in the world. I have advocated for a second destroyer to be included in this year's budget, and I worked with the administration during its careful review and repeated visits to BIW to verify the ability of the shipyard to construct another ship while continuing to complete its current workload," Collins said in a statement shared Monday. "This certification will help keep our Navy strong and support BIW as a steady source of good-paying Maine jobs. I will continue to work to ensure our shipbuilders have the resources to meet the Navy's needs at a time when China is relentlessly expanding its fleet."
In February, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth visited BIW and discussed the Trump administration's goal of rebuilding the country's defense industrial base. Hegseth also praised BIW's employees and touted their shipbuilding capabilities.
"What you're building here in Bath is essential to the arsenal of freedom, and nobody builds it better than you guys," he said.
In August, the Navy christened the USS William Charette at BIW. The vessel is the 43rd Arleigh Burke destroyer and the second Flight III destroyer built at the Maine shipyard.
EDITOR'S NOTE: A previous version of this article stated that Bath Iron Works had been cleared to build two Navy guided-missile destroyers for FY27, but the Senate Appropriations Committee spokesperson provided clarification that this was not the case.

title: Campaign finance reform needs to be our top priority
text:
Beth Franklin of Cumberland worked on Capitol Hill for a Mississippi congressman and has lived in Maine for the last 32 years.
Given the eye-popping revelations about Sen. Susan Collins’ involvement with a pay-to-play arrangement with a campaign donor, it may be time to reexamine how Collins and her opponent, Troy Jackson, are funding their campaigns.
A quick check of Federal Election Commission contribution reports reveals who is giving
money to Collins in her bid to retain the Senate seat she has held since 1997.
The biggest donors in the last several months include the following people: Matthew Steinmetz of Illinois, attorney, whose practice focuses on leveraged buyouts ($100,000); Konstantine Sokolov of Illinois, private equity investor ($100,000); Edward C. Levy Jr. of Michigan, owner of a construction materials company and former president of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee ($250,000); Adam Freede of California, investor ($100,000); Michelle and David Kroin of New York, lawyer and investor ($400,000); Gary Rosenthal of Texas, private equity investor ($50,000); Michael Kassen of Connecticut, investor and former president of the American Israel Political Action Committee ($100,000); J. Blair Frank of Utah, equity portfolio manager and philanthropist ($200,000); Barry MacLean, president of a manufacturing company in Illinois ($50,000).
The most recent entries on the FEC campaign report show that only 24 of the last 100 donors who gave directly to Susan Collins gave under $10,000. All the rest gave what some might refer to as “real money.”
This doesn’t include the donations to the Pine Tree Results Political Action Committee
supporting Sen. Collins. 
Of the most recent donors this year, the top giver to Pine Tree Results was Kenneth Griffin, CEO of Citadel, LLC, a multinational hedge fund based in Florida ($2.5 million). Second runner-up was Stephen Schwarzman, CEO of the Blackstone Group in New York, the world’s largest alternative asset manager ($1 million). Next were Jude and Christopher Reyes, co-chairs of Reyes Holdings in Florida ($1 million, or $500,000 each). More than 20 of the most recent 100 donors to Pine Tree Results gave $100,000 or more.
So, what about Troy Jackson? Given his recent entry into the race, his first FEC report won’t be coming out until October. A quick search of various news outlets painted a different picture of the kinds of donations received by the Jackson campaign.
One report stated that Troy Jackson had 58,000 unique donors in the first few days following his nomination. Another report stated that while Jackson had received a “massive” small donor influx, it was dwarfed by the large sums that continued to pour into the Collins camp.
You don’t have to believe these reports; just watch the evening news. The ads are beginning to all look alike and surely voters are tuning them out. The negative ads about Jackson are double the number that you see about Collins. And if you listen to the fast talk at the end, all those negative ads about Troy Jackson are funded by Pine Tree Results.
What does this say about our candidates? There is no question that Susan Collins’ campaign is being financed by large corporations and investment interests. Does that make her beholden to them? Recent reports about Collins’ alleged “pay-to-play” arrangement with Navatek suggest it may.
But this also points to the broader problem of how campaigns are financed. “Elon Musk-like” money does not always win, but negative ads can sway enough voters to help wealthy interests get the candidates and outcomes they paid for. It’s only when the public makes campaign finance reform their highest priority that this will change.

title: Pregnant mother who was days away from giving birth among 8 killed in mass shooting
text:
ERIE, Pa. (AP) - A man whose toddler was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, said Sunday that the gunman was a grandfather who never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary.
“I think that was a front for him,” Julius Windham said as he stood at a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting, including his 1-year-old daughter Amarianna, her pregnant mother and the woman’s 5-year-old son and unborn baby.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just — you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.
The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.
Those killed include 2 women outside the home
Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 p.m. Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the women and children and the words, “Forever In My Heart.”
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.
Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the 5-year-old boy and 1-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Police decline to discuss motive as investigation continues
Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”
Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, said they’ve known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything.”
“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.
“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. “What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier. ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”

title: Flash-flood risk lingers across the Southwest after Rachel’s remnants swamped Nevada
text:
Forecasters issued flood watches Monday and warned more rain and isolated thunderstorms could hit the Southwest after the remnants of tropical storm Rachel caused severe flooding in Las Vegas over the weekend.
Las Vegas tied an all-time daily rainfall record for the month of October after receiving 1.08 inches of rain into Sunday morning, according to the National Weather Service. The last time that much rain fell on the city in one October day was in 1947.
Videos posted on social media showed a torrent of water rushing through a street near the Las Vegas Strip, with a Ferris wheel and casinos in the background.
Andrew Orrison, a weather service meteorologist, said localized flash flooding was still a risk for the region Monday.
“We’ve seen the worst of what Rachel brought … but unfortunately we are looking at the disturbed weather still lingering,” Orrison said.
The weather service issued flood watches through Monday afternoon for a large swath of Utah, southeast Idaho, and northern and central Arizona, including the Grand Canyon.
The additional rainfall is not associated with Rachel, but a different weather system moving across the West, Orrison said. The precipitation is forecast to end by Wednesday.
Wind, rain, and unusually large waves caused by Rachel battered the Southern California coast over the weekend, forcing oceanside residents in Long Beach to evacuate. Waves tore apart a historic boardwalk and smashed against coastal homes.
The East Coast is forecast to remain clear since Hurricane Isaias has moved well offshore.
At least four deaths have been linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north.
About 158,000 customers remained without power Monday morning in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama, according to poweroutage.com. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he expected nearly everyone to have it restored by Tuesday night.
Drier weather is expected over the next few days across areas of the mid-Atlantic down through the Southeast, including the southern Appalachians.
It will feel “a little summerish” in some of those areas with higher than normal temperatures this week, Orrison said.

title: Archbishop of the U.S. military says Catholic soldiers should not serve on firing squad
text:
Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to Catholics in the U.S. military, is condemning the proposed livestream of the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan.
Broglio, in a statement Monday, also stipulated that any Catholic soldier assigned to the U.S. Army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the livestream plans.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.
The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.
“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”

title: Two American-born economists win Nobel memorial prize in economics
text:
Two American-born economists win Nobel memorial prize in economics
American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation.
Related video: Nobel Peace Prize winnNarges Mohammadi pays tribute to “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement that followed killing of Mahsa AminiDefault
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the two were being honored for work that has helped policymakers deal with economic fluctuations.
“The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement.
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honor, it’s a surprise."
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest themselves and help growth get restarted.
“This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well – until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple tradeoffs – unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “stagflation’’ of the 1970s – when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment – proved the formula was simplistic.
Hall and Woodford set about coming up with an improved model that took into account how consumers and businesses actually made decisions about whether to invest and spend.
“In separate contributions, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford helped build this new foundation for stabilization policy,” Hassler said.
Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growthand human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
___
Dazio reported from Berlin and Wiseman from Washington.

title: Woman arrested after driving recklessly with boyfriend on hood of car, deputies say
text:
LENOIR COUNTY, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - A woman was arrested after she drove nearly five miles with her boyfriend clinging to the hood of her car, according to police.
The Lenoir County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded to reports of a domestic incident on Highway 258 on Saturday.
Janecia Greenfield-Williams, 23, was driving with her boyfriend on the hood of her car. She drove recklessly for 4.6 miles, reaching speeds of up to 60 miles per hour and swerving, according to police.
Authorities said her 3-year-old child was also in the car at the time.
Authorities were able to safely conduct a traffic stop on the car.
The man on the car was assessed and released without injuries, deputies said.
Greenfield-Williams refused to get into the patrol vehicle, but was eventually taken to Lenoir County Jail and faces several charges, including a felony count of assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill, assault with a deadly weapon with a minor present, reckless driving to endanger, resisting a public officer, misdemeanor crime of domestic violence and multiple traffic violations.

title: Passengers injured in deadly Grace Bailey mast failure sue schooner’s owners
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Three people injured in a deadly schooner accident off the coast of Rockland are now suing the boat’s owners.
Just over three years ago, the mast of the schooner Grace Bailey broke during a four-day cruise, killing Dr. Emily Mecklenburg and injuring five others. A sixth passenger was injured when they fell down the galley ladder to avoid the falling mast.
A Coast Guard investigation found that severe internal rot had weakened the mast and that it had not received proper preservation treatments. Court documents say 33 people were on board: 26 passengers and seven crew members.
Three injured passengers are suing Grace Bailey Navigation Company and the schooner, seeking compensation for physical and emotional damages. One of the three is also suing crew members, inspectors, repair workers and the ship’s former owners.
One plaintiff, who lived in Montville at the time of the cruise, was working aboard the vessel as a musician. She says she suffered “serious and numerous physical and emotional injuries” as a result of the incident.
A man from Lubec, who says he was struck by falling debris, also filed a lawsuit. He says he was injured a second time while helping other passengers. His wife, who was also a passenger, joined the suit in an amended filing. She said she heard a “loud crack from above, looked up, [and] saw the mast split and begin to fall.” The complaint says that although she was not physically injured, she was at risk “of traumatic physical harm.”
A Massachusetts woman is the plaintiff in the third lawsuit. According to court documents, she was the passenger injured when she fell down the galley ladder while trying to avoid the mast.

title: 20-year-old father of 2 killed in railcar derailment, officials say
text:
DURANT, Okla. (KXII/Gray News) - A 20-year-old father of two was identified as the rail crew worker who died after a railcar derailed in Oklahoma on Wednesday morning.
The Bryan County Communications Center received a call Wednesday morning about a railroad incident involving a railcar. Several agencies responded, including the Durant Police Department.
Family members identified the worker as Axcell Hernandez. They told KXII that Hernandez was a hard worker and loving father to a toddler and a newborn.
Hernandez was part of a crew loading and moving railcars that were not connected or being moved by an engine.
Durant police Sgt. Nick Spencer said officers “did in fact locate the railcar that was overturned and had witnesses on scene that confirmed that a male employee of a local business had been trapped underneath.”
Spencer said a derailer, “a device known as a derailer was in place and was designed to prevent anything rolling onto an active railway.”
Investigators say the accident happened at the Hardy Farms plant. The plant has so far declined comment.
Specialized equipment was needed for rescue and recovery operations, and Hernandez’s body was recovered during the operation.
Spencer said the department is working to complete a thorough investigation.
“It’s our mission to make sure that we give a thorough investigation to contribute to go along with a much broader investigation. At this time, we’re treating this as a workplace accident,” Spencer said.
The National Transportation Safety Board is also investigating.

title: Where is our declaration of conscience?
text:
To the Editor:
In 1950, Margaret Chase Smith, at the time a freshman senator, delivered her now-famous Declaration of Conscience speech on the floor of the U.S. Senate. She was appalled at the behavior of fellow Sen. Joseph McCarthy, whose attacks on individuals for the unproven sin of being communist. He had smeared people, ruined careers and put individuals at personal risk. She had had enough and went down in history as a person of integrity and courage, who is remembered to this day as someone who was brave enough to stand up for what was right. Today, we, as a country, are faced with an even greater danger. How many lines does the current administration have to cross before someone says enough? Our senator, Susan Collins, has claimed to be a person of integrity during her long career. I believe that she sees the situation as it is but has thus far failed to take a stand that would provide the example that others could emulate. The Maine State motto is Dirigo, which means “I Lead”. Sen. Collins, please live up to that motto. You say you have the integrity, now show the courage. It is what a true “County girl” would do.

title: Maine lobstermen's defamation lawsuit dismissed by appeals court
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine lobstermen's defamation lawsuit against California aquarium dismissed by appeals court
A federal appeals court has ordered the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit that was brought by the Maine Lobstermen's Association and four other groups against the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California.
The lawsuit was filed in March 2023 after Seafood Watch, a conservation program operated by the aquarium, placed lobster from the United States and Canada on its do-not-eat "red list" in 2022 because lobster fishing gear poses an entanglement risk to the endangered North Atlantic right whale. The recommendation prompted some retailers, including Whole Foods, to pull lobster from stores.
The lobster fishing industry pushed back against Seafood Watch's claim, saying it inaccurately portrayed fishing gear as a threat to North Atlantic right whales and constituted defamation that has caused economic harm. The industry claimed that the whales face greater threats from other fishing industries, including the Canadian snow crab fishery.
The Monterey Bay Aquarium made an attempt to have the lawsuit tossed in U.S. District Court in Maine, but Judge John Woodcock ruled in February 2025 that the lawsuit could move forward.
The aquarium then filed an appeal with the Boston-based First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals. During oral arguments held on July 27, one of the appellate judges said that the lawsuit did not strike him as a defamation claim and that he found the case troubling "from a First Amendment perspective."
"The more you broaden the class of people that fall within this, the more it feels like everybody can sue," said Judge Seth Aframe.
In a ruling handed down Friday, the First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals reversed the U.S. District Court's denial of the aquarium's motion to dismiss. The appeals court said that Seafood Watch's comments did not target specific members of a group, which is required under the so-called "group defamation rule." The matter has been remanded to the district court with instructions to dismiss the complaint.
Maine's Total Coverage has contacted the Maine Lobstermen's Association with a request for comment on the appeals court's ruling, but has not yet received a reply.
The groups that joined the Maine Lobstermen's Association in the lawsuit were wholesaler Bean Maine Lobster, the Maine Coast Fishermen's Association, Maine Lobster and Processing, and Maine lobster fishing company Bug Catcher.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: South Portland’s sustainability manager offers 7 tips for an environmentally friendly Halloween
text:
It’s finally October.
The leaves are starting to change, the nights are starting to get cold and things are about to get … spooky.
Waste generation and overconsumption can also be scary.
The Press Herald sat down with Julie Taft, the sustainability program manager for South Portland, to learn some tips to have an environmentally friendly Halloween.
Thrift or make costumes when possible
Nearly 83% of prepackaged Halloween costumes are made of oil-based plastic, Taft said. They’re typically designed for single use and end up in landfills.
Visit town swap shops and thrift stores for whimsical finds. Even a cardboard box can be a costume (you can dress up like a robot! Or a Rubik’s cube!).
Some towns have costume exchanges. Check town websites or Facebook pages for information on upcoming exchanges.
Avoid decorative cobwebs
Although whimsical, these stretchy, fake spiderwebs can trap and kill birds, rodents, insects and other animals. And when they blow away, they can wind up in habitats as litter.
If you want to use these decorations, try reusing them year after year – the material can’t be recycled.
If you want to use plastic skeletons or other spooky plastic decorations, consider used
If you want one of the giant skeletons, or black cats with scrunched backs, consider finding them at swap shops or thrift stores instead of ordering them online.
“Not buying new plastic is not increasing the need for the production of new plastics,” Taft said.
And if you have decorations you don’t use anymore, donate them instead of throwing them away. Maybe the Frankenstein that’s been gathering dust in your basement would make someone else really happy!
Better yet, make scarecrows to decorate your lawn
Pull an old flannel shirt from the back of your closet. Use a pair of pants that don’t quite fit like they used to. Stuff them with leaves from your yard (it’s a win-win). Paint an old pillowcase or bag with a joyful face. And voila, a scarecrow! Extra points if they have fun accessories, like sunglasses, a silly hat or an old necktie.
Dispose of candy wrappers responsibly
Americans purchase nearly 500 million pounds of candy around Halloween each year. That’s a lot of sugar — and a lot of waste.
Most candy wrappers aren’t recyclable, at least not in a traditional blue bin.
South Portland’s Go-Go Refill will have a candy wrapper collection box, in partnership with Terracycle, a recycling company.
Don’t live in South Portland? These candy wrapper collection boxes through Terracycle can be purchased online.
Use all parts of the pumpkin
As gross and slimy as the inside of the pumpkin can seem while gutting it and getting it ready for carving, it’s also a yummy snack.
Make sure you rinse and dry the seeds – if they’re still wet, they’ll be chewy instead of crunchy.
If you like your snacks salty, toss them with paprika and garlic salt to give some more flavor. If you want a sweet, crunchy snack, sprinkle them cinnamon and brown sugar with a pinch of salt.
Compost your pumpkin
Even after your jack-o-lantern has wilted beyond recognition, it can still find a new use.
Many local farms will accept your old pumpkins as feed for their livestock. Pigs and cows deserve a little treat, too.
Portland hosts an annual Pumpkin-Cycle event, usually on the weekend after Halloween, for people to compost their pumpkins. Last year, the event included hammers for people to smash their pumpkins before dumping.

title: SNAP enrollment sinks to 19.8 million in June as states face higher costs and new rules
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SNAP enrollment sinks to 19.8 million in June as states face higher costs and new rules
The number of households enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, fell to 19.8 million in June, according to the latest data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. That's down nearly 12% from the same time last year.
The decline in SNAP participation comes after federal policy changed the program's eligibility rules and work requirements. Participation is now similar to what it was in March 2020. SNAP helps provide food assistance to eligible low-income households.
What changes were made to SNAP?
President Donald Trump signed the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," known as H.R. 1, into law last July, requiring many SNAP recipients to work, volunteer or participate in job training for at least 80 hours a month. The legislation also raised the age limit of people who need to meet these requirements from 54 to 64.
Another change requires states to cover 75% of the program's administrative costs starting Oct. 1, while the federal government will pay the remaining 25%. Starting next year, states will be responsible for covering SNAP benefits costs associated with payment error rates above 6%.
Some states have begun reducing SNAP participation to lower their payment error rates and cut program costs, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
How did monthly SNAP participation change?
With the new stricter requirements, SNAP participation has declined across the country. Arizona, Nevada and Oklahoma had some of the largest drops in household participation from June 2025 to June 2026, at 49%, 28% and 21%, respectively.
Nine states saw more than 100,000 households dropped from the program. Florida had the largest decrease, with more than 293,000 fewer participating households in June.
Alaska was the only state where household participation increased. It was up slightly, by 4%, in June.
See how household participation in SNAP changed in each state from June 2025 to June 2026.

title: Man charged with murder in Indian Township killing; tribal chiefs react
text:
Man charged with murder in Indian Township, Maine, killing; tribal chiefs react
A man from Indian Township is accused of killing a man from Indian Island on Saturday.
The Indian Township Police Department was called to a reported shooting on Peter Dana Point Road in Indian Township at about 9:28 p.m. on Saturday.
The police department, Indian Township Fire Department, Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service and Washington County Sheriff's Office all responded and found Cory Fields, 41, dead.
Maine State Police was then called to investigate. Police ultimately arrested Jeremy Stevens, 46, and charged him with murder. He was taken to the Washington County Jail.
Fields' caused of death was determined to be gunshot wounds.
Police did not release any information on Sunday about a possible cause.
On Sunday, the Chiefs of the Passamaquoddy Tribe and Penobscot Nation, Chief Amkuwiposhehs "Pos" Bassett, Chief William Nichols Sr., and Chief Kirk Francis, released a joint statement to "express our shock and deep sadness" following the death of a Penobscot citizen.
"Family is at the heart of who we are as Wabanaki People. Our communities are connected through generations of kinship, traditions, shared histories, and our responsibility to care for one another. When a life is lost to violence, the pain reaches beyond one family. It is felt throughout our communities and across our Nations," the chiefs wrote. "Every life is precious, and every family deserves to live in peace, safety, and dignity."
The chiefs said tribal law enforcement was working with Maine State Police.
The chiefs said that community response teams and mental health support resources were available in their communities to help those who may be struggling.
"Seeking help is a sign of strength, and no one should feel that they have to carry the weight of this tragedy alone. We encourage our citizens to check on one another, support our elders and young people, and ensure that those who are hurting know they have people and resources they can turn to," the chiefs wrote.
